Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Three weeks after discharge, the father of a baby Ruth cared for on the postnatal ward sends her a social media friend request and invites her for a drink to say thanks. Ruth had no previous relationship with the family. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the friend request but decline the invitation for a drink
Decline both, keeping a clear professional boundary with the family
Accept the drink if a colleague from the ward also attends
Accept both, as the family is no longer in her care
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 20.6: stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including those who have been in your care in the past, their families and carers. Ruth should politely decline both.

n.0: An online friendship with the family of a former patient still blurs the professional boundary that Code 20.6 protects.
n.2: A colleague's presence does not change the nature of a social relationship with a family recently in her care.
n.3: Code 20.6 expressly includes people who have been in your care in the past, so discharge does not end the boundary.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Abi, 24, has given birth to her first baby. She tells the midwife she has decided to formula feed and asks for help with making up feeds. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: "Formula is fine; there is no real difference between breast milk and formula."
"I will show you how to make up feeds safely and how to bottle feed responsively."
"I will note your choice and ask the infant feeding team to discuss it with you."
"Most babies do much better on breast milk, so could you try for a week first?"
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 2.4 and 4.1 require respect for the level of involvement and the decisions a woman makes; Code 6.1 requires evidence-based advice. NG194 supports safe formula preparation and responsive bottle feeding for women who formula feed, and Baby Friendly standards support informed feeding decisions.

n.0: Saying there is no difference is inaccurate; Code 6.1 requires information to be evidence-based.
n.2: Referring her to be persuaded implies her choice needs correcting and delays the practical help she has asked for.
n.3: Pressuring her to try breastfeeding after she has made an informed choice does not respect her decision (Code 2.4).

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Marcus, a registered midwife, has been charged with a criminal offence after an incident outside work. His court hearing is in four months. He has told nobody at work. According to the NMC Code, what must he do?
o: Declare the charge at his next revalidation health and character declaration
Tell his employer now and the NMC if he is convicted
Tell the NMC and his employer about the charge as soon as he can
Tell the NMC and his employer once the court has reached a verdict
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 23.2: tell both the NMC and any employers as soon as you can about any caution or charge against you, or a conditional discharge or finding of guilt. Being honest about a charge upholds public trust in the profession.

n.0: Waiting until revalidation could mean years of delay; Code 23.2 requires notification as soon as he can.
n.1: The NMC must also be told of the charge now; Code 23.2 names both the NMC and employers.
n.3: Code 23.2 is triggered by the charge itself, not by the outcome of the trial.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Ifeoma, a midwife, is a passenger on a long-haul flight when the crew ask for help: a woman is in labour at about 38 weeks. Ifeoma is off duty and has no equipment of her own. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait until the crew confirm no doctor is on board before helping
Offer help within her competence and support the crew's emergency plans
Offer advice but avoid physical contact as she is outside the UK
Stay seated as her employer's indemnity does not cover care on the flight
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 15: always offer help if an emergency arises in your practice setting or anywhere else, acting within the limits of your knowledge and competence (15.1) and arranging for emergency care to be accessed promptly (15.2), taking account of safety (15.3).

n.0: Delaying help while waiting for a doctor wastes time; a midwife is competent to attend a normal birth and should offer help now.
n.2: Code 15 applies anywhere, and a midwife attending a birth in an emergency may give the hands-on care that is needed.
n.3: Indemnity concerns do not remove the professional expectation in Code 15 to offer help in an emergency anywhere.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Siobhan is registered with the NMC as a midwife and holds no other registration. She is preparing to revalidate. What is the minimum number of practice hours she must have completed in the three years since her registration was last renewed?
o: 600 hours
900 hours
450 hours
1,350 hours
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC revalidation requirements: a midwife needs a minimum of 450 practice hours over the three-year period. 900 hours applies to dual nurse and midwife registration (450 for each), and 1,350 to triple registration.

n.0: 600 hours is not an NMC practice hours figure for any registration.
n.1: 900 hours is the requirement for dual registration as a nurse and a midwife.
n.3: 1,350 hours applies to triple registration as a nurse, midwife and nursing associate.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Priya, a midwife, has logged 35 hours of continuing professional development (CPD) for revalidation. Twelve hours were participatory workshops; the rest were e-learning modules she completed alone. Which statement about her CPD is correct?
o: She meets the requirement because she has reached 35 hours in total
She needs 15 more hours of any type of CPD
She needs 8 more hours of participatory learning
She needs 20 more participatory hours on top of her 35
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC revalidation: 35 hours of CPD over three years, of which at least 20 must be participatory (interaction with one or more other professionals). Working: 20 required minus 12 completed = 8 more participatory hours. Solo e-learning is not participatory.

n.0: The total of 35 is met, but the participatory minimum of 20 is not: she has 12.
n.1: Any type of CPD will not fix the shortfall; the gap is specifically in participatory hours, and it is 8 hours, not 15.
n.3: Participatory hours count within the 35, so she needs 8 more, not an extra 20.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Laura, a midwife, is arranging the reflective discussion for her revalidation. She has written her five reflective accounts. Who may she hold the reflective discussion with?
o: A consultant obstetrician registered with the GMC
A retired midwife who has left the NMC register
Another registrant on the NMC register
Her line manager, a registered physiotherapist
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC revalidation: the reflective discussion about the five written reflective accounts must be held with another NMC-registered nurse, midwife or nursing associate.

n.0: A GMC-registered doctor may act as confirmer in some circumstances but cannot hold the reflective discussion, which must be with an NMC registrant.
n.1: A person who has left the NMC register is not a current NMC registrant.
n.3: A physiotherapist is registered with the HCPC, not the NMC, so cannot be the reflective discussion partner.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Tara, a community midwife, has a recurrence of depression. She is finding it hard to concentrate on long home visits and recently forgot to complete a newborn check entry. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her manager and seek support from occupational health
Ask a colleague to double-check her notes until she feels better
Continue working as normal and keep the condition private
Wait to declare the condition at her next revalidation
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 20.9: maintain the level of health needed to carry out the professional role; Code 16.3: tell someone in authority if problems may prevent you working within the Code. Occupational health can advise on adjustments and support (SPM 1.26).

n.1: An informal check by a colleague does not address the health problem or allow formal support and adjustments.
n.2: Keeping the condition private while errors are already occurring risks women's and babies' safety (Code 16.3).
n.3: Revalidation may be years away; the effect on practice needs addressing now.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Rebecca, a midwife, took a career break and has practised for 200 hours in the three years since she last renewed her registration. Her revalidation date is next year. What must she do to renew?
o: Make up the missing hours by extra CPD before renewal
Renew now and complete the remaining hours during the next cycle
Complete a return to practice programme or Test of Competence
Ask her confirmer to sign that her hours are sufficient
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC practice hours requirement: a registrant who has not practised the minimum hours (450 for a midwife) must successfully complete an approved return to practice programme or a Test of Competence before applying to renew.

n.0: CPD hours are a separate requirement and cannot replace practice hours.
n.1: Hours cannot be carried forward; the requirement must be met before the date of the renewal application.
n.3: The confirmer cannot certify hours that were not worked; the shortfall needs a return to practice route.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Gemma is employed as an NHS midwife. At weekends she plans to run private antenatal classes and offer private postnatal home visits. What should she check before starting the private work?
o: That her NMC registration fee covers indemnity for private work
That she has an appropriate indemnity arrangement for the private work
That her employer's indemnity extends to all midwifery work she does
That each woman signs a waiver accepting the absence of indemnity cover
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 12.1: have an appropriate indemnity arrangement in place relevant to your scope of practice. Employer cover relates to employed work, so private practice needs its own arrangement, and indemnity is also declared at revalidation.

n.0: NMC registration does not provide indemnity; it is a separate requirement under Code 12.
n.2: An NHS employer's indemnity covers work done for that employer, not private work she arranges herself.
n.3: A waiver cannot replace the indemnity arrangement that Code 12.1 requires.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Claire, a midwife, receives a letter from the NMC stating that a fitness to practise referral has been made about her care of a woman in labour. Her trust is also investigating. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Add the missing details to the labour records before they are requested
Contact the woman who complained to try to resolve the matter directly
Cooperate with both investigations and seek union or defence advice
Decline to respond to the NMC until the trust investigation has ended
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 23: cooperate with all investigations and audits. Seeking advice from a union or professional indemnity body is appropriate. Altering records breaches Code 10.3, and contacting the complainant is inappropriate.

n.0: Changing records after the event is falsification under Code 10.3; late entries must be marked as late and must not alter what was written.
n.1: Contacting the complainant directly could be seen as pressure and is not part of a fair investigation.
n.3: Code 23 requires cooperation; the NMC process does not wait for permission from the employer's investigation.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Naomi is writing one of her five reflective accounts for revalidation about a postnatal haemorrhage. Her draft includes the woman's full name and the date of birth of the baby. What should Naomi do before her reflective discussion?
o: Remove anything that could identify the woman or her baby
Keep the details as the account stays in her own portfolio
Replace the name with the woman's initials and hospital number
Send the draft to the NMC to be made anonymous
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC revalidation guidance on reflective accounts: they must not include any information that could identify a person, in line with confidentiality (Code 5). Initials, hospital numbers and dates of birth can all identify.

n.1: Confidentiality applies to everything she records, including her portfolio, and the account will be shared in the reflective discussion.
n.2: Initials and a hospital number are identifiers, so the account would still identify the woman.
n.3: The NMC does not anonymise accounts; the registrant must write them without identifying details.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Mia, 31, is 37 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated pregnancy and plans to give birth in an alongside midwifery unit. She asks who is in charge of her care. Who is her lead professional?
o: Her named midwife
A consultant obstetrician
The labour ward coordinator
Her GP
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: For women with uncomplicated pregnancies the midwife is the accountable, autonomous lead professional across the continuum of care (NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives 1.6).

n.1: Obstetric lead care is for women with complications or additional needs, which Mia does not have.
n.2: The coordinator manages the unit's workload; she is not the lead professional for an individual woman's care.
n.3: The GP is not the lead professional for routine maternity care in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Which statement best describes the scope of the midwife set out in the NMC Standards of proficiency for midwives (2019)?
o: Care for women at low risk, ending when complications arise
Care from booking until 10 days after the birth for healthy women
Intrapartum care, with antenatal and postnatal care led by GPs
Universal care for all, plus additional care in partnership with others
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: The 2019 standards describe the midwife providing universal care for all women and newborn infants, and additional care for those with complications, working with the interdisciplinary and multiagency team (SPM 1.7, Domains 3 and 4).

n.0: Midwives continue to care for women who develop complications, coordinating with others, rather than stopping.
n.1: The standards cover all women and newborns across the continuum, not a fixed 10-day window for healthy women.
n.2: Midwives provide antenatal, intrapartum and postnatal care; GPs are not the leads for routine antenatal and postnatal care.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Dani, 28, is 34 weeks pregnant and has been receiving midwife-led care. At a routine appointment her blood pressure is 152/100 mmHg and urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Transfer her to obstetric care and close her midwifery record
Ask her GP to review her blood pressure within the next few days
Arrange same-day obstetric assessment and continue her midwifery care
Continue midwife-led care and recheck her blood pressure next week
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: New hypertension after 20 weeks with dipstick proteinuria raises suspicion of pre-eclampsia. NICE NG201 1.2.26 says a first episode of hypertension (140/90 mmHg or higher) after 20+0 weeks is referred to secondary care to be seen within 24 hours, and NG133 1.2.3 asks for dipstick proteinuria to be quantified with PCR or ACR, so same-day obstetric assessment is the prompt, safe step. The midwife refers for shared care while continuing to provide midwifery care (SPM 1.6).

n.0: The woman still needs midwifery care when obstetric input begins; care becomes shared rather than ended.
n.1: GP review in a few days misses the 24-hour secondary care assessment in NG201 1.2.26; she needs the obstetric team, not primary care.
n.3: A week's delay is unsafe with possible pre-eclampsia; NG201 1.2.26 expects secondary care assessment within 24 hours.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Holly, 33, plans to give birth at home attended only by her doula, without a midwife. The doula has no midwifery or medical qualification. Which statement about the law is correct?
o: The doula may attend in place of a midwife if she has doula training
The midwife must inform the police that an unattended birth is planned
Holly may lawfully freebirth, but the doula must not attend as a midwife
Holly commits an offence by giving birth without a midwife present
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 art 45: a person other than a registered midwife or registered medical practitioner must not attend a woman in childbirth, except in sudden or urgent necessity or as a student in recognised training. The offence applies to the attendant, not to the woman, who may lawfully give birth unassisted.

n.0: Doula training is not a midwifery or medical qualification, so it does not lift the art 45 restriction.
n.1: There is no duty to notify the police of a planned freebirth; the midwife keeps offering care.
n.3: The woman commits no offence; art 45 applies to a person who attends her in childbirth.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: During a woman's induction of labour, the obstetric registrar instructs Sam, a midwife, to increase the oxytocin infusion. The woman is having six contractions in 10 minutes and the CTG has become suspicious. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase the rate, as the instruction transfers accountability to the registrar
Ask another midwife to increase the rate so that she can monitor the CTG
Increase the rate and record the registrar's name with the time of the instruction
Withhold the increase, explain her concerns and escalate to the consultant
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Midwives are accountable for their own actions (SPM 1.6, Code 13 and 16.2). Six contractions in 10 minutes is uterine hyperstimulation: NICE NG235 1.8.55 says reduce or stop oxytocin if contractions are more frequent than 4 in 10 minutes, and NG229 lists reducing or stopping oxytocin among the conservative measures for a concerning CTG. She explains her rationale and escalates.

n.0: Accountability does not transfer by instruction; a midwife who gives an unsafe dose is answerable for it.
n.1: Delegating the increase to a colleague still exposes the woman to the same unsafe action.
n.2: Documenting the instruction does not make an unsafe increase acceptable or protect the woman and baby.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Kiran, 30, has type 1 diabetes and is 16 weeks pregnant. She is under joint diabetes and obstetric care and asks whether she will still see a midwife. Which response is most accurate?
o: "No, your care is now led by doctors, so midwives step back."
"Yes, a midwife will still care for you alongside the specialist team."
"You will see a midwife in labour, but not before then."
"You will see a midwife after the birth, once your diabetes is stable."
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Midwives provide care to all women, including those with complications, working in partnership with the multidisciplinary team (SPM 1.7, Domain 4). Women with pre-existing diabetes have joint care, with midwifery care throughout.

n.0: Midwives do not withdraw when a pregnancy is medically complex; care is shared.
n.2: Midwifery care continues antenatally, not just in labour.
n.3: Midwifery care runs through the whole pregnancy, not just after the birth.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Jo, a midwife in England, was involved in a stillbirth last week and feels distressed. Her manager suggests restorative clinical supervision under the A-EQUIP model. Who provides this?
o: A Professional Midwifery Advocate
The Local Supervising Authority Midwifery Officer
A Supervisor of Midwives
The NMC Midwifery Committee
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Statutory supervision of midwives, including Supervisors of Midwives and Local Supervising Authorities, was removed in 2017. In England the A-EQUIP model replaced it, delivered by Professional Midwifery Advocates who offer restorative clinical supervision.

n.1: The Local Supervising Authority role ended with statutory supervision in 2017.
n.2: Supervisors of Midwives were part of statutory supervision, which ended in 2017.
n.3: The NMC is the regulator; no NMC committee provides individual restorative supervision, which under A-EQUIP comes from a Professional Midwifery Advocate.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: On a busy postnatal ward, Ellie, a midwife, asks a maternity support worker who has been trained and assessed in the task to complete four-hourly observations on a well woman. Which statement about accountability is correct?
o: Accountability for the task passes to the support worker once she accepts it
The support worker's manager becomes accountable for the delegated task
The ward coordinator is accountable as she allocates the staffing
Ellie is accountable for delegating and for checking the outcome is safe
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 11: be accountable for decisions to delegate; delegate within the other person's competence (11.1), make sure they are supervised and supported (11.2) and confirm the outcome meets the required standard (11.3). The support worker is responsible for how she performs the task.

n.0: The support worker is responsible for her own performance, but the midwife's accountability for the delegation decision does not pass to her.
n.1: The support worker's line manager does not take over accountability for a clinical delegation decision made by the midwife.
n.2: Allocating staff does not make the coordinator accountable for an individual midwife's delegation decision.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Farah, 26, attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks. She speaks Dari and very little English. Her husband, who speaks fluent English, offers to interpret for her. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a Dari-speaking care assistant from the ward to interpret
Arrange a professional interpreter for the appointment
Accept the husband's offer as he knows her medical history
Use a translation app and give her English leaflets to take home
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NICE NG201 and the NMC Code (7.2) support independent professional interpreters rather than family members, so the woman can speak freely and the booking enquiries, including routine domestic abuse enquiry, can be made in private.

n.0: A bilingual care assistant is not a trained, independent interpreter and has a separate clinical role.
n.2: A family member as interpreter prevents private disclosure, including routine enquiry about domestic abuse, and may filter what she says.
n.3: An app and English leaflets do not give reliable two-way communication for a full booking history.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Grace, 19, comes to every antenatal appointment with her mother, who answers most questions for her. Grace says little. Which approach by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Ask her mother to wait outside for the rest of the pregnancy
Direct questions to her mother, who seems to know the history well
Continue as now, as Grace has not raised any concerns
Ask Grace privately how she would like her mother involved
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.10 asks midwives to involve partners and family in discussions on the woman's terms. Seeing Grace alone for part of the appointment lets her state her own wishes and allows routine enquiry about safety (NICE NG201).

n.0: Excluding her mother for the whole pregnancy may not be what Grace wants; her own preference should decide this.
n.1: Speaking through her mother bypasses Grace, who is the person receiving care and makes her own decisions.
n.2: A quiet young woman may not raise concerns while a relative is present, so the midwife should create the chance to speak privately.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Bethany, 34, is discussing induction of labour at 41 weeks. She asks the midwife, "What would you do if you were me?" Which response best supports partnership working?
o: "I can't give an opinion on this, so it is your decision."
"Let's look at the options and what matters most to you."
"I would have the induction, so I think you should book it."
"The doctors will decide what is safest for you and your baby."
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.13 and Code 2.3: work in partnership, basing care on the woman's needs, views and preferences, and support shared decision-making with balanced, evidence-based information (NICE NG207 on discussing induction).

n.0: Refusing to engage leaves her without the information and support she needs to decide.
n.2: Telling her what to do substitutes the midwife's preferences for Bethany's own values.
n.3: Decisions about induction are hers to make, with information from the team; doctors do not decide for her.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: After explaining the oral glucose tolerance test to Zainab, 29, the midwife wants to check that she has understood how to prepare. Which method is most effective?
o: Ask, "Do you have any questions about the test?"
Ask, "Is everything clear about the test?"
Give her a leaflet and ask her to call if she has any problems
Ask her to tell you, in her own words, how to prepare for the test
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 7.4: check people's understanding from time to time. Asking the woman to explain in her own words (teach-back) shows what she has understood and any gaps.

n.0: A question about questions often gets 'no' even when understanding is incomplete.
n.1: A closed yes or no question does not show what she has understood.
n.2: A leaflet does not check her understanding of what has just been explained.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Olivia, 27, booked late at 24 weeks. She tells the midwife her last birth was "terrifying" and that staff "didn't listen". She avoids eye contact and asks to keep appointments short. Which approach will best build a trusting relationship?
o: Acknowledge her experience and agree a plan of care together
Reassure her that this hospital is different from her last one
Keep appointments short as asked and focus on clinical checks
Refer her for counselling before continuing the care discussion
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.12 and Code 2: develop trusting, compassionate, person-centred relationships by listening, acknowledging her experience and planning care in partnership. This also supports trauma-informed care.

n.1: Quick reassurance dismisses her experience and does not build trust.
n.2: Focusing on checks only does not address her distrust, which affects engagement with care.
n.3: Counselling may help later, but making it a precondition delays care and does not build the relationship itself.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Lucy and Sarah are a married couple expecting their first baby; Lucy is pregnant. At a postnatal visit, the midwife is completing the newborn records. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Ask the couple how they each wish to be named and involved
Record Sarah as 'friend' until parental responsibility is confirmed
Record Sarah as 'partner' and ask Lucy to answer all questions
Address questions about the baby to Lucy as the birth mother
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.10 and Code 1.3: avoid assumptions, recognise diversity and involve partners and family as the woman wishes. Asking how the couple wish to be named and involved is respectful and person-centred.

n.1: Recording a spouse and co-parent as 'friend' is inaccurate and disrespectful; the couple's own description of their relationship should guide the record.
n.2: Directing everything to Lucy excludes Sarah, who is a parent, without asking the couple's wishes.
n.3: Directing questions to the birth mother alone assumes their roles without asking them.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Precious, 32, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language (BSL). Her hearing partner offers to sign for her during labour. What is the most appropriate arrangement?
o: Ask her partner to interpret, as he is fluent in BSL
Rely on lip-reading, with staff speaking slowly and facing her
Communicate by writing notes throughout labour
Book a registered BSL interpreter for labour and appointments
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 7.2: meet people's language and communication needs. A registered BSL interpreter gives accurate, independent communication, and the partner can support Precious rather than interpret.

n.0: A partner interpreting cannot also act as her birth supporter and may not convey clinical information accurately.
n.1: Lip-reading conveys only part of speech and is unreliable, especially in labour.
n.2: Written notes are slow and impractical during labour and may not be her preferred language.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Ruby, 23, has a mild learning disability and is 12 weeks pregnant. She lives independently with some support. At booking, she seems confused by the information about screening tests. What should the midwife do first?
o: Ask how Ruby prefers to receive information and offer easy read
Record that she lacks capacity to decide about screening
Ask her support worker to make the screening decision for her
Book the screening tests and explain them at the next visit
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(3): take all practicable steps to help a person decide before concluding they cannot. SPM 1.13 and Code 7.2: adapt communication, for example easy read and extra time, to strengthen her own ability to decide.

n.1: Capacity is presumed (MCA s1(2)) and cannot be judged lacking before steps have been taken to help her understand.
n.2: A support worker cannot make health decisions for an adult who has not been shown to lack capacity.
n.3: Booking tests before she understands them means there is no informed consent.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Chloe, a midwife, managed a postpartum haemorrhage at 14:10 and could not write her notes during the emergency. She is now able to document at 16:30. How should she record the events?
o: Write it on a separate sheet to be added to the notes later
Write the entry at the times of the events, as it is accurate
Ask the scribe midwife to write the account in her place
Mark it as a late entry, with the time of writing and of events
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 10.1: complete records at the time or as soon as possible after an event, recording if the notes are written some time after the event. A late entry shows when it was written and the times the events happened (Code 10.4: dated and timed).

n.0: Loose sheets risk loss and break the chronological record; the late entry goes in the notes now.
n.1: Writing as if contemporaneous hides when the entry was made, which is misleading (Code 10.3).
n.2: Each professional records their own care; entries must be attributable to the person who made them (Code 10.4).

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: While reviewing her handwritten antenatal entry, a midwife notices she recorded the symphysis fundal height as 32 cm instead of 28 cm. What is the correct way to amend the paper record?
o: Draw one line through it, then sign, date and time it
Cover the error with correction fluid and write 28 cm over it
Score through the figure until it is unreadable and write 28 cm
Tear out the page and rewrite the entry in full
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Records must be accurate without falsification (Code 10.3) and attributable, dated and timed (10.4). A single line keeps the original readable, and the signed, dated correction shows who changed it and when.

n.1: Correction fluid hides the original entry, which looks like falsification.
n.2: Making the original unreadable removes the audit trail of what was first recorded.
n.3: Removing a page destroys part of the record and is falsification.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Amaka, 30, gave birth by emergency caesarean three weeks ago. At a postnatal visit she asks the community midwife for a copy of her labour records so she can understand what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell her the records belong to the trust and need a solicitor's request
Explain her right to see her records and support her request
Tell her she can request the records once the postnatal period ends
Give her the original records to take home and read
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Women have a legal right of access to their health records under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 (subject access request). SPM 1.24 states records should be available for review by the woman. A debrief offer may also help her understand events.

n.0: A solicitor is not needed; a woman can request her own records directly.
n.2: Her right of access is not delayed until the end of the postnatal period.
n.3: Original records stay with the trust; she is entitled to a copy, not the originals.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Which postnatal record entry best meets the NMC Code's standards for record keeping?
o: "Lochia moderate, red, no clots. Fundus firm, 2 cm below umbilicus."
"Lochia NAD. Fundus OK, well contracted. Pt happy with feeding."
"All observations within normal limits today. Plan as before."
"Seems a bit low today; may have postnatal depression, will monitor."
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 10.4: entries must be clearly written, dated, timed and attributable, without unnecessary abbreviations, jargon or speculation. The keyed entry records specific findings that another midwife could act on.

n.1: Abbreviations such as NAD and vague terms such as OK are unclear (Code 10.4).
n.2: 'All normal' and 'plan as before' do not record the actual findings or plan (Code 10.2).
n.3: A diagnosis guessed from an impression is speculation; mood should be described and assessed, not guessed.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Baby Tom, 3.2 kg, is prescribed an intravenous antibiotic at 5 mg/kg. The vial contains 10 mg in 1 mL. What volume should be drawn up?
o: 3.2 mL
1.6 mL
16 mL
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Dose = 5 mg/kg x 3.2 kg = 16 mg. Volume = 16 mg / 10 mg per mL = 1.6 mL. Accurate numeracy for safe practice is part of SPM 1.23.

n.0: 3.2 mL would give 32 mg, double the prescribed dose.
n.1: 0.16 mL is a tenfold underdose (16 divided by 100 instead of 10).
n.3: 16 mL confuses the dose in mg with the volume in mL, a tenfold overdose.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Baby Ava weighed 3,600 g at birth. On day 3 she weighs 3,240 g. What percentage of her birth weight has she lost?
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Loss = 3,600 - 3,240 = 360 g. Percentage = 360 / 3,600 x 100 = 10%. Calculating weight loss accurately supports feeding assessment (SPM 1.23; NICE NG194).

n.0: 9% would be a loss of 324 g, not 360 g.
n.1: 11% would be a loss of about 396 g, not 360 g.
n.2: 36% confuses the 360 g loss with a percentage.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Sian's electronic patient record login has expired during a night shift. Her colleague offers to stay logged in so Sian can document her care under the colleague's account until IT reset the password in the morning. What should Sian do?
o: Decline and use the trust's downtime process to record her care
Accept and add her initials to each entry made under the account
Accept and copy the entries into her own account in the morning
Decline and write up all her care from memory in the morning
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 10.4: attribute every entry to yourself. Using another person's login makes entries falsely attributed and breaches information governance. Trusts have downtime or paper processes so care can be recorded contemporaneously (Code 10.1; SPM 1.23 digital literacy).

n.1: Initials inside another person's account still leave the entries attributed to the wrong person in the system.
n.2: Using the account overnight already breaches attribution, and copying later duplicates the record.
n.3: Waiting until morning means the records are not contemporaneous, when a downtime process exists now.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: At handover, a midwife suggests sending details of a woman's care plan to the community team through a personal messaging app on her own phone, because it is quicker. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree, and leave the woman's name out of the message
Agree, as the messaging app is encrypted end to end
Disagree, and send the plan through the trust's approved secure system
Disagree, and phone the details to the community midwife's mobile instead
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 10.5: take all steps to keep records secure. Information about women must be shared through approved, secure, auditable systems so the record is complete and confidential (SPM 1.23 and 1.24).

n.0: Leaving out the name does not make a personal app an approved route; other details can still identify her.
n.1: Encryption does not make a personal device an approved, auditable route, and the information sits outside the record.
n.3: A phone call leaves no written, auditable copy of the plan in the record.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Nadia, a midwife, realises she has given Ms Cole, 6 hours after birth, a second dose of an oral analgesic 2 hours early. Ms Cole is resting comfortably. What should Nadia do first?
o: Assess Ms Cole and seek medical advice
Complete an incident report on the trust system
Explain the error to Ms Cole and apologise
Tell the ward manager about the error
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 14.1: act immediately to put right the situation if harm has occurred or could occur. Assessing the woman and getting advice comes first; then explain and apologise (14.2), document and escalate (14.3), and report the incident.

n.1: Reporting matters but comes after making the woman safe.
n.2: Candour with Ms Cole is required promptly, but after checking she is safe and getting advice on any treatment.
n.3: The manager must be told, but assessing the woman's safety is the immediate priority.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Under regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, who holds the statutory duty of candour in England?
o: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The registered provider, such as the NHS trust
The Care Quality Commission
Each registered midwife involved in the incident
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Regulation 20 places the statutory duty of candour on registered persons (providers registered with the CQC). Individual midwives have a professional duty of candour under NMC Code 14.

n.0: The NMC sets the professional duty but does not hold the statutory duty.
n.2: The CQC enforces reg 20; it does not hold the duty itself.
n.3: Individual midwives hold the professional duty under Code 14; reg 20 is placed on the provider.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: After a baby sustains a brachial plexus injury, the midwife who was present wants to apologise to the parents but worries that saying sorry will be treated as admitting negligence. Which statement is accurate?
o: An apology is an admission of liability, so legal advice comes first
An apology may be given once the trust's investigation has ended
An apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence
An apology should come from the consultant rather than the midwife
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Compensation Act 2006 s2: an apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty. Code 14.2 requires explaining fully and promptly and apologising.

n.0: An apology does not by itself admit liability (Compensation Act 2006 s2), so it should not be delayed for legal advice.
n.1: Code 14.2 requires a prompt apology; it should not wait for the investigation's outcome.
n.3: Every professional has the duty of candour under Code 14; the midwife may apologise herself.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: At the start of a night shift, Rhiannon notices that a midwife colleague smells strongly of alcohol and is slurring her words. The colleague is about to take over care of a woman in labour. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Take over the woman's care herself and deal with it after the shift
Escalate to the coordinator now to stop her giving care
Report the colleague directly to the NMC the next day
Speak to the colleague privately at the end of the shift
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 16 (act without delay if there is a risk to patient safety) and 16.1: raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns about patient safety; Code 8.7: support for a colleague must never compromise patient safety. Escalating to the coordinator now stops unsafe care immediately.

n.0: Covering for her leaves the colleague able to care for other women tonight and delays escalation (Code 16).
n.2: An NMC referral may follow, but it does not deal with the immediate risk tonight.
n.3: Waiting until the end of the shift leaves women at risk during the shift.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: For three months, Fatima has reported unsafe staffing on the labour ward to her manager. Nothing has changed, and two near misses have occurred. Her manager says nothing more can be done. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Post a description of the staffing problem on social media
Keep a private record and wait for the annual staff survey
Raise the concern with the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
Write to a national newspaper about the staffing levels
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 16.1: raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns using the available channels. When the line manager does not act, the next step is a higher internal route such as the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian or senior leaders, then prescribed bodies such as the CQC or NMC.

n.0: Social media posts may breach confidentiality and bypass the escalation channels the Code expects.
n.1: Waiting allows the risk to continue; Code 16 requires escalation without delay.
n.3: Going to the press first bypasses internal and regulatory routes and may lose legal protection for the disclosure.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: In a labour room, a registrar begins a vaginal examination on Joy, 25, without explaining it or asking her. Joy looks distressed and pulls away. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the midwife?
o: Report the registrar through the incident system after the shift
Ask the registrar to pause and check Joy's consent
Discuss the registrar's approach with the coordinator later
Hold Joy's hand to reassure her until the examination ends
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.15 and Code 3.4: advocate for women and challenge poor practice. Code 4.2: informed consent before any action. Speaking up at the time protects Joy; reporting can follow.

n.0: Reporting later is appropriate in addition, but does not stop the examination now.
n.2: A later discussion leaves Joy without an advocate at the moment consent is missing.
n.3: Reassuring Joy while an examination continues without consent fails to advocate for her.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: In established labour, Mel, a midwife, classifies Lara's CTG as pathological. The registrar reviews it and says to recheck in an hour. Mel still believes urgent action is needed and the registrar is now in theatre. What should Mel do?
o: Escalate directly to the consultant obstetrician using the policy
Ask a colleague to agree the CTG before taking any action
Accept the registrar's plan and recheck the CTG in one hour
Document her disagreement in the notes and continue monitoring
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.15: know when and how to escalate concerns. A pathological CTG needs urgent obstetric review (NICE NG229). If she remains concerned, she escalates to the consultant using the escalation policy, a lesson of the Ockenden (2022) and East Kent (2022) reports.

n.1: A 'fresh eyes' review is useful, but it should not delay escalation when she already believes urgent action is needed.
n.2: Waiting an hour with a pathological CTG, when she believes action is urgent, may delay life-saving care.
n.3: Documenting disagreement without escalating leaves the risk to the baby unaddressed.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998, what is needed for a midwife raising a concern about patient safety with her employer to be protected as a whistleblower?
o: She reasonably believes the disclosure is in the public interest
She raises the concern anonymously through a hotline
She has written evidence that proves the wrongdoing occurred
She has first raised the concern with the NMC
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: PIDA 1998 (inserting Part IVA into the Employment Rights Act 1996) protects a worker who makes a qualifying disclosure, which requires a reasonable belief that the information tends to show wrongdoing such as danger to health and safety, and that disclosure is in the public interest.

n.1: Anonymity is not a condition of protection; named concerns are protected too.
n.2: Proof is not required; a reasonable belief is enough.
n.3: Raising a concern with the employer first is the normal route; prior NMC contact is not a condition.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: During a planned home birth, Lisa, 30, has been in established labour for 5 hours when her waters break and the liquor is stained with thick meconium. The midwife recommends transfer to the obstetric unit. Lisa asks why. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Call the ambulance first and explain the reasons on the way
Tell her that trust policy requires transfer in this situation
Explain the reasons for transfer and the risks of staying at home
Tell her the doctors will explain the reasons when she arrives
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.18: explain the rationale for judgements and decisions. NICE NG235 advises transfer to obstetric-led care for significant meconium. Lisa needs the clinical reasons and risks so she can make an informed decision (Code 4.2).

n.0: Arranging transfer before explaining denies her the chance to make an informed decision.
n.1: Citing policy without the clinical reasons does not support informed decision-making.
n.3: Deferring the explanation leaves her without the information needed to decide about transfer now.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Reflecting on her practice, Nicole, a midwife, notices she has been slower to offer analgesia to Black women who report severe pain than to White women with similar findings. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Recognise possible bias, seek supervision and change her practice
Keep a list of women she has cared for to compare pain scores
Accept this as a normal variation in clinical judgement
Decide that each woman's pain report is unreliable without objective signs
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.18: recognise and address personal factors that may unduly influence decisions. MBRRACE-UK reports show stark ethnic disparities in maternal outcomes. Acknowledging bias, seeking support (for example from a Professional Midwifery Advocate) and changing practice is the professional response (Code 20.2).

n.1: A personal list of identifiable women breaches confidentiality and does not address the bias.
n.2: Unequal analgesia by ethnicity is a pattern of bias, not acceptable variation, and breaches Code 20.2.
n.3: Doubting women's pain reports in general would worsen the problem; pain is what the woman reports.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: The labour ward coordinator asks Helen, a midwife, to discharge Mrs Ahmed, 1 day after birth, to free a bed. Helen has just recorded a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and Mrs Ahmed has a headache. What should Helen do?
o: Explain why discharge is unsafe and request urgent medical review
Discharge her with advice to see the GP if the headache continues
Recheck the blood pressure in 4 hours before deciding on discharge
Discharge her and arrange a community blood pressure check tomorrow
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: SPM 1.18: recognise external pressures that may unduly influence decisions. A blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg with a headache after birth may be postnatal pre-eclampsia and needs urgent medical assessment (NICE NG133). Helen explains her rationale and escalates rather than discharging.

n.1: Discharging with GP advice ignores a possible postnatal pre-eclampsia that needs urgent review now.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours before acting delays the urgent review that hypertension with headache requires.
n.3: A check tomorrow delays assessment of a woman with hypertension and headache today.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Ffion, a midwife, is in the 13th hour of a shift. She is reviewing a complex CTG and notices she is struggling to concentrate. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Document that she was tired and continue her own review
Make a decision now and review the CTG again later in the shift
Ask a colleague to review the CTG with fresh eyes now
Have a coffee and complete the review after a short break
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 13.3 and 16.3: ask for help and tell someone if problems may stop you working safely. A fresh-eyes review by another clinician is part of systematic CTG review (NICE NG229 1.3.6; Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 4), and recognising fatigue is part of SPM 1.18.

n.0: Recording tiredness does not make her interpretation safe; another clinician should review it.
n.1: A decision made while struggling to concentrate risks an unsafe interpretation of a complex CTG.
n.3: Delaying the review of a complex CTG for a break could delay action the baby needs.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Bryony, a community midwife, finds that her close friend Ellen has been allocated to her caseload for antenatal and intrapartum care. Ellen is pleased. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Provide the care but keep her own notes on Ellen separately
Discuss the relationship with her manager before agreeing to provide care
Ask Ellen to request a different midwife so Bryony need not explain
Provide the care, since Ellen is pleased with the arrangement
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 20.6: stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries; SPM 1.14 and 1.18: act in the woman's best interests and recognise personal factors that may influence decisions. Discussing it with the manager allows an open decision about whether care should be reallocated.

n.0: Separate personal notes breach record keeping (Code 10) and do not address objectivity.
n.2: Putting the burden on Ellen avoids the professional conversation Bryony should have herself.
n.3: Ellen's wishes matter, but a close friendship can affect objectivity and needs an open, managed decision.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Martha, a midwife, holds religious views against contraception. Postnatally, Leanne, 22, asks Martha about contraception options before discharge. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give balanced information on options or arrange a colleague to do so
Explain her views and suggest Leanne waits until her GP check
Tell Leanne that breastfeeding is reliable contraception for now
Give leaflets and avoid discussing her personal views
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 20.7: do not express personal beliefs inappropriately; Code 4.4 on conscientious objection does not cover contraception advice. Leanne must get evidence-based information (Code 6.1), from Martha or a colleague arranged without delay.

n.1: Sharing personal beliefs and delaying advice breaches Code 20.7 and leaves Leanne without information when she wants it.
n.2: Breastfeeding protects reliably only if strict criteria (lactational amenorrhoea) are met; presenting it as reliable is inaccurate.
n.3: Handing out leaflets without discussion does not meet her request for information about options.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Tasha, 28, is 33 weeks pregnant. She phones triage for the third time this week reporting reduced fetal movements. Staff have noted she is 'anxious' and her two previous checks were normal. What should the triage midwife do?
o: Advise her to lie on her left side and count kicks for 2 hours
Invite her in for assessment, including fetal heart and CTG
Book a routine appointment with her community midwife this week
Reassure her by phone as both previous checks were normal
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Each episode of reduced fetal movements needs assessment; recurrent reduced movements after 28 weeks carry higher risk and need an ultrasound scan (Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 3; NICE NG201). SPM 1.18: a label such as 'anxious' must not bias the decision.

n.0: Kick counting at home is not recommended as a replacement for assessment when movements are reduced.
n.2: A routine appointment later in the week delays assessment of reduced movements that needs to happen now.
n.3: Previous normal checks do not exclude a new problem; each episode needs assessment.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Baby Noah is born at term in good condition and is in skin-to-skin contact with his mother. A colleague wants to weigh and dress him straight away to free the room. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: Agree to weigh him but let the mother dress him afterwards
Keep skin-to-skin and delay routine checks for the first hour
Weigh him now and return him for skin-to-skin to finish
Agree, as early weighing helps plan the first feed
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NICE NG235: encourage skin-to-skin as soon as possible and avoid separating the woman and baby within the first hour for routine procedures, such as weighing, unless she asks or they are needed for the baby's immediate care. Best interests of woman and newborn guide the decision (SPM 1.14).

n.0: Weighing still separates them during the first hour without a clinical need.
n.2: Interrupting skin-to-skin for a routine weight goes against NG235's advice for the first hour.
n.3: Weighing is a routine procedure that NG235 advises delaying; feeding plans do not depend on weight in the first hour.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Jess, 29, is 30 weeks pregnant and attends a community antenatal clinic. She tells the midwife that at her last appointment another midwife talked over her and did not answer her questions about birth options. Which theme of the NMC Code is most directly concerned with listening to women and responding to their preferences and concerns?
o: Promote professionalism and trust
Practise effectively
Prioritise people
Preserve safety
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Standard 2 of the NMC Code (2018), 'Listen to people and respond to their preferences and concerns', sits under the theme Prioritise people, alongside dignity (1), assessing needs (3), best interests (4) and confidentiality (5).

n.0: Promote professionalism and trust covers upholding the reputation of the profession, gifts, registration and leadership (standards 20 to 25).
n.1: Practise effectively covers evidence-based practice, communication, teamwork, records and delegation (standards 6 to 12), not listening to the woman's preferences.
n.3: Preserve safety covers working within competence, candour, escalation, medicines and infection control (standards 13 to 19).

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Kelly, a midwife on the postnatal ward, has cared for Mrs Okafor for three days. On discharge, Mrs Okafor hands Kelly a £50 shopping voucher as a personal thank you. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Politely decline the voucher and explain the professional reason
Accept the voucher and record the gift in Mrs Okafor's maternity notes
Accept the voucher because the episode of care has now ended
Accept the voucher and share its value with the ward team
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 21.1: refuse all but the most trivial gifts, favours or hospitality, as accepting them could be interpreted as an attempt to gain preferential treatment. A £50 voucher is not trivial, so the midwife declines kindly and explains why.

n.1: Recording the gift in the clinical notes does not make accepting a £50 voucher compatible with Code 21.1; the notes are a clinical record, not a gifts register.
n.2: Code 21.1 applies to people in your care regardless of discharge timing; the end of the episode does not turn a £50 voucher into a trivial gift.
n.3: Sharing the value with colleagues still means accepting a non-trivial gift, which Code 21.1 asks the midwife to refuse.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: After a busy night shift, Leah, a midwife, drafts a post for a private social media group of local friends: 'Long night with a very demanding woman in room 4 on our labour ward.' The post names the hospital. Which part of the NMC Code does this post most directly breach?
o: Standard 21: cooperate with the media appropriately
Standard 16: act without delay on risks to safety
Standard 10: keep clear and accurate records
Standard 20: use digital communication responsibly
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: Code 20.10 requires registrants to use all forms of spoken, written and digital communication, including social media, responsibly and to respect the right to privacy of others. Naming the unit and room risks identifying the woman and undermines public trust, whether or not the group is private.

n.0: Standard 21.6 concerns dealing with the media; posting in a friends' group is covered by 20.10 on digital communication.
n.1: Standard 16 concerns raising concerns about patient or public safety, which is not what this post does.
n.2: Standard 10 concerns clinical records; a social media post is not a care record.

Professional Accountability & the Code.q: Hannah, a newly registered midwife, is asked by the labour ward coordinator to repair a second-degree perineal tear. Hannah has not yet completed her trust's suturing training and has never sutured independently. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the woman whether she agrees to an untrained midwife suturing
Carry out the repair and ask a senior colleague to check it afterwards
Leave the repair until the next shift when a trained midwife is free
Tell the coordinator she is not yet competent and request a trained colleague
Professional Accountability & the Code.w: NMC Code 13.3 and 13.5: ask for help from a suitably qualified professional for any procedure beyond your competence and complete training before taking on a new role; Code 16.2: raise concerns immediately if asked to practise beyond your training. A trained colleague can repair the tear without delay.

n.0: The woman's agreement cannot make it safe or acceptable to practise beyond competence; Code 13.3 still applies.
n.1: Checking afterwards does not protect the woman from an unsafe repair carried out by someone who is not yet competent (Code 13.3).
n.2: Delaying the repair to another shift prolongs bleeding and discomfort; the right step is a trained colleague now, not later.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Which organisation regulates midwives in all four nations of the United Kingdom?
o: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The General Medical Council
The Health and Care Professions Council
Law, Consent & Rights.w: The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) regulates nurses and midwives across the UK, and nursing associates in England, under the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001.

n.0: The CQC regulates health and care providers in England, not individual midwives.
n.2: The GMC regulates doctors.
n.3: The HCPC regulates allied health professions such as paramedics and physiotherapists.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Jade, 25, gives birth at 22+5 weeks. The baby shows signs of life, including a heartbeat, and dies 30 minutes later. What are the registration requirements?
o: No registration is needed because the birth was before 24 weeks
Issue a certificate of pregnancy loss instead of registering
Register both the birth and the death
Register the baby as a stillbirth because the birth was before 24 weeks
Law, Consent & Rights.w: A baby born alive at any gestation is a live birth. Its birth and death must both be registered. The stillbirth category applies to babies born after 24 completed weeks with no signs of life (Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953).

n.0: The 24-week threshold applies to stillbirth; a baby born alive at any gestation must be registered.
n.1: Voluntary pre-24-week loss certificates are for babies born without signs of life; a live-born baby's birth and death must be registered.
n.3: A stillbirth is a baby born after 24 weeks with no signs of life; this baby was born alive.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Morag, a midwife in Glasgow, is assessing whether an adult woman in labour has capacity to make a decision about her care. Which legislation applies?
o: Mental Capacity Act 2005
Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000
Mental Health Act 1983
Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Capacity law differs between UK nations (SPM 1.2): the Adults with Incapacity (Scotland) Act 2000 applies in Scotland; the Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies in England and Wales; Northern Ireland has the Mental Capacity Act (Northern Ireland) 2016.

n.0: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 applies in England and Wales, not Scotland.
n.2: The Mental Health Act 1983 concerns treatment for mental disorder in England and Wales, not general capacity.
n.3: The 2016 Act applies in Northern Ireland, not Scotland.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Eilidh, a midwife in Scotland, sees a 15-year-old girl at an antenatal appointment and observes signs that FGM has been carried out. Which action is correct?
o: Refer under local child protection procedures without delay
Notify the police within one month under FGM Act 2003 s5B
Wait for the girl to disclose before taking any action
Record the finding and review at the next appointment
Law, Consent & Rights.w: The s5B mandatory notification duty in the FGM Act 2003 extends to England and Wales. In Scotland, FGM is an offence under the Prohibition of Female Genital Mutilation (Scotland) Act 2005, and a girl with FGM is a child protection concern referred without delay under local procedures (SPM 1.2: differentiate between devolved legislatures).

n.1: Section 5B does not extend to Scotland; Scottish child protection procedures apply.
n.2: Observed signs of FGM in a child are a child protection concern whether or not she discloses.
n.3: Delaying to a later appointment leaves a child protection concern without action.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Emma, 32, is told by her trust that home birth services are suspended because of staffing, without any individual discussion of her circumstances. Which Convention right under the Human Rights Act 1998 is most directly engaged by her choice of where to give birth?
o: Article 2: right to life
Article 8: right to respect for private and family life
Article 9: freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 5: right to liberty and security
Law, Consent & Rights.w: The European Court of Human Rights has held that choices about the circumstances of giving birth, including place of birth, fall within Article 8 (Ternovszky v Hungary, 2010). Article 8 is qualified, so any restriction must be lawful, necessary and proportionate.

n.0: Article 2 protects life; it is not the right that covers choice of place of birth.
n.2: Article 9 concerns belief and religion; place of birth is a private life matter under Article 8.
n.3: Article 5 concerns detention and loss of liberty, not birth choices.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: On a busy postnatal ward, a woman who is unwell is left for several hours in heavily blood-soaked bedding despite asking for help. Which Human Rights Act 1998 Convention right, which is absolute, may be engaged?
o: Article 14: prohibition of discrimination
Article 8: right to respect for private and family life
Article 3: prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 6: right to a fair trial
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Article 3 prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment and is an absolute right that cannot be limited. Leaving a woman in degrading conditions may engage it; it also breaches Code 1.1 and 1.2 (dignity and the fundamentals of care).

n.0: Article 14 applies with another Convention right when there is discrimination, which the scenario does not describe.
n.1: Article 8 may also be relevant to dignity, but it is a qualified right, and the question asks for the absolute right.
n.3: Article 6 concerns fair hearings in legal proceedings.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Which statement correctly describes how the Human Rights Act 1998 applies to an NHS trust providing maternity care?
o: It applies to doctors' decisions but not to midwives' decisions
The trust must act compatibly with Convention rights
It applies when a woman has brought a claim in court
It applies to private providers but not to NHS bodies
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Human Rights Act 1998 s6: it is unlawful for a public authority to act in a way that is incompatible with a Convention right. NHS trusts are public authorities, so their staff, including midwives, must act compatibly.

n.0: The trust acts through all its staff, so midwives' decisions are covered too.
n.2: The duty applies to everyday decisions, not just when a court case is brought.
n.3: NHS bodies are core public authorities and are bound by s6.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Student midwife Ben asks to observe a vaginal examination of Chantelle, 26, in labour. Which approach best respects Chantelle's rights to privacy and dignity?
o: Let Ben observe from behind a curtain without disturbing her
Ask Chantelle's partner whether he agrees to Ben observing
Let Ben observe, as students are part of the care team
Ask Chantelle privately whether she agrees to Ben observing
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Article 8 (private life) and Code 5.1 (privacy) and 4.2 (consent) mean Chantelle decides who is present for intimate care. Asking her privately makes it easier to refuse.

n.0: Observing from behind a curtain without asking her still breaches her privacy and right to decide.
n.1: Her partner cannot consent on her behalf to who observes her examination.
n.2: Students learning in practice still need the woman's agreement to be present for intimate care.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Natalie, 35, is having a planned caesarean for her fourth baby and asks for sterilisation at the same time. Her husband tells the midwife he does not agree. Natalie has capacity and has received full counselling. Whose consent is legally needed?
o: Natalie's and her husband's
Natalie's alone
Natalie's, with a second consultant's approval
Her husband's, as it affects the family
Law, Consent & Rights.w: An adult with capacity consents to treatment on her own body; no spouse or partner consent is required. This upholds her sexual and reproductive rights (SPM 1.3) and Article 8.

n.0: A husband has no legal right to consent or veto treatment on his wife's body.
n.2: No second consultant approval is required for sterilisation in an adult with capacity.
n.3: A spouse cannot consent for a woman who has capacity.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Kayla, 15, gave birth 4 weeks ago. At a postnatal visit she asks the midwife for contraception and does not want her parents told. She understands the information and is likely to have sex again. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Tell her she needs a parent's signature before contraception can be supplied
Refuse the request until she is 16
Arrange contraception if she is Gillick competent and the Fraser guidelines are met
Tell her parents, as she is under 16
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985): a young person under 16 may consent if competent, and the Fraser guidelines apply to contraception advice. Confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm. Safeguarding considerations still apply to sex under 16.

n.0: A competent young person can consent without a parent's signature.
n.1: Refusing contraception to a competent young person who is likely to have sex increases her risk of pregnancy.
n.3: Being under 16 does not by itself require parents to be told if she is competent and there is no serious risk.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Bridget, 27, a member of the Irish Traveller community, has no fixed address and is 14 weeks pregnant. A receptionist says she cannot book antenatal care without a permanent address. What is the most appropriate response by the midwife?
o: Book her care now, with a contact method that suits her
Offer to see her for emergencies until she has an address
Agree that a permanent address is needed for booking
Ask her to register with a GP first and then return
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Refusing care because of no fixed address may be indirect discrimination (Equality Act 2010, race includes Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities) and engages Article 14 with Article 8. Lack of an address is not a reason to refuse NHS maternity care; the midwife advocates and books her (SPM 1.3, 1.16).

n.1: Limiting her to emergency care denies her routine antenatal care and screening.
n.2: No fixed address is not a lawful reason to refuse antenatal booking.
n.3: GP registration is not a precondition for booking maternity care, and delaying booking adds risk at 14 weeks.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Which statement about Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, as applied to maternity care, is correct?
o: It can be limited if lawful, necessary and proportionate
It protects the rights of the fetus before birth
It applies once a baby has been born, but not in pregnancy
It is an absolute right, in the same way as Article 3
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Article 8 is a qualified right: interference must be in accordance with the law, pursue a legitimate aim (such as protecting the rights of others) and be necessary and proportionate. Information sharing for safeguarding can meet this test.

n.1: The fetus has no separate legal personality in England and Wales; Article 8 protects the woman's private life.
n.2: Article 8 covers pregnant women's choices, including about birth.
n.3: Article 8 is qualified; absolute rights include Article 3.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Sara, 31, has diabetes and a scan suggests a large baby. Her obstetrician did not mention shoulder dystocia because the risk 'is only a few per cent'. Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], which test decides whether a risk is material and must be disclosed?
o: Whether a responsible body of doctors would disclose the risk
Whether a reasonable person in her position would think it significant
Whether the clinician thinks the risk is relevant to the decision
Whether the risk is above a fixed percentage such as 1%
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11 para 87: a risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or the clinician knows or should know that this particular patient would.

n.0: A responsible body of medical opinion is the Bolam test, which Montgomery replaced for disclosure of risk.
n.2: The test looks at the patient's perspective, not what the clinician alone thinks is relevant.
n.3: Materiality does not depend on a percentage threshold; a rare but serious risk can be material.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Under Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015], when recommending a treatment, what must the clinician take reasonable care to make sure the woman knows about, in addition to its material risks?
o: The clinician's personal preference
The trust's policy on the treatment
Any reasonable alternative treatments
The national rate of complaints for it
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Montgomery para 87: the clinician must take reasonable care to ensure the patient is aware of any material risks involved in recommended treatment and of any reasonable alternative or variant treatments.

n.0: The clinician's personal preference is not part of the Montgomery duty of disclosure.
n.1: Trust policy is not what Montgomery requires to be disclosed.
n.3: Complaint rates are not part of the Montgomery duty of disclosure.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: During a vaginal examination in labour, Abby, 23, who had agreed to the examination, says, "Please stop, it hurts too much." The midwife has nearly finished assessing the cervix. What should the midwife do?
o: Continue, as Abby gave consent before it started
Finish quickly as the examination is nearly complete
Stop the examination at once and talk with Abby
Pause briefly, then continue once Abby has had a contraction
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Consent can be withdrawn at any time. Once Abby asks to stop, continuing would be without consent (Code 4.2; SPM 1.20). The midwife stops, supports her and discusses options.

n.0: Earlier consent does not continue once she has withdrawn it.
n.1: Finishing after consent has been withdrawn is examination without consent, however near completion.
n.3: Continuing after a pause without her renewed agreement still ignores the withdrawal of consent.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: A midwife is about to perform a vaginal examination in labour. Which statement about the form of consent is correct?
o: Consent is implied once a woman is admitted in labour
Written consent is legally required for any intimate examination
Verbal consent is valid and should be documented
Consent can be given by her birth partner on her behalf
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Consent may be verbal, written or non-verbal; what matters is that it is informed, voluntary and given by a person with capacity. Code 4.2: get properly informed consent and document it before any action.

n.0: Admission in labour does not imply consent to each examination; consent is needed for each intervention.
n.1: No law requires written consent for every intimate examination; verbal consent is valid when informed and voluntary.
n.3: A birth partner cannot consent for an adult woman with capacity.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Mei, 30, is pregnant for the first time. When is the best time to give her information about interventions that may be offered in labour, such as episiotomy?
o: In the second stage of labour, when the need arises
Antenatally, then confirmed in labour before any procedure
After the birth, during the postnatal debrief
When she is admitted to the labour ward in early labour
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Informed consent relies on information given when the woman can weigh it (Montgomery; MCA 2005 s3). Discussing interventions antenatally (NICE NG201 antenatal information on labour) and confirming consent at the time supports decision-making.

n.0: Information given for the first time during the second stage is hard to weigh under pain and time pressure.
n.2: Information after the birth cannot inform consent to a procedure that has already happened.
n.3: Early labour is better than the second stage, but antenatal discussion gives her time to consider options.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Mr Jacobs and Ms Lewis are not married. Their baby was born an hour ago and the birth has not been registered. Ms Lewis is in theatre recovery after a caesarean. Mr Jacobs says he consents to the baby's vitamin K injection. What should the midwife do?
o: Give vitamin K as it is a routine procedure
Give vitamin K on Mr Jacobs' consent
Seek Ms Lewis's consent when she is able
Ask the paediatrician to consent on the baby's behalf
Law, Consent & Rights.w: In England and Wales, a mother always has parental responsibility; an unmarried father gains it by joint birth registration, a parental responsibility agreement or a court order (Children Act 1989 s4). Vitamin K is not an emergency, so the midwife seeks consent from Ms Lewis when she is able (SPM 1.20).

n.0: Routine procedures for a newborn still need consent from a person with parental responsibility.
n.1: Mr Jacobs does not yet have parental responsibility, as the birth is not registered and they are not married.
n.3: A paediatrician cannot consent on a baby's behalf for non-emergency treatment when a parent can be asked.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Hollie, 29, is planning a vaginal birth after a previous caesarean. The consultant tells the midwife not to mention the risk of uterine rupture because "she might choose a caesarean instead". What is the most appropriate response by the midwife?
o: Mention the risk briefly if Hollie asks directly
Explain the risk must be discussed so she can make her choice
Agree, as discussing rupture may cause her anxiety
Agree, as the consultant leads her care and holds the duty
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Montgomery [2015] UKSC 11: material risks and reasonable alternatives must be disclosed. The therapeutic exception is narrow and cannot be used to stop a patient making a choice the clinician disagrees with. Uterine rupture is a material risk of VBAC, and SPM 1.15 requires the midwife to challenge.

n.0: Disclosure of material risks does not depend on the woman asking the right question.
n.2: Possible anxiety does not justify withholding a material risk; information can be given sensitively.
n.3: Every professional has a duty to support informed consent; the consultant's lead role does not justify withholding a material risk.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Student midwife Priti will perform a vaginal examination on Marie, 27, under direct supervision. What must happen for Marie's consent to be valid?
o: Marie is told it is a student and agrees to her doing it
Marie signs a form agreeing to all student involvement
Marie's partner agrees to the student taking part
The supervising midwife consents on Marie's behalf
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Valid consent must be informed and voluntary. The woman must know who will perform the procedure, including that the person is a student, and agree (Code 4.2; SPM 1.20).

n.1: A general form for all student involvement is not informed consent to a specific procedure.
n.2: A partner cannot consent for an adult woman with capacity.
n.3: The supervising midwife cannot consent for a woman with capacity.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Anya, 33, is 41+2 weeks in an uncomplicated first pregnancy. After a full discussion of the risks and benefits, she declines induction of labour. What is the most appropriate response by the midwife?
o: Ask her partner to talk with her about changing her decision
Respect her decision and offer extra monitoring from 42 weeks
Refer her to the safeguarding team as the baby may be at risk
Book the induction anyway in case she changes her mind
Law, Consent & Rights.w: A woman with capacity may decline induction. NICE NG207 advises that if she chooses not to have induction, her decision is respected and additional monitoring is offered from 42 weeks (twice-weekly CTG and ultrasound of the maximum amniotic pool depth). SPM 1.21.

n.0: Using her partner to pressure her undermines a voluntary decision.
n.2: Declining induction is a lawful choice, not a safeguarding concern.
