n.3: Booking a procedure she has declined disregards her decision.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Zara, 30, is in labour at term. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration, and an emergency caesarean is recommended. Zara has capacity, understands the risk to her baby and declines. What should the midwife do?
o: Proceed with the caesarean in the baby's best interests
Seek an urgent court order to allow the caesarean
Ask Zara's partner to consent to the caesarean
Respect her refusal, continue care and escalate
Law, Consent & Rights.w: A competent woman may refuse treatment even if this risks the fetus; the fetus has no separate legal personality in England and Wales. The midwife continues to provide care, explains alternatives, documents and involves senior staff (SPM 1.21; Code 2.5).

n.0: The fetus has no separate legal interests that can override a competent woman's refusal.
n.1: A court cannot authorise surgery on a woman who has capacity and refuses it.
n.2: A partner cannot consent for an adult woman with capacity.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Ruth, 28, is a Jehovah's Witness at 20 weeks and tells the midwife she will not accept blood transfusion under any circumstances. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Tell her blood will be given if her life is at risk
Note her religion and take no further action until labour
Ask the hospital chaplain to discuss her decision with her
Arrange a care plan with senior obstetric and anaesthetic staff
Law, Consent & Rights.w: An adult with capacity may refuse blood. SPM 1.22: advocate when decisions are outside guidance and plan to minimise risk. An individual plan records what she will and will not accept (for example cell salvage), optimises haemoglobin and involves senior staff early.

n.0: Giving blood to a competent woman who has refused it would be unlawful.
n.1: Waiting until labour misses the chance to plan and optimise her care.
n.2: Asking a chaplain to discuss her decision suggests pressure to change it rather than respect for it.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Kerry, 34, had a caesarean in her first pregnancy and plans a vaginal birth at home with her second, against obstetric advice. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Advise her to arrange private midwifery care for the birth
Document her plan and refer her to children's social care
Arrange a personalised care planning meeting with a consultant midwife
Tell Kerry midwives cannot attend a home birth after a caesarean
Law, Consent & Rights.w: SPM 1.22: advocate for the woman when her decision is outside guidance, to minimise risk and maintain the relationship. A consultant midwife care planning meeting allows an honest discussion of risks and a plan that supports her choice (Code 2.5).

n.0: Sending her to private care withdraws NHS support instead of advocating for her.
n.1: Choosing a birth outside guidance is not a safeguarding concern.
n.3: The trust still provides midwifery care; a woman's choice of place of birth does not remove midwifery support.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Lily, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. She has no medical or social risk factors and no safeguarding concerns. She declines further antenatal care and plans to give birth at home without a midwife. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that freebirth is unlawful in the UK
Discharge her from maternity services as she has declined care
Respect her decision, keep offering contact and document discussions
Refer to children's social care because she is declining care
Law, Consent & Rights.w: A woman with capacity may decline care and give birth without a professional present; it is lawful for her to do so. With no other concerns, declining care is not itself a safeguarding issue. The midwife keeps the door open, shares information and documents (SPM 1.21).

n.0: Freebirth is lawful; art 45 of the Nursing and Midwifery Order 2001 restricts who may attend, not the woman's choice.
n.1: Discharging her closes the door on care she may later accept.
n.3: Declining care, with no other concerns, is not a reason for a social care referral.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Yasmin, 32, is in labour at term with a previous caesarean. Continuous CTG is recommended, but she declines it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Apply the CTG anyway as she has a uterine scar
Ask the registrar to apply the CTG while the midwife reassures her
Stop monitoring the baby until she agrees to the CTG
Explain why, offer intermittent auscultation and document it
Law, Consent & Rights.w: SPM 1.21: respect the right to decline and provide appropriate care. The midwife explains why continuous monitoring is advised (NICE NG229 for women with a previous caesarean), offers an alternative such as intermittent auscultation and documents the discussion.

n.0: Applying monitoring she has declined is treatment without consent.
n.1: Applying the CTG through another clinician is still monitoring without consent.
n.2: Stopping monitoring removes all fetal assessment; she should be offered an acceptable alternative.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: After a discussion, Tamsin, 27, declines group B streptococcus antibiotics in labour despite known carriage. Which record entry best documents her decision?
o: "Risks and options explained; Tamsin declines and understands."
"Refused antibiotics against medical advice; plan as before."
"Advised strongly but refused. Not my responsibility."
"Declined GBS antibiotics. Aware of risks."
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 2.5: respect, support and document a person's right to refuse care; Code 10.2: record risks and steps taken. The entry shows the information given, her decision and her understanding.

n.1: 'Plan as before' and 'against advice' do not record the information given or a revised plan.
n.2: Disclaiming responsibility is unprofessional and does not record the discussion.
n.3: 'Aware of risks' does not show what information was given.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Parents of baby Harry, born today, decline vitamin K after hearing the information. What should the midwife do next?
o: Give oral vitamin K instead, as it is less invasive
Refer them to children's social care for neglect
Tell them the baby cannot be discharged without vitamin K
Document their decision and explain signs of bleeding
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Parents with parental responsibility may decline vitamin K after informed discussion (SPM 1.20, 1.21). The midwife records the decision, explains signs of vitamin K deficiency bleeding to watch for and informs the paediatric and community teams.

n.0: Oral vitamin K still needs consent; the parents declined vitamin K, not just the injection (Code 4.2).
n.1: An informed decision to decline vitamin K is not by itself neglect.
n.2: Discharge is not conditional on vitamin K; that would be coercion.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Danielle, 25, is in strong labour and declines an epidural, shouting that she wants to cope without one. The registrar says she cannot be making a proper decision while in so much pain. Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what is the starting point?
o: She lacks capacity as she is refusing pain relief
She lacks capacity until her pain has been controlled
She is assumed to have capacity unless shown otherwise
Her birth partner decides while she is in pain
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack capacity. Pain and distress do not by themselves establish incapacity; any doubt needs a decision-specific assessment.

n.0: Refusing a recommended treatment does not show a lack of capacity (s1(4)).
n.1: Pain does not remove capacity automatically; incapacity must be established, not assumed.
n.3: Nobody can decide for an adult who has capacity, including a birth partner.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 s3, a person is unable to make a decision if they cannot do which of the following?
o: Agree with the professional's recommendation about the decision
Explain the reasons for their decision to the clinical team
Understand, retain, use or weigh information, or communicate a decision
Read and write fluently in the language the information is given in
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MCA 2005 s3(1): a person is unable to make a decision if unable to understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it as part of the decision, or communicate the decision by any means.

n.0: Disagreeing with a professional is not a lack of capacity; unwise decisions are protected (s1(4)).
n.1: A person does not have to justify their decision to have capacity.
n.3: Literacy is not part of the test; information can be given in other ways (s3(2)).

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Sophie, 36, has capacity and declines a recommended blood transfusion after a postpartum haemorrhage, saying she prefers iron infusions. Staff feel this is unwise. What does the Mental Capacity Act 2005 say?
o: Staff can override unwise decisions in an emergency
An unwise decision does not mean she lacks capacity
An unwise decision shows that she lacks capacity
Unwise decisions must be reviewed by the Court of Protection
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because they make an unwise decision. Her choice must be respected while care continues.

n.0: A capacitous refusal cannot be overridden, even in an emergency.
n.2: The Act states the opposite: an unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
n.3: The Court of Protection is not needed when a person has capacity.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Emily, 29, is in labour and understands the information about an epidural but forgets the details within about 20 minutes. She has weighed it up and says she wants one. Which statement about her capacity is correct?
o: She lacks capacity as she cannot retain the details for long
She lacks capacity until a psychiatrist has assessed her
She has capacity once her birth partner confirms her wishes
She has capacity, as brief retention is enough to decide
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MCA 2005 s3(3): being able to retain information for a short period only does not prevent a person being regarded as able to make the decision.

n.0: Short retention is enough under s3(3).
n.1: Any professional making the decision can assess capacity; a psychiatrist is not required.
n.2: A partner's confirmation is not part of the capacity test.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Precious, 22, has an eclamptic seizure on the antenatal ward and remains unconscious afterwards. She needs magnesium sulfate urgently. What is the legal basis for treatment?
o: Best interests treatment under the MCA 2005
A Court of Protection order
The consent of her next of kin
Her consent once she regains consciousness
Law, Consent & Rights.w: She lacks capacity at the material time (MCA 2005 s2; temporary impairment counts, s2(2)). Treatment that cannot wait is given in her best interests (s4, s5), taking account of any known wishes.

n.1: A court order is not needed for urgent treatment in an emergency.
n.2: Next of kin cannot consent for an adult unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
n.3: Waiting for consciousness would delay treatment needed to prevent further seizures.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Maria, 34, lacks capacity to make decisions about her birth because of a severe psychotic illness. The team is deciding on a plan in her best interests. Which approach meets the Mental Capacity Act 2005?
o: Ask her mother to choose, as she is next of kin
Choose the option with the shortest stay in hospital
Choose the option the obstetrician thinks is clinically best
Consider Maria's wishes and beliefs and consult those close to her
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MCA 2005 s4: the best interests checklist includes the person's past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values, and the views of those caring for or interested in them; s1(6) requires the least restrictive option. A best interests decision is not just the clinical view.

n.0: Relatives are consulted but do not decide unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney.
n.1: Length of stay is not a best interests consideration in itself.
n.2: Best interests are wider than the clinical view; her wishes and values must be considered.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Lucia, 27, lacks capacity because of a severe learning disability and is 38 weeks pregnant. The team believes a planned caesarean is in her best interests, but she objects and her family disagree. There is no emergency. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask Lucia's GP to make the decision
Wait until labour starts and decide then
Apply to the Court of Protection for a decision
Proceed with the caesarean as a best interests decision
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Where serious medical treatment is proposed for a person lacking capacity and there is disagreement or objection, the Court of Protection can decide what is in her best interests (MCA 2005). Planning ahead avoids an emergency decision.

n.0: A GP has no legal power to decide for an adult who lacks capacity.
n.1: Waiting for labour turns a plannable decision into an emergency with less time to safeguard her rights.
n.3: Proceeding with major surgery against objection and family disagreement, without the court, is not appropriate when time allows an application.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Fern, 30, is in labour and has a needle phobia. She agreed to a caesarean but panics and refuses as the cannula is about to be inserted. The team must decide whether she has capacity for this decision. Which approach is correct?
o: Treat the refusal as valid without any further assessment
Treat her as lacking capacity because she has a phobia
Assess whether panic stops her weighing the information
Proceed, as she agreed to the caesarean earlier
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific (MCA 2005 s2, s3). Panic or phobia may remove capacity only if it stops her using or weighing the information. If she has capacity, her refusal stands; if she lacks it, treatment is in her best interests.

n.0: Where there is real doubt, capacity must be assessed for this decision at this time.
n.1: A phobia is a condition that must not lead to unjustified assumptions about capacity (s2(3)).
n.3: Earlier consent does not override a later refusal if she has capacity now.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Jasmine, 27, is 16 weeks pregnant. While she is in the toilet, her partner asks the midwife for the results of her booking blood tests, including the infection screen. Jasmine has not said whether he may be told. What should the midwife do?
o: Give the results, as he is the baby's father
Explain she will discuss results with Jasmine first
Give the normal results and withhold any abnormal ones
Give the results if he can confirm her date of birth
Law, Consent & Rights.w: NMC Code 5.1 and 5.2: respect privacy and confidentiality; results belong to Jasmine, who decides who is told. The midwife discusses them with her and asks her wishes (SPM 1.24).

n.0: Being the father of the baby does not give a right to the woman's health information.
n.2: Revealing that some results are normal while withholding others still discloses information without consent.
n.3: Knowing her date of birth does not give him permission to receive her results.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: At booking, Hana, 31, discloses a previous termination of pregnancy and asks that her husband is not told. At a later appointment her husband is present and the midwife needs to review her obstetric history. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the husband to leave for every appointment from now on
Ask Hana privately how she wants the history discussed
Skip the obstetric history to avoid the topic
Review the history aloud, as the termination is in her records
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 5.1: respect privacy in all aspects of care. Hana controls who knows about her history. Finding time to speak privately respects her wishes while the review is completed safely.

n.0: Excluding him from every appointment may not be what she wants; she should be asked.
n.2: Skipping the history risks missing relevant clinical information.
n.3: Discussing the termination in front of her husband breaches her confidentiality and her express wish.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: At a home visit, Kirsty, 24, who is 30 weeks pregnant, tells the midwife her partner hit her 2-year-old son last night, leaving a bruise. She begs the midwife not to tell anyone. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain why and refer to children's social care today
Keep it confidential, as Kirsty has asked
Share the information if Kirsty agrees after thinking about it
Advise Kirsty to contact children's social care herself
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 17.1 and 17.2: protect people at risk and share information where someone may be at risk of harm, in line with the law. A child with an injury from an adult is at risk, so the midwife shares without waiting for consent, explaining why to Kirsty where this is safe.

n.1: Confidentiality does not prevent sharing to protect a child at risk of harm.
n.2: Waiting for her agreement delays protection for a child who has been injured.
n.3: Leaving the referral to Kirsty may mean it is not made, and the midwife holds the concern.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: A caller to the postnatal ward says she is the mother of Rosie, 22, who gave birth yesterday, and asks how Rosie and the baby are. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give a brief update as the caller is a close relative
Neither confirm nor deny, and offer to pass a message to Rosie
Confirm Rosie is on the ward but give no clinical details
Give an update if the caller can state Rosie's address
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 5.1 and 5.2: confidentiality includes whether a person is in hospital. The midwife cannot verify the caller, so she offers to pass on a message so Rosie can decide what to share.

n.0: The caller's identity cannot be confirmed, and Rosie has not agreed to updates.
n.2: Confirming that Rosie is on the ward is itself a disclosure of confidential information.
n.3: Knowing an address does not verify identity or give Rosie's consent.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: A police officer arrives on the postnatal ward and asks the midwife for details of injuries to Leanne, 30, who was assaulted, saying it will help their inquiry. Leanne is asleep. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Show the officer Leanne's notes so he can decide what is relevant
Give the details, as the police are investigating a crime
Seek Leanne's consent and advice from the information governance lead
Refuse and ask the officer not to return to the ward
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Information about a person with capacity is normally shared with consent; disclosure without consent needs a legal basis or an overriding public interest, decided carefully (Code 5.4, 17.2). The midwife asks Leanne when she wakes and involves the trust's information governance or Caldicott lead.

n.0: Giving access to the whole record discloses far more than any request could justify.
n.1: A police request alone is not a legal basis to disclose without consent or a public interest assessment.
n.3: Refusing outright and turning the officer away ignores routes such as consent or a lawful public interest disclosure.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: A woman died on the labour ward last month. A journalist contacts a midwife who was present, asking for details of what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give general details, as confidentiality ends at death
Give details if the woman's family agree
Give details anonymously, without naming the woman
Decline and refer the journalist to the trust
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 5.3: the right to privacy and confidentiality continues after death. Code 21.6: cooperate with the media only when appropriate, protecting confidentiality and dignity. Media enquiries go through the trust.

n.0: Confidentiality continues after death (Code 5.3).
n.1: Even with family agreement, an individual midwife should not brief journalists; the trust manages media contact.
n.2: Details of a recent death can identify the woman even without her name.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Two midwives in a crowded hospital lift are talking about a woman's recent stillbirth, using her first name and room number. A third midwife is also in the lift. What should she do?
o: Report both midwives to the NMC after the shift
Leave it to the midwives' own manager to address later
Join the conversation to make sure the details are accurate
Quietly remind them to stop discussing the woman
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 5.1: respect privacy in all aspects of care; Code 16 and 20.3: act on concerns and promote professional behaviour. A prompt, quiet reminder protects the woman's confidentiality now.

n.0: An NMC referral is disproportionate as a first step and does not stop the breach now.
n.1: Leaving it for someone else lets the breach continue now; every registrant should act on poor practice (Code 16, 20.3).
n.2: Joining in adds to the breach of confidentiality.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Lauren, 28, is 24 weeks pregnant and has no children. She discloses that her partner is controlling and has pushed her. She does not want any referral. She has capacity and there is no immediate danger. What should the midwife do first?
o: Complete a risk assessment and offer specialist support
Close the conversation, as she has declined referral
Refer her to the police without her agreement
Tell her partner the midwife is aware of the abuse
Law, Consent & Rights.w: NICE NG201 recommends asking about domestic abuse when the woman is alone. A structured risk assessment (for example DASH) guides action: high risk may justify sharing without consent (for example a MARAC referral), while lower risk means offering specialist support and respecting her decision. The unborn baby is also considered in safeguarding.

n.1: Ending the discussion misses the risk assessment and support she needs.
n.2: Sharing without consent depends on assessed risk, which has not yet been done.
n.3: Telling the partner could put Lauren in danger.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Bella, 29, is 14 weeks pregnant in England and requests a termination because continuing the pregnancy is affecting her mental health. Under the Abortion Act 1967 s1, how many registered medical practitioners must form the opinion that a ground is met?
o: One doctor and one midwife
Three
One
Two
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(1): a pregnancy may be lawfully terminated by a registered medical practitioner when two registered medical practitioners are of the opinion, formed in good faith, that a ground in s1(1)(a) to (d) applies.

n.0: The opinions must be those of two registered medical practitioners; a midwife's opinion does not count towards them.
n.1: The Act requires two, not three, practitioners.
n.2: One practitioner is enough in an emergency under s1(4), which does not apply here.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Under the Abortion Act 1967, what is the time limit for termination on ground (a), risk of injury to the physical or mental health of the woman or her existing children?
o: 12 weeks
20 weeks
28 weeks
24 weeks
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(1)(a): ground (a) applies where the pregnancy has not exceeded its 24th week.

n.0: 12 weeks is not the limit for ground (a) under the 1967 Act.
n.1: 20 weeks is not the limit set by the Act.
n.2: 28 weeks was the old presumption of viability under the Infant Life (Preservation) Act 1929; the Act sets 24 weeks for ground (a).

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Chen, 30, has a scan at 26 weeks showing a serious fetal abnormality. She asks whether termination is still lawful in England. Which statement is correct?
o: Yes, if a court approves the termination first
Yes, under ground (a), as her mental health is affected
Yes, under ground (d), which has no time limit
No, termination is not lawful after 24 weeks on any ground
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(1)(d): substantial risk that the child would suffer physical or mental abnormalities so as to be seriously handicapped. Grounds (b), (c) and (d) have no gestational time limit.

n.0: No court approval is required; two practitioners' opinions are needed.
n.1: Ground (a) is limited to 24 weeks, so it does not apply at 26 weeks.
n.3: Grounds (b) to (d) have no time limit, so termination can be lawful after 24 weeks.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Aoife, a midwife, is moving from a post in Belfast to a new post in Cardiff. She is checking which law on termination of pregnancy will apply to her new role. Which statement about the territorial extent of the Abortion Act 1967 is correct?
o: It extends to England and Wales, but not Scotland
It extends to England, Wales and Scotland
It extends to all four nations of the United Kingdom
It extends to England, Scotland and Northern Ireland
Law, Consent & Rights.w: The Abortion Act 1967 extends to England, Wales and Scotland. Northern Ireland has its own separate legal framework, so the Act will apply in Cardiff but did not apply in Belfast. Midwives must differentiate between UK legislatures (SPM 1.2).

n.0: The Act also extends to Scotland.
n.2: The Act does not extend to Northern Ireland, which has its own framework.
n.3: The Act extends to Wales and does not extend to Northern Ireland.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: A woman at 22 weeks has a severe haemorrhage and the obstetric consultant believes immediate termination is needed to save her life. There is no time to obtain a second opinion. Under the Abortion Act 1967, is this lawful?
o: Yes, under the emergency provision in s1(4)
No, two practitioners must agree before any termination
No, termination must take place in an approved clinic
Yes, if a senior midwife also signs the certificate
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Abortion Act 1967 s1(4): the requirement for two opinions, and the place requirement, do not apply where a registered medical practitioner believes in good faith that termination is immediately necessary to save the life, or prevent grave permanent injury to the physical or mental health, of the pregnant woman.

n.1: Section 1(4) removes the two-opinion requirement in an emergency.
n.2: Section 1(4) also removes the requirement for an NHS hospital or approved place.
n.3: A midwife's signature is not part of the Act's requirements.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Ellen, a midwife, has a conscientious objection to abortion. She is the only midwife available when a woman bleeds heavily after a medical termination and needs urgent care to prevent grave injury. What must Ellen do?
o: Provide the care, as her objection does not cover this situation
Provide care once the woman confirms the termination is complete
Wait for a midwife without an objection to arrive
Refuse, as her objection covers all care related to termination
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Abortion Act 1967 s4(2): conscientious objection does not affect any duty to take part in treatment necessary to save the life or prevent grave permanent injury to the pregnant woman. Code 4.4 and 15 also apply.

n.1: Making care depend on confirmation delays emergency treatment that s4(2) requires.
n.2: Waiting risks the woman's life; the s4(2) exception requires Ellen to act.
n.3: Section 4(2) keeps the duty to take part in treatment needed to save life or prevent grave permanent injury.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Hope, a midwife, has a conscientious objection to taking part in terminations. Under the NMC Code 4.4, what should she do?
o: Decline to tell anyone, as the objection is a private matter
Explain her personal views to women who request a termination
Refuse to care for any woman before or after a termination
Tell her manager and colleagues and ask a colleague to take over
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 4.4: tell colleagues, your manager and the person receiving care about a conscientious objection, and arrange for a suitably qualified colleague to take over. Objection is limited to participation in the termination itself.

n.0: Code 4.4 requires the objection to be made known so care can be arranged.
n.1: Sharing personal beliefs with women breaches Code 20.7.
n.2: Objection does not extend to caring for women before or after termination.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Kathleen, a labour ward coordinator, has a conscientious objection to abortion. She is asked to allocate a midwife to care for a woman having a termination for fetal anomaly. Following the Supreme Court decision in Doogan [2014], what is the position?
o: She must allocate staff, as this is not hands-on participation
She may refuse, as any link to a termination is covered
She may refuse, as allocation is participation in the treatment
She may refuse if she records her objection in writing
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Greater Glasgow Health Board v Doogan [2014] UKSC 68 held that 'participate' in s4 means taking part in a hands-on capacity; managerial and supervisory tasks such as allocating staff are not covered by the objection.

n.1: Doogan rejected a wide reading covering any task linked to termination.
n.2: Doogan held that allocation is not participation in the treatment.
n.3: Recording an objection does not bring allocation within s4, which Doogan held is not participation.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Zoe, 26, tells her community midwife that a café owner asked her to stop breastfeeding her 10-week-old baby or leave. Under the Equality Act 2010, how is this treatment best described?
o: Lawful, as the baby is over 6 weeks old
Pregnancy and maternity discrimination
Lawful, as the owner may set rules for a private business
Discrimination under the Human Rights Act 1998
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Equality Act 2010 s17: in services, treating a woman unfavourably because she is breastfeeding within 26 weeks of the birth is pregnancy and maternity discrimination. After 26 weeks it is treated as sex discrimination (s13).

n.0: Protection in s17 lasts for 26 weeks after the birth; 10 weeks is well within it.
n.2: Service providers, including private businesses, must not discriminate under the Equality Act 2010.
n.3: The Human Rights Act binds public authorities; a private café's conduct falls under the Equality Act.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: According to the MBRRACE-UK data brief on maternal deaths in 2022 to 2024, how did the maternal death rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
o: About ten times higher
About one and a half times higher
About the same
Nearly three times higher
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MBRRACE-UK maternal mortality data brief 2022-24 (September 2026 update): Black women died at nearly three times the rate of White women. SPM 1.17.1: health inequalities and their determinants.

n.0: The figure is nearly three times, not ten.
n.1: The disparity is larger: nearly three times.
n.2: The data show a large disparity, not similar rates.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: The MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 maternal mortality data brief compares women living in the most and least deprived areas. What did it report?
o: Women in the most deprived areas had about twice the rate
Rates were similar across deprivation levels
Women in the most deprived areas had about five times the rate
Women in the least deprived areas had a higher rate
Law, Consent & Rights.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: maternal mortality in the most deprived areas was about twice that in the least deprived. Midwives must understand health inequalities and their determinants (SPM 1.17.1).

n.1: The data show a clear gradient by deprivation.
n.2: The difference was about twice, not five times.
n.3: The gradient runs the other way: higher in the most deprived areas.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: At handover, a colleague says of a Black woman in early labour, "These women always make a fuss about pain; she'll be fine for hours." What is the most appropriate response by the midwife?
o: Agree to review her later, as early labour can be slow
Report the colleague to the NMC before the end of the shift
Assess the woman's pain herself later and raise the remark at appraisal
Challenge the remark now and make sure her pain is assessed
Law, Consent & Rights.w: SPM 1.8: challenge discriminatory behaviour. Code 3.4 and 20.2: challenge discriminatory attitudes and treat people fairly. Challenging at the time and making sure the woman is properly assessed protects her care; MBRRACE-UK reports show stark ethnic disparities.

n.0: Accepting the plan lets a biased judgement delay her assessment.
n.1: An NMC referral is not the first step and does not make sure the woman is assessed now.
n.2: Delaying both the challenge and the assessment lets a discriminatory remark influence her care now.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Gloria, 38, is 20 weeks pregnant and has a significant visual impairment. She says she has not been able to read any of her appointment letters or screening leaflets. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her partner to read all letters and leaflets to her
Phone her before each appointment and stop sending letters
Advise her to contact the RNIB for help reading her letters
Offer large print, audio or another accessible format
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Equality Act 2010 s20: duty to make reasonable adjustments, including providing information in an accessible format. SPM 1.9: take account of the need for adjustments. Code 7.2: meet communication needs.

n.0: Relying on her partner removes her privacy and independence and is not an adjustment by the service.
n.1: Phone calls help but stopping written information denies her a record she can use.
n.2: The duty to adjust lies with the service, not with a charity.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Mirela, 29, is undocumented and 22 weeks pregnant. She has not booked because she fears she will be charged and reported. Under the NHS charging rules in England, what should the midwife tell her?
o: Care is free once she registers with a GP, so she should do that first
Care will start once she has paid a deposit towards the charges
Her care will not be withheld or delayed because of charges
She should return to hospital when she goes into labour
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Under the NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 guidance, maternity care is always treated as immediately necessary and must not be withheld or delayed because of a woman's ability to pay. SPM 1.16: advocate for women made vulnerable by their social circumstances.

n.0: GP registration does not decide charging status, and booking should not wait for it.
n.1: Payment is not a condition of receiving maternity care.
n.3: Delaying care until labour misses screening and antenatal care, increasing risk.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Aisha, 33, wears a hijab and is attending her booking appointment. The midwife is arranging an obstetric referral. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask Aisha's husband about any cultural requirements
Ask Aisha whether she has any preferences about her care
Book a female obstetrician without asking, as this is likely her preference
Book the first available obstetrician without asking about preferences
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Code 1.3: avoid making assumptions and recognise diversity and individual choice. SPM 1.9: provide respectful care and take account of any need for adjustments. Asking the woman herself is person-centred.

n.0: Aisha can state her own preferences; asking her husband bypasses her.
n.2: Booking on an assumption about her religion stereotypes her and may not be her wish.
n.3: Not asking misses any preference that could be accommodated.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Alex, 30, is a trans man who is 28 weeks pregnant. At his first appointment with a new midwife, how should the midwife approach his care?
o: Use the name on his NHS number record until it is changed
Ask how he wishes to be addressed and record his name and pronouns
Refer to him as 'mum' in line with maternity documentation
Refer him to a gender clinic before continuing antenatal care
Law, Consent & Rights.w: Gender reassignment is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010. Code 1.1 and 1.3: treat people with respect and avoid assumptions. Asking how he wishes to be addressed and recording it is respectful, person-centred care (SPM 1.9).

n.0: Using a name he does not use, when he has told staff his name, is disrespectful and avoidable.
n.2: Using 'mum' ignores his identity and how he wishes to be addressed.
n.3: His antenatal care does not depend on a gender clinic referral.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Kate, a community midwife in England, attends Ruth's planned home birth at 40 weeks. Mother and baby are well. Under the NHS Act 2006 s269, within what time must notice of the birth be given?
o: 21 days
36 hours
24 hours
42 days
Law, Consent & Rights.w: NHS Act 2006 s269: the father and any person attending the mother at the birth or within six hours after it must give notice of the birth within 36 hours. In practice the midwife sends the notification. Registration (42 days in England and Wales) is a separate duty of the parents.

n.0: 21 days is the registration period in Scotland, not the notification time in England.
n.2: 24 hours is shorter than the 36 hours set by s269.
n.3: 42 days is the time limit for registering a birth in England and Wales, not for notification.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Isla and Callum live in Edinburgh and had their baby 5 days ago. They ask their community midwife how long they have to register the birth. What is the correct answer?
o: 36 hours
6 weeks
21 days
42 days
Law, Consent & Rights.w: In Scotland a birth must be registered within 21 days (Registration of Births, Deaths and Marriages (Scotland) Act 1965). In England and Wales the period is 42 days (Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953 s2). Midwives differentiate between UK legislatures (SPM 1.2).

n.0: 36 hours is the time limit for notifying a birth in England, not for registering it in Scotland.
n.1: 6 weeks equals the 42-day period in England and Wales, which does not apply in Scotland.
n.3: 42 days is the registration period in England and Wales, not Scotland.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Amina, 16, is booking at 10 weeks in a clinic in England. During the history she tells the midwife that she had FGM when she was 6 years old. What must the midwife do under the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 s5B?
o: Notify the police if Amina consents to the disclosure
Record the FGM and notify the police when Amina turns 18
Refer to children's social care, which will inform the police
Personally notify the police within one month
Law, Consent & Rights.w: FGM Act 2003 s5B (England and Wales): a regulated health professional who is told by a girl under 18 that FGM has been carried out on her must personally notify the police within one month. Local safeguarding procedures are followed as well.

n.0: The duty does not depend on the girl's consent.
n.1: The duty applies now, as Amina is under 18; waiting until 18 would miss the one-month limit.
n.2: The s5B duty is personal to the professional and cannot be passed to social care.

Law, Consent & Rights.q: Leyla, 24, attends booking at 11 weeks in England. During the examination, the midwife observes that Leyla has had FGM, which Leyla confirms was done in childhood abroad. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer Leyla to the police as a victim of a criminal offence
Take no further action, as the FGM happened outside the UK
Record the FGM, then assess risk to the unborn baby and any daughters
Notify the police within one month under the mandatory reporting duty
Law, Consent & Rights.w: The s5B mandatory police notification applies to girls under 18 (FGM Act 2003). For a woman aged 18 or over, the midwife records the FGM, offers support and specialist care, and completes a safeguarding risk assessment for the unborn baby and any daughters.

n.0: Police referral for an adult is not required by s5B and is not the first step; safeguarding assessment is.
n.1: FGM carried out abroad still requires recording, care planning and safeguarding assessment.
n.3: Mandatory reporting under s5B applies to girls under 18; Leyla is 24.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Rosa, 31, is cared for by a continuity team. At 34 weeks she develops gestational hypertension and is referred to the antenatal clinic for obstetric review. Her named midwife is concerned about losing the relationship. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Continue as her named midwife while coordinating care with the obstetric team
Keep her care midwife-led and defer the obstetric referral to 36 weeks
Discharge her from the continuity team and book a new consultant midwife
Transfer her midwifery care to the hospital antenatal clinic midwives
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.5 requires continuity of midwifery carer for women with and without complications and additional care needs. The named midwife remains her midwife and works with the obstetric team (SPM 2.4: work across settings and with other staff to promote continuity of care and carer).

n.1: Gestational hypertension needs obstetric involvement now (NG133); delaying referral to protect continuity would be unsafe.
n.2: Discharging her ends continuity at the point she most benefits from a known carer, and a consultant midwife does not replace obstetric review.
n.3: Handing her to clinic midwives fragments care; SPM 2.5 expects continuity for women with complications as well as without.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A continuity team of six midwives covers its own women in labour on call. One midwife has worked a 13-hour day and is called at 03:00 to a woman in early labour. A second team midwife is available and rested. Which action best balances continuity and safety?
o: Advise the woman to attend the labour ward and be seen by core staff
Ask the rested team midwife, known to the woman, to attend the call
Delay the visit until 07:00 when the midwife has rested for four hours
Attend the call herself because the woman expects her named midwife
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Continuity models work through small teams so a known midwife is available; safety and staff wellbeing must be protected (Code 13 work within limits of competence; NHS England 2022 on safe staffing). A rested team colleague keeps continuity and safety.

n.0: Sending her to an unknown team when a known, rested team member is free loses continuity without any safety gain.
n.2: Delaying assessment of a woman in labour for staff convenience is unsafe and could miss progress or complications.
n.3: Working fatigued after a 13-hour shift risks unsafe care; Code 13 and safe staffing take priority over seeing the named midwife.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Hana, 27, recently arrived in the UK, booked late at 22 weeks and has missed two appointments. She is allocated to a continuity team. Which feature of the model is most likely to improve her engagement?
o: A single extended visit with an interpreter to explain the antenatal schedule
A trusted relationship with a known midwife who can follow up missed contacts
Hospital-based clinics where all specialists can see her together
Fewer appointments so that attendance feels less demanding
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Better Births and NHS England (2022) describe continuity as giving consistent, personalised care; the known relationship builds trust, helps women who find services hard to reach and allows the midwife to follow up missed appointments (SPM 2.5, 2.8).

n.0: One explanatory visit helps understanding but does not create the ongoing relationship that improves engagement over time.
n.2: Centralised clinics may add barriers for a woman struggling to attend; continuity is about the relationship, not the building.
n.3: Reducing contacts for a woman with late booking and missed appointments increases risk; she may need more contact, not less.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A newly qualified midwife joins a trust that has paused its continuity teams because of staffing. She asks how she can still promote continuity of care. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Ask women to request her by name for every future appointment
Coordinate handovers and clear plans so care is consistent across different staff
Restart an informal continuity team with two colleagues on call
Focus on continuity of carer for postnatal visits and stop antenatal handovers
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.4 requires midwives to work across settings and with other staff to promote continuity of care and carer. When a continuity team is not possible, consistent plans, communication and handover maintain continuity of care.

n.0: Asking women to book with one named midwife cannot be guaranteed in a paused model and does not address continuity across settings.
n.2: Setting up an unofficial on-call team bypasses the trust's safe staffing decision and governance.
n.3: Stopping antenatal handovers would worsen continuity of care; good handover is the core of continuity when the same carer is not possible.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Mei, 29, is well and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. She asks about a birth centre in her town that is on a different site from the hospital and has no obstetricians or anaesthetists. Which setting is she describing?
o: An alongside midwifery unit
An obstetric unit
A freestanding midwifery unit
A midwife-led triage unit
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NICE NG235 1.2.1 and 1.3.3 name four birth settings: home, freestanding midwifery unit (on a separate site from an obstetric unit), alongside midwifery unit (same site) and obstetric unit. A unit away from the hospital without obstetric or anaesthetic staff is freestanding (SPM 2.1).

n.0: An alongside midwifery unit is on the same site as an obstetric unit, so transfer does not need an ambulance.
n.1: An obstetric unit has obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal staff on site, which this birth centre lacks.
n.3: Triage assesses women who call or attend with concerns; it is not a place planned for giving birth.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A student midwife is preparing a presentation on the NHS England three year delivery plan for maternity and neonatal services (2023). Which is one of the plan's four themes?
o: Achieving national continuity of carer targets
Growing, retaining and supporting the workforce
Reducing caesarean birth to a set national rate
Centralising births into larger obstetric units
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The three year delivery plan (30 Mar 2023) has four themes: listening to and working with women and families with compassion; growing, retaining and supporting the workforce; developing and sustaining a culture of safety, learning and support; and standards and structures that underpin safer, more personalised and more equitable care (3YP).

n.0: National continuity targets were removed in September 2022; the plan does not set them.
n.2: The plan does not set a caesarean rate target; national reviews warned against using such rates as performance measures.
n.3: Centralisation is not a theme; the plan focuses on listening, workforce, safety culture and standards.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Leila, 33, had her second baby last month. She tells her midwife she would like to help improve how local maternity services are designed for women who do not speak English. Where should the midwife signpost her?
o: The national Maternity and Newborn Safety Investigations
The local Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnership
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The hospital Patient Advice and Liaison Service
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnerships bring together women, families and staff to review and co-produce local maternity services, and feed into the Local Maternity and Neonatal System. Listening to and working with women is the first theme of the three year delivery plan (3YP; SPM 2.1).

n.0: MNSI investigates specific safety incidents; it does not involve service users in local service design.
n.2: The NMC regulates nurses and midwives; it does not design local maternity services.
n.3: PALS helps resolve individual concerns and complaints; it is not the forum for co-producing service design.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: In England, which organisation is responsible for commissioning maternity services for its local population?
o: The UK Health Security Agency
The Care Quality Commission
The NHS trust that runs the maternity unit
The integrated care board
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Since July 2022 integrated care boards commission NHS services, including maternity, for their population; Local Maternity and Neonatal Systems bring partners together to plan and improve care within each integrated care system. SPM 2.1 requires knowledge of the health and social care system.

n.0: UKHSA leads on health protection such as immunisation and infectious disease, not commissioning maternity care.
n.1: The CQC registers, inspects and rates providers; it does not commission services.
n.2: The trust is the provider: it delivers the service that has been commissioned.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: On a busy labour ward, the coordinator notices that one midwife has been caring for two women in established labour for 40 minutes because of sickness absence. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Escalate it as a staffing red flag and seek extra staff to restore one-to-one care
Transfer one woman to the antenatal ward until a midwife becomes available
Continue the arrangement and document the staffing problem at the end of the shift
Ask a maternity support worker to stay with one woman until a midwife is free
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NICE NG235 1.4.5: maternity services should provide a model of care that supports one-to-one care in labour for all women. Being unable to give one-to-one care in established labour is a midwifery staffing red flag (NICE NG4) that must be escalated through the escalation policy (Code 16; SPM 2.3).

n.1: Moving a woman in established labour to a ward without a midwife increases risk and does not solve the staffing gap.
n.2: This accepts unsafe care and delays escalation; Code 16 requires acting without delay on a risk to safety.
n.3: A maternity support worker cannot replace the midwife; one-to-one care in established labour must be by a midwife.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A labour ward coordinator is asked by the bleep holder to take over the care of a woman in active labour because the ward is short of one midwife. The coordinator is currently overseeing eight rooms. What should the coordinator do?
o: Take the woman's care and hand oversight of the ward to the most senior midwife
Stay supernumerary and escalate the shortfall through the escalation policy
Take the woman's care and review the other rooms between contractions
Decline the request and wait for the next shift to address the shortfall
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NHS Resolution's Maternity Incentive Scheme (Year 7, safety action 5) states that the midwifery coordinator in charge of labour ward must have supernumerary status, to keep oversight of all birth activity, with an escalation plan for shortfalls. The coordinator stays supernumerary and escalates the gap (SPM 2.3: factors affecting safe provision, including staffing).

n.0: Taking a caseload removes the coordinator's supernumerary oversight of the whole ward, which the Maternity Incentive Scheme requires for safety.
n.2: Combining a one-to-one caseload with coordination means neither role is done safely.
n.3: Declining without escalation leaves the staffing gap unresolved and the woman without a midwife.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Grace, 30, is low risk in her second pregnancy and is choosing between a freestanding midwifery unit and the obstetric unit. Which disadvantage of the freestanding unit should the midwife include in the discussion?
o: Epidural analgesia is available but is given by a visiting anaesthetist
Outcomes for the baby are worse than in an obstetric unit for multiparous women
Rates of intervention are higher than in an obstetric unit for multiparous women
Transfer by ambulance is needed if complications develop or she wants an epidural
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NICE NG235 1.3.3 and 1.3.7 ask midwives to explain the benefits and risks of each setting. A freestanding unit is on a separate site, so complications or a request for epidural (available in obstetric units only, NG235 1.6.26) mean ambulance transfer (SPM 2.2: positive and negative impacts of ways of organising care).

n.0: Epidurals are provided in obstetric units; a freestanding unit has no anaesthetist (NG235 1.6.26).
n.1: NG235 1.3.3 states there is no difference in outcomes for the baby for low-risk multiparous women.
n.2: For low-risk multiparous women midwife-led units are associated with fewer interventions, not more (NG235 1.3.3).

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A community midwifery manager notices that women living on one housing estate frequently miss hospital antenatal appointments, which involve two bus journeys. Which change is most likely to improve attendance?
o: Hold antenatal clinics in a local family hub on the estate
Offer every appointment as a video call instead of face to face
Send a reminder letter to each woman before every appointment
Discharge women from the clinic list after two missed appointments
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.1 and 2.2 require understanding how settings and the organisation of care affect women. Moving care closer to where women live reduces access barriers while keeping face-to-face assessment (NG201 schedule).

n.1: Video calls cannot provide BP, urine testing or fundal height measurement and may exclude women without devices or data.
n.2: Reminders do not remove the travel barrier that is causing the missed appointments.
n.3: Discharging women who miss appointments increases risk; missed contacts are a warning sign that needs follow-up.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Joy, 32, is pregnant with her third baby. Both previous births were straightforward and she has no risk factors. She asks whether planning a home birth is safe for her baby. What should the midwife tell her?
o: Fewer interventions but a small increase in adverse outcomes for the baby
A higher risk for the baby because this will be her third birth
Similar interventions and no difference in outcome for the baby
Fewer interventions and no difference in outcome for the baby
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk multiparous women, planning birth at home or in a midwife-led unit (freestanding or alongside) is associated with a lower rate of interventions, and the outcome for the baby is no different from an obstetric unit.

n.0: This applies to low-risk nulliparous women; for multiparous women there is no difference for the baby (NG235 1.3.3).
n.1: Having had two previous straightforward births is not a risk factor; NG235 finds no difference for the baby for low-risk multiparous women.
n.2: Planned home birth is associated with a lower rate of interventions for low-risk multiparous women.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Ellie, 26, is having her first baby and has no risk factors. She is considering a home birth. Which information about her baby's safety is accurate according to NICE?
o: Planned home birth carries a lower risk than a midwife-led unit
Planned home birth carries a small increase in adverse outcomes for the baby
Planned home birth carries a large increase in risk and is advised against
Planned home birth carries no difference in outcome for the baby
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk nulliparous women, planning birth at home is associated with a small increase in the risk of an adverse outcome for the baby; the same recommendation says she may choose any setting and must be supported in her choice.

n.0: For nulliparous women the evidence shows a small increase at home, not a lower risk.
n.2: NG235 describes a small increase and supports her choice; it does not advise against home birth.
n.3: No difference applies to midwife-led units for nulliparous women and to home birth for multiparous women, not home birth for a first baby.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Ama, 23, is low risk in her first pregnancy. She asks how an alongside midwifery unit compares with the obstetric unit on the same hospital site. Which statement is accurate?
o: The midwifery unit has fewer interventions with no difference in outcome for the baby
The midwifery unit has the same interventions and outcomes as the obstetric unit
The midwifery unit has more interventions with no difference in outcome for the baby
The midwifery unit has fewer interventions and a small increase in risk for the baby
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.3.3: for low-risk nulliparous women, planning birth in a midwife-led unit (freestanding or alongside) is associated with a lower rate of interventions and the outcome for the baby is no different from an obstetric unit.

n.1: Outcomes for the baby are similar, but interventions are lower in midwife-led units.
n.2: Midwife-led units are associated with a lower, not higher, rate of interventions (NG235 1.3.3).
n.3: The small increase in risk for the baby applies to planned home birth for nulliparous women, not midwife-led units.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Which settings should be offered as options for planned place of birth to a low-risk woman in England, according to NICE NG235?
o: Home or obstetric unit with a midwife present
Home, freestanding or alongside midwifery unit, or obstetric unit
Freestanding or alongside midwifery unit for low-risk women
Alongside midwifery unit or obstetric unit, both on the hospital site
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.3.3: women should be told they may choose any birth setting (home, freestanding midwifery unit, alongside midwifery unit or obstetric unit) and be supported in that choice; NG235 1.2.1 asks that all 4 settings are available (SPM 2.1).

n.0: This omits both kinds of midwifery unit, which NG235 recommends as options.
n.2: Low-risk women may also choose home or an obstetric unit; NG235 does not limit them to midwifery units.
n.3: Restricting options to the hospital site omits home and freestanding units, which NG235 says women may choose.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Lucy, 35, is pregnant with her second baby. Her first birth was complicated by a postpartum haemorrhage of 1,400 mL requiring transfusion. She asks to give birth in the alongside midwifery unit. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree to the alongside unit because it is on the same site as the obstetric unit
Explain her bleeding risk and advise planned birth in the obstetric unit
Agree to the alongside unit with active management of the third stage
Tell her a midwifery unit cannot be offered and book a planned caesarean
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.10.29 lists previous PPH over 1,000 mL or blood transfusion as an antenatal risk factor for which women should be advised to give birth in an obstetric unit. The midwife explains the risk, records the discussion and respects her informed decision (SPM 2.2).

n.0: Being on the same site does not provide the obstetric care advised after a previous PPH over 1,000 mL.
n.2: Active management reduces PPH risk but does not replace the advice for obstetric unit care with this history.
n.3: Previous PPH is not an indication for caesarean, and she keeps the right to make an informed choice.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Fatima, 34, has a BMI of 37 at booking and is otherwise well. At 36 weeks she says she still wants a home birth after a full discussion of the risks with her midwife and an obstetrician. What should the midwife do next?
o: Transfer her care to the GP until she agrees to give birth in the obstetric unit
Support her choice and agree a documented individual plan with senior input
Refuse to attend a home birth because the plan is outside guidance
Tell her she must give birth in the obstetric unit because of her BMI
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 advises obstetric unit birth when BMI is over 35 (1.10.29), but women may decline. SPM 1.21-1.22 require respecting her right to decline and advocating for her when her choice is outside guidance, with an individualised plan involving senior midwives (for example a consultant midwife).

n.0: Transferring care to pressure her abandons her and does not reduce risk.
n.2: A competent woman may choose her place of birth; the midwife has a duty to support and attend, and to plan for safety.
n.3: Midwives can advise but cannot compel; this disregards her autonomy and informed choice.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Sophie, 28, wants a water birth in the alongside midwifery unit but is also keen to have the option of an epidural. What information should the midwife give her?
o: An epidural would mean transfer to the obstetric unit on the same site
An epidural can be sited in the midwifery unit by the on-call anaesthetist
An epidural can be given if she leaves the pool for 2 hours first
An epidural is not available to women who planned a midwife-led birth
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.6.26: regional analgesia is available only in obstetric units. When planning place of birth women should be told which analgesia is available in each setting, and that an epidural in a midwife-led setting requires transfer.

n.1: Epidurals are available in obstetric units only (NG235 1.6.26).
n.2: The 2-hour rule applies to opioids before entering water, not to epidurals in a midwifery unit (NG235 1.6.20).
n.3: She can change her mind and request an epidural; it means transfer to the obstetric unit.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: At a planned home birth, Nadia, 30, is 6 cm dilated. Her pulse is 124 bpm and, 20 minutes later, 126 bpm. Her temperature and blood pressure are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange transfer to an obstetric unit
Offer oral fluids and continue at home
Recheck her pulse in one hour
Transfer if her temperature rises
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.8.20 lists maternal pulse over 120 bpm on 2 occasions 15 to 30 minutes apart as an indication to transfer to obstetric-led care. Here the readings 20 minutes apart are both over 120, so the midwife should arrange transfer.

n.1: Hydration may help, but it does not change the need to transfer once the pulse criterion is met.
n.2: Two readings over 120 bpm taken 15 to 30 minutes apart already meet the transfer criterion (NG235 1.8.20).
n.3: Tachycardia is itself a transfer trigger; waiting for fever delays care for possible sepsis or bleeding.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Hope, 19, attends the maternity unit for the first time at 24 weeks of pregnancy. She has not seen a midwife before and seems anxious when asked why. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a child protection referral because late booking indicates neglect
Arrange a routine booking appointment with her community midwife in 4 weeks
Offer the combined screening test for Down's syndrome at this appointment
Complete her booking today and sensitively explore why she has booked late
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Late booking is a recognised warning sign (for example of domestic abuse, concealed pregnancy or social difficulty). NG201 1.1.4-1.1.5 aims for booking by 10+0 weeks; a late booker should be booked promptly, with a sensitive exploration of reasons and safeguarding questions asked when she is alone (NG201 1.2.5; SPM 2.8).

n.0: Late booking is a warning sign to explore, not proof of harm; a referral is made if the assessment identifies risk.
n.1: She has already missed most of the antenatal schedule; delaying booking another month adds risk.
n.2: The combined test is offered up to 14+1 weeks, so it is no longer available at 24 weeks (FASP).

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Mariam, 28, speaks limited English and attends her booking appointment with her husband, who offers to interpret. What should the midwife do?
o: Use a translation app on the midwife's phone throughout
Accept the husband as interpreter because Mariam agrees
Arrange a professional interpreter for the appointment
Give written English leaflets and rebook with her husband
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG201 advises using independent interpreters rather than family members or friends, so the woman can share information confidentially, including about domestic abuse, and make informed choices (NG201 schedule; SPM 2.8).

n.0: Informal apps are not reliable for clinical information or consent and are not a substitute for an interpreter.
n.1: Family members should not interpret; they may filter information and Mariam cannot be asked about abuse privately.
n.3: Leaflets she cannot read do not support informed choice, and rebooking delays care.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Comfort, 30, is undocumented and 20 weeks pregnant. She tells the midwife she has been avoiding antenatal care because she is afraid of being charged. What is the most accurate information to give her?
o: She will need to pay a deposit before her next antenatal appointment
She should register with a private clinic for the rest of her antenatal care
Antenatal care is deferred until her immigration status is confirmed
Maternity care is immediately necessary and will not be withheld or delayed
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Under the NHS (Charges to Overseas Visitors) Regulations 2015 guidance, maternity services are always treated as immediately necessary and must never be withheld or delayed because of charges. Midwives should help women who fear charging to access care (SPM 2.8).

n.0: Maternity care must not be withheld or delayed pending payment, even when charges apply.
n.1: Sending her to private care adds a barrier and is not needed; NHS maternity care must be provided.
n.2: Care cannot be deferred for immigration checks; maternity services are always immediately necessary.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Kayla, 17, is pregnant with her first baby and lives with her mother. She wants to continue the pregnancy and says she does not know anything about caring for a baby. Which additional service should the midwife offer to refer her to?
o: The Family Nurse Partnership programme
The specialist perinatal mental health team
The adult safeguarding team
The pregnancy options counselling service
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The Family Nurse Partnership is an evidence-based home visiting programme for young first-time parents (usually 19 or under), running from pregnancy until the child is 2. It supports young parents who may find services hard to engage with (SPM 2.8, 2.9).

n.1: There is no indication of mental illness; this team is for moderate to severe perinatal mental health problems.
n.2: Kayla is under 18 and has no identified safeguarding concern; adult safeguarding does not apply.
n.3: She has decided to continue the pregnancy, so options counselling does not meet her needs.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A public health midwife is redesigning antenatal smoking cessation support across a city with large differences in deprivation between areas. Which approach best reflects proportionate universalism?
o: Offer support to women who ask for it at booking
Offer the same level of support to every woman across the city
Offer support to women in the most deprived areas and stop it elsewhere
Offer support to all women, with intensity rising with disadvantage
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Proportionate universalism (Marmot review, Fair Society, Healthy Lives, 2010) means actions are universal but with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. SPM 2.9 asks midwives to consider the impact of social determinants of health.

n.0: Waiting for requests widens inequalities; women facing most disadvantage are least likely to ask.
n.1: Equal provision does not narrow inequalities because need is greater in deprived groups.
n.2: Targeting deprived areas alone misses disadvantaged women elsewhere and is not universal.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Zainab, 25, is 38 weeks pregnant and lives with her toddler in one room of temporary accommodation. She has no cot and plans to share her bed with the new baby. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to contact the housing department herself after the baby is born
Advise her to keep the baby in a pram until she is rehoused
With her consent, liaise with the housing officer and health visitor
Make a child protection referral because the accommodation is unsuitable
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.9 requires midwives to work with other professionals and agencies when social determinants affect health. With consent, liaising with housing and the health visitor (who also supports safe sleep, NG194 1.3.14-1.3.15) addresses her needs.

n.0: Leaving it until after the birth delays help; SPM 2.9 expects the midwife to work with other agencies.
n.1: A pram is not a long-term safe sleeping space and this does not address the housing need.
n.3: Poverty and poor housing alone are not abuse; the priority is multiagency support, with a referral if risk of harm is identified.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Beatriz, 34, works night shifts on a zero-hours contract and has missed three daytime antenatal appointments. She says she cannot afford to lose shifts. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Remind her that missed appointments put her baby at risk
Arrange appointments at times that fit around her shifts
Reduce her schedule to the appointments she can attend
Ask her to attend the triage unit for checks when she is off shift
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.7 requires understanding the social context in which women live; SPM 2.8 requires adapting care provision to meet the needs of women who find services hard to access. Flexible appointment times keep her in routine care.

n.0: Warning her without adapting care ignores the barrier and may damage the relationship.
n.2: Cutting appointments rather than adapting their timing removes routine checks such as BP and urine testing.
n.3: Triage is for urgent concerns; using it for routine antenatal checks gives fragmented care without planned screening or continuity.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Leanne, 26, has a mild learning disability and is pregnant with her first baby. She becomes distressed during a rushed booking appointment. Which adjustment is most appropriate?
o: Give her the standard leaflets to read at home
Ask her mother to make decisions about her care
Refer her to an obstetrician for consultant-led care
Offer longer appointments and Easy Read information
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments for disabled people. NG201 and NG194 recommend information in accessible formats such as Easy Read, and SPM 2.8 asks midwives to adapt care provision for women who find services hard to access.

n.0: Standard leaflets may not be accessible to her, which is the problem the adjustment should solve.
n.1: A learning disability does not remove capacity; decisions remain Leanne's unless she lacks capacity for that decision.
n.2: A mild learning disability is not a medical indication for obstetric-led care.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Baby Noah was born at 39 weeks and is well. Ten minutes after birth, during skin-to-skin contact with his mother, a student midwife suggests weighing and measuring him so the paperwork can be completed. What should the midwife advise?
o: Weigh him now and return him quickly to skin-to-skin contact
Weigh him after his first bath so that he is clean, dry and warm
Weigh him when he and his mother are transferred to the postnatal ward
Keep him in skin-to-skin contact and weigh him after the first hour
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG235 1.11.7-1.11.10: encourage skin-to-skin contact as soon as possible after birth and avoid separating the woman and her baby within the first hour for routine procedures (weighing, measuring, bathing); measure weight and head circumference soon after the first hour (1.11.14).

n.0: NG235 1.11.10 advises avoiding separation in the first hour for routine procedures such as weighing.
n.1: Bathing is also a routine procedure to avoid in the first hour and adds heat loss.
n.2: Weight and head circumference should be measured soon after the first hour, not left to an arbitrary transfer time (NG235 1.11.14).

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Baby Ivy, born at 38 weeks, needs intravenous antibiotics for 36 hours because of maternal risk factors for infection. She is feeding well and her observations are normal. Where should she ideally receive this care?
o: In the neonatal unit until the course of antibiotics is complete
In transitional care, staying with her mother on the postnatal ward
In the neonatal unit, with her mother visiting for each feed
On the postnatal ward, with her mother discharged home first
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.6 requires the needs of the woman and newborn to be considered together. National work on avoiding term admissions into neonatal units supports transitional care so that well babies needing treatment such as antibiotics stay with their mothers.

n.0: Admitting a well term baby to the neonatal unit separates her from her mother without clinical need.
n.2: Visiting for feeds still separates them and disrupts responsive feeding and bonding.
n.3: Discharging the mother separates them; the aim is to keep them together while the baby is treated.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Precious, 29, had an emergency caesarean birth. Her baby, born at 32 weeks, is in the neonatal unit. Precious wants to breastfeed. Which action best supports her and her baby together?
o: Arrange donor milk so that she does not need to express after surgery
Help her hand express colostrum as soon as possible after the birth
Advise her to start expressing once she can walk to the neonatal unit
Advise her to rest and plan breastfeeding when the baby is discharged
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly neonatal standards support mothers of babies in neonatal units to start expressing early after the birth and to express frequently, so the baby receives her own milk and her supply is established. Expressing can begin at the bedside after a caesarean. SPM 2.6 asks midwives to plan for mother and baby together even when they are cared for apart.

n.0: Donor milk may bridge a gap but does not replace support for her own milk, which she wants to give.
n.2: Delaying expression until she is mobile reduces milk supply; expressing can start at the bedside.
n.3: Early expression protects her supply and gives the preterm baby colostrum now.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Olu, 31, is admitted to the intensive care unit after a major postpartum haemorrhage. Her baby is well and is being cared for by her partner on the postnatal ward. What is the most appropriate plan for the baby's care?
o: Start formula feeds because Olu is too unwell to breastfeed
Keep the baby on the postnatal ward until Olu is well enough to return
Discharge the baby home with the partner until Olu is transferred back
Plan regular contact between Olu and her baby and support her feeding wishes
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.6: ensure the needs of women and newborn infants are considered together as a priority in all settings, even when they have to be cared for separately. Contact, skin-to-skin when possible and support for expressing keep the dyad together.

n.0: Her feeding wishes should be explored; she may be able to express or have skin-to-skin contact when stable.
n.1: Separating them for the whole ICU stay ignores the needs of both and her feeding wishes.
n.2: Discharging the baby early increases separation and removes midwifery oversight of the baby.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Sana, 27, develops a temperature of 38.4 C and offensive lochia on day 3 after birth. She is being treated for suspected puerperal sepsis. Her baby is rooming in with her. What should the midwife also do?
o: Advise Sana to stop breastfeeding until her antibiotics finish
Move the baby to the nursery to prevent cross-infection
Assess the baby for signs of infection
Arrange for the baby to start prophylactic antibiotics
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.2.8: if a woman has confirmed or suspected puerperal sepsis, assess the baby for symptoms or signs of infection. This reflects SPM 2.6, planning for woman and newborn together.

n.0: Puerperal sepsis is not a reason to stop breastfeeding; compatible antibiotics can be chosen.
n.1: Separation is not recommended; the baby should be assessed and kept with the mother where possible.
n.3: Antibiotics for the baby depend on assessment; they are not given automatically.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Jade, 30, is on a stable dose of methadone and has given birth to a term baby. Her urine screen shows no other drugs. Her baby is at risk of neonatal abstinence syndrome. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Advise formula feeding because methadone passes into breast milk
Keep the baby in the ward nursery overnight so that Jade can rest
Admit the baby to the neonatal unit for observation for the first 72 hours
Keep the baby with Jade, observe for withdrawal, support breastfeeding
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: UK drug misuse clinical guidelines encourage breastfeeding for women on stable opioid substitution therapy. Keeping mother and baby together, with observation for withdrawal, meets SPM 2.6 (needs of both considered together).

n.0: Breastfeeding is encouraged for women on stable methadone; small amounts in milk may ease withdrawal.
n.1: Night-time separation interrupts responsive feeding and attachment and does not reduce withdrawal.
n.2: Routine admission of a well baby separates them; observation can take place with the mother.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Abi, 24, is 10 days postnatal and has developed symptoms of postpartum psychosis. The perinatal mental health team advises inpatient admission. Which setting best meets the needs of Abi and her baby?
o: An acute adult psychiatric ward, with the baby cared for by family
A medical ward until the psychosis settles, then a psychiatric unit
A specialist mother and baby unit
The postnatal ward with one-to-one mental health nursing
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: CG192: women who need inpatient care for a mental health problem within 12 months of childbirth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit, unless there are specific reasons not to. This keeps mother and baby together (SPM 2.6).

n.0: This separates mother and baby; NICE advises admission to a mother and baby unit unless there are specific reasons not to.
n.1: A medical ward is not appropriate for a psychiatric emergency and separates her from her baby.
n.3: A postnatal ward lacks the specialist psychiatric care she needs for psychosis.
