Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Kiera, 32, is medically fit for discharge on day 2. Her baby needs phototherapy on the postnatal ward for at least another 24 hours. Kiera is breastfeeding. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Discharge Kiera and give the baby formula top-ups overnight
Discharge Kiera and ask her to visit for feeds
Transfer the baby to the neonatal unit so that Kiera can go home
Offer Kiera the option to stay with her baby while treatment continues
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: SPM 2.6 requires planning care for woman and newborn as a unit. Keeping the mother with her baby supports breastfeeding during phototherapy, with breaks for feeds of up to 30 minutes (CG98).

n.0: Breastfed babies having phototherapy should not have extra fluids routinely; expressed breast milk is used if needed (CG98).
n.1: Visiting for feeds separates them and makes responsive breastfeeding difficult.
n.2: Moving a well baby to the neonatal unit for convenience separates them and uses a cot without clinical need.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Tamsin, 28, is transferred home from the birth centre at 18:00 on Monday after an uncomplicated birth. By what time should the first postnatal visit by a midwife take place?
o: By 18:00 on Thursday
By 06:00 on Thursday
By 06:00 on Wednesday
By 18:00 on Wednesday
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.1.14: the first postnatal visit by a midwife takes place within 36 hours after transfer of care from the place of birth or after a home birth, face to face and usually at home. 18:00 Monday plus 36 hours = 06:00 Wednesday.

n.0: This is 72 hours after transfer, which is well beyond the 36-hour standard.
n.1: This is 60 hours after transfer, which is later than the 36-hour standard.
n.3: This is 48 hours after transfer, which is later than the 36-hour standard.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Before a woman is transferred from the maternity unit to community care, which assessment of her own health does NICE specifically recommend?
o: Checking that her lochia has changed from red to brown
Measuring her haemoglobin before she leaves the unit
Measuring the volume of her first void after the birth
Checking that she has opened her bowels after the birth
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer to community care, or before the midwife leaves after a home birth, assess the woman's health and her bladder function by measuring the volume of the first void, assess the baby, and make a feeding plan including observing at least 1 effective feed.

n.0: Lochia remains red for several days; this is not a transfer criterion.
n.1: A routine haemoglobin is not required before transfer for every woman; it is taken if there are signs or risk of anaemia.
n.3: Bowel function is discussed at postnatal contacts, but NICE specifies the first void volume before transfer.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A community midwife is preparing to complete midwifery care for Laila, 29, and her baby on day 14. Which action best ensures a seamless transfer of care?
o: Leave a copy of the notes in Laila's home for the health visitor
Communicate the transfer to the health visitor and inform Laila
Tell Laila that her GP will contact the health visitor at 6 weeks
Ask Laila to phone the health visitor to arrange a visit
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.1.9: midwifery services should ensure the transfer of care from midwife to health visitor is clearly communicated between professionals and that the woman or parents are informed about it (SPM 2.11: coordinator of care arranging seamless transfer).

n.0: Notes left at home are not a professional handover and may not be read.
n.2: This leaves weeks without a known professional and is not how transfer of care is arranged.
n.3: Relying on the woman to arrange the handover risks a gap; NICE expects professionals to communicate the transfer.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: When should the first postnatal health visitor home visit be considered, according to NICE?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from the place of birth
Within 72 hours with the newborn physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery
At 6 to 8 weeks with the GP postnatal check
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care, so contacts are evenly spread.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit, not the health visitor.
n.1: 72 hours is the deadline for the newborn physical examination, not the health visitor visit.
n.3: 6 to 8 weeks is the GP check for the woman and baby, not the first health visitor visit.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Aisha, 30, has type 1 diabetes and books at 8 weeks. She asks who will be in charge of her care now that she will see several specialists. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Keep her under midwife-led care and refer to diabetes services at 28 weeks
Ask her GP to coordinate her care because diabetes is a medical condition
Refer her to the joint diabetes antenatal clinic and remain her midwife
Transfer her care to the diabetes team and discharge her from midwifery care
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG3 recommends joint diabetes and antenatal clinics for women with pre-existing diabetes. SPM 2.11 and 2.4 describe the midwife as coordinator of care within interdisciplinary teams, including for women with complications.

n.0: Type 1 diabetes needs specialist joint care from booking (NG3); waiting until 28 weeks is unsafe.
n.1: The GP is not the lead for her antenatal care; the maternity team coordinates with the specialists.
n.3: Women with complications still need midwifery care; the midwife remains part of her care and coordinates it.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: At a home birth, the midwife arranges transfer to the obstetric unit because of thick meconium-stained liquor. When the ambulance arrives at the unit, which handover approach is most appropriate?
o: A structured verbal handover such as SBAR, supported by the written record
A brief verbal summary to the receptionist so the woman can be booked in
The written labour record handed to the labour ward coordinator
A verbal handover to the obstetrician once the woman has been examined
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Structured communication tools such as SBAR (situation, background, assessment, recommendation) improve the safety of handovers. SPM 2.4 and 2.11 require working across settings and seamless transfer of care; Code 8 asks registrants to share information to keep people safe.

n.1: Handover must be to the clinician taking over care, not to administrative staff.
n.2: Notes alone can miss urgent information; a structured verbal handover is needed as well.
n.3: Handover should happen on arrival so the receiving team knows why she has transferred before acting.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Becky, 22, has a child protection plan for her unborn baby. She is ready for discharge from the postnatal ward on a Saturday evening. What should the midwife do before Becky and her baby leave?
o: Confirm the plan agreed with children's social care is in place
Keep the baby on the ward until the social worker visits on Monday
Discharge them and ask the health visitor to visit within 7 days
Discharge them and email the social worker on Monday morning
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Multiagency working (Working Together to Safeguard Children) requires discharge of a baby subject to a child protection plan to follow the plan agreed with children's social care, using out-of-hours services if needed (SPM 2.4, 2.11).

n.1: There is no legal basis to keep the baby without a plan or order; this action is not the midwife's to take alone.
n.2: The health visitor visit is part of routine care; it does not replace the agreed safeguarding discharge plan.
n.3: Discharging without confirming the agreed plan may leave the baby at risk over the weekend.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: On day 15 the community midwife completes postnatal care for Erin, 33, and her baby. Which information about ongoing care is most accurate to give Erin?
o: Her midwife will return at 6 weeks for a final postnatal check
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 6 to 8 weeks
Her GP will offer a postnatal check for her at 2 weeks
Her health visitor will complete her own postnatal check at 6 to 8 weeks
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.2.7: the woman should have a GP review of her health 6 to 8 weeks after birth. On completing midwifery care the midwife transfers care to the health visitor and GP (SPM 2.11).

n.0: Midwifery care has ended at transfer; the midwife does not routinely return at 6 weeks.
n.2: 2 weeks is not the routine maternal check; the GP check is at 6 to 8 weeks (NG194 1.2.7).
n.3: The maternal 6 to 8 week check is by the GP; health visitors follow the Healthy Child Programme.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Chloe, 26, is breastfeeding her 5-week-old baby in a café when a staff member asks her to feed in the toilets. She asks her midwife what her rights are. What should the midwife tell her?
o: Cafés may ask breastfeeding women to move to a private area
Businesses may refuse breastfeeding if they display a written policy
Her right to breastfeed in public applies until the baby is 6 months old
The Equality Act 2010 protects her right to breastfeed in any public space
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.5.5: inform women and partners that under the Equality Act 2010 women have the right to breastfeed in any public space. SPM 2.10 includes protection for women to breastfeed in all settings.

n.0: Asking her to move because she is breastfeeding is unlawful discrimination under the Equality Act 2010.
n.1: A written policy does not make discrimination lawful.
n.2: The protection for breastfeeding in public spaces is not limited to babies under 6 months.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A representative from a formula company offers the postnatal ward free sample packs of first infant formula to give to new mothers. What should the ward manager do?
o: Accept the samples and store them for use if a baby needs supplements
Accept the samples and give them to mothers who choose formula
Accept the samples if the packs carry no brand logos
Decline the samples because this breaches the WHO Code
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes (WHO, 1981) prohibits free samples to mothers and promotion of breastmilk substitutes in health facilities. UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Stage 1 requires no promotion of breastmilk substitutes, bottles, teats or dummies.

n.0: Supplies for clinical use must be purchased through normal channels, not accepted as promotional gifts.
n.1: Free samples to mothers are prohibited by the WHO Code whatever the feeding choice.
n.2: Removing logos does not change the prohibition on free samples to mothers.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Tara, 31, is returning to work when her baby is 7 months old and wants to continue breastfeeding. She asks what her employer must do. What is the most accurate answer?
o: Offer flexible working that suits her feeding pattern
Assess workplace risks and provide somewhere suitable to rest
Give her paid breaks to express milk during each shift
Provide a private room with a fridge for expressing her milk
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Employers must assess workplace risks for an employee who is breastfeeding (Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999 reg 16; HSE guidance) and provide suitable facilities for a nursing mother to rest (Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 reg 25). Helping women know their rights supports breastfeeding in all settings (SPM 2.10).

n.0: She can request flexible working, but the employer does not have to grant it.
n.2: UK law does not give a statutory right to paid breastfeeding breaks; this is good practice, not a legal duty.
n.3: HSE describes a private room and fridge as good practice; the legal duty is a risk assessment and suitable rest facilities.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Dawn, 29, is breastfeeding her 2-week-old baby. Her GP prescribes a new medicine and tells her she will need to stop breastfeeding while taking it. She is upset. What should the midwife do first?
o: Check the medicine with a specialist breastfeeding medicines service
Advise her to stop breastfeeding and express to maintain her supply
Advise her to take the medicine and continue breastfeeding
Advise her to continue breastfeeding and not take the medicine
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.5.6: professionals supporting breastfeeding should know appropriate resources for safe medicine use and prescribing for breastfeeding women (for example the UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service). Many medicines are compatible with breastfeeding (SPM 2.10).

n.1: Advising her to stop before checking the evidence may end breastfeeding unnecessarily.
n.2: Telling her it is safe without checking the evidence is outside the midwife's knowledge and unsafe.
n.3: Stopping a prescribed medicine without review may harm her health.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Sam is the partner of Nia, who is breastfeeding their first baby. He tells the midwife he feels left out because he cannot feed the baby. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Suggest giving one bottle of formula a day so he can share feeds
Reassure him that fathers bond with babies once feeding is finished
Suggest Nia expresses a bottle each evening from day 3 for him to give
Explain how he can support Nia and bond through skin-to-skin contact
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.5.3: give information about how the partner can support the woman to breastfeed, including the value of their involvement and how they can comfort and bond with the baby (SPM 2.12).

n.0: Introducing formula early can reduce Nia's milk supply and is not needed for bonding.
n.1: This dismisses his concerns and misses the chance to involve him now.
n.2: Routine early bottles can interfere with establishing breastfeeding and do not address his role.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Grace, 24, has decided to formula feed her baby after an informed discussion. Which action by the midwife best supports her decision?
o: Advise her to feed her baby to a fixed 3-hourly schedule
Advise her to change to a follow-on formula at 3 months old
Show her how to make up feeds safely and feed responsively
Give her a list of formula brands that are best for newborns
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NG194 1.5.17-1.5.19: first infant formula is the only formula needed in the first year unless there is a medical need; give information on safe preparation and responsive bottle feeding. Baby Friendly Stage 3 includes supporting parents to make informed decisions.

n.0: Responsive feeding to the baby's cues is recommended rather than fixed schedules.
n.1: Follow-on formula is not needed; first infant formula is suitable for the first year.
n.3: Recommending brands is promotion; any first infant formula meets a baby's needs.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Ruth, 35, was discharged home on day 2 and is breastfeeding. On day 5 she tells her community midwife she has sore nipples and is thinking of stopping. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Advise her to give formula for 24 hours to let the nipples heal
Advise her to feed for 10 minutes on each breast to rest the nipples
Observe a feed, help with attachment and refer to peer support
Recommend nipple shields for each feed until the soreness settles
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Sore nipples usually reflect poor attachment. NG194 1.5.14 lists assessing a feed and breast and nipple condition; professionals should support common problems (1.5.6) and work with other agencies such as peer support services to sustain breastfeeding (SPM 2.10).

n.0: Missed feeds reduce supply and may end breastfeeding, which she has not chosen.
n.1: Limiting feed length does not fix attachment and can reduce intake and supply.
n.3: Shields do not correct the usual cause, poor attachment, and can reduce milk transfer.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A maternity unit is preparing for UNICEF UK Baby Friendly assessment. A formula company offers to sponsor the infant feeding study day for staff. What should the infant feeding lead do?
o: Accept the sponsorship if the company has no speaking role on the day
Accept the sponsorship if the study day covers breastfeeding as well
Decline the sponsorship because it promotes breastmilk substitutes to staff
Accept the sponsorship and declare it in the study day programme
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The WHO Code and UNICEF UK Baby Friendly Stage 1 (building a firm foundation) prohibit promotion of breastmilk substitutes in health settings, including sponsorship of staff education by manufacturers (SPM 2.10).

n.0: Sponsorship itself is a form of promotion to health workers, prohibited by the WHO Code.
n.1: Covering breastfeeding does not make company sponsorship acceptable.
n.3: Declaring sponsorship does not remove the conflict of interest the Code is designed to prevent.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: Amara, 24, is booking for her first pregnancy. She has read that her local trust offers midwifery continuity of carer and asks the midwife what this means for her. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Her electronic records are shared between the GP, hospital and community teams
The same consultant obstetrician reviews her at each hospital antenatal appointment
A known midwife or small team cares for her across pregnancy, birth and the postnatal period
A community midwife provides her antenatal care and hands over to the labour ward team
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: Midwifery continuity of carer means a named midwife, working within a small team, provides care throughout pregnancy, labour, birth and the postnatal period (Better Births, National Maternity Review 2016; SPM 2.5: continuity of midwifery carer across the whole continuum of care).

n.0: Shared records give continuity of information, not continuity of carer; she could still meet a different midwife at every contact.
n.1: Continuity of carer in Better Births and SPM 2.5 is a midwifery relationship model; an obstetrician seeing her antenatally does not cover birth and the postnatal period.
n.3: This is the traditional fragmented model: the relationship ends at labour, which is what continuity of carer aims to change.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A student midwife asks why continuity of midwifery carer models were recommended nationally. Which outcome is associated with midwife-led continuity models compared with other models of care?
o: Fewer instrumental births and more episiotomies
More spontaneous vaginal births and fewer instrumental births
Fewer preterm births and a lower neonatal death rate
More spontaneous vaginal births and more caesarean births
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The 2024 Cochrane review of midwife continuity of care models (Sandall et al., 17 studies, 18,533 women) found they likely increase spontaneous vaginal birth (66% to 70%) and likely reduce caesarean section (16% to 15%) and instrumental birth (14% to 13%), with little or no difference in preterm birth. This evidence supports continuity models such as those set out in Better Births (2016).

n.0: Instrumental birth was likely reduced, but episiotomy may be reduced (23% to 19%), not increased.
n.2: The 2024 review found little or no difference in preterm birth (6% in both models), and the effect on neonatal death is very uncertain. The older 2016 review's preterm finding has been superseded.
n.3: Spontaneous vaginal birth was more likely, but caesarean section was likely reduced (16% to 15%), not increased.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A maternity service cannot meet safe minimum midwifery staffing even for its existing continuity of carer teams. According to the NHS England letter of 21 September 2022, what should the trust do?
o: Restrict booking to women from the most deprived areas and continue
Suspend continuity provision and safely transfer women to other pathways
Continue existing teams and pause any further roll out to new areas
Keep booking women into the teams to meet the national target date
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: The NHS England letter (21 Sep 2022) removed the national target date for MCoC. Trusts unable to meet safe minimum staffing for existing provision should immediately suspend it, safely transfer women to alternative pathways according to their needs and support the midwives into other areas.

n.0: Prioritising disadvantaged women applies where staffing allows; it does not override the instruction to suspend when staffing is unsafe.
n.2: This is the action for trusts that can staff existing provision but not expansion; here even existing provision cannot be staffed safely.
n.3: The 2022 letter removed the national target date, so there is no target to meet and safety must come first.

Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.q: A local maternity system is planning where to expand midwifery continuity of carer as staffing improves. Which group of women should the service prioritise?
o: Women from Black, Asian and mixed ethnic groups and the most deprived areas
Women with pre-existing medical conditions under consultant care
Women who request a home birth at the booking appointment
Low-risk nulliparous women who are planning to give birth in a midwifery unit
Continuity of Carer & Maternity Systems.w: NHS England (2022) states MCoC can improve outcomes for most women and especially women of Black, Asian and mixed ethnicity and those in the most deprived neighbourhoods, and services should focus continuity on women from vulnerable groups who will benefit most.

n.1: These women need obstetric input and may receive continuity within mixed teams, but they are not the national priority group named for MCoC.
n.2: Planned place of birth does not determine priority for continuity; the evidence of greatest benefit is for disadvantaged groups.
n.3: Low clinical risk is not the basis for prioritisation; national advice focuses on women facing the greatest inequalities.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A local audit finds that stillbirth occurred in 8 per 1,000 births to women who smoked and 4 per 1,000 births to women who did not smoke. A woman asks how much smoking raises the risk. Which figure is the relative risk?
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Relative risk = risk in exposed group / risk in unexposed group = (8/1,000) / (4/1,000) = 2. The absolute risk difference is 4 per 1,000. SPM 3.2 requires midwives to interpret data and use it in conversations with women.

n.0: 4 per 1,000 is the absolute risk difference, not the relative risk.
n.1: 0.5 is the ratio the wrong way round (non-smokers compared with smokers).
n.3: 8 per 1,000 is the absolute risk among smokers, not a ratio.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Zara, 33, has read that a treatment doubles the risk of a rare complication and is frightened. The baseline risk is 1 in 10,000. How should the midwife best present this risk?
o: Explain that her risk of the complication is doubled
Explain that the risk increases by 100% compared with no treatment
Explain that the complication is too rare to be worth discussing
Explain that the risk rises from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NICE NG197 (shared decision making) recommends presenting risks as absolute numbers using natural frequencies with a consistent denominator, rather than relative risk alone. SPM 3.2 and 3.3 ask midwives to interpret evidence and share it in a way that supports evidence-informed decisions.

n.0: Relative risk alone exaggerates the change and does not help her weigh the decision.
n.1: This is still a relative figure and is likely to be misunderstood.
n.2: Dismissing the risk does not respect her concern or support informed decision making.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: At a booking appointment, a midwife explains to Maya, 25, why care in pregnancy and birth matters for her baby's health in adulthood. Which statement is accurate?
o: Birthweight has no measurable link with the child's later health
Early life influences on health are fixed by the end of the first trimester
Low birthweight is linked to more heart disease and type 2 diabetes in adult life
High birthweight protects against type 2 diabetes in adult life
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: The developmental origins of health and disease (Barker) show that fetal growth and early life influence lifelong health, with low birthweight linked to cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. SPM 3.5 requires understanding the importance of birth to public health across the life course.

n.0: Large cohort studies show birthweight and early life conditions are linked to later health.
n.1: Influences continue through pregnancy, birth and early childhood, not just the first trimester.
n.3: High birthweight is itself associated with later obesity and diabetes risk, so it is not protective.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Ines, 28, moved to a new city for work, is 30 weeks pregnant and tells her midwife she knows nobody locally and feels lonely. Her mood screening questions are negative. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange extra antenatal appointments so she sees a midwife weekly
Advise her to move closer to family before the birth
Tell her about local antenatal groups and family hub activities
Refer her to the specialist perinatal mental health team
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SPM 3.1 requires understanding the woman's lived experience and enabling access to community resources. Social isolation is a risk to wellbeing; linking her to peer groups and family hubs supports her and her transition to parenthood.

n.0: Extra clinical contacts do not address social isolation and are not clinically indicated.
n.1: This ignores her circumstances and is not a realistic or person-centred response.
n.3: Her screening is negative and loneliness alone does not meet the threshold for specialist mental health care.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Lucy, 29, is planning her first pregnancy and has no medical conditions. She asks about folic acid. What should the midwife advise?
o: Take 400 micrograms daily before conception until 12 weeks
Take 5 mg daily before conception until 12 weeks
Take 400 micrograms daily throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding
Take 400 micrograms daily from the positive test until 20 weeks
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 1.1.3-1.1.4: take 400 micrograms folic acid daily when planning pregnancy (ideally from 3 months before) and for the first 12 weeks.

n.1: 5 mg is for women at increased risk of neural tube defects, which Lucy is not (NG247 1.1.5).
n.2: Routine folic acid is recommended until 12 weeks; vitamin D is the supplement recommended beyond that.
n.3: Folic acid should start before conception, ideally 3 months before, and continue to 12 weeks.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Priya, 31, has type 2 diabetes and is planning a pregnancy. Which folic acid regimen should be recommended?
o: 5 mg daily from before conception until 12 weeks
400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks, rising to 5 mg if her HbA1c is high
400 micrograms daily from before conception until 12 weeks
5 mg daily from confirmation of pregnancy until 12 weeks
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 1.1.5: high-dose 5 mg folic acid for women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes (and other specified risks), from before conception to 12 weeks. NG3 1.1.11 is consistent.

n.1: The 5 mg dose is indicated by type 1 or 2 diabetes itself, not by HbA1c level.
n.2: Diabetes is a high-risk factor, so the standard dose is not enough (NG247 1.1.5).
n.3: Supplementation should start before conception because the neural tube closes early in pregnancy.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Hannah, 27, has a BMI of 33 and no other medical history. She is planning a pregnancy and has read that women with a high BMI need a higher dose of folic acid. What is the current advice?
o: Take 5 mg daily, because a BMI of 30 or more needs the higher dose
Take 400 micrograms daily, as BMI alone does not need the higher dose
Take 5 mg daily, because a BMI of 30 or more raises pre-eclampsia risk
Take 400 micrograms daily, rising to 5 mg if her BMI rises above 35
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 1.1.6-1.1.7 (January 2025): women with a BMI of 25 or above, or at increased risk of pre-eclampsia, do not need more than 400 micrograms unless a 1.1.5 risk factor applies.

n.0: NG247 1.1.6 changed older teaching: BMI alone does not indicate the 5 mg dose.
n.2: Increased risk of pre-eclampsia does not, by itself, indicate 5 mg folic acid (NG247 1.1.7).
n.3: There is no BMI threshold for 5 mg in NG247; it depends on the listed risk factors.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Grace, 34, is 16 weeks pregnant in November. She asks whether she needs any vitamin supplements now. What should the midwife advise?
o: Vitamin D 25 micrograms daily
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily
Vitamin D 10 micrograms daily
Vitamin A 700 micrograms daily
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 1.1.12: all pregnant or breastfeeding women should take vitamin D 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily from October to March, and all year if at increased risk of deficiency.

n.0: The recommended dose in pregnancy is 10 micrograms (400 IU) daily.
n.1: Routine folic acid is recommended to 12 weeks; at 16 weeks it is no longer needed.
n.3: Vitamin A supplements are avoided in pregnancy because high intake can harm the baby.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Adaeze, 26, has dark skin and usually covers most of her skin when outdoors. She is 20 weeks pregnant in June. What vitamin D advice should she receive?
o: Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily if a blood test shows deficiency
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily from 28 weeks until the birth
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily from October to March
Take vitamin D 10 micrograms daily all year round
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 1.1.12: vitamin D 10 micrograms daily October to March for all pregnant or breastfeeding women, and all year for those at increased risk (for example darker skin, or skin rarely exposed to the sun).

n.0: Supplementation is recommended without testing for women at increased risk.
n.1: There is no gestation restriction; it is recommended throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding.
n.2: Women at increased risk of deficiency, such as those with darker skin or little sun exposure, should take it all year.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Kirsty, 30, has epilepsy controlled with an antiepileptic medicine. She tells her midwife at a preconception clinic that she plans to start trying for a baby. Which folic acid dose should she take?
o: 400 micrograms daily
10 mg daily
800 micrograms daily
5 mg daily
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 1.1.5: offer 5 mg folic acid to women taking medicines that affect folate, such as antiepileptic or HIV medicines. She should also be referred for specialist preconception review of her medicine.

n.0: Antiepileptic medicines affect folate, so she needs the high dose (NG247 1.1.5).
n.1: There is no recommendation for 10 mg; the high dose is 5 mg.
n.2: This is not a UK recommended dose; the choices are 400 micrograms or 5 mg.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Sky, 17, is 12 weeks pregnant. She lives with her mother, who works full time and does not receive benefits. Sky asks if she can get help with buying healthy food. What should the midwife tell her?
o: She does not qualify because her household does not receive benefits
She qualifies for Healthy Start once the baby is born
She qualifies for Healthy Start because she is pregnant and under 18
She qualifies for Healthy Start from 20 weeks of pregnancy
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: The NHS Healthy Start scheme helps with milk, fruit, vegetables and pulses and gives free vitamins. Pregnant women under 18 are eligible whatever their income; women 18 and over qualify through benefits. SPM 3.3 includes supporting access to resources and services.

n.0: Benefit criteria apply to women aged 18 and over; pregnant under 18s are eligible regardless.
n.1: Pregnant women under 18 are eligible during pregnancy, not after the birth.
n.3: Eligibility is from 10 weeks of pregnancy, so she can apply now.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Olivia, 32, is 10 weeks pregnant. Each day she drinks two mugs of filter coffee (about 140 mg caffeine each) and one can of cola (about 40 mg). What advice should the midwife give?
o: Continue, as her intake of about 320 mg is within the daily limit for pregnancy
Reduce caffeine, as her intake of about 320 mg exceeds the 200 mg daily limit
Stop the cola but continue the coffee, as cola caffeine is more harmful
Reduce caffeine, as her intake of about 180 mg is close to the daily limit
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NHS and Food Standards Agency advice: limit caffeine to 200 mg a day in pregnancy, because high intake is linked to low birthweight and miscarriage. Working: 2 x 140 mg + 40 mg = 320 mg, above the limit (SPM 3.3).

n.0: The NHS limit in pregnancy is 200 mg a day; 2 x 140 + 40 = 320 mg is above it.
n.2: Caffeine from any source counts towards the limit; two filter coffees alone give 280 mg.
n.3: This miscalculates the total: 2 x 140 + 40 = 320 mg, not 180 mg.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: At which antenatal contacts should carbon monoxide testing be offered routinely to every pregnant woman, according to Saving Babies' Lives version 3?
o: At booking and at the 28-week appointment
At booking and at the 36-week appointment
At booking, then at every appointment for all women
At the 16-week and 36-week appointments
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SBL3 element 1 and NG209 1.18.1: CO testing for all pregnant women at the first antenatal (booking) appointment and at 36 weeks, and at all other appointments for those who smoke, are quitting, used to smoke or tested 4 ppm or above at booking.

n.0: Routine testing is at booking and 36 weeks; 28 weeks is not one of the routine points.
n.2: Testing at every appointment is for women who smoke, are quitting, used to smoke or had a raised reading.
n.3: The first routine test is at booking, not 16 weeks.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Kelly, 24, is booking at 9 weeks. She says she smokes about 10 cigarettes a day and is not ready to stop. Her carbon monoxide reading is 12 ppm. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a referral to the stop-smoking service if she agrees to set a quit date today
Give her a leaflet and advise her to contact her GP to stop
Explain the reading and make an opt-out referral to stop-smoking support
Record that she declined support and offer it again at 36 weeks
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SBL3 1.4 and NG209 1.18.2: provide an opt-out referral for women who say they smoke, have stopped in the past 2 weeks or have a CO reading of 4 ppm or above, and explain that referral is normal practice and what the reading means (NG209 1.18.3).

n.0: An opt-out referral does not depend on readiness to set a quit date.
n.1: Signposting is less effective than an opt-out referral to an in-house tobacco dependence adviser.
n.3: Referral is opt-out: she is referred unless she actively declines after an explanation, not left until 36 weeks.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Ruby, 29, says she has never smoked and lives alone, but her carbon monoxide reading at booking is 14 ppm. What should the midwife do?
o: Advise her about possible carbon monoxide poisoning and the Gas Emergency Line
Record the reading as a faulty device and retest at her next visit
Make an opt-out referral to the stop-smoking service as a smoker
Record the reading and repeat the carbon monoxide test at the 36-week appointment
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG209 1.18.5: if a woman has a high CO reading (more than 10 ppm) but says she does not smoke, advise about possible carbon monoxide poisoning, ask her to contact the Gas Emergency Line for gas safety advice and phrase further questions about smoking sensitively.

n.1: Assuming a device fault delays action on a potentially dangerous exposure.
n.2: Treating her as a smoker misses a possible environmental CO source, although further questions should be sensitive.
n.3: A reading over 10 ppm in a non-smoker needs action now because of possible CO poisoning.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Tia, 26, does not smoke, but her partner smokes 20 cigarettes a day indoors. Her carbon monoxide reading is 3 ppm. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Make an opt-out referral for Tia to stop-smoking support
Offer her partner stop-smoking support and discuss a smoke-free home
Reassure Tia that a reading of 3 ppm is normal and needs no action
Advise Tia to ask her partner to smoke by an open window
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG209 1.18.4: a non-smoker with CO 3 ppm or more should be helped to identify and reduce the source, such as household secondhand smoke. NG209 1.20.18 and NG201 1.2.4: offer partners who smoke help to stop.

n.0: Tia does not smoke and her reading is below 4 ppm; the support is needed by her partner.
n.2: NG209 1.18.4 asks midwives to help a non-smoker with 3 ppm or more identify and reduce the source.
n.3: Smoking by a window still exposes Tia and later the baby to secondhand smoke.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Anya, 31, is 8 weeks pregnant. She is worried because she drank two glasses of wine at a party before she knew she was pregnant. What should the midwife tell her?
o: Limit drinking to 1 to 2 units once or twice a week for the rest of pregnancy
A scan is needed at 12 weeks to look for alcohol-related harm
Avoid alcohol from now; the risk from small amounts early is likely to be low
Drinking in the first weeks causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorder in most cases
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG201 1.3.10: there is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy and the safest approach is to avoid alcohol altogether. UK Chief Medical Officers (2016) advise the risk of harm is likely to be low if a woman drank small amounts before she knew she was pregnant.

n.0: This was older advice; there is no known safe level of alcohol in pregnancy.
n.1: A scan cannot exclude alcohol-related harm and is not indicated for this.
n.3: This overstates the risk of small amounts and causes unnecessary distress.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Jess, 27, smokes 15 cigarettes a day and wants to stop. Her tobacco dependence adviser suggests nicotine patches. She is worried nicotine will harm her baby. What information should the midwife give?
o: NRT risks are much lower than smoking, and patches should be removed at bedtime
NRT is safe in pregnancy and patches should be worn for 24 hours a day
NRT carries the same risks as smoking, so cutting down is safer
NRT should be avoided until 12 weeks, when varenicline is a safer choice
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG209 1.20.6-1.20.11: consider NRT with behavioural support at the earliest opportunity; explain that risks from NRT are much lower than smoking; advise removing patches before bed; do not offer varenicline, bupropion or cytisinicline in pregnancy.

n.1: NICE advises removing patches before going to bed in pregnancy (NG209 1.20.9).
n.2: Most smoking harm comes from other components of smoke, not nicotine; NRT is much safer.
n.3: Varenicline is not offered in pregnancy, and NRT should be considered at the earliest opportunity.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Leah, 30, is 10 weeks pregnant and uses heroin daily. She tells her midwife she plans to stop suddenly today for the baby's sake. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Support her plan and arrange weekly midwife visits to monitor her
Advise her to reduce her heroin use gradually by herself over 4 weeks
Refer her to the obstetrician and wait for that review before giving any advice
Advise against stopping suddenly and refer to the specialist drug service
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: UK drug misuse clinical guidelines advise against abrupt withdrawal from opioids in pregnancy, because of risks to the fetus and of relapse; women should be referred to specialist drug services for opioid substitution therapy with joint maternity care (SPM 3.1, 3.3).

n.0: Abrupt opioid withdrawal in pregnancy carries risks to the fetus and of relapse; it needs specialist management.
n.1: Unsupported reduction is unsafe; specialist services can offer opioid substitution therapy.
n.2: She needs advice now; delaying risks a sudden withdrawal today.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Erin, 35, is 14 weeks pregnant and drinks about a bottle of wine every evening. She has had shakes and sweating in the mornings. She wants to stop drinking straight away. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend a mutual support group before referral
Refer urgently to the specialist alcohol service for assisted withdrawal
Advise her to stop drinking tonight and contact the midwife if unwell
Advise her to cut down to 14 units a week for the rest of the pregnancy
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Morning shakes and sweating suggest alcohol dependence. Abrupt cessation risks withdrawal seizures, so she needs urgent specialist referral for medically assisted withdrawal, while continuing antenatal care. NG201 1.3.10: no safe level of alcohol in pregnancy (SPM 3.1, 3.3).

n.0: Peer support helps later, but her withdrawal symptoms show dependence needing specialist care now.
n.2: Sudden withdrawal in alcohol dependence can cause seizures and needs medical management.
n.3: There is no safe level in pregnancy, and 14 units is the general adult low-risk guideline.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Megan, 25, is 20 weeks pregnant and has just had her anomaly scan. She asks when she should have the whooping cough vaccine. What should the midwife advise?
o: Now, as it is given from 16 weeks and ideally before 32 weeks
At 28 weeks, as it is given with the RSV vaccine
After the birth, as it protects the baby through breastfeeding
At 36 weeks, as protection is highest closer to the birth
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 24: pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks, usually around the mid-pregnancy scan (about 20 weeks), ideally before 32 weeks for best passive protection of the baby.

n.1: Pertussis vaccine can be given from 16 weeks; there is no need to wait until 28 weeks.
n.2: Vaccination in pregnancy gives passive antibody protection to the baby before birth.
n.3: Vaccination ideally before 32 weeks gives better passive protection for the baby.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Nadia, 29, is 28 weeks pregnant. Which vaccine does she become eligible for at this gestation that she was not offered earlier in pregnancy?
o: MMR vaccine
RSV vaccine
Inactivated influenza vaccine
Pertussis vaccine
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 27a: the RSV vaccine (Abrysvo) is offered to all pregnant women from 28 weeks, ideally in week 28 or soon after, in every pregnancy, and can be given up to delivery.

n.0: MMR is a live vaccine and is not given in pregnancy.
n.2: Flu vaccine is offered at any stage of pregnancy in season.
n.3: Pertussis vaccine is offered from 16 weeks, so she was eligible earlier.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Bella, 32, is 9 weeks pregnant in October. She asks whether she should wait until later in pregnancy to have the flu vaccine. What should the midwife advise?
o: Wait until 28 weeks so the baby gets the most antibodies
Wait until 16 weeks, as flu vaccine is not given in the first trimester
Have the inactivated flu vaccine now, as it can be given at any stage
Have the nasal spray vaccine now, as it is the most effective type
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 19 (Aug 2026): pregnant women should be offered inactivated influenza vaccine at any stage of pregnancy (any trimester); inactivated vaccine is the preferred vaccine in pregnancy.

n.0: Waiting leaves her unprotected through the flu season; she should have it now.
n.1: The inactivated flu vaccine can be given in any trimester.
n.3: The live nasal spray is the children's programme vaccine; in pregnancy the inactivated injected vaccine is the one offered and preferred.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Jasmine, 31, had the whooping cough vaccine in her last pregnancy 18 months ago. She is now 18 weeks pregnant again. What should the midwife advise?
o: No vaccine is needed, as she is protected for 5 years
Have the vaccine again in this pregnancy
Have the vaccine if her baby is born before 32 weeks
Have a blood test to check her antibody level first
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 24: pertussis vaccine is recommended in every pregnancy, because antibodies wane and the aim is to maximise passive protection for each new baby.

n.0: Maternal antibody levels fall, so vaccination is needed every pregnancy to protect each baby.
n.2: The vaccine is offered every pregnancy, not according to the baby's gestation at birth.
n.3: No antibody test is needed; vaccination is recommended in every pregnancy.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Chantelle, 27, is 35 weeks pregnant and has not had the whooping cough vaccine. She asks if it is too late. What should the midwife advise?
o: It can still be given, though it gives the baby less passive protection
It can still be given and gives the same protection as at 20 weeks
It is too late, so the baby should be vaccinated at birth instead
It is too late, as it cannot be given after 32 weeks
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 24: the vaccine can still be given later in pregnancy, including up to birth. It may offer less passive protection to the baby but protects the mother, reducing the baby's exposure.

n.1: Vaccinating after 32 weeks may give the baby less passive protection than earlier vaccination.
n.2: Pertussis vaccination of babies starts at 8 weeks in the routine schedule, not at birth.
n.3: It can still be given after 32 weeks; it may offer less passive protection but protects the mother.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Sara, 30, tells the midwife at her 16-week appointment that her children are having the nasal spray flu vaccine at school and asks if she can have the same one. What should the midwife advise?
o: She should wait until after the birth to have any flu vaccine
She should have the nasal spray after 20 weeks
She can have the nasal spray, as it is a low-dose vaccine
She should have the injected inactivated vaccine instead
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 19 (Aug 2026): pregnant women should be offered inactivated injected flu vaccine at any stage of pregnancy, and inactivated vaccine is preferred in pregnancy. The live nasal spray is the children's programme vaccine, and her children having it does not change her own vaccine.

n.0: Pregnant women are offered inactivated flu vaccine at any stage of pregnancy.
n.1: Gestation does not change this; inactivated injected vaccine is the one offered at any stage of pregnancy.
n.2: The nasal spray is the live children's programme vaccine, not the one offered in pregnancy; inactivated vaccine is preferred.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: At booking, Hope, 24, says she never had the MMR vaccine as a child. She is 11 weeks pregnant. What should the midwife advise?
o: Have a rubella immunity blood test at booking
Have MMR after the birth and avoid pregnancy for 1 month after it
Have MMR now, as it protects the baby against rubella
Have MMR at the 6 to 8 week check and avoid pregnancy for 3 months
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Rubella screening in pregnancy stopped in April 2016 (IDPS). Women who have not had 2 doses of MMR should be offered it after the birth. MMR is a live vaccine, so it is not given in pregnancy and pregnancy should be avoided for 1 month after vaccination (Green Book).

n.0: Routine antenatal rubella susceptibility screening stopped in England in April 2016.
n.2: MMR is a live vaccine and is not given during pregnancy.
n.3: MMR is given after the birth, but pregnancy should be avoided for 1 month after vaccination, not 3 months.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Baby Kai is born at 30 weeks in November. His mother was not vaccinated against RSV in pregnancy. Which protection against RSV is he eligible for?
o: No RSV protection, as his mother missed the vaccine
RSV vaccine at 8 weeks with his routine vaccines
RSV vaccine for his mother now, to protect him through breastfeeding
A long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 27a (June 2026): very or extremely preterm infants (born under 32 weeks) are offered a long-acting RSV monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab or clesrovimab).

n.0: Very preterm infants are offered RSV protection directly.
n.1: The RSV vaccine is given to pregnant women, not to babies in the routine schedule.
n.2: Maternal vaccination protects the baby through placental antibody transfer in pregnancy, not breast milk after birth.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A midwife has completed a vaginal examination wearing sterile gloves. She removes her gloves before recording the findings. What should she do next?
o: Record the findings and then decontaminate her hands
Put on a new pair of gloves to write the notes
Wipe her hands with the paper towel from the trolley
Decontaminate her hands
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: The WHO 5 moments for hand hygiene include after body fluid exposure risk, which includes after removing gloves. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene (SPM 3.10: principles of infection prevention and control).

n.0: Hand hygiene is needed immediately after glove removal and body fluid exposure risk, before touching notes.
n.1: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene and are not needed for writing.
n.2: Wiping with a paper towel does not decontaminate hands.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Hannah, 26, is on the postnatal ward with profuse diarrhoea. Clostridioides difficile infection is suspected. Which hand hygiene method should staff use after caring for her?
o: Antiseptic hand wipes
Gloves without hand hygiene
Alcohol-based hand rub
Soap and water
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Alcohol hand rub is ineffective against spore-forming organisms such as C. difficile and against norovirus; hands should be washed with soap and water (national infection prevention and control manual; SPM 3.10).

n.0: Wipes do not remove spores as effectively as washing with soap and water.
n.1: Gloves do not replace hand hygiene after removal.
n.2: Alcohol rub does not kill C. difficile spores; washing with soap and water removes them.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: At booking, which infections are offered screening in every pregnancy by the NHS Infectious Diseases in Pregnancy Screening Programme?
o: HIV, hepatitis C and syphilis
HIV, hepatitis B and group B streptococcus
HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis and rubella
HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: IDPS screens for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis in every pregnancy, offered as early as possible. Rubella susceptibility screening stopped on 1 April 2016 (IDPS).

n.0: Hepatitis C is not part of the IDPS programme; hepatitis B is.
n.1: Group B streptococcus is not one of the infections in the IDPS programme, which covers HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis.
n.2: Rubella susceptibility screening stopped in England on 1 April 2016.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Remi, 28, had negative booking screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis. At 30 weeks she tells her midwife she has a new sexual partner. What should the midwife offer?
o: Reassurance, as her booking screening was negative
Repeat screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis
A swab for group B streptococcus at 36 weeks
Repeat screening at the 6 to 8 week postnatal check
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: IDPS: offer repeat testing if there is a new partner, injecting drug use, sex work, an infected partner, a partner sexually active with others, or an STI diagnosed in pregnancy.

n.0: A negative booking result does not cover new exposure later in pregnancy.
n.2: GBS carriage is not linked to a new sexual partner and is not part of the IDPS repeat-testing offer; a new partner is a trigger to repeat HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis screening.
n.3: Waiting until after the birth misses the chance to prevent transmission to the baby.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Lin, 33, is hepatitis B positive. Her baby has just been born at term and is well. When should the baby receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine?
o: Within 7 days of birth
Within 24 hours of birth
After the newborn blood spot test on day 5
At 8 weeks with the routine vaccines
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Green Book ch 18: babies born to hepatitis B positive mothers should receive the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth, within 24 hours (with hepatitis B immunoglobulin if indicated), then further doses.

n.0: The first dose should be given as soon as possible and within 24 hours.
n.2: Waiting until day 5 delays protection and is not linked to blood spot screening.
n.3: Babies of hepatitis B positive mothers need a dose at birth; 8 weeks is too late to prevent transmission.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Amira, 30, has received intravenous antibiotics for 48 hours for suspected endometritis. She is now apyrexial and well, and her blood cultures are negative. Which action best reflects antimicrobial stewardship?
o: Stop the antibiotics herself, as the cultures are negative
Add a second antibiotic to prevent resistance developing
Ask the prescriber to review whether to stop or switch to oral
Continue intravenous antibiotics for a full 7-day course
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: UKHSA Start Smart then Focus: review antibiotics at 48 to 72 hours with a clear decision to stop, switch IV to oral, change, continue or move to outpatient therapy. SPM 3.10 covers antimicrobial resistance and stewardship.

n.0: Stopping is a prescribing decision; the midwife should prompt a review, not stop treatment unilaterally.
n.1: Adding antibiotics without indication increases, rather than prevents, resistance.
n.3: Continuing IV therapy without review ignores her response and culture results.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Becca, 31, is 39 weeks pregnant. A vaginal swab at 35 weeks found group B streptococcus. She phones to say her waters broke an hour ago and she has no contractions. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Offer expectant management for up to 24 hours at home
Offer immediate induction of labour with intrapartum antibiotics
Offer expectant management with 4-hourly temperature checks
Offer a speculum examination and review again in 12 hours
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG235 1.7.11 and NG207 1.2.16: offer immediate induction of labour (or caesarean if planned) to women with PROM at term who are known GBS positive in this pregnancy; intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is offered for known carriage.

n.0: Expectant management is for low-risk PROM; GBS carriage in this pregnancy means immediate induction is offered.
n.2: Temperature checks are part of expectant management, which is not recommended when she carries GBS.
n.3: Delaying 12 hours increases the time for ascending infection in a known GBS carrier.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: While suturing a perineal tear, a midwife sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle. What should she do first?
o: Suck the wound, apply a plaster and report it at the end of the shift
Finish the repair, then report it to the ward manager the next week
Scrub the wound with an alcohol rub and report it the next day
Let it bleed, wash with soap and running water, then report urgently
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Sharps injury first aid: allow the area to bleed (do not squeeze), wash with soap and running water, do not suck or scrub, cover, then report immediately to occupational health or the emergency department for risk assessment and possible post-exposure prophylaxis (Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013).

n.0: Sucking is unsafe and delayed reporting may miss the window for post-exposure prophylaxis.
n.1: Reporting must be immediate so the source can be tested and treatment started if needed.
n.2: Scrubbing damages tissue, and delay may miss the time-critical window for post-exposure treatment.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Ellie, 27, is exclusively breastfeeding her 10-day-old baby. She asks when she could become pregnant again if she does not use contraception. What should the midwife tell her?
o: From 6 weeks after the birth, after her postnatal check
From 3 weeks after the birth, even while breastfeeding
Once her periods have returned
Once she stops breastfeeding completely
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Women can become pregnant from 3 weeks (day 21) after giving birth, including when breastfeeding and before periods return (NHS; FSRH Contraception After Pregnancy). NG194 1.2.1 asks midwives to discuss contraception at postnatal contacts (SPM 3.4).

n.0: Ovulation can occur from about day 21, before the 6 to 8 week check.
n.2: Ovulation happens before the first period, so she can conceive before any bleeding.
n.3: Breastfeeding reduces but does not remove the chance of pregnancy unless all LAM criteria are met.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Maisie, 30, would like a copper intrauterine device after the birth of her baby, which is due in 2 weeks. When can the device be fitted?
o: From 3 weeks after, once the risk of infection has passed
Within 7 days of the birth, or from 6 weeks after
Within 48 hours of the birth, or from 4 weeks after
From 6 weeks after, at her postnatal check
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: If an IUD or IUS is not fitted within 48 hours of giving birth, it is recommended to wait until 4 weeks after (NHS; FSRH Contraception After Pregnancy). SPM 3.4 requires offering information on contraception.

n.0: Between 48 hours and 4 weeks fitting is not recommended because of expulsion and perforation risk.
n.1: The early window is 48 hours, not 7 days, and fitting can resume from 4 weeks.
n.3: Fitting is possible earlier, within 48 hours or from 4 weeks.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Tola, 25, is breastfeeding her 2-week-old baby and asks to restart the combined contraceptive pill she used before pregnancy. What should the midwife advise?
o: Wait until at least 6 weeks after the birth before starting it
Start it at 3 weeks if she has no blood clot risk factors
Wait until she stops breastfeeding before using any hormonal method
Start it now, as it does not affect breastfeeding
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: If breastfeeding, women are usually advised to wait until at least 6 weeks after birth before starting the combined pill, ring or patch; if not breastfeeding and with no VTE risk factors, they can start at 3 weeks (NHS; FSRH).

n.1: The 3-week start applies to women who are not breastfeeding.
n.2: Progestogen-only methods such as the implant or pill can be started immediately while breastfeeding.
n.3: Combined hormonal methods are usually avoided until at least 6 weeks when breastfeeding.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Dani, 22, is formula feeding her baby and has no risk factors for blood clots. She would like to use the combined pill. When can she start it?
o: 6 weeks after the birth
Immediately after the birth
3 weeks after the birth
After her first period
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Women who are not breastfeeding and have no VTE risk factors can start the combined pill, ring or patch 3 weeks after the birth (NHS; FSRH). VTE risk is raised in the early postnatal period.

n.0: The 6-week wait applies to women who are breastfeeding.
n.1: Combined methods are avoided in the first 3 weeks because of the raised VTE risk after birth.
n.3: Waiting for a period risks pregnancy, as ovulation comes first.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Rosie, 29, has a 3-month-old baby and has used the lactational amenorrhoea method so far. She has now started giving a formula feed at night so her partner can help. What should the midwife advise?
o: Continue LAM, adding condoms when the baby reaches 6 months
Continue LAM until her periods return
Start another method, as LAM is no longer reliable
Continue LAM, as her baby is under 6 months old
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: LAM is reliable only if the baby is under 6 months, the woman is fully or nearly fully breastfeeding and she has no periods. Giving formula, stopping night feeds or longer intervals between feeds mean another method should be used (NHS; FSRH).

n.0: She needs another method now because she is giving formula.
n.1: Return of periods is one trigger, but giving formula also ends LAM reliability.
n.3: LAM relies on exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding, which has stopped.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Jade, 19, has just given birth and is breastfeeding. She wants long-acting contraception before she goes home on day 1. Which method can be started now?
o: A diaphragm with spermicide
A progestogen-only implant
A combined vaginal ring
A combined patch
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: The implant, injection, progestogen-only pill, condoms and IUD or IUS (within 48 hours) can be started straight after the birth, including when breastfeeding (NHS; FSRH).

n.0: A diaphragm is usually fitted from about 6 weeks after the birth.
n.2: Combined methods are avoided for at least 6 weeks when breastfeeding.
n.3: Combined methods are avoided for at least 6 weeks when breastfeeding.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Neha, 33, had her baby 4 weeks ago. She says she would like another baby as soon as possible so the children are close in age. What information should the midwife give?
o: The interval between pregnancies has no effect on outcomes
Waiting at least 3 months before conceiving again lowers some risks
Waiting at least 12 months before conceiving again lowers some risks
Conceiving within 6 months lowers the risk of low birthweight
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: It is usually recommended to wait at least 12 months after giving birth before becoming pregnant again, because a shorter interval may increase risks such as low birthweight (NHS). SPM 3.4 includes information on reproductive health.

n.0: Short interpregnancy intervals are linked to adverse outcomes such as low birthweight.
n.1: Three months is too short; the recommendation is at least 12 months.
n.3: Short intervals are linked to increased, not reduced, risk of low birthweight.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Kiara, 20, is attending her 10-day postnatal visit. She tells the midwife she is worried she may have caught a sexually transmitted infection from a previous partner. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure her that negative booking screening means she is clear
Signpost her to a free, confidential sexual health service
Advise her to wait for testing at her 6 to 8 week GP check
Advise her to ask her previous partner to be tested first
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SPM 3.4 requires offering information and access to sexual and reproductive health services. Sexual health clinics provide free, confidential testing and treatment, and NG194 1.2.1 includes sexual health and contraception in postnatal discussions.

n.0: Booking IDPS screening does not cover infections such as chlamydia or new exposures.
n.2: Waiting delays diagnosis and treatment; sexual health services can be accessed now.
n.3: Her own testing should not depend on a previous partner.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Gemma, 28, attends her booking appointment with her partner, who answers most of the questions for her. When should the midwife ask Gemma about domestic abuse?
o: At 28 weeks, once a relationship of trust has been built
Now, in front of her partner, so he knows it is routine
When Gemma shows physical signs of injury
When Gemma is alone, at booking or the earliest opportunity
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at the booking appointment or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, with an opportunity for a private one-to-one discussion (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Enquiry should be at booking or the earliest opportunity; waiting delays help.
n.1: Asking in front of a partner may put her at risk and prevents an honest answer.
n.2: Routine enquiry is for all women; most abuse has no visible signs.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Aisha, 16, is 12 weeks pregnant. At booking she tells the midwife she had FGM as a young child in another country. What must the midwife do under the FGM mandatory reporting duty?
o: Refer her to children's social care within one month
Record it in her notes and report if she has a daughter
Report it to the police within one year
Report it to the police within one month
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: FGM Act 2003 s5B (England and Wales): a regulated professional who is told by a girl under 18 that FGM has been carried out, or observes physical signs, must notify the police before the end of one month. Safeguarding procedures also apply (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Social care referral may also be needed, but the mandatory duty is to notify the police.
n.1: For a girl under 18, the duty applies now, not when she has a daughter.
n.2: The deadline is one month from the disclosure, not one year.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Fadumo, 29, is 20 weeks pregnant with a girl. On examination the midwife finds she has had type 3 FGM as a child. Fadumo has a 4-year-old daughter. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the FGM, complete a safeguarding risk assessment and plan care
Record the FGM and continue her routine midwife-led antenatal care
Report the FGM to the police within one month of the examination
Refer her daughter for a medical examination for FGM
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: For women aged 18 or over, FGM is recorded and a safeguarding risk assessment is completed, especially for daughters and an unborn girl; police notification under s5B applies to girls under 18. NG235 1.9.20 covers planning care for infibulated women (SPM 3.7).

n.1: Type 3 FGM needs a birth plan, including possible deinfibulation, and a safeguarding assessment.
n.2: The mandatory police reporting duty applies to girls under 18, not adult women.
n.3: Examination is not automatic; risk is assessed first and referral made if there is concern.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Lauren, 30, tells the midwife that her partner checks her phone, controls all the money and stops her seeing friends. She has never been physically hurt. How should the midwife understand this?
o: As a safeguarding concern if the partner has a criminal record
As domestic abuse if it continues after the birth
As relationship difficulties, as there has been no violence
As domestic abuse, including coercive control and economic abuse
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s1 defines domestic abuse to include controlling or coercive behaviour, economic abuse and psychological and emotional abuse as well as physical violence (SPM 3.7).

n.0: A criminal record is not part of the definition of domestic abuse.
n.1: It already meets the definition of domestic abuse.
n.2: Abuse does not need physical violence; controlling and economic behaviour are abuse.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Kim, 26, discloses that her partner has strangled her and threatened to kill her. The midwife completes a domestic abuse risk checklist (DASH), and Kim answers yes to 16 questions. What should the midwife do next?
o: Tell Kim she must report the abuse to the police before referral
Give her a helpline number and review her at the next appointment
Refer Kim to the MARAC and to an independent domestic violence adviser
Arrange a joint appointment with Kim and her partner to discuss safety
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SafeLives DASH: 14 or more yes answers, or professional judgement, indicates high risk and needs referral to a multi-agency risk assessment conference (MARAC) and an independent domestic violence adviser. Strangulation is a high-risk indicator (SPM 3.7).

n.0: MARAC referral does not depend on Kim making a police report.
n.1: A score of 14 or more indicates high risk and needs a multiagency response now.
n.3: Involving the abuser increases the risk to Kim.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Paige, 24, is 18 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed from her care because of neglect, and she still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to the health visitor to monitor the baby after the birth
Wait until after the birth to see how she cares for the baby
Tell Paige the baby will be removed at birth
Refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Midwives safeguard unborn babies. Previous children removed for neglect with the same circumstances is a significant concern needing referral to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment, in line with Working Together to Safeguard Children and local procedures (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Health visitor involvement is not enough when there are known significant safeguarding concerns.
n.1: Waiting removes the chance to plan support and protection before the baby is born.
n.2: Removal is not decided by the midwife and is not certain; this damages trust.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: At a day 5 postnatal visit, the midwife notices a small bruise on the cheek of a 5-day-old baby. The parents say they do not know how it happened. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure the parents that bruising is common in newborns
Record the bruise in the notes and check it again at the next visit
Follow child protection procedures with urgent paediatric review
Ask the parents to take the baby to their GP within a week
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NICE CG89 (child maltreatment): suspect maltreatment if there is bruising in a child who is not independently mobile. Follow local safeguarding procedures with urgent paediatric assessment (SPM 3.7).

n.0: Bruises in non-mobile babies are uncommon and must be investigated.
n.1: Bruising in a baby who is not mobile must not be left for review; it needs action now.
n.3: This delays assessment and leaves the baby at possible risk.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Mia, 27, discloses domestic abuse at a postnatal visit and asks the midwife not to tell anyone. Her partner has hit her in front of their 2-year-old son. What should the midwife do?
o: Keep the disclosure confidential as Mia has requested
Wait until Mia agrees before sharing any information
Advise Mia to leave her partner before any referral is made
Explain that she will share the concern to protect the children
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Children who see or hear domestic abuse are victims of it (Domestic Abuse Act 2021). Information may be shared without consent to protect children, and the midwife should explain this to Mia unless doing so would increase risk, then follow local safeguarding procedures (Code 5.4, 17; SPM 3.7).

n.0: Confidentiality does not stop sharing information to protect children at risk of harm.
n.1: Consent is not required to share information to protect a child.
n.2: Leaving can increase risk, and safeguarding action does not depend on her leaving.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Charlotte, 30, is 29 weeks pregnant. She asks whether her sleeping position matters at this stage of pregnancy. What should the midwife advise?
o: Go to sleep on her side rather than on her back
Go to sleep on her back if she has no heartburn or back pain
Go to sleep on her back with a pillow under her knees
Go to sleep in whatever position is most comfortable
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG201 1.3.25-1.3.26: advise women to avoid going to sleep on their back after 28 weeks, explaining that there may be a link between going to sleep on the back and stillbirth in late pregnancy, so they should go to sleep on their side.

n.1: The stillbirth association with going to sleep on the back applies whatever her symptoms.
n.2: Going to sleep on the back after 28 weeks is associated with stillbirth.
n.3: Position matters after 28 weeks; she should go to sleep on her side.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Leanne, 26, smokes 10 cigarettes a day outside the house. She plans to share a bed with her baby to make night feeds easier. What advice should the midwife give?
o: Bed sharing is safe if she smokes outside the house
Bed sharing is safe if she uses a pillow to wedge the baby
Strongly advise her not to share a bed with the baby
Bed sharing is safe if the baby sleeps between both parents
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.3.15: strongly advise parents not to share a bed with their baby if the baby was low birth weight or either parent has had 2 or more units of alcohol, smokes, has taken medicine that causes drowsiness, or has used recreational drugs.

n.0: Parental smoking is a strong risk factor for SIDS when bed sharing, wherever she smokes.
n.1: Pillows near the baby increase the risk of suffocation.
n.3: Placing the baby between parents does not remove the risk from smoking and adds a hazard.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Isla and Tom have a healthy term baby and plan to bed share. Neither smokes, drinks or takes medication. Which advice about safer bed sharing is accurate?
o: Place the baby on a soft mattress topper, lying on her side to feed
Place the baby on the sofa with a parent when very tired
Use a firm, flat mattress with the baby face up, away from pillows
Place the baby between the parents with the duvet tucked in
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.3.14: discuss safer bed sharing: firm, flat mattress; baby lying face up; not sleeping on a sofa or chair with the baby; no pillows or duvets near the baby; no other children or pets in the bed.

n.0: Babies should sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface.
n.1: Sleeping with a baby on a sofa or chair is particularly dangerous.
n.3: Duvets and pillows near the baby, and lying between parents, increase risk.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Baby Arlo was born at 37 weeks weighing 2.2 kg. His parents do not smoke or drink and ask whether they can share a bed with him. What should the midwife advise?
o: Bed sharing is safe if he is swaddled tightly
Bed sharing is safe once he reaches 2.5 kg
Bed sharing is safe because the parents do not smoke or drink
Strongly advise against bed sharing because of his low birth weight
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.3.15: strongly advise parents not to share a bed with their baby if the baby was low birth weight (under 2.5 kg) or either parent smokes, has drunk 2 or more units of alcohol, or has taken drowsiness-causing medicine or recreational drugs.

n.0: Swaddling does not reduce the risk and can cause overheating.
n.1: The advice relates to his low birth weight; there is no weight at which it becomes safe.
n.2: Low birth weight is an independent risk factor; NICE advises strongly against bed sharing.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: At an antenatal visit at 32 weeks, Sian and her partner ask how they can help their baby feel secure after the birth. Which advice best supports attachment?
o: Keep to a fixed feeding and sleeping routine from the first day
Respond to her cues, with face-to-face time and skin-to-skin contact
Limit holding the baby so she does not become too dependent
Leave the baby to cry so she learns to settle herself
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.3.16-1.3.17: discuss bonding and attachment before and after birth, and encourage face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding appropriately to the baby's cues (SPM 3.9).

n.0: Responsive care, not fixed routines, supports attachment in the newborn period.
n.2: Holding and closeness support, rather than harm, attachment.
n.3: Newborns need responsive care; leaving them to cry does not build secure attachment.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Cara, 25, had an emergency caesarean after a long labour. On day 4 she tells the midwife she does not feel close to her baby and keeps reliving the birth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Discuss her feelings, assess her mental health and offer support
Refer her to the health visitor to discuss bonding at 6 weeks
Advise her to spend less time with the baby until she feels better
Reassure her that bonding will improve once she is home
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.3.18: discuss aspects of the postnatal period that may affect bonding, including traumatic birth. NG194 1.2.2 and CG192: assess psychological wellbeing at each contact and offer support or referral (SPM 3.9).

n.1: She needs assessment and support now, not in several weeks.
n.2: Reducing contact does not help bonding and may worsen her distress.
n.3: Reassurance without assessment misses possible birth trauma or depression; difficulties after a traumatic birth may persist.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Before transfer home, Leon and Priya ask how they will know if their baby is unwell. What information should the midwife give?
o: Contact the GP surgery whatever the urgency of the concern
Seek advice if their baby has a temperature over 39 C
Wait for the health visitor visit before seeking any advice
Use Baby Check to help decide, and call 999 if seriously ill
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.3.12-1.3.13: consider giving parents information about the Baby Check scoring system; advise them to seek advice if they think their baby is unwell and to call 999 if they think the baby is seriously ill (SPM 3.8).

n.0: If they think the baby is seriously ill they should call emergency services.
n.1: In a young baby, a lower temperature or other signs may indicate serious illness.
n.2: Parents should seek advice whenever they think their baby is unwell.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A midwife is planning group antenatal education sessions for women expecting their first baby. Which content and format best meet the needs of parents?
o: Interactive sessions with partners on birth, feeding and parenthood
Online videos for women, covering the pain relief options in labour
A single session at 36 weeks, covering labour, birth and pain relief
Lectures for women on their own, covering the stages of labour in detail
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SPM 3.8 requires midwives to provide parent education and preparation for parenthood for individuals and groups. NG201 and NG194 support antenatal education that involves partners and includes birth, infant feeding, attachment and emotional wellbeing.

n.1: Videos alone do not allow discussion and cover a narrow range of topics.
n.2: One late session leaves no time to prepare for feeding and the transition to parenthood.
n.3: Lectures on labour alone miss feeding, parenting and mental health, and exclude partners.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Jade, 28, is 30 weeks pregnant and undecided about how to feed her baby. She asks what health benefits breastfeeding has for her as a mother. Which answer is accurate?
