o: A lower risk of breast and ovarian cancer
A lower risk of pelvic girdle pain after the birth
A lower risk of postpartum haemorrhage after 6 weeks
A lower risk of haemorrhoids after the birth
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Breastfeeding reduces the mother's risk of breast and ovarian cancer and type 2 diabetes (NG194 1.5.2 asks midwives to discuss health benefits for both baby and woman). SPM 3.6: the importance of breastfeeding to public health.

n.1: Pelvic girdle pain is a musculoskeletal problem and is not reduced by breastfeeding.
n.2: Late postnatal bleeding is not reduced by breastfeeding in this way.
n.3: Haemorrhoids after birth relate to pregnancy, straining and constipation; breastfeeding is not a recognised protection against them.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Which health benefit for the baby should a midwife include when discussing breastfeeding with expectant parents?
o: A lower risk of developmental dysplasia of the hip
A lower risk of physiological jaundice
Fewer gastrointestinal and respiratory infections
A lower risk of tongue-tie
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Breastfed babies have fewer gastrointestinal, respiratory and ear infections and a lower risk of sudden infant death. NG194 1.5.2: discuss nutritional and health benefits for the baby (SPM 3.6).

n.0: Hip dysplasia is not influenced by feeding method.
n.1: Breastfed babies are not at lower risk of jaundice; jaundice can be more prolonged.
n.3: Tongue-tie is congenital and not affected by feeding method.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Rachel, 26, gave birth 20 minutes ago and wants to breastfeed. Her baby is well and in skin-to-skin contact. When should breastfeeding ideally start?
o: After the baby has been weighed and dressed
Within 6 hours of birth, once she has rested
As soon as possible, ideally within the first hour
After the first 24 hours, when the milk comes in
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG235 1.11.11: encourage women to initiate breastfeeding as soon as possible after the birth, ideally within 1 hour. NG194 1.5.7: early skin-to-skin contact so breastfeeding can start when baby and mother are ready (SPM 3.6).

n.0: Weighing and dressing should wait until after the first hour so they do not delay feeding.
n.1: Waiting several hours misses the baby's alert period after birth.
n.3: Colostrum is available from birth and early feeding helps establish supply.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A maternity unit is working towards UNICEF UK Baby Friendly accreditation. Which stage focuses on making sure staff have the knowledge and skills to support families?
o: Achieving Sustainability: the Gold award
Stage 1: building a firm foundation
Stage 3: parents' experiences of care
Stage 2: an educated workforce
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: UNICEF UK Baby Friendly: Stage 1 building a firm foundation; Stage 2 an educated workforce; Stage 3 changes to care (parents' experiences); then Achieving Sustainability (Gold) (BFI; SPM 3.6).

n.0: Gold is about sustaining the standards over time.
n.1: Stage 1 covers policies, guidelines and no promotion of breastmilk substitutes.
n.2: Stage 3 assesses changes in care as experienced by mothers and babies.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Maya, 31, is exclusively breastfeeding her 3-day-old baby. She asks whether her baby needs any supplements. What should the midwife advise?
o: Give the baby daily vitamin D drops of 8.5 to 10 micrograms
Give vitamin D drops if the baby is having under 500 mL of formula
Give vitamin D drops from 6 months, when solids start
No supplements are needed while she is breastfeeding
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG247 (table 1): breastfed babies should have a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms from birth; formula-fed babies having 500 mL or more of formula a day do not need one.

n.1: This threshold applies to formula-fed babies, but Maya's baby is breastfed and needs drops from birth.
n.2: Supplements are recommended from birth for breastfed babies.
n.3: Breastfed babies are recommended vitamin D from birth.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Ella, 23, says she will breastfeed for 2 weeks and then switch to formula because she is returning to college. She asks if it is worth breastfeeding at all. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain that breastfeeding has benefits even for a short time and support her plan
Advise mixed feeding from birth so the switch to formula is easier
Encourage her to defer college so she can breastfeed for 6 months
Explain that benefits begin after 6 months, so formula from birth is simpler
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.5.1-1.5.2: be respectful of parents' choices and explain that breastfeeding can have benefits even if done for a short time. Baby Friendly supports informed decisions (SPM 3.6).

n.1: Formula from birth without need reduces milk supply and the benefits she wants.
n.2: This disregards her circumstances and choice; care should be respectful of her decision.
n.3: Breastfeeding has benefits even when done for a short time (NG194 1.5.2).

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Before transfer home on day 1, Jo, 27, says breastfeeding is going well. The midwife has not yet observed a feed. What does NICE recommend before transfer?
o: Observe at least one effective feed as part of the feeding plan
Give a formula top-up so the baby is settled for the journey
Weigh the baby to confirm feeding is effective
Accept Jo's report and arrange a feed check on day 5
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: NG194 1.1.10: before transfer, make sure there is a plan for feeding the baby, including observing at least 1 effective feed; NG194 1.5.14 lists what to assess (SPM 3.6).

n.1: A top-up without clinical need can undermine breastfeeding.
n.2: Weight on day 1 does not show feeding effectiveness; normal weight loss occurs early.
n.3: NICE expects an effective feed to be observed before transfer.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A local authority asks the maternity service how it can raise breastfeeding rates among young mothers in a deprived area. Which intervention is most likely to help?
o: Community peer support linked with skilled midwifery feeding help
Posters in GP surgeries showing the benefits of breastfeeding
Free formula vouchers for mothers who stop breastfeeding
Leaflets about breastfeeding benefits given at booking
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: SPM 3.6 asks midwives to protect, promote and enable breastfeeding with the woman and family. Face-to-face support, including peer support, combined with skilled professional help improves breastfeeding duration (NG194 1.5 on breastfeeding support; Baby Friendly).

n.1: Posters raise awareness but do not give the practical support young mothers need.
n.2: This would promote breastmilk substitutes and is contrary to the WHO Code.
n.3: Leaflets alone rarely change behaviour or address practical barriers.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A community midwife is reviewing local data for a public health report. She needs a measure of the number of new cases of gestational diabetes diagnosed among women giving birth in the area during 2025. Which epidemiological term describes this?
o: Prevalence
Mortality rate
Relative risk
Incidence
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: Incidence is the number of new cases arising in a defined population over a specified period. SPM 3.2 requires midwives to understand epidemiological principles and interpret public health data.

n.0: Prevalence counts all existing cases at a point or period, not just new ones.
n.1: A mortality rate counts deaths in a population, not new diagnoses.
n.2: Relative risk compares the risk in an exposed group with an unexposed group.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: A student midwife is summarising the MBRRACE-UK data brief on maternal deaths in 2022-24. Which statement about these data is accurate?
o: Women in the most and least deprived areas died at similar rates
The maternal mortality rate fell by 20% compared with 2009-11
Cardiac disease was the leading cause of death up to 6 weeks after birth
Black women died at nearly three times the rate of White women
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 (Sept 2026 data brief): 12.80 maternal deaths per 100,000 maternities, 20% higher than 2009-11; Black women nearly three times the rate of White women; most deprived areas twice the least deprived; thrombosis and thromboembolism leading cause up to 6 weeks (SPM 3.2).

n.0: Women in the most deprived areas died at twice the rate of those in the least deprived.
n.1: The rate was 20% higher, not lower, than in 2009-11.
n.2: Thrombosis and thromboembolism was the leading cause during pregnancy and up to 6 weeks; cardiac disease was second.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Which was the leading cause of maternal death between 6 weeks and 1 year after the end of pregnancy in the MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 data?
o: Cardiac disease
Sepsis
Thrombosis and thromboembolism
Maternal suicide
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: maternal suicide was the leading cause of death from 6 weeks to 1 year after pregnancy; psychiatric causes accounted for 33% of late maternal deaths. This underlines the midwife's public health role in perinatal mental health (SPM 3.2).

n.0: Cardiac disease was the second leading cause up to 6 weeks after pregnancy.
n.1: Sepsis is an important cause but was not the leading cause from 6 weeks to 1 year.
n.2: This was the leading cause during pregnancy and up to 6 weeks after, not from 6 weeks to 1 year.

Public Health & Health Promotion.q: Fiona, 30, is 14 weeks pregnant and asks how much physical activity is recommended now that she is pregnant. She is healthy and was active before pregnancy. What should the midwife advise?
o: At least 30 minutes of light walking on most days of the week
Reduce her usual activity by half until after the birth
At least 150 minutes of moderate activity spread across each week
At least 75 minutes of vigorous activity across each week
Public Health & Health Promotion.w: The UK Chief Medical Officers' physical activity guidelines (2019) recommend that pregnant women do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity every week, plus muscle strengthening twice a week. SPM 3.3 asks midwives to share public health information so women can make evidence-informed decisions.

n.0: Light activity alone falls short of the moderate-intensity amount recommended in pregnancy.
n.1: There is no need to halve activity; women who were active can continue at moderate intensity.
n.3: 75 minutes of vigorous activity is an option in the general adult guideline; the pregnancy guideline recommends 150 minutes of moderate activity.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: A student midwife asks Tara, a registered midwife, to explain fetal circulation before a teaching session. Which statement about the umbilical cord vessels is accurate?
o: The two umbilical arteries carry oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus
The umbilical arteries and vein each carry mixed blood of equal oxygen content
The single umbilical vein carries oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus
The umbilical vein returns deoxygenated blood from the fetus to the placenta
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: A normal cord has one vein and two arteries. The umbilical vein carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus (via the ductus venosus to the inferior vena cava); the umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood from the fetal internal iliac arteries to the placenta (SPM 3.13.1).

n.0: The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus to the placenta.
n.1: The vessels carry blood of clearly different oxygen content, which is why cord gas samples are taken from both artery and vein.
n.3: This reverses the roles: the vein brings oxygenated blood to the fetus.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Sara, 30, attends a preconception appointment and asks why she should start folic acid 400 micrograms before trying to conceive rather than waiting for a positive pregnancy test. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: The placenta cannot transfer folate until the end of the first trimester
The neural tube closes at about 12 weeks, so earlier doses build up maternal stores
Folic acid mainly protects the fetus from anaemia in the third trimester
The neural tube closes about 4 weeks after conception, often before pregnancy is confirmed
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: The neural tube closes around day 28 after conception (about 6 weeks of gestation), when many women do not yet know they are pregnant. Folic acid 400 micrograms daily is advised when planning pregnancy and for the first 12 weeks to reduce neural tube defects (NICE NG247 1.1.3, 1.1.4; SPM 3.13.1).

n.0: Folate crosses to the embryo from early pregnancy; the reason for early dosing is the timing of neural tube closure.
n.1: The neural tube closes in the fourth week after conception, not at 12 weeks; 12 weeks is when supplementation can stop.
n.2: The purpose of periconceptional folic acid is prevention of neural tube defects, not third-trimester fetal anaemia.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Amina, 26, and her partner are both carriers of sickle cell (HbAS), confirmed through antenatal screening. Amina is 11 weeks pregnant and asks what the chance is that this baby will have sickle cell disease. What is the correct answer?
o: 1 in 4 in each pregnancy
1 in 2 in each pregnancy
1 in 4 for the first baby and lower for later babies
No chance, because neither parent has the disease
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive. When both parents are carriers, each pregnancy independently has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected baby, a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and a 1 in 4 chance of an unaffected non-carrier. Prenatal diagnosis should be offered (NHS SCT screening; SPM 3.11).

n.1: 1 in 2 is the chance of the baby being a carrier, not of having the disease.
n.2: The chance is the same in every pregnancy; earlier outcomes do not change it.
n.3: Two carriers can each pass on the sickle gene, so the baby can inherit two copies and have the disease.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: At a parent education class, Lola, 22, asks the midwife whether smoking in pregnancy can affect her baby's health as an adult even though it cannot change the baby's genes. Which explanation best describes epigenetics?
o: Exposures in pregnancy alter the DNA sequence the baby passes to its own children
Exposures affect the baby's health through the placenta and leave gene activity unchanged
Gene expression is fixed at conception and cannot be influenced by the environment
Exposures can change how genes are switched on or off without altering the DNA sequence
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Epigenetics describes changes in gene expression (for example DNA methylation) that do not alter the DNA sequence. Maternal smoking, nutrition and stress in pregnancy can cause epigenetic changes linked to later health, which is part of why midwives promote healthy behaviours (SPM 3.12, 3.13).

n.0: Epigenetic change alters gene activity, not the DNA sequence itself; this describes mutation.
n.1: Placental effects are real, but the question is about gene activity: epigenetic changes do alter how genes are expressed.
n.2: Gene expression is responsive to the environment throughout life, which is the core idea of epigenetics.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Megan, 32, has moved to the area and refers herself to the maternity service when she is 11+1 weeks pregnant. She has not yet seen a midwife in this pregnancy. According to NICE antenatal care guidance, when should her booking appointment take place?
o: Within 2 weeks of her contacting the service, if possible
At the routine 16-week appointment to avoid duplicating checks
At her dating scan, which must be done before 14+1 weeks
Within 4 weeks, as the 10-week target no longer applies to her
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Booking should ideally be by 10+0 weeks; when a woman contacts or is referred to maternity services later than 9+0 weeks, offer a booking appointment within 2 weeks if possible (NICE NG201 1.1.4, 1.1.5). This keeps screening windows such as the combined test (up to 14+1) open.

n.1: Waiting until 16 weeks would miss the window for first-trimester combined screening and delay risk assessment.
n.2: The dating scan is a separate contact; booking includes history, bloods and risk assessment that should not wait for or be merged into the scan.
n.3: NICE sets a 2-week target for late referrals; a 4-week wait is too long.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Nadia, 19, attends her first antenatal appointment at 23 weeks of pregnancy. She seems withdrawn and her partner answers most questions. She has not seen any health professional during this pregnancy. What should the midwife do first in addition to the usual booking care?
o: Ask Nadia, sensitively, about the reasons she has booked late
Make a safeguarding referral because late booking is a safeguarding concern
Arrange an urgent growth scan before completing any history
Record that she did not engage with early care and continue the booking
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.1.6: if a woman books late, ask about the reasons because it may reveal social, psychological or medical issues that need to be addressed. Her presentation also means she should be given the chance to talk alone (NG201 1.2.5).

n.1: Late booking is a trigger to explore reasons, but a referral should follow assessment of what is found rather than replacing it.
n.2: A growth scan may be needed later, but the history and risk assessment come first and determine what investigations are required.
n.3: Recording non-engagement without exploring it misses the purpose of asking: identifying abuse, mental health or social needs.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Fatima, 28, speaks limited English and attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks with her husband, who offers to interpret. The midwife needs to take a full history, including questions about her mental health and safety at home. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange an independent professional interpreter for the appointment
Use a translated leaflet and ask her to nod in answer to questions
Accept her husband's offer because he knows her medical history
Ask a bilingual healthcare assistant from the ward to interpret
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.1.11: interpreters should be independent of the woman rather than a family member or friend. A family interpreter can filter what is said and prevents safe disclosure of domestic abuse or mental health concerns (NG201 1.2.5; SPM 3.22).

n.1: Nodding to a leaflet does not allow informed discussion or a reliable history, and screening choices need full information.
n.2: Family members should not interpret; her husband's presence also blocks private enquiry about domestic abuse.
n.3: An untrained colleague is not a reliable interpreting service and confidentiality and accuracy cannot be assured.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Chloe, 25, attends her booking appointment at 8 weeks. Her partner stays with her throughout and has said he will come to every appointment. The midwife has not been able to ask about domestic abuse. Which is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange time alone with Chloe, such as during a urine test, and ask then
Ask about domestic abuse in front of her partner so the question is covered
Leave the question until the 36-week appointment when trust is established
Record that routine enquiry was declined because her partner was present
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.2.5: ask about domestic abuse at booking, or at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, and ensure there is an opportunity for a private one-to-one discussion. Midwives create that opportunity, for example by seeing the woman alone for part of the appointment.

n.1: Asking in front of a partner is unsafe and unlikely to lead to disclosure; it could increase risk if he is abusive.
n.2: Enquiry should happen at the earliest opportunity when she is alone, not deferred to late pregnancy.
n.3: Chloe has not declined; the question was never asked. Recording a refusal would be inaccurate.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Rosa, 33, is booking at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her BMI is 32 and her mother has type 2 diabetes. Her first baby weighed 3.6 kg. She has no other risk factors. Which plan for gestational diabetes is most appropriate?
o: Arrange a random blood glucose test today and repeat it at 28 weeks
Test her urine for glucose at every antenatal appointment
Check HbA1c at booking and repeat it at 28 weeks
Offer a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Rosa has two risk factors for gestational diabetes (BMI above 30 and a first-degree relative with diabetes). NICE recommends a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks (NG201 1.2.22; NG3 1.2.2). NG3 1.2.3 states that fasting or random glucose, HbA1c, glucose challenge or urinalysis for glucose should not be used to assess GDM risk.

n.0: Random blood glucose is not a recommended test for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.3).
n.1: Urinalysis for glucose is not a valid test for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.3).
n.2: HbA1c is not recommended for assessing gestational diabetes risk in pregnancy (NG3 1.2.3).

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Jade, 30, is booking at 7 weeks. Her BMI is 36. She has no diabetes, no personal or family history of neural tube defects and takes no regular medicines. She has been taking folic acid 400 micrograms daily and asks whether she needs the higher dose. What is the correct advice?
o: Change to 5 mg daily for the whole pregnancy
Change to 5 mg daily until 12 weeks because of her BMI
Continue 400 micrograms daily until 12 weeks
Stop folic acid now, as the neural tube has already closed
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG247 (January 2025) recommends 400 micrograms daily for the first 12 weeks. A BMI of 25 or more alone does not need a higher dose; 5 mg is for women with an increased risk of neural tube defect or congenital malformation, such as diabetes, previous affected pregnancy or anti-epileptic medicines (NG247 1.1.5, 1.1.6).

n.0: The higher dose is not indicated for her, and the standard duration of supplementation is the first 12 weeks.
n.1: Raised BMI on its own is no longer an indication for 5 mg under NG247 1.1.6; this reflects older teaching.
n.3: Supplementation is advised for the first 12 weeks of pregnancy; stopping at 7 weeks does not follow the guidance.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Lauren, 27, is 9 weeks pregnant and smokes about 10 cigarettes a day. At booking her carbon monoxide reading is 12 ppm. She says she would like to stop but has failed before. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to cut down to five cigarettes a day to protect the baby
Ask her GP to prescribe varenicline to support her quit attempt
Make an opt-out referral to the tobacco dependence adviser
Give her a stop smoking leaflet and ask her to self-refer when ready
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Saving Babies' Lives v3 element 1 and NICE NG209: CO testing is offered at booking, and women with CO of 4 ppm or above, or who self-report smoking, receive an opt-out referral to an in-house tobacco dependence adviser. NRT can be offered as part of that support.

n.0: Cutting down is not the recommended goal; specialist support aims for complete cessation.
n.1: Varenicline is not recommended in pregnancy (NG209); NRT is the pharmacological option.
n.3: Self-referral leaflets have lower uptake; SBL v3 requires an opt-out referral at 4 ppm or above.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Hodan, 26, is booking at 10 weeks in her first pregnancy. During the history she tells the midwife she had type 3 FGM (infibulation) as a child in Somalia. She has no daughters. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Document the FGM type, refer to the specialist FGM service and plan care with her
Report the FGM to the police under the mandatory reporting duty
Advise her that a planned caesarean birth will be needed because of the FGM
Record it in her notes and plan no further action as she is an adult
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Assess and discuss FGM sensitively at booking and act in line with government safeguarding guidance (NICE NG201 1.2.6): record the type, refer for specialist assessment (including possible deinfibulation), and complete a safeguarding risk assessment for any future daughter. NG235 1.9.20 explains labour risks and possible deinfibulation, so vaginal birth remains possible.

n.1: The mandatory police reporting duty (FGM Act 2003 s5B) applies to FGM in girls under 18, not to an adult woman.
n.2: Infibulation is managed with deinfibulation antenatally or in labour; it does not of itself mean a caesarean is required.
n.3: Recording alone misses specialist referral, birth planning and the safeguarding assessment for her unborn baby if a girl.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Olivia, 31, is pregnant with her second baby after an uncomplicated first pregnancy and birth. She is now 13 weeks with no risk factors and asks how many routine antenatal appointments she should expect. What is the correct answer under NICE guidance?
o: 10 appointments
5 appointments
7 appointments
12 appointments
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.1.8: plan 7 routine antenatal appointments for parous women with an uncomplicated pregnancy (booking, 16, 28, 34, 36, 38 and 41 weeks if not given birth). Additional or longer appointments are offered if needed (NG201 1.1.10).

n.0: 10 appointments is the schedule for nulliparous women, who also have 25, 31 and 40-week contacts (NG201 1.1.7).
n.1: 5 appointments is fewer than NICE plans for any woman with an uncomplicated pregnancy.
n.3: 12 appointments exceeds the routine schedule; extra contacts are added for clinical need, not routinely.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Aisha, 24, is expecting her first baby and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. Her older sister, who has two children, says she was not seen at 25 weeks and asks why Aisha has an appointment then. Which explanation is accurate?
o: The 25-week appointment replaces the 28-week bloods for first pregnancies
The 25, 31 and 40-week appointments are for women having their first baby
The 25-week appointment is for women with a raised BMI at booking
Every woman is offered a 25-week appointment, but her sister missed it
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: The NICE NG201 schedule adds appointments at 25, 31 and 40 weeks for nulliparous women, giving 10 routine contacts compared with 7 for parous women (NG201 1.1.7, 1.1.8 and schedule of appointments).

n.0: Bloods (FBC, group and antibodies) are still offered at 28 weeks for all women; the 25-week contact does not replace them.
n.2: The extra contacts are based on parity, not BMI.
n.3: Parous women with uncomplicated pregnancies are not routinely offered a 25-week appointment.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Bethany, 29, is 36+2 weeks pregnant with her first baby and has an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy. On abdominal palpation the midwife feels a hard, round, ballotable mass at the fundus and suspects breech presentation. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Recheck the presentation by palpation at the 38-week appointment
Offer external cephalic version at today's appointment
Book an elective caesarean birth at 39 weeks
Offer an ultrasound scan to confirm the presentation
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.2.36 and 1.2.37: offer abdominal palpation at all appointments after 36+0 weeks and, if breech is suspected, offer an ultrasound scan to determine the presentation. Options such as ECV are discussed once breech is confirmed (NG201 1.2.38).

n.0: Waiting 2 weeks delays confirmation and reduces the time available for ECV.
n.1: ECV is offered after breech is confirmed by scan and options are discussed; it is not done on palpation findings alone.
n.2: Mode of birth cannot be planned on a suspected presentation; it must be confirmed and options discussed first.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Emma, 33, is 36+5 weeks pregnant. A scan has confirmed an uncomplicated singleton breech presentation. After discussion of the options she says she would prefer to have a vaginal birth with the baby head down if possible. What should be offered?
o: External cephalic version
A planned vaginal breech birth
Induction of labour at 37 weeks
A repeat scan at 40 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.2.38: for an uncomplicated singleton breech confirmed after 36+0 weeks, discuss ECV, vaginal breech birth and elective caesarean, and offer ECV to women who prefer cephalic vaginal birth.

n.1: Vaginal breech birth is one option, but she wants a head-down birth, which ECV aims to achieve.
n.2: Induction is not generally recommended for a breech baby (NG207 1.2.21) and does not turn the baby.
n.3: Waiting for a repeat scan delays ECV, which is offered from 36+0 weeks when the woman wishes.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Leah, 28, is 32 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy. Her fundal height measurements are plotted and following her growth curve. A friend had a 'reassurance' growth scan at 32 weeks and Leah asks for one too. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer her for a scan because a request indicates reduced fetal movements
Explain routine scans are not offered after 28 weeks; SFH checks continue
Arrange fortnightly growth scans until birth to provide reassurance
Book a growth scan today, as every woman should have one at 32 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.2.33: do not routinely offer ultrasound scans after 28 weeks for uncomplicated singleton pregnancies. Serial SFH measurement plotted on a chart continues (NG201 1.2.30), and a scan is offered if SFH is small for gestational age or there are other concerns.

n.0: She has not reported any change in movements; a request for reassurance is not the same as reduced fetal movements.
n.2: Serial scans are for women with risk factors or concerns, not for an uncomplicated pregnancy with normal SFH.
n.3: Routine third-trimester scans are not recommended for uncomplicated pregnancies.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Zara, 26, is RhD positive and at her 28-week appointment. Her booking antibody screen was negative. The student midwife suggests that, as she is RhD positive, only a full blood count is needed. Which blood tests should be offered?
o: Full blood count and a glucose tolerance test
Full blood count, plus blood group and antibody screen
Blood group and antibodies, with Hb checked at 34 weeks
Full blood count, as her antibody screen was negative at booking
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.2.16: at 28 weeks offer all women a full blood count and blood group and antibody testing; anti-D prophylaxis is added for RhD-negative women who are not sensitised. Atypical red cell antibodies other than anti-D can develop in RhD-positive women.

n.0: An OGTT is offered at 24 to 28 weeks only when GDM risk factors are present, and does not replace group and antibodies.
n.2: The FBC is recommended at 28 weeks to detect anaemia in time to treat it before birth.
n.3: A negative booking screen does not exclude antibodies developing later, so testing is repeated at 28 weeks.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Isla, 30, is 38 weeks pregnant with her first baby and the pregnancy is uncomplicated. Her BP is 116/74 mmHg and urinalysis shows no protein. In addition to routine checks, which discussion is specifically recommended at this appointment?
o: Whether she would like the second-trimester screening tests
Options for managing a pregnancy that goes beyond term
Arranging her first measurement of symphysis fundal height
Her first discussion about birth preferences and place of birth
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.3.17: from 38 weeks discuss prolonged pregnancy and the options for managing it, in line with NG207 (membrane sweep after 39+0 and induction discussion from 41+0).

n.0: Screening windows closed long before 38 weeks; the quadruple test runs to 20+0 weeks.
n.2: SFH is measured at each appointment after 24+0 weeks, with the first by 28+6, not first at 38 weeks.
n.3: Birth preferences should be raised before 28 weeks (NG201 1.3.14), so 38 weeks is too late for a first discussion.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Mia, 27, is 31 weeks pregnant with her first baby and has an uncomplicated pregnancy. Which set of assessments is routinely offered at this appointment?
o: Blood pressure, full blood count and an oral glucose tolerance test
Blood pressure, urine dipstick and palpation to confirm presentation
Blood pressure, urine dipstick and a cardiotocograph of the fetal heart
Blood pressure, urine dipstick for protein and plotted fundal height
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: At every routine face-to-face contact NICE recommends BP and urine dipstick for proteinuria (NG201 1.2.24, 1.2.28), and SFH plotted on a chart after 24+0 weeks (NG201 1.2.30). Babies' movements are also discussed (1.2.34).

n.0: FBC is offered at booking and 28 weeks, and OGTT only for women with GDM risk factors at 24 to 28 weeks.
n.1: Routine palpation for presentation starts after 36+0 weeks (NG201 1.2.36).
n.2: CTG is not part of routine antenatal care for an uncomplicated pregnancy.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Kemi, 34, transferred her care from abroad and books at 15+3 weeks. Her dating scan has confirmed the gestation. After discussion she would like screening for Down's syndrome. Which test should be offered?
o: Amniocentesis to give a definite result
The combined test with a nuchal translucency measurement
The quadruple blood test, which screens for Down's syndrome
Non-invasive prenatal testing as the first screening test
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: The combined test is available from 10+0 to 14+1 weeks. After that, the quadruple test (second trimester, up to 20+0 weeks) is offered and screens for Down's syndrome only (NHS FASP). NIPT is offered after a higher-chance screening result, and diagnostic tests follow a higher-chance result if chosen.

n.0: Amniocentesis is a diagnostic test with a miscarriage risk, offered after a higher-chance result if she chooses it, not as first-line screening.
n.1: The combined test window ends at 14+1 weeks, so at 15+3 it is no longer available.
n.3: In the NHS programme NIPT is offered as a further test after a higher-chance result, not as the first-line screen.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Priti, 38, has a combined test result giving a 1 in 80 chance of Down's syndrome. She is upset and asks what this means and what happens next. Which response by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Explain that the baby has Down's syndrome and arrange counselling about the pregnancy
Advise a repeat combined test in 2 weeks to see whether the chance changes
Explain it is a higher-chance result and offer NIPT, a diagnostic test or no further testing
Book an amniocentesis, as this is the next step after any higher-chance result
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: FASP classes a chance of 1 in 2 to 1 in 150 as a higher-chance result. Screening does not diagnose; she is offered a choice of NIPT, a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis) or no further testing, and every step is her informed choice (NHS FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.0: A screening result gives a chance, not a diagnosis; 79 in 80 babies with this result would not have Down's syndrome.
n.1: The combined test is not repeated; further information comes from NIPT or diagnostic testing.
n.3: Diagnostic testing is one option among several; it is her choice, not an automatic next step.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Grace, 29, receives her combined screening result: a 1 in 2,400 chance of Down's syndrome and a 1 in 10,000 chance of Edwards' or Patau's syndrome. She asks whether she should have more tests. What is the most accurate explanation?
o: This is a higher-chance result, so NIPT should be offered next
This result excludes chromosomal conditions, so the 20-week scan is unnecessary
This is a lower-chance result, so no further screening for these conditions is offered
This result is borderline, so a quadruple test should be offered at 16 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: FASP: results of 1 in 151 or lower chance are lower-chance results and no further screening for these conditions is offered. She should still be offered the 20-week anomaly scan, which screens for a different set of physical conditions.

n.0: A higher-chance result is 1 in 2 to 1 in 150; 1 in 2,400 is well below that.
n.1: A lower-chance result does not exclude a condition, and the 20-week scan screens for 11 other physical conditions.
n.3: There is no borderline category leading to a quadruple test after a combined test result.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Laila, 36, chose NIPT after a higher-chance combined test. The NIPT result shows a high chance of Down's syndrome. She asks whether this means the diagnosis is certain. What is the most accurate response?
o: NIPT is diagnostic for Down's but not for Edwards' or Patau's syndromes
NIPT is diagnostic, so the result is certain and no more tests are needed
A repeat NIPT will confirm the result without any miscarriage risk
NIPT is a screening test; a diagnosis needs CVS or amniocentesis
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NIPT analyses cell-free DNA mostly from the placenta and is highly accurate, but it remains a screening test. A diagnosis needs an invasive diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), which she can choose or decline (NHS FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.0: NIPT is a screening test for all three conditions; none is diagnosed by it.
n.1: NIPT is not diagnostic; false positives occur, for example from placental mosaicism.
n.2: Repeating a screening test does not provide a diagnosis; confirmation needs a diagnostic test.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ruth, 31, is 9 weeks pregnant. After the booking discussion she says she does not want any screening for Down's, Edwards' or Patau's syndromes or the 20-week anomaly scan, because she would continue the pregnancy whatever the result. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that the 20-week scan is required to check the position of the placenta
Respect and record her decision and offer the dating scan to confirm gestation
Refer her to an obstetrician to discuss the reasons for declining screening
Ask her to sign a disclaimer stating she accepts the risks of declining
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Every screening test is a personal choice and she can accept or decline any part (NICE NG201 1.2.13; FASP). The dating scan determines gestational age and multiple pregnancy, and screening is added only if she opts for it (NG201 1.2.14). Her decision is respected and documented.

n.0: Placental location is part of the 18 to 20+6 week scan (NG201 1.2.15), but she may decline it; she should be informed of what it offers, not told it is required.
n.2: Declining screening is a valid informed choice and is not a reason for obstetric referral.
n.3: A disclaimer is not required; documenting the informed discussion and her decision is the standard.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Tamsin, 30, had her first baby in 2014 and remembers a blood test for rubella immunity. At her booking appointment she asks why rubella is not on the list of infectious diseases screening offered this time. What is the correct explanation?
o: Rubella screening is offered to women who have had a previous baby
Rubella immunity is checked at the 28-week appointment instead
Antenatal rubella susceptibility screening stopped in 2016
Rubella is tested for as part of the hepatitis B screening sample
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: The NHS infectious diseases in pregnancy screening programme offers screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis in every pregnancy. Rubella susceptibility screening in pregnancy stopped on 1 April 2016 (IDPS programme overview).

n.0: Rubella screening stopped for all pregnant women, not according to parity.
n.1: 28-week bloods are FBC, blood group and antibodies; rubella is not tested then.
n.3: IDPS screens for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis; rubella is no longer part of it.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Danielle, 23, screened negative for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis at booking. At 30 weeks she tells the midwife she has a new partner who injects drugs. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Offer repeat screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis
Reassure her that her negative booking results cover the whole pregnancy
Offer screening after the birth so the baby can be tested at the same time
Refer her partner to a drug service and take no action for her
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: IDPS: repeat testing is offered if a woman has a new partner, injects drugs, has a partner who injects drugs or is infected, or is otherwise at new risk during pregnancy. Early diagnosis allows treatment that reduces transmission to the baby (SPM 3.20).

n.1: A negative booking result reflects risk at that time; new exposure means repeat testing is recommended.
n.2: Delaying until after birth loses the chance to reduce vertical transmission during pregnancy and birth.
n.3: Supporting her partner is reasonable, but Danielle has a new risk of infection and needs to be offered testing herself.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Emily, 27, is booked for her 20-week scan. She asks the midwife whether a normal scan means her baby will definitely be healthy. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It screens for 11 specific physical conditions and cannot detect every problem
It is a diagnostic test, so any condition it does not find can be ruled out
It confirms or excludes Down's syndrome, which is the main condition it looks for
It checks for all physical and chromosomal conditions, so a normal scan is reassuring
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: The FASP 20-week scan (18+0 to 20+6 weeks) looks for 11 physical conditions, including spina bifida, anencephaly, cleft lip, congenital heart disease and Edwards' and Patau's syndromes. Some conditions are not detectable on scan, so a normal result cannot guarantee a healthy baby (FASP; SPM 3.20).

n.1: The anomaly scan is a screening test; a normal scan does not rule out every condition.
n.2: Down's syndrome is not one of the 11 conditions; it is screened for by the combined or quadruple test.
n.3: The scan looks for a defined list of conditions and many conditions cannot be seen on ultrasound.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Naomi, 35, is booking at 10 weeks in her second pregnancy. In her first pregnancy she developed pre-eclampsia at 35 weeks. Her blood pressure today is 122/78 mmHg. What advice about aspirin is most appropriate?
o: Aspirin is not needed as her blood pressure is now normal
Take 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth
Take 75 mg daily from 20 weeks until 36 weeks
Take 300 mg daily from booking until 28 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy is a high-risk factor; one high-risk factor is enough. Advise aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth (NICE NG133 1.1.2). Aspirin for this use must be prescribed.

n.0: Risk is based on her history, not her current BP; previous pre-eclampsia is a high-risk factor.
n.2: Starting at 20 weeks and stopping at 36 weeks does not match the recommended timing of 12 weeks until birth.
n.3: 300 mg exceeds the recommended 75 to 150 mg dose, and stopping at 28 weeks is too early.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Sophie, 30, is booking at 9 weeks in her first pregnancy. Her BMI is 37 and she has no medical conditions. Her sister and mother have never had pre-eclampsia. Should aspirin be advised to reduce her risk of pre-eclampsia?
o: Yes, because a BMI over 35 is a high-risk factor
Yes, because she has two moderate risk factors
No, because she has no high-risk factors
No, because a BMI of 37 is a single moderate risk factor
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Nulliparity and a BMI of 35 or more at first visit are both moderate risk factors. More than one moderate risk factor means aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth is advised (NICE NG133 1.1.3).

n.0: BMI of 35 or more is a moderate, not a high, risk factor; the high-risk list is previous hypertensive disease, CKD, autoimmune disease, diabetes and chronic hypertension.
n.2: Aspirin is also advised for more than one moderate risk factor, even with no high-risk factor.
n.3: Being nulliparous is a second moderate factor, so she has two, not one.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Bernadette, 41, is booking at 8 weeks in her third pregnancy. Her previous pregnancies, 3 and 6 years ago, were normotensive. Her BMI is 27 and she has no medical conditions or family history of pre-eclampsia. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Aspirin from 12 weeks, as age 40 or over is a high-risk factor
Aspirin from 12 weeks, as any moderate risk factor qualifies
Weekly BP checks from booking, as her age needs closer surveillance
Routine BP and urine checks, with no aspirin indicated
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Age 40 or over is a moderate risk factor. NICE advises aspirin when there is more than one moderate factor or any high-risk factor (NG133 1.1.2, 1.1.3). With a single moderate factor she continues routine BP and urine monitoring at every appointment (NG201 1.2.24, 1.2.28) and is reassessed in the second trimester (NG201 1.2.23).

n.0: Age 40 or over is classed as a moderate, not a high, risk factor.
n.1: One moderate factor alone does not meet the NICE threshold of more than one moderate factor.
n.2: There is no recommendation for weekly BP checks on the basis of age alone in an otherwise uncomplicated pregnancy.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Kayleigh, 27, is 26 weeks pregnant. At a routine community appointment her BP is 146/94 mmHg, and 144/92 mmHg on repeat. Booking BP was 112/70 mmHg. Urinalysis shows no protein and she has no symptoms. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck her BP at the next routine appointment in 2 weeks
Advise rest at home and ask her GP to recheck in a week
Refer her to secondary care to be seen within 24 hours
Refer her for an urgent same-day obstetric admission
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: A first episode of hypertension (140/90 mmHg or more) after 20+0 weeks needs referral to secondary care to be seen within 24 hours (NICE NG201 1.2.26). Severe hypertension (160/110 or more) needs same-day review (NG201 1.2.27).

n.0: Waiting 2 weeks delays assessment of new hypertension, which may be the start of pre-eclampsia.
n.1: New hypertension after 20 weeks is assessed in secondary care; rest and a delayed GP check do not meet NICE guidance.
n.3: Same-day referral is for severe hypertension of 160/110 mmHg or more, or according to clinical assessment; her readings fit the 24-hour pathway.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ngozi, 32, is 33 weeks pregnant. At a community appointment her BP is 164/112 mmHg on two readings. She has a mild headache. Urinalysis shows 2+ protein. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her to the day assessment unit within 24 hours
Arrange same-day urgent assessment in the obstetric unit
Send urine for a protein:creatinine ratio and review the result tomorrow
Repeat the BP in 4 hours and refer if it remains raised
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: BP of 160/110 mmHg or more is severe hypertension and needs urgent referral to be seen on the same day, with urgency set by overall clinical assessment (NICE NG201 1.2.27). Headache and proteinuria raise concern for pre-eclampsia, so she should be seen without delay.

n.0: The 24-hour pathway is for non-severe new hypertension; severe readings with symptoms need same-day assessment.
n.2: Quantifying proteinuria is part of her hospital assessment and must not delay urgent referral.
n.3: Delaying referral for a further reading leaves severe hypertension with symptoms unassessed.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Freya, 29, is 30 weeks pregnant. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and she feels well. A dipstick shows 1+ protein, with no leucocytes or nitrites. Under NICE hypertension in pregnancy guidance, what should happen next to assess the proteinuria?
o: Send a first morning urine sample to measure protein
Repeat the dipstick at her next routine appointment
Arrange a 24-hour urine collection to measure total protein
Quantify with a protein:creatinine or albumin:creatinine ratio
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: If dipstick screening is positive (1+ or more), use albumin:creatinine ratio or protein:creatinine ratio to quantify proteinuria, interpreted alongside a full clinical review (NICE NG133 1.2.1, 1.2.3).

n.0: NICE advises not to use a first morning void to quantify proteinuria (NG133 1.2.4).
n.1: A positive dipstick needs quantification now; waiting for the next routine visit delays assessment.
n.2: NICE advises against routine 24-hour urine collection to quantify proteinuria (NG133 1.2.5).

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ava, 31, is 34 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Booking BP was 110/70 mmHg. Today in the day assessment unit her BP is 148/96 mmHg and her urine protein:creatinine ratio is 42 mg/mmol. How should these findings be interpreted?
o: Chronic hypertension, as her blood pressure has been raised before 20 weeks
Gestational hypertension, as proteinuria is below the significant threshold
Pre-eclampsia is excluded, as her BP is below 160/110 mmHg
New hypertension with significant proteinuria, consistent with pre-eclampsia
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria or organ or uteroplacental dysfunction. NICE uses a PCR of 30 mg/mmol as the threshold for significant proteinuria (NG133 1.2.6), so 42 mg/mmol is significant.

n.0: Her booking BP was normal, so this hypertension is new after 20 weeks, not chronic.
n.1: Gestational hypertension is new hypertension without significant proteinuria; 42 mg/mmol is above the 30 mg/mmol threshold.
n.2: 160/110 mmHg defines severe hypertension; pre-eclampsia is diagnosed from 140/90 mmHg with significant proteinuria or organ dysfunction.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Lily, 24, is 28 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Her BP and urinalysis are normal. The midwife is giving her information about pre-eclampsia. Which advice is most accurate?
o: Seek help immediately for severe headache, blurred vision or pain below the ribs
Seek help if she has heartburn after large meals that settles with an antacid
Wait for her next appointment to mention new headaches, as BP is checked then
Seek help if her ankles swell by evening and settle overnight with feet raised
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG133 1.1.1: advise pregnant women to see a healthcare professional immediately if they have symptoms of pre-eclampsia: severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet.

n.1: Heartburn relieved by antacids is a common symptom; severe pain just below the ribs is the warning sign.
n.2: New severe headache needs immediate assessment; waiting for a routine appointment could delay diagnosis.
n.3: Gradual dependent ankle swelling that resolves overnight is common in pregnancy; it is sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet that is a warning sign.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ellen, 28, is at low risk of fetal growth restriction and is 22 weeks pregnant. She asks when the midwife will start measuring her bump. Which plan follows NICE and Saving Babies' Lives v3 guidance?
o: Measure SFH at every appointment from 16 weeks, with weekly checks after 36
Measure SFH at each appointment after 24+0 weeks, with the first by 28+6 weeks
Measure SFH at each appointment after 32 weeks, with the first by 34 weeks
Measure SFH once at 36 weeks to assess the size of the baby at term
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: For women at low risk of FGR, offer serial SFH at each antenatal appointment after 24+0 weeks (no more often than every 2 weeks), with the first by 28+6 weeks, plotted on a growth chart by trained staff (NICE NG201 1.2.30; SBL v3 intervention 2.10).

n.0: SFH starts after 24+0 weeks, not 16 weeks, and is not repeated more often than every 2 weeks.
n.2: Starting at 32 weeks would miss earlier detection of growth problems; the first measurement should be by 28+6 weeks.
n.3: A single measurement cannot show growth velocity; serial plotted measurements are needed.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Harriet, 30, is 32 weeks pregnant and at low risk of fetal growth restriction. Her previous SFH measurements followed the 50th centile. Today's measurement, plotted on her customised chart, falls below the 10th centile. Movements are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a colleague to remeasure today and document if the result is the same
Reassure her, as SFH varies with the baby's position at this gestation
Remeasure SFH at her next routine appointment in 2 weeks
Refer for an ultrasound scan of fetal growth and wellbeing
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: If SFH suggests a small-for-gestational-age baby, offer an ultrasound scan for fetal growth and wellbeing; urgency depends on additional findings such as reduced movements or raised BP (NICE NG201 1.2.32; SBL v3 element 2). A drop in centile is a referral trigger.

n.0: A second measurement may be reasonable, but the plotted finding needs a scan referral rather than documentation alone.
n.1: A fall across centiles is a recognised referral criterion and should not be explained away.
n.2: Waiting 2 weeks delays assessment of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Esme, 34, had a baby with a birthweight below the 3rd centile in her last pregnancy. She has been placed on a pathway of 3 to 4-weekly growth scans from 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height?
o: Stop SFH measurement, as she is on serial scan surveillance
Measure SFH at alternate appointments to reduce duplication
Measure and plot SFH as well as reviewing each scan result
Measure SFH weekly between scans to detect any change
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Saving Babies' Lives v3 intervention 2.12: women undergoing planned serial scan surveillance should stop SFH measurement once surveillance begins. Women at increased risk of FGR have 3 to 4-weekly scans until birth (2.13). The midwife still discusses movements and checks BP and urine.

n.1: Alternating SFH with scans is not part of the SBL v3 pathway; SFH stops.
n.2: SBL v3 states SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance begins.
n.3: Weekly SFH adds no useful information alongside scans and SFH should not be done more often than every 2 weeks anyway.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ruby, 26, is 30 weeks pregnant. At 20:00 she phones the maternity triage line saying her baby has moved less than usual since the morning. This is the first time she has noticed this. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Attend the maternity unit now for assessment
Have a cold sugary drink and lie on her left side for an hour
Attend the antenatal clinic first thing tomorrow morning
Count ten movements over the next 2 hours, then call back
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Women should contact maternity services at any time of day or night if they are concerned about reduced movements and should be assessed (NICE NG201 1.2.34; SBL v3 element 3). Delays in attending with RFM have been repeatedly identified in stillbirth reviews.

n.1: Trying to stimulate movements at home delays assessment and is not a recommended approach.
n.2: Waiting until the next day delays assessment of possible fetal compromise.
n.3: Counting a set number of movements before calling back delays assessment and is not recommended.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Molly, 25, is 32 weeks pregnant and attends with her first episode of reduced fetal movements. The fetal heart is heard, the computerised CTG meets criteria, SFH is on her centile line and she has no risk factors. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Arrange induction of labour at 37 weeks because of the episode
Book an ultrasound scan for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler
Admit her for daily CTG monitoring until movements return to normal
Explain the results and advise her to return if movements reduce again
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: SBL v3 element 3: after a first episode of RFM with a normal cCTG and no other indication, a scan is not required; results are explained and she is encouraged to reattend with further concerns. A scan for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler is offered for recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks or if there is another indication.

n.0: Induction for RFM alone before 39+0 weeks is not recommended (SBL v3 element 3).
n.1: A scan is offered at a first presentation only when another indication exists, such as suspected SGA.
n.2: Admission for daily CTG is not indicated when assessment is normal and there are no risk factors.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Alice, 29, is 34 weeks pregnant and attends for the second time in 10 days with reduced fetal movements. Her computerised CTG today meets criteria and her SFH is on her usual centile. Her last scan was at 20 weeks. What should be offered?
o: A repeat computerised CTG in 1 week, without an ultrasound scan
Reassurance, as a normal CTG excludes placental insufficiency
Induction of labour now because the episode is recurrent
A scan for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: SBL v3 element 3 checklist: offer an ultrasound scan for fetal growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler to women presenting with recurrent RFM after 28+0 weeks, unless a growth scan was done in the previous 2 weeks.

n.0: A repeat CTG alone does not assess growth or placental function, which is the concern in recurrent RFM.
n.1: A normal CTG reflects current wellbeing and does not exclude placental insufficiency or FGR.
n.2: Birth for recurrent RFM is offered after 38+6 weeks; at 34 weeks the next step is a scan.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Poppy, 31, is 39+2 weeks pregnant and attends with a first episode of reduced fetal movements. The CTG is normal and her SFH is on her usual centile. Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Explain induction is not considered until 41+0 weeks of pregnancy
Discuss induction of labour with her, as she is beyond 38+6 weeks
Arrange twice-weekly CTGs until she reaches 41 weeks
Recommend an expedited caesarean birth today
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: SBL v3 element 3: for RFM after 38+6 weeks, discuss induction of labour with all women (risks, benefits and her wishes), and offer birth to those with recurrent RFM after 38+6 weeks. At 39 weeks and beyond induction is not associated with more caesarean births.

n.0: 41+0 is the threshold for discussing induction for prolonged pregnancy (NG207), not for RFM after 38+6 weeks.
n.2: Serial CTG monitoring is not the recommended response; a discussion about induction is.
n.3: There is no indication for caesarean birth with a normal CTG; induction is discussed as an option.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Jasmine, 27, is 37+2 weeks pregnant. She had one episode of reduced fetal movements yesterday. Today her computerised CTG and a growth scan are normal, and movements have returned. She asks to be induced now 'to be safe'. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain induction for reduced movements alone is not recommended before 39 weeks
Advise that induction is not available until 42 weeks
Agree to induction today, as any reduced movements at term justify birth
Book induction for 38 weeks, as this is the standard timing after reduced movements
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: SBL v3 element 3: induction before 39+0 weeks is recommended only where there is evidence of fetal compromise or other concerns in addition to RFM. Her concerns are explored, she is encouraged to reattend if movements reduce again, and her preferences are revisited as pregnancy continues.

n.1: NG207 discusses induction from 41+0 weeks for prolonged pregnancy, and 42 weeks is not a cut-off for availability.
n.2: Induction for RFM alone before 39 weeks is not recommended and carries risks of early term birth.
n.3: There is no standard 38-week induction after RFM; SBL v3 uses 38+6 weeks as the point for discussion.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Lucy, 30, is RhD negative and 28 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. Her booking antibody screen was negative and she has had no bleeding or trauma. Which care should be offered at this appointment?
o: Weekly antibody screens from 28 weeks instead of anti-D prophylaxis
Blood group and antibody screen, FBC and routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis
FBC and antibody screen, with anti-D given if the screen is positive
Anti-D prophylaxis after the birth, when the baby's blood group is known
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: At 28 weeks offer FBC, blood group and antibodies, and anti-D prophylaxis to RhD-negative women who are not known to be sensitised (NICE NG201 1.2.16; NICE TA156 1.1). RAADP protects against sensitisation from silent fetomaternal haemorrhage in late pregnancy.

n.0: Repeated antibody screening detects sensitisation after it happens; it does not prevent it.
n.2: A positive anti-D antibody screen would mean she is already sensitised, when prophylaxis no longer helps; RAADP is for women who are not sensitised.
n.3: Postnatal anti-D is also given if the baby is RhD positive, but it does not replace antenatal prophylaxis.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Kirsty, 32, asks why she needs an anti-D injection at 28 weeks when she feels well and has had no bleeding. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It reduces her risk of bleeding heavily at the birth
It is a vaccine that protects her baby from jaundice after birth
It stops her forming antibodies that could harm a future RhD-positive baby
It treats anaemia caused by her baby's blood entering her circulation
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Small, unnoticed fetomaternal haemorrhages can expose an RhD-negative woman to RhD-positive fetal cells. Anti-D prophylaxis prevents her immune system forming anti-D antibodies, which could cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in this or a future pregnancy (NICE TA156; SPM 3.20).

n.0: Anti-D has no effect on postpartum haemorrhage risk.
n.1: Anti-D is an immunoglobulin given to the mother, not a vaccine for the baby.
n.3: Anti-D does not treat maternal anaemia; it prevents sensitisation.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Saira, 27, is RhD negative and 22 weeks pregnant. She attends the community clinic with a small amount of fresh vaginal bleeding that started an hour ago. She has no pain and her baby is moving. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure her, as painless bleeding at 22 weeks needs no treatment
Give anti-D at home and review her at the next routine appointment
Refer to secondary care for review and offer anti-D immunoglobulin
Offer anti-D at 28 weeks with her routine prophylaxis
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Refer women with unexplained vaginal bleeding after 13 weeks to secondary care for review (NICE NG201 1.4.17), and offer anti-D immunoglobulin to RhD-negative women at risk of isoimmunisation who bleed after 13 weeks (NG201 1.4.16). Placental localisation is also offered if the site is unknown (1.4.19).

n.0: Painless bleeding may indicate a low-lying placenta and needs assessment; RhD-negative women also need anti-D.
n.1: Anti-D is needed, but unexplained bleeding after 13 weeks also needs secondary care assessment, for example for abruption or a low-lying placenta.
n.3: Routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks does not cover a sensitising event that has happened at 22 weeks.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Bella, 29, is RhD negative and received routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. At 31 weeks she trips and falls onto her abdomen. She has mild tenderness and the baby is moving. What is the most appropriate plan regarding anti-D?
o: Withhold anti-D unless she develops vaginal bleeding in the next 72 hours
Give anti-D at the birth, combined with her postnatal dose
Withhold anti-D, as her 28-week prophylaxis covers her until the birth
Arrange obstetric assessment and offer anti-D for this sensitising event
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Abdominal trauma is a potentially sensitising event. Anti-D given for a sensitising event is separate from routine prophylaxis, so RAADP does not replace it. She also needs obstetric assessment after abdominal trauma because of the risk of placental abruption.

n.0: Trauma can cause fetomaternal haemorrhage without visible bleeding, so anti-D is not conditional on bleeding.
n.1: Delaying until birth leaves her unprotected after a possible fetomaternal haemorrhage now.
n.2: Routine prophylaxis does not replace the anti-D needed after a sensitising event.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Charlotte, 31, is RhD negative. A non-invasive test of cell-free fetal DNA in her blood shows that her baby is predicted to be RhD negative. At 28 weeks she asks whether she still needs anti-D prophylaxis. What is the most accurate response?
o: Anti-D prophylaxis is not needed, as the baby is predicted to be RhD negative
Anti-D prophylaxis is not needed, as her own RhD status is now irrelevant
Anti-D prophylaxis is still needed, as fetal genotyping does not change care
Anti-D prophylaxis is needed at 28 and 34 weeks, as the result may be wrong
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: High-throughput non-invasive prenatal testing for fetal RHD genotype (NICE DG25, referenced in NG201 1.2.16) identifies women carrying an RhD-negative baby, who do not need antenatal anti-D. Where the baby is predicted RhD positive or the result is inconclusive, prophylaxis is offered.

n.1: Her RhD-negative status remains relevant; it is the baby's predicted group that removes the need for prophylaxis in this pregnancy.
n.2: The purpose of fetal RHD genotyping is to target anti-D, avoiding unnecessary doses when the baby is RhD negative.
n.3: The test is highly accurate; a predicted RhD-negative result means prophylaxis is not offered.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Grace, 34, is RhD negative and has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth. Cord blood shows that her baby is RhD positive. She received routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks. What is the correct plan?
o: Offer anti-D within 72 hours of the birth
Offer anti-D at her 6-week postnatal check
Anti-D is not needed, as she had antenatal prophylaxis
Offer anti-D in her next pregnancy at booking
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: After the birth of an RhD-positive baby to an RhD-negative woman who is not sensitised, anti-D is given as soon as possible and within 72 hours, with a test to assess the size of any fetomaternal haemorrhage. Antenatal prophylaxis does not cover exposure at birth.

n.1: Six weeks is far too late; sensitisation can occur within days of exposure.
n.2: Birth is a separate sensitising event; antenatal prophylaxis does not cover it.
n.3: Waiting until the next pregnancy allows sensitisation to occur after this birth.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Maya, 28, is RhD positive. Her 28-week antibody screen detects an atypical red cell antibody (anti-c), which was not present at booking. She is well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Offer routine anti-D prophylaxis to neutralise the antibody
Reassure her, as atypical antibodies matter in RhD-negative women
Refer for obstetric review of antibody levels and the baby
Repeat the screen at 36 weeks before deciding on any referral
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Red cell antibodies other than anti-D, such as anti-c and anti-Kell, can cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn. This is why group and antibodies are checked at 28 weeks in all women (NICE NG201 1.2.16). An unexpected result needs referral according to local pathways (NG201 1.2.17), usually obstetric or fetal medicine review with antibody levels.

n.0: Anti-D prevents RhD sensitisation; it does not neutralise anti-c or any existing antibody.
n.1: Atypical antibodies can affect the baby whatever the woman's RhD status.
n.3: Waiting 8 weeks delays monitoring for fetal anaemia.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Hannah, 33, is RhD negative and booking at 9 weeks in her third pregnancy. Her antibody screen shows immune anti-D antibodies, which were first detected after her second baby's birth. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Give routine anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks as usual
Repeat the antibody screen at 28 weeks before making any referral
Give anti-D now to remove the existing antibodies
Refer for obstetric monitoring, as prophylaxis cannot help now
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: RAADP is for RhD-negative women who are not known to be sensitised (NICE TA156 1.1). Once immune anti-D is present, prophylaxis cannot reverse sensitisation; the pregnancy needs obstetric or fetal medicine monitoring of antibody levels and the fetus for anaemia.

n.0: Prophylaxis is not given to women already sensitised to RhD.
n.1: Her sensitisation is known now, so referral for monitoring should not wait until 28 weeks.
n.2: Anti-D immunoglobulin prevents sensitisation; it cannot remove antibodies already formed.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Daisy, 25, is at her booking appointment at 9 weeks. As part of a general conversation about her wellbeing, the midwife plans to ask about her mental health. Which approach follows NICE antenatal and postnatal mental health guidance?
o: Ask about mental health at the 28-week appointment once rapport is built
Ask whether she has ever been prescribed antidepressants by her GP
Ask her to complete the full EPDS questionnaire before any discussion
Ask the two depression identification questions and the GAD-2 questions
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE CG192 1.5.4: at the booking visit and in the early postnatal period, consider asking the two depression identification (Whooley) questions and the 2-item GAD scale as part of a general discussion about mental health and wellbeing. Fuller tools such as the EPDS or PHQ-9 follow a positive response or concern (1.5.5).

n.0: Enquiry is recommended at booking; delaying until 28 weeks may miss early illness.
n.1: Medication history is useful, but it does not identify current depression or anxiety.
n.2: The EPDS or PHQ-9 is used as part of a full assessment after a positive response or concern, not as the first step.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Asha, 29, is 16 weeks pregnant. When asked, she says that during the past month she has often felt down and hopeless, but she still enjoys time with friends. She has no history of mental illness and no thoughts of self-harm. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Use the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a fuller assessment, or refer to her GP
Refer her to the crisis team for same-day mental health assessment
Repeat the same two questions at her 28-week appointment
Reassure her, as a positive answer needs both questions to be answered yes
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE CG192 1.5.5: if a woman responds positively to either depression identification question, is at risk or there is clinical concern, consider using the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment or referring her to her GP (or a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.1: There are no features of a severe or urgent problem, so crisis referral is not indicated on these facts.
n.2: Waiting 12 weeks delays assessment of possible depression that was identified today.
n.3: A positive answer to either question is enough to prompt further assessment.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ella, 31, is 24 weeks pregnant. On the GAD-2 she says she has felt nervous and on edge 'more than half the days' and has been unable to stop worrying 'several days' over the last 2 weeks. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Consider the GAD-7 for further assessment or refer her to her GP
Reassure her, as her GAD-2 score is below the threshold for action
Ask her to keep a worry diary and review it at her next appointment
Refer her for urgent assessment by the perinatal mental health team today
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: GAD-2 scoring: 'more than half the days' scores 2 and 'several days' scores 1, giving 3. NICE CG192 1.5.6: if a woman scores 3 or more, consider using the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring her to her GP (or a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.1: Her score is 3, which meets the threshold for further assessment.
n.2: A diary delays recommended assessment after a positive GAD-2 score.
n.3: Nothing suggests a severe or urgent problem, so same-day specialist assessment is not indicated.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Victoria, 34, books at 8 weeks. She has bipolar disorder diagnosed 6 years ago and has been well on medication for 3 years. She is under the care of her GP only. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to stop her medication now to protect the baby
Refer her to a specialist perinatal mental health service
Record the history and plan routine care as she is currently well
Ask her GP to review her at 36 weeks before she gives birth
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE CG192 1.5.10: refer all women who have or are suspected to have severe mental illness, or have any history of severe mental illness, to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal service), and ensure the GP knows. Women with bipolar disorder are at high risk of postpartum relapse and psychosis.

n.0: Stopping medication abruptly can trigger relapse; changes should be planned with her prescriber, considering the specific drug's risks.
n.2: Being currently well does not remove the need for referral when there is any history of severe mental illness.
n.3: A review at 36 weeks is too late to plan care; referral is recommended at first contact.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Freya, 27, books at 10 weeks. She has no personal history of mental illness. Her mother had postpartum psychosis after Freya's birth. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Advise her GP to start medication to prevent psychosis after birth
Refer her for immediate mental health assessment within 4 hours
Reassure her, as a family history does not affect her own risk
Record it and watch for postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE CG192 1.5.9 and 1.5.11: ask about severe perinatal mental illness in a first-degree relative, and if present be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after childbirth. The history should be shared in her care plan so the postnatal team is aware.

n.0: There is no indication for preventive medication in a woman with no personal history of mental illness.
n.1: The 4-hour pathway is for sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis, which she does not have.
n.2: A first-degree family history of severe perinatal mental illness does increase her risk.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Megan, 23, is 10 weeks pregnant after an unplanned conception. She tells the midwife she feels 'all over the place': sometimes excited, sometimes unsure she wants a baby, and occasionally tearful. She is sleeping and eating well and answers no to both depression identification questions. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Complete an EPDS at every appointment until 20 weeks
Refer her to the perinatal mental health service for assessment of ambivalence
Ask her GP to start an antidepressant to stabilise her mood
Explain mixed feelings are common and revisit her wellbeing at each visit
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Emotional lability and ambivalence are common normal psychological responses in early pregnancy, especially when unplanned (SPM 3.17.1). With negative screening questions and normal function, she needs information and support, with mental health discussed at every contact (NICE CG192 1.5.8; NG201 1.2.10).

n.0: Routine repeated EPDS without a positive response or concern is not the recommended approach; ongoing discussion at each contact is.
n.1: Normal ambivalence without signs of a mental health problem does not need specialist referral.
n.2: There is no evidence of depression, so medication is not indicated.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Kayla, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. She becomes tearful when asked about her mood and says she has not told anyone how low she feels because she is afraid her baby will be taken into care. Which response by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Acknowledge her fear and explain help aims to support her to care for her baby
Advise her to wait until after the birth to seek help, when it will be easier
Tell her social care becomes involved when a mother declines treatment
Reassure her that the information will stay between the two of them
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE CG192 1.5.1 recognises that women may not disclose mental health problems for fear of stigma or that their baby will be taken into care. Responding with compassion and acknowledging her role in caring for her baby (CG192 1.3.1) supports disclosure and access to help, while being honest about information sharing.

n.1: Delaying help is unsafe; untreated perinatal depression affects the woman and baby.
n.2: This is inaccurate; safeguarding involvement depends on risk to the child, not on refusing treatment.
n.3: Midwives cannot promise absolute confidentiality, as information may need to be shared with the team or for safeguarding.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Nicole, 32, is 22 weeks pregnant. Her first birth 3 years ago was an emergency caesarean under general anaesthetic. She describes nightmares and flashbacks about it, avoids driving past the hospital and feels panic when thinking about this birth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Book an elective caesarean so she does not have to face labour again
Arrange mental health assessment, as these features suggest possible PTSD
Reassure her that fear of birth is normal and will pass after this baby
Advise her to avoid talking about the previous birth to reduce distress
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Nightmares, flashbacks and avoidance suggest post-traumatic stress disorder after a traumatic birth. She needs assessment through her GP or perinatal mental health service so that treatment such as trauma-focused psychological therapy can be offered (NICE CG192; NG201 1.2.10 on discussing previous traumatic birth).

n.0: Mode of birth is discussed with an obstetrician as part of her plan, but it does not treat the underlying trauma symptoms.
n.2: These symptoms go beyond normal fear of birth and need assessment rather than reassurance.
n.3: Avoidance is a symptom of PTSD; discouraging discussion does not help recovery.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Phoebe, 28, is 38+4 weeks pregnant with her first baby and the pregnancy is uncomplicated. She has read about membrane sweeping and asks when it can be offered. What is the correct answer under NICE induction guidance?
o: From 41+0 weeks, when induction of labour is being discussed
At antenatal visits after 39+0 weeks, with her verbal consent
