At antenatal visits after 37+0 weeks, with her written consent
From 42+0 weeks, once the pregnancy is post-term
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.3.2: at antenatal visits after 39+0 weeks, discuss whether she would like a vaginal examination for membrane sweeping and, if so, obtain verbal consent. She should be told that it may make spontaneous labour more likely and can cause discomfort and bleeding (1.3.1).

n.0: Sweeping is offered from 39+0, before the induction discussion at 41+0 weeks.
n.2: 37+0 weeks is earlier than NICE recommends, and verbal consent is sufficient.
n.3: Waiting until 42+0 weeks is later than recommended; sweeping is offered from 39+0.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Isabel, 33, is 40+1 weeks pregnant and asks for a membrane sweep. Her notes show that the 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta, and there is no record of a follow-up scan. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Perform the sweep gently, as most low-lying placentas move up by term
Ask her to sign a consent form accepting the bleeding risk, then sweep
Perform the sweep and observe her for bleeding for 1 hour afterwards
Do not sweep; clarify placental position with the obstetric team first
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.7.6: check that there is no evidence of a low-lying placenta on previous scans before membrane sweeping and before induction. With no follow-up scan documented, the placental site must be clarified before any vaginal examination for sweeping.

n.0: Many placentas do move away from the cervix, but this must be confirmed by scan, not assumed.
n.1: A signed form does not make an unsafe procedure safe; the placental site must be checked first.
n.2: Observing for bleeding afterwards does not prevent haemorrhage from a placenta that may be low lying.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Sienna, 30, is 40+5 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated first pregnancy. She asks the midwife at what point induction of labour will be discussed with her. What is the most accurate answer?
o: From 41+0 weeks, as some risks rise if the pregnancy continues beyond then
From 39+0 weeks, as part of the routine membrane sweep discussion
From 42+0 weeks, as risks do not increase until the pregnancy is post-term
From 40+0 weeks, as every pregnancy should be induced at the due date
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.2.3 and 1.2.4: explain that risks such as caesarean birth, neonatal unit admission, stillbirth and neonatal death may increase beyond 41+0 weeks, and discuss that induction from 41+0 weeks may reduce these risks, alongside its impact on her birth experience.

n.1: From 39+0 weeks sweeping is discussed; induction for prolonged pregnancy is discussed from 41+0.
n.2: NG207 describes rising risks after 41+0 weeks, so waiting until 42+0 to discuss is too late.
n.3: Induction is not offered routinely at the due date in an uncomplicated pregnancy.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Layla, 31, is 41+3 weeks pregnant. After a full discussion of benefits and risks she declines induction and wishes to wait for labour to start naturally. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Refer her to the safeguarding team because of the risk to the baby
Discharge her to routine care with no further appointments until labour
Respect and record her decision; discuss extra monitoring from 42 weeks
Explain that induction must be booked once a pregnancy passes 41 weeks
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.2.6 to 1.2.8: if she declines induction, discuss her options, record her decision, discuss additional fetal monitoring from 42 weeks (explaining it gives a snapshot and cannot predict later problems) and offer her the chance to revisit her decision at later reviews.

n.0: Declining a recommended intervention is not a safeguarding issue; an unborn baby has no separate legal rights over her decision.
n.1: She should be offered ongoing review and monitoring from 42 weeks and the chance to change her mind.
n.3: A woman with capacity can decline induction (NG207 1.2.19); it is not compulsory.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Rachel, 29, is 41+2 weeks pregnant with her first baby and has chosen induction. She has no previous uterine surgery. The fetal head is engaged, the CTG is normal and her Bishop score is 4. Which method is most appropriate to offer first?
o: An intravenous oxytocin infusion with membranes left intact
Vaginal dinoprostone or low-dose oral misoprostol
Amniotomy followed by an intravenous oxytocin infusion
Oral mifepristone followed by vaginal misoprostol
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.3.7: for a Bishop score of 6 or less, offer induction with dinoprostone (vaginal tablet, gel or controlled-release system) or low-dose (25 microgram) oral misoprostol. A mechanical method may be considered if pharmacological methods are unsuitable or she prefers it (1.3.8).

n.0: Intravenous oxytocin alone is not supported by the evidence for induction (NG207 1.4.1).
n.2: Amniotomy with oxytocin is offered when the Bishop score is more than 6 (NG207 1.3.9).
n.3: Mifepristone with misoprostol is a regimen for induction after intrauterine fetal death (NG207 1.2.31).

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Tanya, 34, is 41+1 weeks pregnant. Her first baby was born by caesarean. After discussion of the risks, including uterine rupture, she chooses induction of labour. Her Bishop score is 3. Which method should be considered?
o: Amniotomy and immediate oxytocin infusion
Vaginal dinoprostone gel as the standard first choice
Low-dose oral misoprostol, repeated every 2 hours
A mechanical method such as a balloon catheter
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.3.8 and 1.2.17: for a Bishop score of 6 or less, consider a mechanical method if pharmacological methods are not suitable, for example after a previous caesarean birth. The marketing authorisations for dinoprostone and misoprostol contraindicate their use for induction in women with a uterine scar.

n.0: Amniotomy and oxytocin are offered when the Bishop score is more than 6; a score of 3 needs cervical ripening first.
n.1: Dinoprostone's marketing authorisation contraindicates it for induction with a uterine scar because of uterine rupture risk.
n.2: Misoprostol is likewise contraindicated for induction with a uterine scar.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Olivia, 30, is being induced with a dinoprostone vaginal delivery system. Two hours later she is having 6 contractions in 10 minutes and the CTG shows a new rise in baseline with reduced variability. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Remove the pessary, assess the fetus and request urgent obstetric review
Leave the pessary in and recheck contractions and CTG in 30 minutes
Start an oxytocin infusion to make the contractions more effective
Give a second dose of dinoprostone to establish regular labour
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: This is uterine hyperstimulation with fetal heart changes. NICE NG207 1.7.1: carry out a fetal assessment, give no further doses and remove any vaginal pessary or delivery system if possible, and consider tocolysis, which needs urgent obstetric review.

n.1: Leaving the pessary in continues the drug effect while the fetus is showing signs of compromise.
n.2: Oxytocin would increase contraction frequency further and is contraindicated with excessive contractions.
n.3: Further doses would worsen hyperstimulation.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Megan, 27, is 41+4 weeks pregnant and admitted for induction. On vaginal examination her Bishop score is 8 and the fetal head is well applied to the cervix. Which method should be offered?
o: Amniotomy and an intravenous oxytocin infusion
Low-dose oral misoprostol every 2 hours
Vaginal dinoprostone controlled-release pessary
A balloon catheter for 12 hours before amniotomy
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG207 1.3.9: for a Bishop score of more than 6, offer induction with amniotomy and intravenous oxytocin. She can choose whether or when to start oxytocin, knowing that delaying may lengthen labour and may raise the risk of neonatal infection (1.3.10).

n.1: Oral misoprostol is offered for a Bishop score of 6 or less.
n.2: Pharmacological ripening is offered when the Bishop score is 6 or less; her cervix is already favourable.
n.3: Mechanical ripening is for an unfavourable cervix (Bishop score 6 or less).

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Chloe, 26, is 9 weeks pregnant. She has nausea most mornings and vomits once or twice a week. She is drinking well, passing urine normally and working. She would prefer not to take medicines. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Advise her to stop eating until the nausea passes to rest her stomach
Suggest she tries ginger, and explain symptoms usually settle by 16 to 20 weeks
Advise her GP to prescribe an antiemetic, as ginger is unsafe in pregnancy
Refer her to hospital for intravenous fluids to prevent dehydration
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.4.1 and 1.4.3: reassure women that mild to moderate nausea and vomiting are common and likely to resolve before 16 to 20 weeks, and suggest ginger for those with mild to moderate symptoms who prefer a non-pharmacological option.

n.0: Avoiding food is not recommended and risks dehydration and ketosis; small frequent meals are usually advised.
n.2: Ginger is a NICE-suggested option; an antiemetic is offered if she chooses a medicine.
n.3: She is mildly affected and well hydrated, so IV fluids are not indicated.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Amira, 24, is 11 weeks pregnant. She has vomited everything, including water, for 3 days. She feels dizzy on standing, her urine shows 3+ ketones and she has lost 6% of her booking weight. Oral antiemetics from her GP have not helped. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer her the same day to hospital for assessment and intravenous fluids
Ask her GP to change to a different oral antiemetic and review in 3 days
Advise ginger capsules and small frequent meals, with review in a week
Reassure her that vomiting usually resolves by 16 weeks of pregnancy
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Persistent vomiting with dehydration, ketonuria and weight loss over 5% despite oral antiemetics suggests hyperemesis gravidarum. NICE NG201 1.4.6 and 1.4.7: consider intravenous fluids and consider inpatient care if vomiting is severe and not responding to primary care or outpatient management; VTE risk should also be assessed.

n.1: Changing tablets she cannot keep down delays fluid replacement and assessment.
n.2: Ginger is for mild to moderate symptoms; she has signs of dehydration needing urgent treatment.
n.3: Reassurance is for mild to moderate symptoms; her dehydration and weight loss need treatment now.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Lauren, 28, is 30 weeks pregnant. She has a burning feeling behind her breastbone after large meals and when lying down at night. BP is 112/70 mmHg, urinalysis shows no protein, and she has no headache or visual symptoms. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Refer her to the day assessment unit to exclude pre-eclampsia
Ask her GP to arrange an urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
Give lifestyle and diet advice and consider an antacid or alginate
Advise her to stop eating after 4 pm until the baby is born
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: This is typical heartburn with normal BP and urine. NICE NG201 1.4.8 and 1.4.9: give lifestyle and dietary advice and consider a trial of an antacid or alginate.

n.0: Her BP and urine are normal and the pain is typical reflux, so urgent pre-eclampsia assessment is not needed on these facts.
n.1: Endoscopy is not indicated for typical pregnancy heartburn without red flags.
n.3: Fasting from mid-afternoon is not recommended; smaller meals and not eating close to bedtime are the usual advice.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Pooja, 33, is 34 weeks pregnant. She phones saying she has 'bad heartburn' that started this morning: severe pain just below her ribs on the right, not eased by antacids, with a headache. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to attend the maternity unit now for BP, urine and blood tests
Book a GP appointment for this week to review her indigestion
Advise paracetamol for the headache and to sleep propped up on pillows
Advise a stronger alginate and to call back if it persists tomorrow
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Severe pain just below the ribs with headache is a recognised symptom of pre-eclampsia (NICE NG133 1.1.1), which can be mistaken for heartburn. She needs immediate assessment of BP, proteinuria and bloods (platelets, liver and renal function).

n.1: Waiting for a GP appointment delays urgent assessment of pre-eclampsia symptoms.
n.2: Masking the headache delays diagnosis; these symptoms need assessment now.
n.3: Treating as heartburn delays assessment of possible pre-eclampsia or HELLP.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Sophie, 29, is 22 weeks pregnant and has noticed more vaginal discharge than usual. It is thin, white and odourless, with no itching, soreness or pain on passing urine. She is worried something is wrong. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain increased discharge is common and which changes to report
Refer her for a sexual health screen at the local clinic
Offer a vaginal imidazole pessary in case of thrush
Take a high vaginal swab to exclude infection before reassuring her
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: NICE NG201 1.4.10: advise that vaginal discharge is common in pregnancy, but that itching, soreness, an unpleasant smell or pain on passing urine may indicate an infection that needs investigation. A swab is considered when discharge is symptomatic and the cause is in doubt (1.4.11).

n.1: There is nothing to suggest a sexually transmitted infection on these facts.
n.2: Treatment for candidiasis is for women with symptoms of thrush.
n.3: Swabs are considered for symptomatic discharge where the cause is in doubt; hers is asymptomatic.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Rebecca, 31, is 26 weeks pregnant. She has a thick white vaginal discharge with itching and soreness. She has no abdominal pain, fever or urinary symptoms. Which treatment is recommended by NICE?
o: Oral fluconazole as a single 150 mg dose
Oral metronidazole tablets for 7 days
A vaginal imidazole such as clotrimazole
Douching with diluted vinegar daily
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Thick white discharge with itching and soreness suggests vaginal candidiasis. NICE NG201 1.4.13: offer a vaginal imidazole (such as clotrimazole or econazole) to treat vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy.

n.0: Oral antifungals such as fluconazole are avoided in pregnancy; NICE recommends a vaginal imidazole.
n.1: Metronidazole treats bacterial vaginosis, which typically causes thin grey discharge with a fishy odour, not itching.
n.3: Douching is not a recommended treatment and can disturb normal vaginal flora.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Jodie, 30, is 28 weeks pregnant. She has pain over her pubic bone and the backs of her pelvis that is worse when climbing stairs, turning in bed and standing on one leg. She has no bleeding or contractions. What is the most appropriate management?
o: Consider physiotherapy referral for exercise advice or a pelvic belt
Advise strict bed rest until the pain resolves
Advise her to avoid all exercise for the rest of the pregnancy
Refer her for an urgent obstetric review to consider early induction
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: These are typical features of pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain. NICE NG201 1.4.15: consider referral to physiotherapy for exercise advice and/or a non-rigid lumbopelvic belt.

n.1: Bed rest is not recommended and increases VTE risk and deconditioning.
n.2: Appropriate exercise is part of physiotherapy management; avoiding all activity is not advised.
n.3: Pelvic girdle pain is not an indication for early birth; physiotherapy is the first step.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Natalie, 27, is 32 weeks pregnant. She describes intense itching on her palms and the soles of her feet, worse at night, for a week. There is no rash apart from scratch marks. BP and urinalysis are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recommend an emollient and reassure her that itching is due to skin stretching
Arrange blood tests for bile acids and liver function
Advise cool baths and loose cotton clothing, with no further tests
Advise an antihistamine and review at her next routine appointment
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Itching of the palms and soles without a rash in the third trimester suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, which needs bile acid and liver function testing and obstetric review (RCOG Green-top Guideline 43). NHS advice is that itchy palms and soles, often worse at night, need urgent assessment for cholestasis.

n.0: Itching from skin stretching usually affects the abdomen; palm and sole itching without a rash needs investigation.
n.2: Comfort measures alone miss a condition associated with adverse fetal outcomes.
n.3: An antihistamine may ease symptoms but does not exclude cholestasis, which needs testing now.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Priya, 29, is 26 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her haemoglobin at booking was 128 g/L and is now 112 g/L. She is well, eats a varied diet and asks why her result has fallen. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Red cell production in the bone marrow slows during the second trimester
The placenta removes maternal red cells to supply iron to the fetus
Increased red cell breakdown in the spleen shortens their lifespan in pregnancy
Plasma volume rises proportionally more than red cell mass, diluting the haemoglobin
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: In normal pregnancy plasma volume expands by roughly 40 to 50% while red cell mass rises by about 20 to 30%, so haemoglobin concentration falls (physiological haemodilution). A fall to 112 g/L at 26 weeks in a well woman is consistent with this normal adaptation (SPM 3.12.1).

n.0: Red cell mass and erythropoiesis increase in pregnancy under the influence of erythropoietin; they do not slow.
n.1: The placenta transfers iron actively from maternal plasma; it does not take up whole maternal red cells.
n.2: Red cell survival is not shortened in normal pregnancy; the fall reflects dilution, not haemolysis.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Grace, 31, is 34 weeks pregnant. While lying flat on her back for an abdominal examination she says she feels dizzy and sick. She looks pale and her blood pressure has dropped from 118/72 to 92/54 mmHg. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Raise her legs on pillows while she stays flat on her back
Turn her onto her left side to relieve pressure on the inferior vena cava
Ask her to sit fully upright and continue the abdominal palpation
Give her a glass of water and repeat the blood pressure in 30 minutes
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: This is supine hypotension: in late pregnancy the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the woman lies flat, reducing venous return and cardiac output. Turning her to the left lateral position (or a left tilt) relieves aortocaval compression and restores blood pressure (SPM 3.12.1; NICE NG235 1.9.5 notes lying flat reduces BP and placental flow).

n.0: Leg elevation while supine leaves the uterus resting on the vena cava, so the cause of the hypotension continues.
n.2: Sitting up may help, but carrying on with the examination while she is hypotensive delays correction; lateral positioning is the recognised first step.
n.3: Fluids and a delayed recheck leave caval compression in place while she is symptomatic now.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Ellie, 24, is 22 weeks pregnant. She says she feels she needs to breathe more deeply than usual even at rest, but has no cough, chest pain or palpitations. Her respiratory rate is 16, oxygen saturation 99% and pulse 84. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Progesterone increases tidal volume, so she breathes more air with each breath
Her respiratory rate has doubled to meet the oxygen demands of the fetus
The enlarging uterus has already reduced her lung capacity by about half
Oestrogen narrows the airways and increases the effort of breathing
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Progesterone acts on the respiratory centre to increase tidal volume and minute ventilation (respiratory rate changes little), lowering maternal PaCO2 and creating the gradient that clears fetal CO2. Many women notice this as a normal awareness of breathing. Her observations are normal, so no red flags are present (SPM 3.12.1).

n.1: Respiratory rate stays broadly unchanged in pregnancy; her rate of 16 is normal.
n.2: Total lung capacity is only slightly reduced in late pregnancy as the diaphragm rises; it is not halved, and at 22 weeks the effect is small.
n.3: Airway resistance tends to fall in pregnancy because progesterone relaxes smooth muscle; it is not increased by oestrogen.

Antenatal Assessment & Screening.q: Hannah, 27, is 12 weeks pregnant and asks why she has been told to keep moving on long journeys and to report any calf swelling. Which physiological change best explains her higher risk of venous thromboembolism?
o: Platelet counts rise steeply throughout the first trimester
Clotting factors rise and natural anticoagulant activity falls
Plasma volume falls, making the blood more concentrated and viscous
Blood flow in the leg veins speeds up as cardiac output increases
Antenatal Assessment & Screening.w: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state: fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII and X rise, protein S falls and fibrinolysis is reduced, preparing for haemostasis at birth. Combined with venous stasis this raises VTE risk, which is why VTE risk is assessed at booking and after any admission (NICE NG201 1.2.18; SPM 3.12.1).

n.0: Platelet counts usually stay similar or fall slightly in pregnancy; they do not rise steeply.
n.2: Plasma volume increases in pregnancy, which lowers viscosity; it does not fall.
n.3: Venous flow in the legs slows in pregnancy (progesterone and uterine pressure on pelvic veins), which adds to the risk rather than reducing it.

Labour & Birth.q: A student asks the midwife why the fetal head usually enters the pelvis in a transverse or oblique position but is born with the occiput under the symphysis pubis. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: The pelvis is round throughout, so rotation is caused by the mother's position
The head rotates because the cervix pulls the occiput forward as it dilates
The pelvic inlet is widest transversely and the outlet widest anteroposteriorly
The pelvic inlet is widest anteroposteriorly and the outlet widest transversely
Labour & Birth.w: In a gynaecoid pelvis the inlet's widest diameter is transverse, while the outlet's widest diameter is anteroposterior. The head enters in the transverse or oblique diameter and rotates internally on the sloping pelvic floor so its longest diameter fits the outlet (SPM 3.12.2).

n.0: The pelvic diameters change from inlet to outlet; that change, with the pelvic floor, drives rotation.
n.1: Internal rotation is guided by the pelvic floor and pelvic shape, not traction from the cervix.
n.3: This reverses the shape: the inlet is widest transversely and the outlet anteroposteriorly.

Labour & Birth.q: Ruth, 29, is in her first labour. A student midwife notes that the upper part of the uterus feels thicker after each contraction, while the lower part is thin. Which process explains this?
o: Polarity: the lower segment contracts more strongly than the upper
Retraction: upper segment fibres stay shorter after each contraction
Hypertonus: the uterus fails to relax between contractions
Effacement: the upper segment is taken up into the cervix
Labour & Birth.w: Retraction is the progressive, permanent shortening of the muscle fibres of the active upper uterine segment after each contraction. The upper segment thickens and draws up the passive lower segment and cervix, causing effacement and dilatation (SPM 3.12.2).

n.0: Polarity describes the upper segment contracting strongly while the lower segment relaxes; it is not the lower segment contracting more.
n.2: Hypertonus is a contraction lasting 2 minutes or more, an abnormal finding (NICE NG229), not the normal thickening of the upper segment.
n.3: Effacement is the cervix being taken up into the lower segment, not the upper segment entering the cervix.

Labour & Birth.q: Grace, 34, is in her third labour. Her cervix is 4 cm dilated but only partly effaced. A student midwife asks whether this is unusual. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Partial effacement at 4 cm is a sign of obstructed labour
In parous women effacement and dilatation often happen together
Partial effacement at 4 cm means she is still in the latent first stage
In parous women dilatation cannot begin until effacement is complete
Labour & Birth.w: In a first labour the cervix usually effaces before it dilates. In parous women effacement and dilatation commonly occur together, so a partly effaced cervix at 4 cm is normal. NICE defines established first stage as regular contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm (NG235 1.8.1).

n.0: Partial effacement is normal in parous women and is not a sign of obstruction.
n.2: Established labour is defined by regular contractions and progressive dilatation from 4 cm, not by complete effacement.
n.3: Effacement before dilatation is the usual pattern in first labours, not in parous women.

Labour & Birth.q: After the placenta is delivered, Lily, 28, has a firm, well-contracted uterus at the level of the umbilicus and only a small blood loss. A student asks what mainly stops bleeding from the placental site. What is the correct answer?
o: Vasoconstriction of the uterine arteries by circulating adrenaline
Pressure from the full bladder pressing on the placental site
Rapid formation of clot over the placental site by clotting factors
Uterine muscle contraction and retraction compressing the vessels
Labour & Birth.w: The interlacing, oblique fibres of the myometrium contract and retract around the spiral arteries, acting as 'living ligatures'. Clotting helps, but uterine tone is the main mechanism, which is why atony is the commonest cause of PPH (SPM 3.12.3).

n.0: Adrenaline-driven vasoconstriction is not the main way placental site bleeding is controlled.
n.1: A full bladder impedes uterine contraction and increases bleeding risk; it does not compress the placental site.
n.2: Clotting contributes, but without uterine contraction bleeding continues; uterine tone is the main mechanism.

Labour & Birth.q: Holly, 25, is 39+3 weeks pregnant with her first baby and has a low-risk pregnancy. She attends the midwifery-led unit with irregular painful contractions for 6 hours. Her observations and the fetal heart are normal. On examination her cervix is soft, central and 2 cm dilated. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Offer support and analgesia and encourage her to go home with a plan
Admit her to the unit and start a partogram to record her progress
Perform an amniotomy to help establish labour
Transfer her to the obstetric unit for assessment of slow progress
Labour & Birth.w: Holly is in the latent first stage (contractions with cervical change up to 4 cm; NICE NG235 1.8.1). NG235 1.8.6: recognise that latent labour can be painful, offer individualised support and analgesia, and encourage her to remain at or return home unless this risks birth without a midwife or distress.

n.1: The partogram is used once labour is established (NG235 1.8.22), not in the latent phase.
n.2: Amniotomy is not routinely performed when labour is progressing normally (NG235 1.8.39) and is not used to establish labour.
n.3: Latent labour has no time limit for delay; there is no indication for obstetric transfer.

Labour & Birth.q: Eve, 30, is in her second labour at 40 weeks. She is contracting regularly 3 to 4 times in 10 minutes. On vaginal examination her cervix is fully effaced and 5 cm dilated, having been 3 cm 2 hours ago. Which statement about her labour is correct?
o: She is in the latent first stage, as labour starts at full effacement
She is in the second stage, as the cervix is fully effaced
She is in the latent first stage until the cervix reaches 6 cm
She is in the established first stage, and a partogram should be started
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.1: established first stage is regular contractions with progressive cervical dilatation from 4 cm. Use a partogram once labour is established (NG235 1.8.22).

n.0: Effacement alone does not define the stages; the definition is based on regular contractions and dilatation from 4 cm.
n.1: The second stage begins at full dilatation of the cervix, not full effacement (NG235 1.9.1).
n.2: NICE uses 4 cm, not 6 cm, as the start of the established first stage.

Labour & Birth.q: Kat, 28, is 40 weeks pregnant and phones the birth centre at 02:00 because she has had contractions every 8 to 10 minutes for 3 hours. She is coping and her pregnancy is low risk. As part of the telephone triage, which question is most important to include?
o: Whether she has eaten anything in the last 6 hours
Whether her partner is able to drive her in
Whether her baby's movements have changed
Whether she has written a birth plan
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.4: any early or triage assessment of labour should include asking about the baby's movements, including any changes, as well as her wishes and concerns, information about latent labour, and an agreed plan of whom to contact and when. The triage midwife documents the guidance given (1.8.5).

n.0: Food intake is not a key triage question; women can eat a light diet in labour if they wish (NG235 1.8.18).
n.1: Transport is practical, but it does not assess the wellbeing of the woman or baby.
n.3: Birth preferences matter, but they do not identify risk at triage the way a change in movements can.

Labour & Birth.q: Laura, 33, is 39 weeks pregnant. She reports a small gush of fluid an hour ago followed by dampness, but no contractions. The midwife cannot see liquor draining on inspection and is unsure whether the membranes have ruptured. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Perform a digital vaginal examination to feel for intact membranes
Take a lower vaginal swab and measure C-reactive protein
Offer a speculum examination and avoid digital vaginal examination
Advise induction of labour as soon as possible
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.7.4: if it is uncertain whether prelabour rupture of membranes has occurred, offer a speculum examination, and avoid digital vaginal examination in the absence of contractions because of the infection risk. If rupture is certain, a speculum is not needed (1.7.3).

n.0: Digital examination without contractions should be avoided as it increases infection risk.
n.1: NICE advises against lower vaginal swabs and CRP in women with PROM at term (NG235 1.7.8).
n.3: Management choices follow confirmation of rupture; induction is not advised before confirming it.

Labour & Birth.q: Nicola, 29, is 39+2 weeks pregnant. Her membranes ruptured 2 hours ago with clear liquor. She is not contracting, she feels well, her temperature is 36.8 C, the fetal heart is normal and she has no GBS history. Which options should be offered?
o: Immediate induction of labour, as expectant management is unsafe
Expectant management with intravenous antibiotics until labour starts
Expectant management for up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible
Expectant management for up to 72 hours before induction is discussed
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.7.6 and 1.7.7: offer women with PROM at or after 37+0 weeks a choice of expectant management for up to 24 hours or induction as soon as possible, discussing benefits and risks; offer induction if labour has not started after about 24 hours. About 60% go into labour within 24 hours (1.7.5).

n.0: Immediate induction is one choice; expectant management for up to 24 hours is also safe to offer without risk factors.
n.1: Antibiotics are not given without signs of infection or another indication such as GBS.
n.3: NICE offers induction at about 24 hours, not 72 hours, although she may choose to wait longer.

Labour & Birth.q: Bella, 31, has prelabour rupture of membranes at 40 weeks and chooses expectant management at home. Which advice is most appropriate while she waits for labour?
o: Attend daily for a vaginal swab and a C-reactive protein blood test
Take her temperature 4-hourly while awake and report changes in loss
Insert a fresh tampon every 4 hours to monitor the colour of the liquor
Avoid baths and showers, as bathing increases the risk of infection
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.7.8: advise her to record her temperature every 4 hours during waking hours and to report immediately any change in the colour or smell of her vaginal loss; bathing or showering is not associated with increased infection, but sexual intercourse may be. Fetal movements and heart rate are assessed every 24 hours (1.7.9).

n.0: NICE advises against lower vaginal swabs and CRP during expectant management.
n.2: Tampons should not be used after rupture of membranes; a pad allows liquor to be observed.
n.3: Bathing and showering are not associated with an increase in infection.

Labour & Birth.q: Yasmin, 27, is 38+5 weeks pregnant. Group B streptococcus was found on a urine culture at 30 weeks. She phones to say her membranes ruptured 30 minutes ago with clear fluid and she has no contractions. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Wait at home for up to 24 hours, taking oral antibiotics
Attend within 12 hours for a speculum examination
Wait at home for up to 24 hours, then attend for induction
Attend now; immediate induction of labour should be offered
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.7.11 (and NG207 1.2.16): if a woman has PROM at term and a positive GBS test at any time in the current pregnancy, offer immediate induction (or caesarean if planned). Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance. GBS carriage is also a phone triage risk factor needing urgent in-person review (1.7.1).

n.0: Oral antibiotics at home do not replace intrapartum IV prophylaxis and immediate induction.
n.1: The 12-hour review applies to women with no risk factors on phone triage; GBS carriage requires immediate attendance.
n.2: Expectant management for 24 hours is for women without risk factors; GBS positive women are offered immediate induction.

Labour & Birth.q: Faye, 30, gave birth at term 34 hours after her membranes ruptured; labour began 28 hours after rupture. She had no signs of infection and her baby is well at birth. What care does NICE recommend for the baby?
o: Observation at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours, with no routine antibiotics
Admission to the neonatal unit for observation for 24 hours
Blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics for 48 hours
Routine postnatal care, as the baby is well at birth
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.11.31 and 1.11.32: closely observe a baby born to a woman with PROM more than 24 hours before established labour at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours (temperature, heart rate, breathing, colour, perfusion, tone, feeding). If there are no signs of infection, do not give antibiotics to the woman or baby.

n.1: Observation can take place in any setting with the woman; neonatal unit admission is not needed for a well baby.
n.2: Antibiotics and cultures are not given to an asymptomatic baby when there are no signs of infection (1.11.32, 1.11.35).
n.3: Routine care alone misses the recommended observations during the first 12 hours, when infection risk is greatest.

Labour & Birth.q: Martha, 29, is in established labour with her first baby in a midwifery-led unit. Her pregnancy was low risk and she is coping well. Which observation schedule does NICE recommend during the first stage?
o: Contractions half-hourly; pulse hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate 4-hourly
Contractions half-hourly; pulse 4-hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate hourly
Contractions 4-hourly; pulse hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate half-hourly
Contractions hourly; pulse half-hourly; temperature, BP and respiratory rate 2-hourly
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.19: record half-hourly frequency of contractions, hourly pulse, 4-hourly temperature, BP and respiratory rate, and offer 4-hourly vaginal examination. An hourly risk assessment is also carried out (1.8.20) and bladder care reviewed at least every 4 hours (1.8.25).

n.1: Pulse is checked hourly, and temperature, BP and respiratory rate are 4-hourly, not hourly.
n.2: This reverses the frequencies; contractions are documented half-hourly.
n.3: Contractions are recorded half-hourly and pulse hourly; vital signs are 4-hourly, not 2-hourly.

Labour & Birth.q: Toni, 32, is in established labour at a freestanding midwifery unit. Her pulse was 124 beats per minute, and 126 on repeat 20 minutes later. She is drinking and passing urine, her temperature is 37.1 C and the fetal heart is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start intravenous fluids and continue care in the midwifery unit
Arrange transfer to obstetric-led care, explaining the reason to Toni
Continue midwifery-led care, as her temperature is normal
Encourage oral fluids and recheck her pulse in 1 hour
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.20: a maternal pulse over 120 beats per minute on 2 occasions 15 to 30 minutes apart is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care, following the principles in section 1.5 (discuss reasons, obtain consent, arrange transfer as soon as possible).

n.0: Treating the pulse in the midwifery unit does not address the need for obstetric assessment.
n.2: A persistent tachycardia over 120 is a trigger on its own, whatever her temperature.
n.3: Waiting an hour delays action on a recognised transfer criterion that may indicate sepsis or haemorrhage.

Labour & Birth.q: Saskia, 27, is in established labour in an alongside midwifery unit. At 14:00 her temperature is 37.6 C and at 15:00 it is 37.7 C. Her pulse is 98 and the fetal heart is normal. Which action follows NICE guidance?
o: Transfer her to obstetric-led care for review
Give paracetamol and continue midwifery-led care
Recheck her temperature in 4 hours, as it is under 38 C
Recheck in 1 hour and transfer if it reaches 38 C
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.20: a temperature of 38 C or above on a single reading, or 37.5 C or above on 2 consecutive occasions 1 hour apart, is a trigger for transfer to obstetric-led care. Intrapartum antibiotics follow NICE neonatal infection guidance.

n.1: Antipyretics may mask infection and do not replace transfer for review.
n.2: Two consecutive readings of 37.5 C or above 1 hour apart already meet the transfer criterion.
n.3: The 38 C single-reading threshold is not needed when the 37.5 C two-reading criterion is met.

Labour & Birth.q: Ellie, 26, is in her first labour with intact membranes. Four hours ago her cervix was 4 cm dilated; it is now 5 cm. Contractions are 2 in 10 minutes, she is well hydrated and the fetal heart is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Transfer her to obstetric-led care for confirmed delay
Start an oxytocin infusion to increase contraction frequency
Offer support and pain relief and re-examine in 2 hours
Perform an amniotomy now, as delay has been confirmed
Labour & Birth.w: Under 2 cm in 4 hours in a first labour means delay is suspected (NICE NG235 1.8.42). Discuss findings, offer support and pain relief (1.8.41, 1.8.43, 1.8.44) and advise a VE 2 hours later; delay is diagnosed if progress is under 1 cm (1.8.45). Amniotomy is then considered (1.8.46).

n.0: Delay has not yet been diagnosed, so transfer is not indicated on progress alone.
n.1: Oxytocin is considered by an obstetrician after confirmed delay, not as a first step for suspected delay.
n.3: Delay is suspected, not confirmed; amniotomy is considered once delay is diagnosed after the 2-hour re-examination.

Labour & Birth.q: Ruth, 30, is in her first labour in a midwifery-led unit. Delay was suspected 2 hours ago and she has now progressed from 5 cm to 5.5 cm. Her membranes are intact, she and the baby are well, and she has no other risk factors. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start an oxytocin infusion in the midwifery unit and re-examine in 4 hours
Wait another 2 hours before diagnosing delay, as she has made progress
Transfer her to the obstetric unit so that an amniotomy can be performed
Diagnose delay, offer amniotomy in the unit and re-examine 2 hours later
Labour & Birth.w: Progress of under 1 cm in 2 hours confirms delay (NICE NG235 1.8.45). Consider amniotomy after explaining it shortens labour by about an hour and may make contractions stronger (1.8.46). Do not transfer for amniotomy alone (1.8.47); re-examine 2 hours later (1.8.48).

n.0: Oxytocin needs obstetric assessment and is not started in a midwifery-led unit.
n.1: Progress under 1 cm in 2 hours already meets the definition of delay.
n.2: NICE advises not to transfer to obstetric-led care for amniotomy alone.

Labour & Birth.q: Lily, 29, is in a midwifery-led unit. Delay in the first stage was diagnosed and an amniotomy was performed 2 hours ago. On re-examination her cervix has not changed. She is well and the fetal heart is normal. What should happen next?
o: Start an oxytocin infusion in the midwifery unit
Encourage mobilisation and re-examine in 4 hours
Diagnose delay and transfer her to obstetric-led care
Perform a further vaginal examination in another 2 hours
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.49: if there is no progress 2 hours after amniotomy, diagnose delay and transfer to obstetric-led care, where an obstetrician offers a full assessment including consideration of oxytocin (1.8.50).

n.0: Oxytocin is considered by an obstetrician after full assessment of confirmed delay (NG235 1.8.50); it is not started in a midwifery-led unit.
n.1: Waiting a further 4 hours delays obstetric assessment of confirmed delay.
n.3: No progress 2 hours after amniotomy is the point at which delay is diagnosed and transfer is made.

Labour & Birth.q: Sian, 31, is on an oxytocin infusion for delay in the first stage. The CTG has just been categorised as pathological by the midwife and the coordinator. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Increase the oxytocin to achieve 5 contractions in 10 minutes
Reduce the oxytocin rate by half and recheck the CTG in 30 minutes
Stop the oxytocin and seek urgent obstetric review
Continue the oxytocin, as contractions are not more than 4 in 10
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.56: oxytocin must be discontinued immediately if the CTG is pathological, and urgent obstetrician or senior midwife review sought. It may be restarted after review if the CTG is no longer pathological and the woman agrees (1.8.57).

n.0: The aim is 3 to 4 contractions in 10; more than 4 is excessive and harmful with a pathological trace.
n.1: Reducing the dose is the response to more than 4 contractions in 10 (1.8.55); a pathological CTG needs oxytocin stopped.
n.3: A pathological CTG requires oxytocin to stop whatever the contraction frequency.

Labour & Birth.q: Amy, 34, is in her third labour without an epidural. She has been actively pushing for 1 hour. The head has descended but birth is not imminent. She and the baby are well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer for senior review and a decision on place and mode of birth
Start an oxytocin infusion to strengthen her contractions
Perform an episiotomy to shorten the second stage
Encourage her to continue pushing for another hour before review
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.9.26: for a multiparous woman without an epidural, birth is expected within 2 hours of the start of active second stage; reassess after 30 minutes of pushing, and if birth is not imminent after 1 hour of pushing, refer for senior review and a decision on place and mode of birth.

n.1: Oxytocin in the second stage follows in-person obstetric assessment (1.9.31), not as a midwife's first step.
n.2: Routine episiotomy is not recommended (1.9.16); it is performed for clinical need such as fetal compromise.
n.3: Waiting another hour before review applies to nulliparous women (senior review if not imminent after 2 hours of pushing).

Labour & Birth.q: Jo, 28, is in established first stage of labour at a birth centre. She has a low-risk pregnancy and has chosen intermittent auscultation. How should the midwife carry out and record intermittent auscultation?
o: Listen between contractions for 15 seconds, every 5 minutes, as a range
Listen after a contraction for 1 minute, every 30 minutes, as a single rate
Listen during a contraction for 30 seconds, every 15 minutes, as a range
Listen after a contraction for 1 minute, every 15 minutes, as one rate
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG229 1.2.9: in established first stage, auscultate immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, at least every 15 minutes, recording a single rate and any accelerations or decelerations, and palpate the maternal pulse hourly (or more often if concerned).

n.0: Every 5 minutes is the second-stage frequency, and 15 seconds is too short to detect decelerations.
n.1: In the first stage, auscultation is at least every 15 minutes, not every 30.
n.2: Auscultation is done immediately after a contraction for at least 1 minute and recorded as a single rate.

Labour & Birth.q: Kim, 31, has a low-risk labour and is now actively pushing in the second stage. The midwife is using intermittent auscultation with a handheld Doppler. Which approach is correct?
o: Auscultate after a contraction for 1 minute at least every 15 minutes, palpating her pulse
Auscultate during every contraction and record the lowest rate heard
Auscultate every 10 minutes and check her pulse once an hour
Auscultate after a contraction for 1 minute at least every 5 minutes, palpating her pulse
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG229 1.2.10: in the second stage, auscultate immediately after a palpated contraction for at least 1 minute, at least every 5 minutes, recording a single rate, and palpate the woman's pulse simultaneously to differentiate maternal and fetal heart rates.

n.0: Every 15 minutes is the first-stage frequency; the second stage needs at least every 5 minutes.
n.1: Auscultation is performed after the contraction and recorded as a single rate.
n.2: Every 10 minutes is too infrequent, and the maternal pulse should be palpated at the same time in the second stage.

Labour & Birth.q: Nina, 29, is in established labour with intermittent auscultation. At the start of labour the fetal heart rate was 125 beats per minute. Three hours later the rate after contractions is consistently 148, with no decelerations heard. Her temperature is 37.2 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start continuous CTG immediately and transfer without further review
Auscultate more often and carry out a full review of the clinical picture
Give intravenous fluids, as a rising fetal heart rate means dehydration
Continue auscultation every 15 minutes, as 148 is within the normal range
Labour & Birth.w: A rise of 20 beats per minute or more from the start of labour is significant even within 110 to 160. NICE NG229 1.2.11: auscultate more frequently (for example after 3 consecutive contractions) and carry out a full review of risk factors, maternal observations, contractions and progress. If concerns are confirmed, advise continuous CTG and transfer (1.2.12).

n.0: CTG is advised if concerns are confirmed after review; NICE first asks for more frequent auscultation and a full review.
n.2: IV fluids are not given for fetal heart rate changes unless the woman is hypotensive or septic (NG229 1.5.11).
n.3: A rise of 23 beats per minute is a concern even though the rate is under 160; it may indicate infection or hypoxia.

Labour & Birth.q: Ola, 33, is on continuous CTG in established labour. Contractions are 4 in 10 minutes, the baseline is 140 beats per minute and there are no decelerations. Variability has been 3 to 4 beats per minute for the last 40 minutes. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Suspicious
Normal
Need for urgent intervention
Pathological
Labour & Birth.w: Variability under 5 beats per minute for 30 to 50 minutes is an amber feature (NICE NG229 1.4.18). Contractions, baseline and decelerations are white. One amber feature makes the CTG suspicious (NG229 1.4.32), prompting a full risk assessment and conservative measures.

n.1: A normal CTG has all four features white; reduced variability for 40 minutes is amber.
n.2: NG229 uses normal, suspicious and pathological; this is not one of its categories.
n.3: Pathological needs one red feature or two or more amber features; there is one amber feature.

Labour & Birth.q: Pria, 30, has a CTG in labour showing contractions 4 in 10 minutes, a baseline of 105 beats per minute, variability under 5 beats per minute for 35 minutes, and no decelerations. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Suspicious
Normal
Suspicious, becoming pathological at 50 minutes
Pathological
Labour & Birth.w: A baseline of 100 to 109 is amber, and variability under 5 for 30 to 50 minutes is amber (NICE NG229 1.4.15, 1.4.18). Two or more amber features make the CTG pathological (NG229 1.4.32), needing urgent review by an obstetrician and senior midwife (1.5.7).

n.0: Suspicious means exactly one amber feature; there are two.
n.1: A normal CTG has all four features white.
n.2: Two amber features already make the trace pathological; it does not wait for variability to become red.

Labour & Birth.q: Rhian, 27, is on continuous CTG in labour. The baseline is 135, variability is 10 beats per minute and contractions are 3 in 10. For the last 15 minutes there have been late decelerations with each contraction. How should the CTG be categorised?
o: Pathological, needing urgent obstetric and senior midwife review
Suspicious, needing review if they continue for 30 minutes
Normal, as baseline and variability are reassuring
Suspicious, as the decelerations have lasted under 30 minutes
Labour & Birth.w: Late decelerations are a red feature regardless of how long they have been present (NICE NG229 1.4.24, amended 2025). Any red feature makes the CTG pathological (1.4.32), requiring urgent review by an obstetrician and senior midwife, exclusion of acute events and conservative measures (1.5.7).

n.1: Late decelerations are red at any duration, so the trace is already pathological.
n.2: Reassuring baseline and variability do not offset a red feature.
n.3: The 30-minute timing applies to variable decelerations with concerning characteristics, not late decelerations.

Labour & Birth.q: Sadie, 32, is in established labour with no oxytocin. The CTG suddenly shows the fetal heart rate fall to 80 beats per minute, and it has stayed there for 3 minutes. There is no cord visible and no bleeding. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start intravenous fluids to correct presumed dehydration and recheck in 15 minutes
Give facial oxygen by mask and continue to observe the CTG for 10 minutes
Seek urgent obstetric review, start conservative measures and prepare for urgent birth
Call for obstetric review if the bradycardia is still present at 9 minutes
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG229 1.5.9: for an acute bradycardia or a prolonged deceleration of 3 minutes or more, urgently seek obstetric review, expedite birth if there is an acute event, start conservative measures (such as position change), prepare for urgent birth with neonatal support, and expedite birth if the bradycardia persists for 9 minutes (or sooner with risk factors).

n.0: IV fluids are not given for fetal heart rate abnormalities unless the woman is hypotensive or septic (NG229 1.5.11).
n.1: Maternal facial oxygen is not offered as a conservative measure because it may harm the baby (NG229 1.5.12).
n.3: 9 minutes is when birth should be expedited; obstetric review is sought immediately.

Labour & Birth.q: Tilly, 29, was started on CTG during labour in a midwifery-led unit because a deceleration was heard on intermittent auscultation. She has no other risk factors. After 20 minutes the CTG is categorised as normal. What should happen next?
o: Continue CTG for a further 2 hours before deciding
Continue the CTG until the birth, as a deceleration was heard
Return to intermittent auscultation, unless she prefers CTG
Transfer her to obstetric-led care for continuous monitoring
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG229 1.2.13: return to intermittent auscultation if continuous CTG was started because of concerns from IA but the trace is normal after 20 minutes, unless the woman decides to remain on CTG.

n.0: NICE uses 20 minutes of normal CTG, not 2 hours, before returning to IA.
n.1: A normal CTG after 20 minutes with no risk factors allows a return to IA.
n.3: Transfer is not needed when the concern has resolved and there are no risk factors.

Labour & Birth.q: Hana, 27, is in the latent first stage of her first labour at home. She is finding contractions painful and asks the midwife what might help at this stage. Which advice is supported by NICE?
o: Intramuscular diamorphine so that she can rest at home
Breathing exercises, a warm shower or bath, and massage
Lidocaine spray to numb the perineum during contractions
Aromatherapy oils, yoga positions and acupressure
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.3: advise that breathing exercises, a shower or bath, and massage may reduce pain in the latent first stage. NG235 1.6.4 advises not to offer aromatherapy, yoga or acupressure for latent-phase pain (though her choice to use them is supported).

n.0: Opioids at home in the latent phase are not the NICE-advised first step and carry maternal and neonatal side effects.
n.2: Lidocaine spray is not offered for labour pain (NG235 1.9.15 advises against it in the second stage) and does not relieve contraction pain.
n.3: NICE advises not to offer or advise aromatherapy, yoga or acupressure for latent-phase pain relief.

Labour & Birth.q: Leah, 30, is labouring in a birthing pool at a midwifery-led unit. Her pregnancy is low risk. Which monitoring is required while she is in the water?
o: Check the water temperature hourly, keeping it at or above 38 C for comfort
Check her temperature 4-hourly and the water temperature once at the start
Check the water temperature every 4 hours, keeping it between 38 and 39 C
Check both temperatures hourly, keeping water at or below 37.5 C
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.11: for women labouring in water, monitor the temperature of the woman and the water hourly to ensure she is comfortable and not becoming pyrexial; the water should not be above 37.5 C.

n.0: Water at 38 C or above exceeds the NICE limit of 37.5 C.
n.1: Both her temperature and the water temperature need hourly checks.
n.2: Water above 37.5 C risks maternal pyrexia and fetal tachycardia; checks must be hourly.

Labour & Birth.q: Fiona, 29, received intramuscular diamorphine for pain in established labour 1 hour ago. She now feels alert and asks to get into the birthing pool. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Help her into the pool and keep the water at 38 C to aid relaxation
Help her into the pool now, as she feels alert
Explain the pool is unsuitable for the rest of labour after any opioid
Explain she should wait until 2 hours after the opioid before entering water
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.20: women should not enter water within 2 hours of opioid administration or if they feel drowsy, because of sedation and the risk of drowning. Water temperature should not exceed 37.5 C (1.6.11).

n.0: The 2-hour rule still applies, and 38 C exceeds the 37.5 C limit.
n.1: Feeling alert does not override the 2-hour rule after opioids.
n.2: After 2 hours, if she is not drowsy, she can enter the water; it is not excluded for the rest of labour.

Labour & Birth.q: Ruby, 31, is in established labour in an obstetric unit and asks for pethidine. The midwife explains its effects and Ruby consents. Under NICE intrapartum guidance, what else should be given with the intramuscular opioid?
o: Continuous oxygen by face mask
An antiemetic
Naloxone, to prevent respiratory depression
Intravenous fluids
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.19: if an intravenous or intramuscular opioid is used, also administer an antiemetic. She should be told opioids give limited pain relief and may cause drowsiness, nausea and vomiting, and neonatal respiratory depression that may affect breastfeeding (1.6.18).

n.0: Routine oxygen is not part of opioid administration.
n.2: Naloxone reverses opioid effects when respiratory depression occurs; it is not given routinely alongside the opioid.
n.3: IV fluids are not routinely needed with an IM opioid.

Labour & Birth.q: Grace, 26, is in established labour and is considering an epidural. She has heard that it causes long-term backache and makes a caesarean more likely. Which information is accurate?
o: It lengthens the first stage of labour and is less effective than opioids
It causes long-term backache but does not affect the second stage of labour
It is not linked to long-term backache but is linked to more forceps or ventouse births
It increases the chance of an unplanned caesarean birth and shortens the second stage
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.26: epidural gives more effective pain relief than opioids; it is not associated with long-term backache, a longer first stage or an increased chance of unplanned caesarean birth; it is associated with a longer second stage and an increased chance of forceps or ventouse birth.

n.0: Epidural is not associated with a longer first stage and is more effective than opioids.
n.1: Epidural is not associated with long-term backache, and it does lengthen the second stage.
n.3: Epidural is not associated with more unplanned caesarean births and is associated with a longer, not shorter, second stage.

Labour & Birth.q: Zoe, 33, has just received a 10 mL top-up of low-dose epidural solution in established labour. Which observations should the midwife carry out?
o: BP every 15 minutes for 1 hour and intermittent auscultation every 15 minutes
Pulse every 30 minutes and CTG for 10 minutes after the top-up
BP once after 30 minutes and a check of the sensory block after 4 hours
BP every 5 minutes for 15 minutes and continuous CTG for at least 30 minutes
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.30 and 1.6.36: after establishing regional analgesia or after boluses of 10 mL or more, measure BP every 5 minutes for 15 minutes and perform continuous CTG for at least 30 minutes. Sensory block is assessed hourly.

n.0: BP is measured every 5 minutes for the first 15 minutes, and continuous CTG is needed for at least 30 minutes.
n.1: These checks are too infrequent and too short to detect hypotension and fetal heart changes.
n.2: A single BP at 30 minutes would miss early hypotension, and sensory block is checked hourly.

Labour & Birth.q: Amy, 28, had an epidural top-up 30 minutes ago. She still feels strong pain with contractions on her left side. Her BP is 118/72 mmHg and the CTG is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise her to wait another hour for the top-up to work
Remove the epidural catheter and offer Entonox
Ask the anaesthetist to review the epidural
Give a further bolus from the epidural pump yourself
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.30: if the woman is not pain-free 30 minutes after each administration of local anaesthetic or opioid solution, ask the anaesthetist to review. An epidural may need adjusting or replacing (1.6.26).

n.0: Waiting another hour delays review; NICE sets 30 minutes as the trigger.
n.1: Removing the catheter is an anaesthetic decision; the block may be fixable by adjustment.
n.3: Extra boluses outside the prescribed regimen are not given without anaesthetic review of an inadequate block.

Labour & Birth.q: Esther, 30, is in established labour with severe lower back pain. The baby is in an occipito-posterior position. She does not want an epidural or opioids. The midwife is trained in sterile water injections. Which information about this option is accurate?
o: A single injection into the lumbar spine gives pain relief for the rest of labour
The injections are painless and relieve contraction pain at the front of the abdomen
Injections are given into each buttock and relieve pain within 1 minute
Four injections around the Rhombus of Michaelis may ease back pain for up to 3 hours
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.14 to 1.6.16: consider intracutaneous or subcutaneous sterile water injections for back pain in labour, given at 4 points around the Rhombus of Michaelis (0.1 mL intracutaneously or 0.5 mL subcutaneously). Relief starts from about 10 minutes and lasts up to 3 hours; there is initial stinging.

n.0: The technique uses four superficial injections, and relief lasts up to about 3 hours, not the whole labour.
n.1: There is an initial stinging sensation, and the injections target back pain.
n.2: Injections are given around the Rhombus of Michaelis, and relief starts after about 10 minutes.

Labour & Birth.q: Sophie, 28, is in established labour in a midwifery-led unit and is coping well with her partner present. The unit is busy and her midwife is asked to help another woman for 40 minutes. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Leave Sophie with the call bell and check on her every 15 minutes
Stay with Sophie and ask the coordinator to find support elsewhere
Ask a maternity support worker to stay with Sophie while she is away
Leave Sophie with her partner, as a birth companion is present
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.4.5 and 1.4.6: services should support one-to-one care in labour, and a woman in established labour should not be left alone except for short periods or at her request. Escalating staffing pressure to the coordinator is the appropriate response.

n.0: Leaving her for 40 minutes with periodic checks is not one-to-one care.
n.2: A support worker cannot provide the midwifery care, assessment and monitoring needed in established labour.
n.3: A birth companion does not replace one-to-one midwifery care in established labour.

Labour & Birth.q: Rosa, 30, is in established labour without an epidural. She has been lying flat on her back on the bed because she thought this was expected. What should the midwife advise about positions?
o: Lie on her back with her knees bent, as this opens the pelvis
Stay on the bed in a semi-recumbent position for monitoring
Use any position she finds comfortable, except lying flat on her back
Kneel on all fours throughout labour, as this is the best position
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.4.12: encourage and help the woman to move and adopt whatever positions she finds most comfortable throughout labour, except lying flat on her back. Lying flat reduces BP and placental blood flow (1.9.6), and upright, mobile positions may help (1.9.6).

n.0: Lying flat on her back is the position NICE advises against.
n.1: Restricting her to the bed is not needed in a low-risk labour and limits mobility.
n.3: No single position is mandated; she chooses what is comfortable.

Labour & Birth.q: Isla, 26, is in established labour. Her mother has told her to drink at least a litre of water every hour to keep her strength up. Which advice about drinking in labour is most accurate?
o: Avoid all fluids, as drinking increases the risk of aspiration
Drink plain water, as isotonic drinks raise the risk of hyponatraemia
Drink at least a litre an hour to prevent dehydration and ketosis
Drink when thirsty, as excess fluid can cause harm
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.17 and 1.8.26 (updated 2025): drink when thirsty; isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; there is no benefit to drinking more than normal, and excessive oral or IV fluid can cause hyponatraemia (sodium under 130 mmol/L), with maternal and neonatal seizures or death.

n.0: Women should drink in labour when thirsty; fluid restriction is not advised.
n.1: Isotonic drinks may be more beneficial than water; excess water is the hyponatraemia risk.
n.2: Drinking a litre an hour risks fluid overload and hyponatraemia.

Labour & Birth.q: Nadia, 31, is in established labour in an alongside midwifery unit. Her fluid balance chart shows a positive balance of 1,600 mL. She has a headache and feels nauseated. Her BP is 116/72 mmHg. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage her to drink an isotonic sports drink and recheck in 1 hour
Explain possible hyponatraemia, seek obstetric review, offer sodium test
Offer paracetamol for the headache and continue the fluid chart
Start intravenous fluids to treat her nausea and continue midwifery care
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.28: with a positive fluid balance of 1,500 mL or more, or clinical concerns such as signs of hyponatraemia, explain she may be developing hyponatraemia, request an obstetric review, offer a blood test for sodium and advise transfer to an obstetric setting from a midwifery-led setting.

n.0: More oral fluid adds to a positive balance when hyponatraemia is possible.
n.2: Headache and nausea may be signs of hyponatraemia; treating symptoms alone delays assessment.
n.3: IV fluids could worsen hyponatraemia and she needs obstetric review and transfer.

Labour & Birth.q: Leila, 29, is in established labour and has not passed urine for 4 hours. She has been drinking well and says she cannot feel any need to pass urine. Her bladder is palpable above the symphysis. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait until after the birth, as bladder sensation returns then
Encourage her to drink more to stimulate her to pass urine
Start fluid balance monitoring and offer to insert a catheter
Reduce her oral fluids and recheck her bladder in 4 hours
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.25 and 1.8.27: review bladder care at least every 4 hours, including frequency of passing urine and bladder sensation; monitor fluid balance if sensation is abnormal or she cannot pass urine; offer a catheter if there are ongoing concerns about her ability to pass urine. A full bladder can impede descent and damage the bladder.

n.0: Leaving a distended bladder risks overdistension injury and can delay progress.
n.1: Extra fluid adds to bladder distension and hyponatraemia risk.
n.3: Restricting fluids does not empty a full bladder and the next review would be too late.

Labour & Birth.q: Megan, 27, is in established labour in a low-risk setting. She has not had opioids and has no risk factors that make a caesarean birth more likely. She says she is hungry. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: She can eat a light diet if she wishes
She should eat a large meal to keep up her energy
She may drink water but must not eat anything
She should be nil by mouth until after the birth
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.18: inform the woman that she can eat a light diet in established labour if she wishes, unless she has received opioids or develops risk factors that make a caesarean birth more likely.

n.1: NICE refers to a light diet, not a large meal.
n.2: Restricting her to water is unnecessary; a light diet is acceptable.
n.3: Nil by mouth is not needed for a low-risk woman without opioids or caesarean risk factors.

Labour & Birth.q: Hollie, 25, is in established labour in a birth room with her partner. She wants a calm, private environment. Which action by the midwife best supports this?
o: Knocking and waiting before entering, and asking others to do the same
Asking her partner to wait outside during each vaginal examination
Turning on the main lights so that her colour can be observed
Keeping the door open so staff can see her progress from the corridor
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.4.11: respect the woman's personal space, privacy and dignity, and ask others to do the same, for example by knocking and waiting before entering. A calm, private environment supports oxytocin release and physiological labour (SPM 3.24).

n.1: Her birth companion of choice should be supported to stay (NG235 1.4.13) unless she asks otherwise.
n.2: Bright lighting is not needed for routine observation and can disturb a calm environment.
n.3: An open door undermines privacy and dignity.

Labour & Birth.q: Chantelle, 30, is in established labour progressing at 1 cm an hour with intact membranes. She and the baby are well. A student midwife suggests an amniotomy to speed labour up. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree, as amniotomy should be done at 6 cm in every labour
Explain intervention is not advised when labour is progressing well
Suggest starting oxytocin as a gentler alternative to amniotomy
Agree, as amniotomy reduces the risk of infection in labour
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.8.37 and 1.8.39: do not offer or advise clinical intervention if labour is progressing with no complications and the woman and baby are well, and do not routinely perform amniotomy in that situation.

n.0: There is no routine amniotomy at any dilatation in a normally progressing labour.
n.2: Oxytocin is for confirmed delay after obstetric review, not normal labour.
n.3: Amniotomy does not reduce infection risk; ruptured membranes can increase it.

Labour & Birth.q: Abbie, 29, is in the active second stage of her first labour on a birthing stool. The baby's head is starting to distend her perineum. She has asked for help to reduce her chance of a tear. Which measure does NICE recommend offering?
o: A routine episiotomy as the head distends the perineum
A warm, wet compress on the perineum until the birth
Lidocaine spray to the perineum as the head crowns
Fundal pressure to shorten the time the perineum is stretched
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.9.13: once the presenting part distends the perineum, offer a warm wet compress and continue until birth, checking it is a comfortable temperature (not for births in water). Perineal massage with a water-soluble lubricant may be considered if she prefers (1.9.14).

n.0: Routine episiotomy is not performed during spontaneous vaginal birth (NG235 1.9.16).
n.2: NICE advises not to offer lidocaine spray in the second stage (NG235 1.9.15).
n.3: Fundal pressure is not a recommended technique to reduce perineal trauma and can cause harm.

Labour & Birth.q: Dee, 31, is having a spontaneous vaginal birth. The fetal heart has been normal throughout. The midwife needs to perform an episiotomy because the perineum is rigid and not stretching after a long second stage. What must happen before the incision?
o: Wait for the next contraction to reduce pain from the incision
Perform a rectal examination to check the anal sphincter
Obtain written consent signed by Dee and her partner
Confirm that tested, effective analgesia is in place
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.9.23: provide tested, effective analgesia before an episiotomy, except in an emergency because of acute fetal compromise. If performed, it should be mediolateral from the fourchette, usually to the right, at 45 to 60 degrees to the vertical at the time of the cut (1.9.21).

n.0: Timing the cut with a contraction does not replace the need for tested, effective analgesia.
n.1: Rectal examination is part of the systematic assessment after birth, not a prerequisite for episiotomy.
n.2: Verbal informed consent is required, but written consent is not the standard for episiotomy.

Labour & Birth.q: Lauren, 33, had a third-degree tear in her first birth, repaired with a good recovery and no continence symptoms. She is now 36 weeks and asks whether she will need an episiotomy and how likely another severe tear is. Which response is accurate?
o: An episiotomy will be performed to protect the repaired sphincter
A planned caesarean birth is required after any third-degree tear
No routine episiotomy, and her risk of a repeat severe tear is not raised
Her risk of a repeat severe tear is raised, so an episiotomy is advised
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.9.17 and 1.9.18: inform a woman with previous severe perineal trauma that her risk of repeat severe trauma is not increased compared with women having their first baby, and do not offer episiotomy routinely after previous third- or fourth-degree trauma. Mode of birth is discussed considering symptoms and previous repair (1.9.19).

n.0: Routine episiotomy is not recommended after previous third-degree trauma.
n.1: Caesarean is not required; mode of birth is an informed choice considering her symptoms and history.
n.3: NICE states the risk of repeat severe trauma is not increased compared with a first birth.

Labour & Birth.q: After a spontaneous birth, the midwife assesses Kemi's perineum with good lighting and analgesia. The tear involves the perineal muscles and about 60% of the thickness of the external anal sphincter. The internal anal sphincter and anal mucosa are intact. How is this tear classified?
o: Third degree, 3b
Fourth degree
Third degree, 3c
Third degree, 3a
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.12.3: 3a is less than 50% of external anal sphincter thickness torn; 3b is more than 50% of EAS thickness torn; 3c involves the internal anal sphincter; fourth degree involves both sphincters and the anal epithelium.

n.1: A fourth-degree tear involves the anal epithelium, which is intact.
n.2: 3c requires a tear of the internal anal sphincter, which is intact.
n.3: 3a is less than 50% of the external sphincter thickness; this tear is 60%.

Labour & Birth.q: Nisha, 27, has just had a spontaneous vaginal birth. On visual inspection there appears to be a small tear involving the skin and perineal muscle. She is comfortable and has good analgesia. What should the midwife's systematic assessment include before classifying the tear?
o: A careful visual inspection, as the tear looks second degree
A rectal examination, with consent, to check the anal sphincters
A rectal examination after the repair is completed
A speculum examination of the cervix as the first step
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.12.5 and 1.12.7: offer all women systematic assessment including a rectal examination to exclude all genital tract trauma, including buttonhole tears and sphincter injury, with explanation, consent and tested analgesia, before repair.

n.0: Visual inspection alone can miss anal sphincter injury and buttonhole tears.
n.2: Assessment must happen before repair so that sphincter injury is identified and repaired correctly.
n.3: Cervical inspection is not the first step of perineal assessment and does not assess the sphincters.

Labour & Birth.q: Amal, 25, is in early established labour with her first baby. She has type 3 FGM (infibulation) and no deinfibulation was performed antenatally. Which information should the midwife give her?
o: A caesarean birth is needed because vaginal birth is unsafe with infibulation
Reinfibulation will be offered after the birth if she requests it
Infibulation does not affect labour, so no special plan is needed
Examinations may be difficult and deinfibulation may be needed in labour
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.9.20: inform women with infibulated FGM of the risks of difficulty with vaginal examination, catheterisation and fetal scalp electrode application, and of delay in the second stage and spontaneous laceration, with the possible need for deinfibulation in labour.

n.0: Infibulation is managed with deinfibulation; it is not of itself an indication for caesarean birth.
n.1: Reinfibulation after birth counts as FGM, so it is unlawful (Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003 in England, Wales and Northern Ireland; the 2005 Act in Scotland) and must not be offered.
n.2: Infibulation affects examinations and the second stage, so a plan is needed.

Labour & Birth.q: Ellen, 30, is having her first baby with an effective epidural. Her cervix is fully dilated, she has no urge to push, the head is not visible and the CTG is normal. What should the midwife advise?
o: Delay pushing for up to 4 hours to allow the head to descend fully
Delay pushing for up to 2 hours unless she gets an urge or the head shows
Start an oxytocin infusion to help bring on an urge to push
Start directed pushing now to avoid a prolonged active second stage
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.6.34 and 1.9.9: with regional analgesia, pushing may be delayed up to 2 hours for nulliparous women (1 hour for multiparous) after full dilatation unless she has an urge to push or the head is visible. Oxytocin is not routinely used in the second stage with an epidural (1.6.35).

n.0: The passive second stage with an epidural is up to 2 hours, not 4.
n.2: Oxytocin is not used routinely in the second stage for women with regional analgesia.
n.3: Delayed directed pushing may shorten the active second stage for nulliparous women with an epidural.

Labour & Birth.q: Bryony, 28, has just had a ventouse birth with an episiotomy. The baby is well. Under NICE intrapartum guidance, which medicine should be offered to reduce her risk of infection?
o: A single dose of IV co-amoxiclav before the ventouse is applied
Oral co-amoxiclav for 7 days starting on day 1
No antibiotics unless she develops a fever
A single dose of IV co-amoxiclav within 6 hours of cord clamping
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.9.43: offer women who have had a birth with forceps or ventouse a single dose of intravenous co-amoxiclav (or a locally agreed alternative if allergic to penicillin) within 6 hours after cord clamping.

n.0: The dose is given after cord clamping, within 6 hours, not before the procedure.
n.1: NICE recommends a single IV dose, not a 7-day oral course.
n.2: Prophylaxis is recommended after assisted birth, not withheld until fever develops.

Labour & Birth.q: Tara, 32, has pre-eclampsia treated with labetalol and has just given birth vaginally. She chose active management of the third stage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate?
o: Ergometrine 500 micrograms by intravenous injection
Carbetocin by slow intravenous injection
Oxytocin 10 units by intramuscular injection
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
Labour & Birth.w: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease (NICE NG235 1.10.9). Oxytocin 10 units IM given after the birth of the baby, before cord clamping, is appropriate (1.10.11).

n.0: Ergometrine raises blood pressure and is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia by any route.
n.1: NICE recommends carbetocin for women having a caesarean birth (1.10.13), not after vaginal birth.
n.3: Ergometrine-containing preparations are contraindicated in pre-eclampsia because they raise blood pressure.

Labour & Birth.q: Mei, 36, has just had a vaginal birth after a long labour augmented with oxytocin. She had a 1,200 mL PPH in her last pregnancy. Her BP is 118/74 mmHg and she has no cardiac, liver or kidney disease. She has chosen active management. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Carbetocin IV, as it is the first choice after any vaginal birth
Physiological management to avoid uterotonic side effects
Oxytocin 10 units IM, as ergometrine is reserved for treatment
Oxytocin plus ergometrine IM, with an antiemetic
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.10.9 and 1.10.10: oxytocin plus ergometrine may be more effective than oxytocin alone and is advised when there are risk factors for PPH (here previous PPH and augmented, prolonged labour), unless contraindicated; offer an antiemetic such as cyclizine because of nausea and vomiting.

n.0: Carbetocin is recommended for prevention of PPH at caesarean birth, not vaginal birth.
n.1: She has chosen active management, which lowers PPH risk; physiological management would increase her risk.
n.2: Oxytocin alone is less effective; with PPH risk factors and no contraindication, oxytocin plus ergometrine is advised.
