Labour & Birth.q: Jess, 27, has just given birth. The baby cried at birth, has good tone and a heart rate over 100, and is skin to skin. Jess has chosen active management. When should the cord be clamped?
o: No earlier than 1 minute after birth, and before 5 minutes for traction
After the cord stops pulsating, then give the uterotonic
Immediately after the uterotonic is given, to allow cord traction
No earlier than 10 minutes after birth, to maximise placental transfusion
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.10.14: after the uterotonic, do not clamp the cord earlier than 1 minute after birth unless there is concern about cord integrity or the baby's heart rate is below 60 and not increasing; clamp before 5 minutes to perform controlled cord traction, and support a request for later clamping.

n.1: Waiting for pulsation to stop is part of physiological management; in active management the uterotonic is given before clamping.
n.2: Immediate clamping is not recommended for a well baby; wait at least 1 minute.
n.3: In active management the cord is clamped before 5 minutes for controlled cord traction unless she requests otherwise.

Labour & Birth.q: Ana, 30, has had a straightforward birth and chose active management. She received IM oxytocin when the baby was born. At 3 minutes the cord is clamped and cut. The uterus is soft and the cord has not lengthened. When should controlled cord traction begin?
o: At the next contraction, whether or not separation has occurred
Immediately after the cord is cut, to speed up the third stage
After signs of separation, such as cord lengthening and a gush of blood
After 30 minutes, if the placenta has not delivered spontaneously
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.10.15: perform controlled cord traction as part of active management only after oxytocin and signs of placental separation (lengthening of the cord, a small gush of blood, the uterus becoming firm and rising). Traction before separation risks cord snapping or uterine inversion.

n.0: Contractions alone do not show separation; traction waits for signs of separation.
n.1: Traction before separation risks cord avulsion or uterine inversion.
n.3: 30 minutes is when a prolonged third stage is diagnosed in active management, not the timing of traction.

Labour & Birth.q: Emma, 26, is low risk and asks for a physiological third stage after a spontaneous birth at home. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree, and explain that there is no difference in bleeding risk
Explain that active management is required after every home birth
Agree, and give a uterotonic before clamping the cord
Discuss her level of risk, support her choice and document the decision
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.10.6 to 1.10.8: advise that active management is associated with a lower risk of PPH and transfusion; if she requests physiological management, discuss her level of risk so she can make an informed decision, support her choice and document it.

n.0: Active management is associated with a lower risk of PPH and transfusion, so this would be inaccurate information.
n.1: Physiological management is a valid choice for a woman at low risk, in any setting.
n.2: Physiological management involves no routine uterotonic; giving one before clamping is active management.

Labour & Birth.q: Gemma, 29, chose a physiological third stage at a birth centre. One hour after the birth the placenta has not delivered. Her blood loss is 250 mL and her observations are normal. What should the midwife advise?
o: Manual removal of the placenta in the birth centre
Controlled cord traction without a uterotonic
Continue to wait, as physiological third stage has no time limit
A change to active management
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.10.17 and 1.10.20: advise a change from physiological to active management if there is haemorrhage or the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour of birth. A third stage over 60 minutes with physiological management is prolonged.

n.0: Manual removal needs anaesthesia and is not done in a birth centre (NG235 1.10.28).
n.1: Controlled cord traction is performed after a uterotonic and signs of separation, as part of active management.
n.2: Physiological third stage is prolonged after 60 minutes, so a change is advised.

Labour & Birth.q: Isla, 31, had active management of the third stage in a freestanding midwifery unit. Forty minutes after the birth the placenta has not delivered. Her blood loss is 300 mL and she is stable. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Attempt manual removal with Entonox as analgesia
Inject oxytocin into the umbilical vein to release the placenta
Secure IV access, explain why and arrange transfer to obstetric care
Start an intravenous oxytocin infusion and wait a further hour
Labour & Birth.w: A third stage over 30 minutes with active management is prolonged (NICE NG235 1.10.20). For a retained placenta: secure IV access and explain why (1.10.21), do not use umbilical vein agents (1.10.22), do not use IV oxytocics routinely unless bleeding excessively (1.10.23, 1.10.24), and arrange transfer if not in an obstetric unit (1.10.27).

n.0: Manual removal must not be attempted without an anaesthetic (NG235 1.10.28).
n.1: NICE advises not to use umbilical vein agents for a retained placenta.
n.3: IV oxytocics are not used routinely for a retained placenta unless she is bleeding excessively.

Labour & Birth.q: Rachel, 28, has given birth and the baby is well. The midwife is about to give the uterotonic for an active third stage. Rachel received an oxytocin infusion during labour and now has an IV cannula. Which route and timing for oxytocin is appropriate?
o: 10 units added to the infusion, after the cord has stopped pulsating
5 units by IV injection over 3 to 5 minutes, after controlled cord traction
10 units by rapid IV bolus, after the placenta has delivered
5 units by slow IV injection over 3 to 5 minutes, before the cord is clamped
Labour & Birth.w: NICE NG235 1.10.11 and 1.10.12: give 10 units IM, or 5 units IV by slow injection over 3 to 5 minutes for women who received oxytocin in labour, immediately after the birth of the baby and before the cord is clamped and cut.

n.0: Waiting for the cord to stop pulsating is part of physiological management, and a 10-unit infusion is not the prophylactic regimen.
n.1: The uterotonic is given before cord clamping and traction, not after traction.
n.2: Oxytocin is not given as a rapid 10-unit IV bolus, and it is given after the baby's birth, not after the placenta.

Labour & Birth.q: A student midwife caring for Jess, 27, in established labour asks why contractions often become stronger once the baby's head is well applied to the cervix. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Pressure on the cervix triggers adrenaline release, which strengthens contractions
Pressure on the cervix releases relaxin, which strengthens contractions
Pressure on the cervix lowers prostaglandin levels, which strengthens contractions
Pressure on the cervix triggers oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions
Labour & Birth.w: The Ferguson reflex: stretch of the cervix and upper vagina by the presenting part sends signals to the hypothalamus, causing posterior pituitary release of oxytocin. Stronger contractions push the head down further, a positive feedback loop (SPM 3.12.2).

n.0: Adrenaline (catecholamines) tends to inhibit oxytocin and slow contractions, especially in early labour.
n.1: Relaxin softens ligaments and connective tissue; it does not drive this feedback loop.
n.2: Prostaglandins rise in labour and help cervical ripening and contractions; they do not fall.

Labour & Birth.q: Sarah, 30, is in early established labour in a busy, brightly lit room. She is frightened, keeps being interrupted and her contractions have spaced out from 3 to 1 in 10 minutes. Which physiological explanation is most likely?
o: Stress hormones are inhibiting oxytocin release and slowing contractions
Prostaglandin levels have peaked and are now suppressing contractions
Endorphin release has numbed the uterus and reduced contractions
High oxytocin levels have exhausted the uterine muscle early
Labour & Birth.w: Fear and disturbance raise catecholamines (adrenaline), which inhibit oxytocin release and can slow or stall labour. A calm, private, dimly lit environment with continuous support helps restore oxytocin release (SPM 3.21, 3.24; NICE NG235 1.4.3 and 1.4.11).

n.1: Prostaglandins support cervical change and contractions; they do not suppress them.
n.2: Endorphins help women cope with pain but do not suppress contractions in this way.
n.3: Uterine exhaustion from excess oxytocin is not the explanation for early labour slowing after distress.

Labour & Birth.q: Ana, 26, is having a vaginal examination in labour. The midwife feels a small triangular fontanelle at the front of the pelvis, just behind the symphysis pubis. The larger diamond-shaped fontanelle cannot be felt. What does this finding indicate?
o: An occipito-anterior position with a well-flexed head
A brow presentation with the head partly extended
An occipito-posterior position with a deflexed head
A face presentation with the head fully extended
Labour & Birth.w: The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is small and triangular and marks the occiput. Feeling it anteriorly, with the anterior fontanelle (bregma) out of reach, indicates an occipito-anterior position with good flexion, presenting the smallest diameter (suboccipitobregmatic, about 9.5 cm) (SPM 3.12.2).

n.1: In a brow presentation the anterior fontanelle and supraorbital ridges are felt, not the posterior fontanelle anteriorly.
n.2: In an occipito-posterior position the occiput, and so the posterior fontanelle, lies towards the sacrum, and the anterior fontanelle is often easily felt.
n.3: In a face presentation the facial features are felt, not either fontanelle.

Labour & Birth.q: Mia, 32, has just given birth to her baby's head in a left occipito-anterior position. Before the next contraction, the head turns a little to the left without any help. Which part of the mechanism of labour is this?
o: Extension of the head
Internal rotation of the head
Restitution
Lateral flexion
Labour & Birth.w: After the head is born, it untwists to realign with the shoulders, which are still in the oblique diameter of the pelvis. This is restitution. External rotation follows as the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior diameter of the outlet (SPM 3.12.3).

n.0: Extension is how the head is born, pivoting under the symphysis; it occurs before restitution.
n.1: Internal rotation of the head happens inside the pelvis before the head is born, bringing the occiput under the symphysis.
n.3: Lateral flexion is the sideways bending of the body as the shoulders and trunk are born, after external rotation.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Chloe, 24, had a second-degree tear sutured after a vaginal birth 5 days ago. At a home visit she reports increasing perineal pain and needs more pain relief than before. On examination the wound edges have separated with a small amount of discharge. Her observations are within normal limits. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise warm salt baths and review the wound at the next visit in 2 days
Refer her urgently to specialist maternity services to be seen the same day
Take a wound swab and decide on referral once the result is available
Ask the GP to examine the wound at her 6 to 8 week postnatal check
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.20: if the perineal wound breaks down or there are ongoing healing concerns, refer urgently to specialist maternity services, to be seen the same day in the case of a perineal wound breakdown. Increasing pain and need for analgesia are warning features (1.2.15).

n.0: Self-care and a delayed review do not meet the same-day standard for wound breakdown.
n.2: A swab may be useful, but referral must not wait for results when the wound has broken down.
n.3: Waiting for the 6 to 8 week GP review would leave a broken-down wound unassessed for weeks.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Mei, 34, is 10 days after the birth of her third baby and phones the community midwife about heavier vaginal bleeding. Her records show a booking weight of 47 kg, a postnatal haemoglobin of 92 g/L, and that she is exclusively breastfeeding. Which features in her history may worsen the consequences of a secondary postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Her age over 30 years and exclusive breastfeeding
Exclusive breastfeeding and her parity of three
Her booking weight under 50 kg and her anaemia
Her parity of three and her age over 30 years
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.14: when a woman seeks advice about bleeding after birth, assess severity and be aware that anaemia and a weight of less than 50 kg at booking may worsen the consequences of secondary postpartum haemorrhage.

n.0: Neither age nor breastfeeding is listed in NG194 as worsening the consequences of secondary PPH.
n.1: Breastfeeding does not worsen the consequences of secondary PPH and parity is not a listed factor.
n.3: Parity and age are not the factors NG194 lists as worsening the consequences of secondary PPH.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Hannah, 22, had a first-degree tear repaired yesterday. She asks the midwife on the postnatal ward how to look after her stitches and reduce the chance of infection once she is home. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Change pads twice a day and clean the perineum with alcohol wipes each time
Use sitz baths instead of showering until the sutures have fully dissolved
Shower the perineum daily, change pads often, wash hands before and after
Apply antiseptic cream to the sutures after each visit to the toilet
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.16: advise the woman about good perineal hygiene, including daily showering of the perineum, frequent changing of sanitary pads, and hand washing before and after doing this.

n.0: Pads should be changed frequently, and alcohol wipes on a healing wound are painful and not recommended.
n.1: Daily showering is recommended; there is no need to avoid showers until sutures dissolve.
n.3: Routine antiseptic creams are not part of NG194 perineal hygiene advice.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: A midwife attends Ruth, 30, at a planned home birth. Three hours after the birth Ruth is well and has had a cup of tea, but has not yet passed urine. The baby has had one effective breastfeed and has not passed meconium. Before the midwife leaves the home, which action is the priority?
o: Wait to measure the volume of Ruth's first void after the birth
Observe a second effective feed before leaving the family
Stay until the baby has passed meconium for the first time
Complete the full newborn physical examination before leaving
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.10 applies before the midwife leaves after a home birth: measure the volume of the first void, assess the baby, make a feeding plan including at least 1 effective feed observed, and if meconium has not been passed, advise parents to seek advice if it is not passed within 24 hours. The feed requirement is already met, so the outstanding item is the first void.

n.1: NG194 requires at least 1 effective feed to be observed, which has already happened.
n.2: The midwife advises the parents to seek help if meconium is not passed within 24 hours of birth; she does not wait for it.
n.3: The NIPE newborn examination should be completed within 72 hours, so it is not a precondition for leaving after the birth.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Sophie, 28, is 4 days after a vaginal birth with epidural analgesia. At a home visit she reports a persistent, severe headache that paracetamol has not eased. She is otherwise well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Check her blood pressure and urine and arrange urgent medical review
Advise rest, extra fluids and caffeine for a likely post-dural headache
Reassure her that headache is common with broken sleep and review in 2 days
Advise her to raise the headache with the GP at the 6 to 8 week check
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4: persistent or severe headache after birth could indicate hypertension, pre-eclampsia, post-dural puncture headache, migraine, intracranial pathology or infection, and needs medical advice without delay. The midwife assesses BP and urine and escalates rather than assuming a benign cause.

n.1: Assuming a post-dural cause without assessment could miss postnatal pre-eclampsia or intracranial pathology.
n.2: A persistent severe headache is a warning symptom in NG194 and must not wait 2 days.
n.3: Deferring to the 6 to 8 week check ignores a red flag that needs same-day review.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Ellie, 25, is visited at home 3 days after an assisted vaginal birth. She has been shivering, her lochia smells offensive and she feels unwell. Observations: heart rate 134 bpm, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, temperature 38.3 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat the observations in 1 hour before deciding on transfer
Take a high vaginal swab and plan review when the result is back
Arrange emergency transfer to hospital by 999 with a pre-alert
Ask the GP to prescribe oral antibiotics and review her tomorrow
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG255 (2025): a recently pregnant woman with any high-risk criterion outside hospital needs emergency transfer, usually by 999, with a pre-alert (1.6.1, 1.6.2). A heart rate over 130 bpm is a high-risk criterion (Table 1); assisted birth and offensive lochia add to her risk (1.2.1).

n.0: A high-risk criterion is already present, so delaying transfer for repeat observations is unsafe.
n.1: Waiting for swab results delays treatment of suspected high-risk sepsis.
n.3: Oral antibiotics in the community delay the hospital assessment and IV antibiotics within 1 hour that NG255 requires for high risk.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Jess, 30, is breastfeeding her 10-day-old baby. She noticed a red, tender, wedge-shaped area on her left breast this morning. Her temperature is 37.6 C and she feels otherwise well. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Express as much milk as possible after every feed to empty the left breast
Continue feeding on both sides and seek advice if it persists beyond 24 hours
Stop feeding from the left breast until the redness and tenderness settle
Contact the GP today for antibiotics to treat infective mastitis early
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4: worsening redness and swelling of the breast persisting for more than 24 hours despite self-management could indicate mastitis and needs medical advice. Self-management includes continuing to breastfeed, good positioning and attachment, rest and simple analgesia (NHS mastitis advice).

n.0: Over-expressing beyond the baby's needs increases supply and can perpetuate engorgement.
n.2: Stopping feeds on the affected side causes stasis and makes mastitis worse.
n.3: Most early mastitis settles with self-management; antibiotics are for symptoms that persist or worsen.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Abi, 27, had pre-eclampsia and gave birth 2 days ago. She is not taking antihypertensive medicine. Her blood pressure is now 152/102 mmHg on two readings and she has no symptoms. According to NICE NG133, what is the most appropriate next step?
o: Plan transfer home, as she has no symptoms of pre-eclampsia
Recheck in 4 hours and treat if her blood pressure reaches 160/110
Start antihypertensive treatment now, as her BP is 150/100 or higher
Reduce blood pressure checks to once daily now that the baby is born
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG133 (postnatal care, pre-eclampsia): start antihypertensive treatment if blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher. Inpatients with pre-eclampsia need BP measured at least 4 times a day.

n.0: Transfer criteria include BP of 150/100 or less, which she does not meet.
n.1: 160/110 is the threshold for severe hypertension; postnatal treatment starts at 150/100.
n.3: NG133 requires at least 4 BP checks a day while she is an inpatient with pre-eclampsia.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Ruby, 32, took methyldopa for gestational hypertension during pregnancy. She gave birth yesterday and is breastfeeding. Her blood pressure remains raised and she still needs treatment. Which change to her medicines is recommended by NICE?
o: Stop all antihypertensives at birth and recheck her blood pressure at 2 weeks
Continue methyldopa unchanged until her 6 to 8 week GP review
Stop methyldopa within 2 days of birth and change to another antihypertensive
Increase the methyldopa dose, as blood pressure peaks on days 3 to 5
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG133: if a woman has taken methyldopa in pregnancy, stop it within 2 days of birth and change to an alternative antihypertensive. Enalapril is the suggested first choice postnatally and is compatible with breastfeeding.

n.0: She still needs treatment, so stopping all medicines risks severe postnatal hypertension.
n.1: NG133 advises stopping methyldopa within 2 days of birth and changing to an alternative, not continuing it.
n.3: Methyldopa should be replaced, not increased, after the birth.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Nadia, 4 days after birth, had pre-eclampsia and takes enalapril. Her blood pressure is 146/96 mmHg, she has no symptoms and her blood results are stable. She asks to go home. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: Keep her in hospital until her blood pressure is below 130/80 mmHg
Transfer with no medical follow-up, as her BP is below 150/100 mmHg
Transfer home with a medical review 2 weeks after the birth
Keep her in hospital until the enalapril can be stopped completely
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG133: transfer to community care is appropriate when there are no symptoms of pre-eclampsia, BP is 150/100 mmHg or less and blood results are stable or improving. Women still on antihypertensives need medical review at 2 weeks, plus the 6 to 8 week review.

n.0: 130/80 is a treatment target, not a requirement for transfer home.
n.1: Women discharged on antihypertensives need a review at 2 weeks and again at 6 to 8 weeks.
n.3: Treatment can be reduced in the community; it does not need to stop before transfer.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Fatima, 35, is 5 days after a caesarean birth. At a home visit the edge of her wound is red with an offensive discharge. Her temperature is 37.9 C, heart rate 96 bpm and other observations are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Clean the wound and review it again at the next routine visit
Arrange a same-day medical review of the wound and observations
Advise her to mention the wound at the 6 to 8 week GP review
Give a course of antibiotics using the midwives exemptions
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.3 and 1.2.4: assess wound healing and signs of infection after caesarean; infection symptoms need medical advice without delay. Signs of wound infection are a moderate to high risk criterion for sepsis in NG255, so a prompt medical assessment is needed.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays assessment of a probable wound infection.
n.2: A 6 to 8 week review is far too late for an infected wound.
n.3: Antibiotics are not among the medicines midwives may supply or administer under the HMR 2012 Schedule 17 exemptions.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Lucy, 31, had gestational diabetes treated with metformin. She gave birth yesterday and her baby is well. She asks what happens to her diabetes care now. Which plan is in line with NICE NG3?
o: Stop metformin straight after the birth and offer a fasting plasma glucose test at 6 to 13 weeks
Continue metformin while breastfeeding and arrange an annual HbA1c from 1 year
Stop metformin after the birth and check an HbA1c at the 2-week postnatal visit
Continue metformin until the 6 to 8 week GP check, then perform a glucose tolerance test
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG3 1.6.3, 1.6.11: women with gestational diabetes should stop blood glucose-lowering therapy immediately after the birth; offer a fasting plasma glucose test 6 to 13 weeks after the birth to exclude diabetes, then an annual HbA1c if the result is normal.

n.1: Metformin is stopped after the birth in gestational diabetes; annual HbA1c follows a normal postnatal test.
n.2: An HbA1c at 2 weeks reflects pregnancy glucose levels; NG3 recommends a fasting plasma glucose at 6 to 13 weeks.
n.3: Glucose-lowering therapy is stopped immediately after the birth, not continued to 6 to 8 weeks.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Olivia, 29, had a caesarean birth in labour for failure to progress. Her BMI is 24, she does not smoke and has no other risk factors. The midwife completes her postnatal VTE risk assessment using the RCOG score. Which plan is most appropriate?
o: LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 10 days after the birth
Anti-embolism stockings until mobile, with no LMWH needed
Early mobilisation and good hydration, with no LMWH needed
LMWH thromboprophylaxis for 6 weeks after the birth
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: RCOG GTG 37a risk assessment (amended by the RCOG position statement, Sept 2026): caesarean section in labour scores 2. A postnatal score of 2 or more means considering LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 10 days.

n.1: Her score of 2 meets the threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis; stockings are for women who cannot have LMWH.
n.2: Mobilisation and hydration are advised for everyone, but a score of 2 means LMWH should also be considered.
n.3: 6 weeks is for high-risk women such as those with previous VTE; a score of 2 indicates at least 10 days.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Bethany, 33, had an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis 4 years ago. She has just had a straightforward vaginal birth and is otherwise well. Which postnatal thromboprophylaxis plan should the midwife expect?
o: LMWH for 10 days, as she had an uncomplicated vaginal birth
No prophylaxis, as her thrombosis was more than 2 years ago
LMWH (or warfarin) for at least 6 weeks after the birth
Anti-embolism stockings for 6 weeks, without anticoagulation
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: RCOG GTG 37a: all women with a previous confirmed VTE should be offered thromboprophylaxis with LMWH or warfarin for at least 6 weeks postpartum, regardless of mode of delivery. Previous VTE (other than one linked to major surgery) scores 4.

n.0: Mode of birth does not reduce the duration; previous VTE needs at least 6 weeks.
n.1: There is no time limit after which previous VTE stops counting as a risk factor.
n.3: Stockings are not a substitute for anticoagulation in a woman with previous VTE.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Chen, 31, has been prescribed 10 days of low molecular weight heparin after her caesarean birth. She is breastfeeding and asks the midwife whether the injections will affect her baby. Which response is accurate?
o: She should express and discard milk for 4 hours after each dose
She should give formula until the 10-day course is finished
LMWH is considered safe to use while breastfeeding
A direct oral anticoagulant tablet is preferred while breastfeeding
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: RCOG GTG 37a: LMWH is safe in breastfeeding (warfarin is also safe). Use of direct oral anticoagulants (NOACs) is not recommended in women who are breastfeeding.

n.0: There is no need to discard milk; LMWH is safe in breastfeeding.
n.1: Interrupting breastfeeding is unnecessary and could undermine her milk supply.
n.3: GTG 37a advises that NOACs are not recommended in breastfeeding women.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Freya, 27, had a caesarean birth under combined spinal-epidural anaesthesia, and the epidural catheter was removed at 10:00. There has been no postpartum haemorrhage. She is prescribed prophylactic LMWH. What is the earliest time the first dose should be given?
o: 22:00 on the same day
14:00 on the same day
11:00 on the same day
10:00 on the following day
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: RCOG GTG 37a: LMWH should not be given for 4 hours after spinal anaesthesia or after the epidural catheter has been removed. The first postnatal dose is otherwise given as soon as possible after delivery, so the earliest time is 10:00 plus 4 hours = 14:00.

n.0: 12 hours is the interval after an LMWH dose before a catheter is removed, not the wait after removal.
n.2: 1 hour is too soon after catheter removal and risks spinal haematoma.
n.3: Waiting 24 hours leaves her unprotected longer than necessary.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Grace, 34, is 6 days after a vaginal birth. At a home visit she reports that her left calf has become swollen and tender over the past day. She is not breathless and has no chest pain. Her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the GP to see her at the 6 to 8 week postnatal check
Advise leg elevation and stockings and review her in 2 days
Arrange an urgent same-day hospital assessment for suspected DVT
Advise more walking and fluids, and review at the next routine visit
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4: leg swelling and tenderness could indicate venous thromboembolism and needs medical advice without delay. Suspected DVT needs same-day assessment and imaging so that treatment can start.

n.0: Deferring to the 6 to 8 week check ignores a warning sign that needs same-day review.
n.1: A 2-day delay for a suspected DVT risks extension or pulmonary embolism.
n.3: Mobility and hydration do not replace urgent assessment of a suspected DVT.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Nia, 26, is 10 days after a caesarean birth. She phones the community midwife reporting sudden breathlessness and sharp chest pain on breathing in. When the midwife arrives, her heart rate is 122 bpm and oxygen saturation 93% on air. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Book an urgent GP appointment for later today
Call 999 for emergency transfer to hospital
Advise rest and recheck her observations in 1 hour
Start her remaining LMWH injections and monitor
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4: shortness of breath or chest pain could indicate VTE or a cardiac problem. With tachycardia and low saturations this is a suspected pulmonary embolism, an emergency needing immediate transfer. Thrombosis and thromboembolism is the leading cause of maternal death up to 6 weeks (MBRRACE-UK 2022-24).

n.0: A GP appointment later in the day delays emergency care for suspected PE.
n.2: Waiting an hour with tachycardia and hypoxia is unsafe.
n.3: Prophylactic LMWH does not treat an established PE and delays transfer.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Kate, 37, smokes 10 cigarettes a day. She has had a spontaneous vaginal birth at term with no complications. Her BMI is 27 and she has no other risk factors. Using the RCOG VTE score, which postnatal plan is most appropriate?
o: No LMWH, as her postnatal score is below the threshold of 3
Consider LMWH for at least 10 days after the birth
LMWH until she has stopped smoking cigarettes
LMWH for 6 weeks after the birth
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: RCOG GTG 37a score: age over 35 = 1, smoker = 1, total 2. A postnatal score of 2 or more means considering LMWH thromboprophylaxis for at least 10 days. A BMI of 27 does not score.

n.0: The postnatal threshold is 2, not 3 (3 is the antenatal threshold for prophylaxis from 28 weeks).
n.2: Duration is set by the risk assessment, not by ongoing smoking; smoking cessation support is offered separately.
n.3: 6 weeks is for high-risk women such as previous VTE; a score of 2 indicates at least 10 days.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Precious, 30, had a booking BMI of 52 kg/m2. She has no other VTE risk factors and gives birth vaginally at term. Under the current RCOG position (September 2026, aligned with the NHS England Maternal Care Bundle), which postnatal thromboprophylaxis should she be offered?
o: LMWH for 10 days after the birth
LMWH until she is fully mobile on the ward
LMWH for 6 weeks after the birth
Anti-embolism stockings until discharge
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: RCOG GTG 37a position statement (Sept 2026): women with a booking BMI of 50 kg/m2 or more should be offered LMWH during pregnancy and for 6 weeks postpartum. BMI 50 or more now scores 4 on the amended risk assessment.

n.0: 10 days was the older advice for class 3 obesity; BMI 50 or more now means 6 weeks.
n.1: Stopping at mobility on the ward falls far short of the 6-week recommendation.
n.3: Stockings do not replace LMWH for a woman at this level of risk.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Ama, 27, is breastfeeding her 5-day-old baby. She tells the midwife that milk leaks from her breasts whenever she hears her baby cry, and asks why. Which hormone is mainly responsible for this response?
o: Progesterone from the placenta, causing milk secretion
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, causing milk ejection
Oestrogen from the ovaries, causing alveolar growth
Prolactin from the anterior pituitary, causing milk synthesis
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: The let-down (milk ejection) reflex is mediated by oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli. It can be conditioned by the baby's cry or sight. Prolactin drives milk production (SPM 3.14 lactation physiology).

n.0: The fall in placental progesterone after birth allows copious milk production; progesterone does not cause let-down.
n.2: Oestrogen promotes breast development in pregnancy and high levels inhibit milk production.
n.3: Prolactin stimulates milk production in the alveoli; it does not eject milk.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Becky, 23, is breastfeeding her 3-day-old baby. She is tired and asks whether giving formula overnight would let her breasts 'fill up' so she has more milk in the morning. Which explanation by the midwife is accurate?
o: Frequent, effective milk removal signals the breasts to make more milk
Milk supply is fixed by breast size and is set by the third day
Supply depends mainly on how much water she drinks each day
Resting the breasts overnight builds a larger store for the next day
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: Breastfeeding works on supply and demand (NICE NG194 1.5.12): regular, effective milk removal, including at night, drives continued production. Replacing feeds with formula reduces stimulation and can lower supply (NG194 1.5.17).

n.1: Breast size does not determine supply; production responds to milk removal throughout lactation.
n.2: Drinking to thirst is enough; fluid intake does not drive milk supply.
n.3: Leaving milk in the breast signals the breast to slow production, so supply falls.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Mariam, 31, is breastfeeding on the first day after birth. She is worried because she can only express a few drops of thick yellow milk and thinks her baby is not getting enough. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Colostrum is low in antibodies, which rise once her mature milk arrives
Colostrum comes in small amounts, is rich in antibodies and suits a newborn's needs
Colostrum is too concentrated for a newborn and should be expressed and discarded
Colostrum is mainly water, so formula top-ups are needed until her milk comes in
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: Colostrum is produced in small volumes in the first days, is concentrated and rich in immunoglobulins (especially secretory IgA) and protective factors, and meets the needs of a healthy term newborn. NG194 1.5.12 asks midwives to explain how much milk is produced in the early stages.

n.0: Colostrum has the highest concentration of antibodies of any milk.
n.2: Colostrum should be given to the baby, not discarded.
n.3: Colostrum is nutrient-dense, not mainly water; routine formula top-ups are not clinically indicated (NG194 1.5.12).

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Jade, 20, is breastfeeding her first baby and asks the midwife how often she should feed. Which advice reflects responsive breastfeeding?
o: Feed whenever the baby shows cues, for comfort as well as hunger
Feed for 10 minutes on each breast every 3 hours during the day
Wait until the baby cries, as crying is the earliest sign of hunger
Feed every 4 hours by the clock to set a routine from the start
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 defines responsive breastfeeding as feeding in response to the baby's cues, recognising that feeds are also for love, comfort and reassurance, and that a mother can also feed for her own comfort or convenience.

n.1: Fixed durations and intervals do not reflect individual variation in feeding (NG194 1.5.12).
n.2: Crying is a late hunger cue; earlier cues include rooting, stirring and hand to mouth.
n.3: Clock-timed feeds ignore the baby's cues and can reduce milk supply.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Priya, 28, plans to breastfeed and give one bottle of formula each evening. She asks whether her baby could be overfed with either method. Which statement is accurate?
o: A breastfed baby cannot be overfed but a formula-fed baby can, so pace bottles
Either method can lead to overfeeding, so both should be limited to set volumes
A formula-fed baby cannot be overfed, as the baby stops when the bottle is finished
A breastfed baby can be overfed if feeds last longer than 20 minutes
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.12 and 1.5.19: it is not possible to overfeed a breastfed baby, but it is possible to overfeed a formula-fed baby, so parents should pace bottle feeds and recognise signs the baby has had enough.

n.1: Breastfed babies regulate their own intake, so set volumes for breastfeeding are not appropriate.
n.2: Encouraging a baby to finish the bottle is how formula-fed babies become overfed.
n.3: Long feeds at the breast do not cause overfeeding; NG194 states a breastfed baby cannot be overfed.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Leila, 26, is exclusively breastfeeding her 2-week-old baby in June. She is taking a vitamin D supplement herself and asks whether her baby needs one too. What should the midwife advise?
o: Give the baby a daily vitamin D supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms
Start the baby's vitamin D at 6 months, when solid foods begin
Give the baby vitamin D from October to March each year
No supplement is needed while she takes vitamin D herself
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG247 (table 1): breastfed babies should be given a daily supplement of 8.5 to 10 micrograms of vitamin D from birth, all year round. Formula-fed babies taking 500 mL or more of formula a day do not need one because formula is fortified.

n.1: Breastfed babies need vitamin D from birth, not from 6 months.
n.2: The October to March advice applies to adults; breastfed babies need vitamin D all year.
n.3: The mother's supplement does not provide enough vitamin D for the baby through breast milk.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Toni, 19, says she will breastfeed 'for a couple of weeks' before returning to college, and asks whether it is worth it for such a short time. Which response is most accurate?
o: Benefits begin once she has breastfed without formula for 6 months
Colostrum helps, but later milk gives no advantage over formula
Breastfeeding benefits her and the baby even if done for a short time
Short spells of breastfeeding confuse the baby and are best avoided
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.2: discussions about breastfeeding should include how it can have benefits even if only done for a short time, and how it can soothe and comfort the baby. Advice respects the parents' choices (1.5.1).

n.0: There is no 6-month threshold before benefits begin; NG194 states short-term breastfeeding still helps.
n.1: Breast milk continues to provide immune and nutritional benefits beyond the first week.
n.3: Any breastfeeding is beneficial; there is no evidence that short spells confuse the baby.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Holly, 30, gave birth 2 days ago. Her baby has died in the neonatal unit. She does not want to breastfeed and asks how to stop her milk coming in comfortably. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Express fully every 3 hours so the breasts do not become engorged
Avoid all pain relief, because analgesia delays lactation suppression
Bind the breasts tightly and reduce fluid intake until the milk dries up
Wear a supportive bra, avoid stimulation and express sparingly for comfort
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.21: after the death of a baby, discuss lactation suppression, including avoiding breast stimulation, a supportive bra, ice packs, over-the-counter pain relief, expressing sparingly to ease engorgement, medicines that can suppress lactation and the possibility of becoming a milk donor.

n.0: Full, regular expressing stimulates milk production and delays suppression.
n.1: Over-the-counter pain relief is part of the NG194 self-help advice.
n.2: Tight binding and fluid restriction are not recommended and cause discomfort.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: A midwife is observing Saira breastfeed her 2-day-old baby on the postnatal ward. Which observation best indicates that the baby is well attached?
o: The baby's cheeks dimple inwards with each suck during the feed
The baby's cheeks are full and rounded, with rhythmic sucks and swallows
More areola is visible below the bottom lip than above the top lip
Rapid shallow sucks continue throughout, with clicking sounds
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: Signs of good attachment include a wide-open mouth, chin touching the breast, more areola visible above the top lip than below, full rounded cheeks, and rhythmic sucking with audible swallowing (NICE NG194 1.5.6, 1.5.14).

n.0: Dimpled or sucked-in cheeks suggest the baby is sucking on the nipple rather than well attached.
n.2: With good attachment the lower jaw takes in more areola, so more is visible above the top lip.
n.3: Persistent rapid shallow sucks and clicking suggest poor attachment and ineffective milk transfer.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Lauren, 25, is breastfeeding on day 3. She says feeds are very painful and her nipple looks flattened, like a new lipstick, when the baby comes off. The baby is feeding frequently and seems unsettled. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Advise nipple shields for every feed until the pain settles
Observe a full feed and support her with positioning and attachment
Rest the nipples for 24 hours by giving the baby formula feeds
Recommend a nipple cream and advise her that pain is expected
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.12 and 1.5.15: pain when breastfeeding and a misshapen nipple after feeds suggest poor attachment. The first step is to observe a feed and adjust positioning and attachment; persisting concerns may need further support or tongue-tie assessment.

n.0: Nipple shields do not correct the underlying attachment problem and can reduce milk transfer.
n.2: Replacing feeds with formula reduces milk removal and supply and does not fix attachment.
n.3: Ongoing pain is not normal; NG194 tells women to seek help for pain when breastfeeding.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: A student midwife is supporting Mia, 22, to breastfeed for the first time. The baby is struggling to latch and the student is about to guide the baby's head and Mia's breast with her hands. What should the student do first?
o: Explain the technique afterwards once the baby has latched
Ask Mia's permission before giving any hands-on help
Help the baby latch quickly before the baby becomes upset
Ask Mia's partner to leave so that Mia can concentrate
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.8: those providing breastfeeding support should obtain consent before offering physical assistance, respect the woman's personal space, cultural influences and preferences, and build her confidence. NMC Code 4.2 requires consent before any action.

n.0: Explaining after the event does not obtain consent for physical contact.
n.2: Speed does not override consent; hands-on help must be agreed first.
n.3: The partner should be involved according to Mia's wishes (NG194 1.1.3), not sent away by staff.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Hope, 29, is breastfeeding and plans to go home today, 18 hours after the birth. The midwife observed a full effective feed at 6 hours. Which statement about breastfeeding assessment in the first week reflects NICE NG194?
o: A feed observed before discharge and another at the 6 to 8 week check
A feed observed in the first 24 hours and at least one more in week one
Hope keeps a feeding diary, which is reviewed by the midwife at day 10
The baby is weighed before and after feeds for the first 48 hours
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.14: as part of breastfeeding assessment, observe a feed within the first 24 hours after the birth and at least 1 other feed within the first week, alongside asking about feed frequency, sucking and swallowing, contentment, nappies and weight.

n.0: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks misses the first-week observation that NG194 recommends.
n.2: A diary may help, but NG194 requires observed feeds within the first week.
n.3: Test weighing around feeds is not part of the NG194 breastfeeding assessment.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Day 5: Esi's baby is still not feeding well despite two observed feeds with help on attachment. Esi has sore nipples, the baby makes a clicking noise, and the baby's tongue looks heart-shaped and cannot lift to the roof of the mouth. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise Esi to stop breastfeeding and express for bottle feeds
Advise formula top-ups after every feed until the baby is older
Arrange a tongue-tie assessment and keep supporting breastfeeding
Reassure Esi and review feeding again at the 6 to 8 week check
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.15: if breastfeeding concerns persist, consider observing more feeds, adjusting positioning, giving expressed milk, referring for additional support such as a lactation consultant, and assessing for tongue-tie. The signs described suggest tongue-tie.

n.0: Stopping breastfeeding is not indicated when a treatable cause is suspected and support is ongoing.
n.1: Routine formula top-ups reduce milk supply and do not address the cause.
n.3: Waiting 6 weeks risks poor weight gain, nipple damage and early cessation of breastfeeding.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Dani, 24, is formula feeding her baby. The midwife watches her prepare a feed at home. Which step is correct?
o: Warm a made-up feed in the microwave and shake it before use
Use boiled water cooled in the fridge so the feed is ready faster
Use water boiled no more than 30 minutes ago, so it is at least 70 C
Put the powder in the bottle first, then add water up to the line
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NHS formula guidance (NICE NG194 1.5.17 safe preparation): boil fresh water and leave it for no more than 30 minutes so it stays at least 70 C, which kills harmful bacteria in powdered formula. Put the water in the bottle first, then add the powder.

n.0: Microwaves heat unevenly and can scald the baby's mouth.
n.1: Water below 70 C will not kill bacteria that can be present in powdered formula.
n.3: Water goes in first so the powder-to-water ratio is correct.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Kayla, 21, is bottle feeding with formula. Her baby often takes the whole bottle quickly and then brings back milk. Which advice best reflects responsive bottle feeding?
o: Prop the bottle on a cushion so the baby can feed at their own pace
Hold the baby close, pace the feed and let the baby decide when to stop
Share feeds among relatives so the baby bonds with many people
Encourage the baby to finish each bottle so feeds stay regular
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.19: responsive bottle feeding involves holding the baby close, pacing feeds, recognising signs the baby has had enough (because formula-fed babies can be overfed), the dangers of prop feeding, and minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby.

n.0: Prop feeding is dangerous (choking) and removes the close contact of feeding.
n.2: NG194 notes a potential benefit of minimising the number of people regularly feeding the baby.
n.3: Pushing the baby to finish the bottle risks overfeeding.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Ben and Laila are formula feeding their 6-week-old son, who is growing well. They ask the health visitor whether to switch to follow-on milk or a 'hungry baby' formula because he wakes at night. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Switch to follow-on formula now that he is over 6 weeks old
Add a little baby rice to the evening bottle to settle him
Change to a hungry baby formula to help him sleep longer
Keep to first infant formula, which meets his needs in year one
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.17: first infant formula is the only formula milk babies need in the first year of life, unless there are specific medical needs. Night waking is normal in young babies.

n.0: Follow-on formula is not needed and is not suitable for babies under 6 months.
n.1: Cereal must not be added to bottles; it alters the feed and is a choking and overfeeding risk.
n.2: Hungry baby formulas are not needed for a well-growing baby; first infant formula is sufficient.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Kirsty, 27, is 4 days after the birth of her first baby. She has been tearful and irritable since yesterday but is sleeping when the baby sleeps, enjoys caring for the baby and has no thoughts of harm. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain this is postnatal depression and ask the GP to start an antidepressant
Refer her urgently to the perinatal mental health team for assessment today
Reassure her that these feelings normally last for about 3 months after birth
Explain the baby blues usually settle within 2 weeks and when to seek help
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: Feeling down, anxious or irritable for a few days after the birth is very common (the baby blues) and usually goes away within 2 weeks; if it continues or worsens she should seek help (NHS postnatal depression guidance). NG194 1.2.2: assess emotional wellbeing at every contact and arrange further assessment if there are concerns.

n.0: Transient tearfulness on day 4 does not meet the picture of postnatal depression, and medication is not indicated.
n.1: Her symptoms fit the baby blues with no risk features, so urgent specialist referral is not indicated.
n.2: The baby blues usually resolve within 2 weeks; symptoms lasting months suggest depression and need assessment.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Rachel, 32, has bipolar disorder and is 6 days postnatal. Her partner phones the midwife: Rachel has not slept for 2 nights, is talking rapidly and believes strangers are watching the baby through the windows. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to specialist mental health services for assessment within 4 hours
Advise rest and sleep tonight and visit again early tomorrow morning
Ask Rachel the Whooley questions at her next routine visit
Book a routine GP appointment for her within the next 2 weeks
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE CG192 1.5.11, 1.5.12: be alert for postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks in women with a history of severe mental illness such as bipolar disorder. If psychosis is suspected, refer to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal service) for assessment within 4 hours of referral.

n.1: Postpartum psychosis can deteriorate rapidly; delaying overnight puts Rachel and the baby at risk.
n.2: Screening questions are for identifying depression; she needs urgent assessment now.
n.3: 2 weeks is the CG192 timeframe for assessment after routine mental health referral, not suspected psychosis.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: At a 10-day postnatal visit the midwife asks Nadia, 30, questions to help recognise depression, as recommended by NICE CG192. Which question is one of the Whooley questions?
o: Over the last 2 weeks, have you felt nervous, anxious or on edge most days?
Do you feel your baby is harder to settle than other babies of the same age?
During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?
In the past year, have you had any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE CG192 1.5.4: at the first contact in primary care, booking and early postnatal period, ask the two depression identification (Whooley) questions about feeling down, depressed or hopeless, and having little interest or pleasure in doing things, during the past month.

n.0: This is from the GAD-2 anxiety questions, which use a 2-week timeframe.
n.1: This asks about the baby's temperament, not the woman's mood or interest.
n.3: Risk questions matter but are not one of the two Whooley questions.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Day 14: Ama, 26, answers 'yes' to both Whooley questions. She has no thoughts of self-harm, is caring for her baby and has family support. Which next step is in line with NICE CG192?
o: Explain this is the baby blues, which will settle by itself
Offer a fuller assessment, such as the EPDS, or refer her to her GP
Repeat the Whooley questions at the 6 to 8 week GP check before acting
Refer her to the crisis team for same-day assessment
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE CG192 1.5.5: if a woman answers yes to either Whooley question, or there are concerns, consider using the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or refer her to her GP (or to a mental health professional if there is a severe illness).

n.0: Symptoms present at 2 weeks with positive Whooley answers need assessment rather than reassurance.
n.2: A positive screen needs action now, not a delay of several weeks.
n.3: There are no features of severe illness or risk, so crisis referral is not the next step.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Molly, 33, is 10 days after an emergency caesarean under general anaesthetic. She tells the midwife she keeps replaying the birth, which she found frightening, and has questions about what happened. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she requests a copy of her notes and reads them through on her own
Advise her to ask about the birth at her 6 to 8 week GP check
Give her time to talk about the birth and offer the birth reflection service
Reassure her that she and the baby are well now, so it is best to move on
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.5: at each postnatal contact, give the woman the opportunity to talk about her birth experience and provide information about relevant support and birth reflection services. CG192 also covers care after traumatic birth.

n.0: Reading clinical notes alone without support may increase distress and does not answer her questions.
n.1: NG194 asks midwives to offer this opportunity at each contact rather than deferring it.
n.3: Dismissing her distress misses a chance to support her and identify trauma symptoms.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Sam, the partner of Lucy, who is breastfeeding their 1-week-old baby, tells the midwife he feels left out and is worried he will not bond with the baby. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Wait until the baby is weaned, when fathers usually begin to bond
Give the baby a bottle of formula each night so that he can bond through feeding
Wait until the baby starts smiling at around 6 weeks to build a bond
Spend skin-to-skin and face-to-face time with the baby and respond to the baby's cues
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.3.17: encourage parents to value time with their baby to promote attachment, including face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding to the baby's cues. NG194 1.5.3: partners can comfort and bond with the baby and support breastfeeding.

n.0: Bonding starts from birth; there is no need to wait until weaning.
n.1: Introducing formula can affect breastfeeding; partners can bond in other ways.
n.2: Attachment develops through early interaction; waiting for smiles delays it unnecessarily.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: A community midwife is reviewing her caseload of four new mothers. According to NICE NG194, which mother is most likely to need additional support with bonding and emotional attachment?
o: Ann, 34, who plans to return to work when the baby is 9 months
Josie, 19, who grew up in local authority care
Mae, 30, a second-time mother with an uncomplicated birth
Lia, 28, who has chosen to formula feed her baby
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.3.19: some parents may need additional support with bonding and emotional attachment, for example those who have been through the care system, have experienced adverse childhood events or a traumatic birth, or have complex psychosocial needs.

n.0: Planning a return to work is not listed as a factor needing extra attachment support.
n.2: An uncomplicated second birth is not one of the NG194 factors for additional bonding support.
n.3: Formula feeding by choice does not by itself indicate a need for attachment support; parents can bond when bottle feeding (NG194 1.5.19).

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: At a home visit 3 weeks after the birth, Tom, the partner of a woman in the midwife's care, says he has felt low, irritable and unable to sleep for the past 3 weeks and is struggling to cope. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest he raises it at his partner's 6 to 8 week postnatal GP check
Explain that postnatal depression affects birthing mothers rather than partners
Acknowledge his feelings and advise him to contact his GP or NHS Talking Therapies
Note his comments in the woman's records and take no further action
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: Fathers and partners can also have depression after the birth of a baby (NHS postnatal depression guidance), and adults can self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies. SPM 3.16.1 requires midwives to recognise and respond to the needs of adults in the family.

n.0: His partner's check is about her health, and his symptoms need attention now.
n.1: Partners can develop depression after a birth; dismissing this misses a treatable condition.
n.3: Recording without acting fails to support him or signpost help.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Hamida, 24, speaks little English. Her husband offers to interpret at her day 3 postnatal check, which includes questions about her mood, bleeding and contraception. What should the midwife do?
o: Use a translation app and give her an English leaflet
Book a professional interpreter rather than her husband
Ask her teenage daughter to interpret, as she is fluent
Accept her husband's offer, as he knows her history best
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.5: information should be translated by an appropriate interpreter. NG201 advises independent interpreters rather than family members, so that the woman can speak freely about sensitive issues such as mood and domestic abuse.

n.0: An app and an English leaflet do not ensure she understands or can ask questions.
n.2: Using a child to interpret is inappropriate, particularly for intimate health topics.
n.3: Family interpreters may filter information and prevent disclosure of sensitive issues such as abuse.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Lan, 29, tells the midwife that in her culture new mothers rest at home for a month, are cared for by their mothers, and avoid showering in the early weeks. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record that she has declined postnatal care because of her cultural beliefs
Explore her wishes and adapt care, offering hygiene advice for her to weigh up
Ask her mother to decide which postnatal care is acceptable
Tell her the tradition is unsafe and that she must shower every day from now
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: SPM 3.22 and 3.27: midwives support the needs and preferences that women identify and provide culturally sensitive care. NG194 1.1.1 and 1.1.5: listen and respond to her preferences and give individualised information so she can make informed decisions, including perineal hygiene advice (1.2.16).

n.0: She has not declined care; her cultural practices can be accommodated within postnatal care.
n.2: Decisions about her care are hers; her mother is involved only as she wishes.
n.3: A directive, dismissive response undermines trust and her right to make informed choices.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Aisha, 31, is on day 2 and has a perineal tear. She asks that her perineal examination is carried out by a female practitioner for religious reasons. The midwife on shift is male. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Explain that patients cannot choose the gender of NHS staff
Postpone the examination until her 6 to 8 week GP check
Arrange for a female midwife to carry out the examination
Ask her husband to consent to the examination by the male midwife
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: SPM 3.27: provide culturally sensitive and individualised care. The NMC Code requires listening and responding to people's preferences (standard 2) and getting properly informed consent before any action (4.2). A reasonable request for a same-gender practitioner should be accommodated where possible without delaying care.

n.0: Reasonable preferences about the gender of the examiner should be accommodated where possible.
n.1: Delaying a perineal assessment for weeks could miss infection or poor healing.
n.3: Only Aisha can consent to her own examination; her husband cannot consent on her behalf.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Grace, 35, who is Black British, is 3 days after a caesarean. She mentions feeling 'not quite right' but her observations are within normal limits. Which principle from NICE NG194 should guide the midwife's response?
o: Ethnicity is no longer relevant to risk once the birth has been uncomplicated
Higher maternal mortality in Black women is explained by older maternal age
Closer monitoring is reserved for women living in the most deprived areas
Some minority ethnic groups have higher mortality and may need closer monitoring
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.2: MBRRACE-UK reports show that women from some minority ethnic backgrounds, and those in deprived areas, have a higher risk of death and may need closer monitoring. Her concern should be taken seriously and explored.

n.0: Increased risk continues into the postnatal period; ethnicity remains relevant after birth.
n.1: The disparity is not explained by age; MBRRACE-UK shows higher risk across groups.
n.2: NG194 identifies both minority ethnic background and deprivation as reasons for closer monitoring.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Fatou, 22, is an asylum seeker living in temporary accommodation. She gave birth 2 days ago and is anxious because she may be moved to another area. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Give her written information in English and close her midwifery care
Reduce her visits, because she may soon be moved to another area
Ask the Home Office to confirm her status before her next visit
Continue her postnatal care and link her with local support services
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.7: follow the NICE guideline on pregnancy and complex social factors for women who may need additional support, including recent migrants, asylum seekers and refugees. SPM 3.27: care irrespective of social situation. NG194 1.1.8 supports clear handover if she moves.

n.0: Closing care early and giving English-only information fails her additional needs.
n.1: Women with complex social factors need more support, not fewer visits.
n.2: Her immigration status is not a precondition for postnatal midwifery care.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Chantelle, 17, lives with her mother and plans to breastfeed her first baby. According to NICE NG194, which approach to her feeding support is most appropriate?
o: Hand all feeding support to her mother from the first day
Offer extra face-to-face support and continuity from a known team
Give her a leaflet and helpline number in place of visits
Suggest formula feeding, as young mothers seldom keep breastfeeding
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.5.11: younger women and women from a low income or disadvantaged background may need more support and encouragement to start and continue breastfeeding, and continuity of carer is particularly important for them.

n.0: Family support helps, but professional breastfeeding support remains part of postnatal care.
n.2: Written and phone support supplement, but do not replace, face-to-face support (NG194 1.5.9).
n.3: Steering her away from her choice is not respectful (NG194 1.5.1) and assumes failure.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Rosie, 26, has a mild learning disability and lives with her partner. She is going home with her baby tomorrow and the midwife needs to give her information about postnatal recovery and warning signs. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Keep information brief and leave out the warning signs
Give information in Easy Read format and check her understanding
Give the standard leaflet and ask her to sign that she has read it
Give the information to her mother, who can explain it later
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.5 and 1.1.6: tailor the content and format of information to the woman's needs (for example Easy Read), and check that she understands it and how it relates to her. Reasonable adjustments are required under the Equality Act 2010.

n.0: Warning signs are essential safety information that every woman needs (NG194 1.2.4).
n.2: A signature does not show she has understood the information.
n.3: Information should be given to Rosie herself in an accessible way; others are involved as she wishes.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Jo and her wife Priti have a 3-day-old baby; Jo gave birth. At the postnatal visit the student midwife directs all questions to Jo and does not include Priti, who looks uncomfortable. Jo wants Priti fully involved. What should the midwife do?
o: Ask Priti to step out during discussions about the baby's care
Involve Priti in care and discussions in line with Jo's wishes
Record Priti as a visitor until parental status is confirmed
Address advice to Jo, as she is the birth mother of the baby
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.3: a woman may be supported by her partner, who should be involved according to her wishes; NG194 defines partner and parents inclusively. SPM 3.22 and 3.27: individualised, respectful care for all families. Code 20.2: treat people fairly and without discrimination.

n.0: Excluding a parent from the baby's care discussions is unjustified and discriminatory.
n.2: Recording Priti as a visitor disregards her role and Jo's wishes.
n.3: Jo has asked for Priti to be involved, so excluding her goes against Jo's wishes.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Amara, 29, gave birth vaginally 6 hours ago on the postnatal ward and would like to go home this evening. Her observations are normal and her baby has fed well at the breast. She has not yet passed urine since the birth. Which bladder assessment should the midwife complete before Amara is transferred to community care?
o: Measure the volume of her first void after the birth
Dipstick her first urine sample for protein and leucocytes
Perform a routine bladder scan at 6 hours after the birth
Record that she has voided, without measuring the volume
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.10: before transfer to community care (or before the midwife leaves after a home birth), assess bladder function by measuring the volume of the first void after giving birth. Undetected urinary retention can cause long-term bladder damage.

n.1: Urinalysis does not assess bladder emptying; NG194 asks for the volume of the first void.
n.2: NG194 does not recommend routine bladder scanning for every woman; measuring the first void is the required assessment.
n.3: Noting that she has voided without a volume cannot identify retention or incomplete emptying.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Grace, 31, is 7 days after the birth of her second baby. She asks the community midwife how her womb returns to normal size and why she gets cramping pains when she breastfeeds. Which explanation by the midwife is accurate?
o: Oxytocin released during feeds makes the uterus contract, which aids involution
The uterus should still be felt at the level of the umbilicus at one week
Breastfeeding slows involution because prolactin relaxes the uterine muscle
Cramping during feeds suggests retained placental tissue and needs a scan
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: Suckling releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary; as well as milk ejection it causes uterine contractions ('afterpains'), which are common in multiparous women and help involution. The uterus is at about the umbilicus just after birth and is usually no longer palpable abdominally by around 10 to 14 days (SPM 3.12.4 postpartum physiology).

n.1: The fundus is at about the umbilicus immediately after birth and descends steadily, so at one week it is well below the umbilicus.
n.2: Breastfeeding speeds involution through oxytocin; prolactin drives milk synthesis, not uterine relaxation.
n.3: Afterpains during feeds are a normal oxytocin effect; retained tissue presents with heavy or increasing bleeding or infection signs (NG194 1.2.4).

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Leah, 26, is on day 2 after a vaginal birth. Her lochia is bright red and moderate. At her first postnatal midwife contact she asks when she should seek advice about bleeding. Which symptom should the midwife tell her needs medical advice without delay?
o: Loss that changes from red to pinkish brown within a week
A pale yellowish discharge still present at 4 weeks
A slightly heavier loss for a few minutes during a feed
Bleeding that increases after it had started to settle
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.2.4 and 1.2.13: advise women to seek advice without delay if bleeding is sudden or very heavy, persistent or increasing, if they pass clots, placental tissue or membranes, or if there are infection signs, because this could indicate retained placental tissue or endometritis.

n.0: Lochia normally changes from red (rubra) to pinkish brown (serosa) over the first week or so.
n.1: A pale yellowish-white discharge (alba) can continue for several weeks and is normal without other symptoms.
n.2: A transient increase in loss with feeding reflects oxytocin-driven uterine contraction and is expected.

Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.q: Zainab, 33, has an uncomplicated birth on a midwife-led unit and is transferred home 20 hours later with her baby. She lives with her partner and has no safeguarding concerns. According to NICE postnatal guidance, when should her first postnatal visit by a midwife take place?
o: Between 7 and 14 days, jointly with the health visitor
On day 5, timed to coincide with the newborn blood spot test
Within 36 hours of transfer, face-to-face and usually at home
Within 72 hours of transfer, by telephone if she feels well
Postnatal Care & Infant Feeding.w: NICE NG194 1.1.14: ensure the first postnatal visit by a midwife takes place within 36 hours after transfer of care from the place of birth (or after a home birth). It should be face-to-face and usually at the woman's home.

n.0: 7 to 14 days after transfer from midwifery care is the suggested timing for the first health visitor visit (NG194 1.1.15).
n.1: Day 5 is the usual timing for blood spot sampling, which is later than the 36-hour standard for the first visit.
n.3: NG194 sets 36 hours, not 72, and the visit should be face-to-face rather than by telephone.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ayo is born through thick meconium-stained liquor. She cries immediately, has good tone and a heart rate over 100 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate care?
o: Avoid suction; dry and warm her and plan close observation
Suction her mouth and nose, then dry her and keep her warm
Intubate to check the trachea for meconium below the cords
Give 5 inflation breaths to clear meconium from her lungs
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.25: in the presence of any meconium, do not suction the upper airways before the birth of the shoulders and trunk, and do not suction or intubate if the baby has normal respiration, heart rate and tone. Significant meconium needs close observation (1.11.27).

n.1: NG235 1.11.25: do not suction the upper airways if breathing, heart rate and tone are normal.
n.2: Intubation is not indicated in a vigorous baby.
n.3: Inflation breaths are for a baby who is not breathing adequately, not a vigorous crying baby (RCUK 2025 NLS).

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Lily is born in a freestanding midwifery unit. There was significant meconium in the liquor, but she is breathing normally with good tone and heart rate. How should her observations be planned?
o: At 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours of age in any birth setting
At 1 and 2 hours of age in the birth centre, then stop if both are normal
Hourly for 24 hours following admission to the neonatal unit
At 1 and 2 hours, then 2-hourly to 12 hours, with neonatologist access
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.27: after significant meconium, a healthy baby is closely observed within a unit with immediate access to a neonatologist, at 1 and 2 hours old and then 2-hourly until 12 hours old. 1.11.28: after non-significant meconium, observe at 1 and 2 hours in all settings.

n.0: 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours is the schedule after prolonged prelabour rupture of membranes (NG235 1.11.31).
n.1: Observations at 1 and 2 hours alone are for non-significant meconium.
n.2: A well baby does not need neonatal unit admission; observation is with access to a neonatologist.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Noah was born through meconium-stained liquor 2 hours ago. His observations: respiratory rate 66 breaths/min, heart rate 150 bpm, temperature 37.3 C, oxygen saturation 97%. Which finding means a neonatologist should assess him?
o: Heart rate of 150 beats per minute
Oxygen saturation of 97%
Respiratory rate of 66 breaths/min
Temperature of 37.3 C on one reading
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.29: after any meconium, ask a neonatologist to assess the baby if respiratory rate is above 60, there is grunting, heart rate is below 100 or above 160, capillary refill is over 3 seconds, temperature is 38 C or more (or 37.5 C twice 15 to 30 minutes apart), saturation is below 95% or there is central cyanosis.

n.0: A heart rate of 150 is within the 100 to 160 range.
n.1: 97% is above the 95% threshold.
n.3: 37.3 C is below the 37.5 C and 38 C triggers.

The Newborn Infant.q: Joy, 30, took sertraline throughout pregnancy for anxiety. Her baby is born at term in good condition. Which plan for the baby is in line with NICE NG235?
o: Advise Joy to stop sertraline now to protect the breastfed baby
Routine care, as sertraline is considered safe in pregnancy
Admission to the neonatal unit for 72 hours of observation
Additional monitoring for signs of PPHN or neonatal withdrawal
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.17: undertake additional monitoring of babies whose mothers took SSRI or SNRI antidepressants in pregnancy, because of a small increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) or neonatal withdrawal symptoms.

n.0: Stopping her medicine abruptly risks relapse; decisions about it belong to her prescriber with her.
n.1: NG235 recognises a small increased risk, so additional monitoring is advised.
n.2: A well baby can stay with the mother; routine neonatal unit admission is not required.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Isla was born at 09:00 on Monday in a midwife-led unit and is well. Under the NHS NIPE screening programme, by when should her newborn physical examination be completed at the latest?
o: By 09:00 on Tuesday
By 09:00 on Wednesday
By 09:00 on Thursday
By 09:00 on Saturday
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE programme handbook: the newborn screening examination (eyes, heart, hips and testes) should be completed before, or at, 72 hours of age (KPI NP1). 72 hours after 09:00 Monday is 09:00 Thursday. NG194 1.3.3 also requires a complete examination within 72 hours.

n.0: Tuesday 09:00 is 24 hours, earlier than the latest permitted time.
n.1: Wednesday 09:00 is 48 hours; the standard is 72 hours.
n.3: Saturday 09:00 is 5 days, beyond the 72-hour standard.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ruby was breech at 37 weeks. A successful external cephalic version was performed and she was born head first at 40 weeks. Her hip examination at the NIPE newborn check is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Refer for hip ultrasound, as she has a NIPE hip risk factor
Rely on the 6 to 8 week hip examination to detect any problem
Refer for a hip X-ray at 6 months of age
No further action, as she was head first at birth with normal hips
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE handbook: breech presentation at or after 36 completed weeks, irrespective of presentation at birth or mode of delivery (including after successful ECV), is a hip risk factor. Babies with risk factors are screen positive and need hip ultrasound, usually at 4 to 6 weeks.

n.1: A risk factor means referral for ultrasound now, not reliance on later clinical examination.
n.2: Hip ultrasound, not X-ray, is the NIPE screening test in early infancy.
n.3: Presentation at birth does not remove the risk factor; breech at 36 weeks or later counts even after ECV.

The Newborn Infant.q: During the NIPE newborn examination of baby Leo, the midwife finds that the red reflex in his left eye is absent and the pupil looks white. The right eye is normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer to a community optician for an eye test at 1 year
Refer urgently so he is seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks
Repeat the red reflex check at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Refer for an ophthalmology appointment within 6 weeks
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE handbook 12.11: babies with screen positive (abnormal) red reflex results should be urgently referred and seen by an ophthalmologist within 2 weeks of the newborn examination; an absent or white reflex may indicate congenital cataract or retinoblastoma.

n.0: An optician at 1 year is far too late; surgery for severe congenital cataract is time-critical.
n.2: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks delays assessment of a possible cataract or retinoblastoma.
n.3: The NIPE standard is assessment within 2 weeks, not 6.

The Newborn Infant.q: A student midwife is learning the heart component of the NIPE newborn examination. Which statement is accurate?
o: Every baby in England has routine pulse oximetry as part of NIPE
Critical congenital heart disease may be present without a murmur
Auscultation at the apex is enough to exclude heart disease
A murmur heard at 24 hours confirms congenital heart disease
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE handbook 13.7 and 13.8: critical congenital heart disease does not always present with a murmur, so auscultation cannot be used alone to exclude it. The UK NSC does not currently advocate universal pulse oximetry, but it forms part of the diagnostic assessment if there are concerns.

n.0: Universal pulse oximetry is not currently part of the NIPE heart screen.
n.2: Auscultation should cover all key areas, and even then cannot exclude disease.
n.3: A murmur makes the screen positive for review; it does not confirm heart disease.

The Newborn Infant.q: At the NIPE newborn examination of baby Sami, born at 39 weeks, neither testis can be palpated in the scrotum, groin or perineum. There is no hypospadias. What is the most appropriate action?
