o: Refer to paediatric urology for review at 6 months
Arrange review by a senior paediatrician within 24 hours
Refer for GP review at the 6 to 8 week infant check
Reassure the parents that the testes will descend by 1 year
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE handbook 15.10: bilateral impalpable testes need urgent review by a consultant paediatrician or associate specialist within 24 hours of the newborn examination, because they may indicate a disorder of sex development.

n.0: Specialist review at 6 months is too late for bilateral impalpable testes.
n.2: GP review at 6 to 8 weeks is the non-urgent pathway, used when testes are palpable but undescended without hypospadias.
n.3: Bilateral impalpable testes need urgent assessment, not reassurance.

The Newborn Infant.q: At the NIPE newborn examination of baby Theo, born at 40 weeks, the right testis is in the scrotum. The left testis is palpable in the groin but cannot be brought into the scrotum. There is no hypospadias. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Non-urgent review by the GP at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
Reassurance with no follow-up, as one testis is in the scrotum
Review by a senior paediatrician within 24 hours of the examination
Testicular ultrasound within 2 weeks of the examination
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE handbook: one or both testes palpable but not in the scrotum, without hypospadias, is screen positive on the non-urgent pathway: GP review at the 6 to 8 week NIPE infant examination. Urgent 24-hour review is for impalpable testes or hypospadias with an undescended testis.

n.1: A unilateral undescended testis is screen positive and needs follow-up.
n.2: 24-hour senior review is for bilateral or unilateral impalpable testes, or a palpable undescended testis with hypospadias.
n.3: Ultrasound within 2 weeks is not part of the NIPE testes pathway.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ella, born at 39 weeks with no risk factors, has a palpable clunk on the Ortolani manoeuvre of her left hip at the NIPE newborn examination. What is the expected screening pathway?
o: Hip ultrasound at 4 to 6 weeks, outcome decided by 6 weeks
Repeat the hip examination at the 6 to 8 week infant check
Referral for review by an orthopaedic surgeon by 10 weeks
Hip ultrasound between 38 and 40 weeks corrected age
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE hip screen positive pathway: for babies born at 34+0 weeks or more, perform hip ultrasound between 4 and 6 weeks of age, with an orthopaedic outcome decision by 6 weeks. A palpable clunk on Ortolani or Barlow is a screen positive finding.

n.1: A screen positive newborn hip needs ultrasound, not just a repeat clinical check.
n.2: Being seen by 10 weeks applies to babies found screen positive at the 6 to 8 week infant examination.
n.3: 38 to 40 weeks corrected age is the scan timing for babies born before 34 weeks.

The Newborn Infant.q: Kemi and her partner tell the midwife they do not want their baby to have the NIPE newborn examination. They have no other concerns about their baby. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Carry out the examination anyway, as it is in the baby's best interests overall
Accept the decision without further discussion and keep no written record of it
Make a safeguarding referral, as declining screening suggests neglect
Explain the screen, then record their decision and tell the GP and health visitor
The Newborn Infant.w: NIPE handbook: parents can decline all or part of the NIPE examination. They should be fully informed of each element and why screening is offered; the decision is recorded (SMaRT4NIPE and the personal child health record) and communicated to the GP and health visitor. NG235 1.11.18: examinations need parental consent.

n.0: Examining without consent is unlawful when there is no emergency.
n.1: Parents should be informed of the implications, and the decision must be documented and shared.
n.2: Declining screening is an informed choice, not in itself a safeguarding concern.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Amira was born at 23:00 on a Tuesday and is well. The community midwife is planning her newborn blood spot test. On which day should the sample ideally be taken?
o: On the Saturday
On the Monday
On the Sunday
On the Friday
The Newborn Infant.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: the sample is usually taken on day 5, counting the day of birth as day 0. Tuesday is day 0, so day 5 is Sunday, regardless of the time of birth.

n.0: Saturday is day 4, which is earlier than recommended.
n.1: Monday is day 6; the sample should ideally be taken on day 5.
n.3: Friday is day 3, which is too early for reliable results.

The Newborn Infant.q: On day 5, the parents of baby Omar ask the student midwife which conditions his blood spot test will look for. Which of these conditions is included in the current NHS newborn blood spot programme in England?
o: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Tyrosinaemia type 1
Biotinidase deficiency
Classic galactosaemia
The Newborn Infant.w: The NHS newborn blood spot programme screens for 10 conditions: sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1, homocystinuria and tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1, added in 2025).

n.0: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia is not part of the national blood spot programme.
n.2: Biotinidase deficiency is not part of the national blood spot programme.
n.3: Galactosaemia is not one of the 10 conditions screened in England.

The Newborn Infant.q: Daniel and Mia agree to newborn blood spot screening for their son but do not want him screened for cystic fibrosis. What should the midwife explain?
o: They can decline CF and still have the other conditions screened
They need a consultant's written agreement to decline CF screening
CF screening is a legal requirement and cannot be declined
Declining CF screening means declining the whole blood spot test
The Newborn Infant.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: parents can decline screening for sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis and congenital hypothyroidism individually; the inherited metabolic diseases can be declined only as a group. Screening is voluntary and based on verbal consent.

n.1: Parents give or decline consent themselves after information; no consultant agreement is needed.
n.2: Newborn screening is voluntary, so parents can decline any part that is allowed to be declined separately.
n.3: CF can be declined individually without declining the other conditions.

The Newborn Infant.q: Parents of a 5-day-old baby tell the midwife they want blood spot screening but would like to decline screening for phenylketonuria (PKU). They are happy for the other conditions to be tested. What should the midwife explain?
o: PKU screening is mandatory because PKU is the most common condition
They can decline PKU while keeping screening for the other metabolic diseases
Declining PKU means they must also decline sickle cell screening
The inherited metabolic diseases, including PKU, can be declined as a group
The Newborn Infant.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis and congenital hypothyroidism can be declined individually, but the 7 inherited metabolic diseases (PKU, MCADD, MSUD, IVA, GA1, homocystinuria, HT1) can be declined only as a group.

n.0: No part of newborn screening is mandatory; it is offered with consent.
n.1: PKU cannot be declined on its own; the IMDs are accepted or declined together.
n.2: Sickle cell disease is screened separately and can be accepted or declined independently of the IMDs.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Dev is 10 weeks old and has just moved to England from abroad. He has not had newborn blood spot screening. What should the health professional offer?
o: No screening, as blood spot screening ends at 8 weeks of age
Blood spot screening for the conditions except cystic fibrosis
Blood spot screening for all 10 conditions in the usual way
Cystic fibrosis screening, as the other tests are now too late
The Newborn Infant.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening: babies are eligible up to 1 year of age, except for cystic fibrosis screening, which is unreliable after 8 weeks. At 10 weeks Dev should be offered screening for the other conditions.

n.0: Eligibility continues to 1 year for the other conditions.
n.2: CF screening is unreliable after 8 weeks, so it is not offered at 10 weeks.
n.3: CF is the one test that is too late; the other conditions can still be screened.

The Newborn Infant.q: A midwife is about to take a blood spot sample from baby Ivy on day 5. Her mother asks whether she needs to sign anything. Which approach to consent is correct?
o: Obtain written consent from the parent with parental responsibility
Treat consent as implied and take the sample
Obtain written consent signed by both parents
Give information, obtain verbal consent and record it
The Newborn Infant.w: NHS newborn blood spot screening is offered with verbal consent after parents have been given information about the screening, and the decision is recorded. Written consent is not required.

n.0: Verbal consent is the standard; a signed form is not required.
n.1: Consent must be actively obtained after information; it cannot be assumed.
n.2: Written consent from both parents is not required for blood spot screening.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Finn was discharged home at 8 hours of age before his newborn hearing screen was done. His parents ask when it can still be carried out. What should the midwife tell them?
o: At the 6 to 8 week GP infant examination
Within 72 hours, at the same time as the NIPE newborn examination
At 12 months, alongside his routine vaccinations
Ideally in the first 4 weeks, but it can be done up to 3 months
The Newborn Infant.w: NHS newborn hearing screening (Screening tests for you and your baby): the automated otoacoustic emission (AOAE) screen is ideally done in the first 4 weeks but can be done up to 3 months of age.

n.0: Hearing screening is a separate programme and is not part of the GP 6 to 8 week check.
n.1: Hearing screening is not tied to the 72-hour NIPE deadline and can be done later.
n.2: 12 months is far beyond the 3-month screening window.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Zara's newborn hearing screen did not show a clear response in one ear, and she has been referred to audiology. Her mother is distressed and asks what this means. What is the most appropriate explanation?
o: It does not mean she has hearing loss; audiology within 4 weeks
The screen will be repeated at her 1-year health review
It confirms permanent hearing loss, so hearing aids will be fitted
Audiology will see her at 6 months if parents notice problems
The Newborn Infant.w: Newborn hearing screening: no clear response can be due to fluid or debris in the ear, an unsettled baby or background noise, and does not mean the baby has hearing loss. Babies referred should have an audiology appointment within 4 weeks (Screening tests for you and your baby).

n.1: A referred baby needs audiology within 4 weeks, not a repeat screen at 1 year.
n.2: A screening result does not diagnose hearing loss; audiology assessment is needed.
n.3: Audiology follow-up is arranged now, not left to parental concern.

The Newborn Infant.q: Before the birth of their first baby, Yusuf and Hana ask the midwife why vitamin K is offered to newborn babies. Which explanation is accurate?
o: To strengthen the baby's immunity against early-onset infection
To prevent newborn jaundice developing in the first week of life
To prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious disorder
To prevent anaemia in babies who had delayed cord clamping
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.12 (recommendation reintroduced 2026): offer parents vitamin K prophylaxis for their babies and explain it is to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare but serious and sometimes fatal disorder.

n.0: Vitamin K has no role in immunity against infection.
n.1: Vitamin K supports clotting; it does not prevent jaundice.
n.3: Delayed cord clamping improves iron stores; vitamin K prevents bleeding, not anaemia.

The Newborn Infant.q: Parents ask the midwife which way of giving vitamin K to their baby is recommended. According to NICE NG235, what should the midwife advise?
o: A subcutaneous injection into the abdomen after the first feed
An intramuscular injection, because this method works best
An intravenous injection for all babies born at term
Oral drops, because a single dose works as well as an injection
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.13: give vitamin K as an injection into the muscle because this is the method that works best. If parents do not want the injection, offer oral vitamin K, which may need multiple doses.

n.0: Vitamin K prophylaxis is given IM (or orally), not subcutaneously.
n.2: IV vitamin K is reserved for specific situations, such as very low birth weight preterm babies who cannot have IM.
n.3: Oral vitamin K may need multiple doses, including after discharge, and is less effective than IM.

The Newborn Infant.q: Ella and Joe have been given information about vitamin K but do not want their baby to have an injection. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Record that they have declined vitamin K and take no further action
Explain that the injection is required by law for all newborn babies
Offer oral vitamin K, explaining that more doses may be needed after going home
Advise that vitamin K taken by the mother will protect the breastfed baby
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.13: if parents do not want vitamin K by injection, offer oral vitamin K as an alternative, advising that it may need to be given as multiple doses, including after the baby goes home, at the dose and time in the manufacturer's instructions.

n.0: Declining the injection is not declining vitamin K; the oral alternative should be offered.
n.1: Vitamin K prophylaxis is offered with parental consent; it is not a legal requirement.
n.3: Maternal vitamin K is not a substitute for neonatal prophylaxis.

The Newborn Infant.q: A midwife is preparing intramuscular vitamin K (phytomenadione) for baby Rhys, born at 40 weeks weighing 3.4 kg. Which dose should she expect to give?
o: 1 mg as a single dose
2 mg as a single dose
400 micrograms as a single dose
3.4 mg, at 1 mg per kilogram
The Newborn Infant.w: BNF for Children (phytomenadione): neonatal prophylaxis of vitamin K deficiency bleeding by intramuscular injection is 1 mg as a single dose at birth for a term neonate. The weight-based dose of 400 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg) is for preterm neonates.

n.1: 2 mg is the oral dose of Konakion MM Paediatric, not the IM dose.
n.2: 400 micrograms is the per-kilogram preterm dose, not the term dose.
n.3: IM prophylaxis is not 1 mg per kilogram; the term dose is a single 1 mg.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Kai is born at 32 weeks weighing 1.5 kg. The neonatal team prescribe intramuscular phytomenadione at 400 micrograms/kg (maximum 1 mg). What dose should be given?
o: 1 mg intramuscularly
600 micrograms intramuscularly
1.5 mg intramuscularly
400 micrograms intramuscularly
The Newborn Infant.w: BNF for Children: preterm neonate IM prophylaxis 400 micrograms/kg (max 1 mg per dose) at birth. 400 micrograms x 1.5 kg = 600 micrograms, which is below the 1 mg maximum.

n.0: 1 mg is the term dose and the preterm maximum; Kai's weight-based dose is lower.
n.2: 1.5 mg is 1 mg/kg and also exceeds the 1 mg maximum.
n.3: 400 micrograms ignores his weight; the dose is per kilogram.

The Newborn Infant.q: Parents choose oral vitamin K for their baby, who is being exclusively breastfed. The unit uses Konakion MM Paediatric. Which regimen should the midwife explain, following the BNFC and manufacturer's directions?
o: 2 mg at birth and 2 mg at 4 to 7 days, with no later dose
2 mg at birth, 2 mg at 4 to 7 days and 2 mg at 1 month
A single oral dose of 1 mg given at birth
2 mg each week for the first 12 weeks of life
The Newborn Infant.w: BNF for Children (Konakion MM Paediatric by mouth): 2 mg at birth, then 2 mg at 4 to 7 days; exclusively breastfed babies need a further 2 mg at 1 month. NICE NG235 1.11.13: oral vitamin K may need multiple doses, including after discharge, per the manufacturer's instructions.

n.0: Two doses suit babies who are not exclusively breastfed; exclusively breastfed babies need a third dose at 1 month.
n.2: A single 1 mg oral dose at birth does not protect against late vitamin K deficiency bleeding with this product.
n.3: Weekly dosing for 12 weeks is not the Konakion MM Paediatric regimen.

The Newborn Infant.q: A student midwife asks whether a registered midwife needs a prescription to give intramuscular phytomenadione (vitamin K) to a healthy term newborn. Which answer is correct?
o: Yes: it needs a written prescription signed by a doctor before each dose
No: midwives may give it under the HMR 2012 midwives exemptions
No: any registered nurse or midwife may give it without a prescription
Yes: midwives may give oral vitamin K but need a prescription for the injection
The Newborn Infant.w: Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Schedule 17 Part 3: registered midwives may administer parenteral phytomenadione in the course of their professional practice without a prescription. Student midwives may administer it under the direct supervision of a registered midwife (the exclusions for students are diamorphine, morphine and pethidine).

n.0: Phytomenadione is on the midwives exemptions list, so a prescription is not needed.
n.2: The Schedule 17 exemption covers registered midwives (and student midwives under direct supervision), not registered nurses.
n.3: The injection is the form listed in Part 3 (parenteral administration).

The Newborn Infant.q: After a full discussion of the benefits and risks, the parents of baby Arlo decide against vitamin K by any route. They understand the information and are clear in their decision. What should the midwife do?
o: Give the injection anyway, as it is in the baby's best interests
Make a safeguarding referral, as declining vitamin K is neglect
Respect and record their decision and explain bleeding signs to report
Tell them the baby cannot be discharged home until vitamin K is given
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.12, 1.11.18: vitamin K is offered and any treatment of the baby needs parental consent. An informed decision to decline should be respected and documented, with information on warning signs (such as bleeding or bruising) and how to seek help (NG194 1.3.13).

n.0: Giving treatment without parental consent, when there is no emergency, is unlawful.
n.1: An informed refusal of prophylaxis is not in itself a safeguarding concern.
n.3: Discharge cannot be made conditional on accepting an optional treatment.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Lena, born at 39 weeks, is 18 hours old. During a routine check the midwife notices that her skin and sclerae look yellow. She is feeding and otherwise well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start phototherapy on the ward before a bilirubin level is taken
Use a transcutaneous bilirubinometer and repeat it in 24 hours
Reassure the parents that this is physiological jaundice
Serum bilirubin within 2 hours and urgent medical review
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.2.10-1.2.12: jaundice visible in the first 24 hours is a risk factor for pathological hyperbilirubinaemia. Measure serum bilirubin urgently (within 2 hours), repeat 6-hourly until stable, and arrange urgent medical review within 6 hours.

n.0: Treatment decisions are based on a measured serum bilirubin plotted on the threshold graph.
n.1: Serum bilirubin, not a transcutaneous reading, is required in the first 24 hours (CG98 1.2.15).
n.2: Jaundice in the first 24 hours needs urgent serum bilirubin and medical review within 6 hours to exclude pathological causes (CG98 1.2.10-1.2.12).

The Newborn Infant.q: A midwife is assessing four babies on the postnatal ward. Using NICE CG98, which baby has the most risk factors for developing significant hyperbilirubinaemia?
o: Born at 41 weeks; mixed feeding; first child with no siblings
Born at 36 weeks; sibling had phototherapy; exclusive breastfeeding planned
Born at 38+2 weeks; formula fed; mother had gestational diabetes
Born at 39 weeks by caesarean; formula fed; no family history of jaundice
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.2.1 risk factors: gestational age under 38 weeks, a previous sibling who needed phototherapy, mother's intention to breastfeed exclusively, and visible jaundice in the first 24 hours. The baby born at 36 weeks has three of these factors.

n.0: 41 weeks with mixed feeding and no sibling history gives no CG98 risk factors.
n.2: 38+2 weeks is not under 38 weeks, and formula feeding is not a risk factor.
n.3: Caesarean birth and formula feeding at 39 weeks are not CG98 risk factors.

The Newborn Infant.q: A student midwife is learning to check babies for jaundice on the postnatal ward. Which technique reflects NICE CG98?
o: Use visual inspection of skin colour to estimate the baby's bilirubin level
Check the clothed baby's face under the cot's artificial light at night
Examine the naked baby in bright natural light, including sclerae and gums
Check the face, as jaundice not yet reaching the trunk is safe
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.2.5, 1.2.6: check for jaundice with the baby naked in bright and preferably natural light; examine sclerae, gums and blanched skin, which is especially important in babies with darker skin tones. Visual inspection should not be used to estimate the bilirubin level.

n.0: CG98 advises against relying on visual inspection to estimate bilirubin levels.
n.1: Clothing and dim artificial light make jaundice harder to see.
n.3: The spread of jaundice is not a safe guide to its level; any concern needs measurement.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Omar was born at 38 weeks and is 40 hours old. At a home visit the midwife sees that he looks jaundiced; he is feeding well and alert. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Measure serum bilirubin within 2 hours and arrange urgent review
Measure bilirubin with a transcutaneous bilirubinometer within 6 hours
Estimate the level visually and recheck at the next routine visit
Check bilirubin at the next routine visit in 48 hours
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.2.14, 1.2.16: in babies over 24 hours with suspected jaundice, measure the bilirubin within 6 hours; use a transcutaneous bilirubinometer in babies of 35 weeks or more and over 24 hours old.

n.0: Serum bilirubin within 2 hours is for jaundice in the first 24 hours of life.
n.2: Visual estimation is unreliable and CG98 requires measurement.
n.3: Waiting 48 hours exceeds the 6-hour measurement window.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Grace, born at 40 weeks, is 60 hours old. Her transcutaneous bilirubin reading is 262 micromol/L. She is feeding well. What should the midwife do next?
o: Start phototherapy based on the transcutaneous reading
Measure serum bilirubin to confirm the level
Reassure the parents, as the reading is below 300
Repeat the transcutaneous reading in 6 hours
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.2.16: use serum bilirubin measurement if a transcutaneous bilirubinometer gives a reading above 250 micromol/L; the serum value is then plotted on the treatment threshold graph.

n.0: Treatment decisions use serum bilirubin when the transcutaneous reading exceeds 250.
n.2: There is no 300 reassurance threshold; readings over 250 need serum confirmation.
n.3: A reading above 250 needs a serum measurement, not a repeat transcutaneous reading.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ruby, born at term and breastfed, is having phototherapy for jaundice. Her mother asks about feeding during treatment. Which advice is in line with NICE CG98?
o: Keep phototherapy continuous and give feeds by nasogastric tube
Take breaks of up to 30 minutes to breastfeed, without extra fluids
Give extra water or dextrose between feeds to flush out the bilirubin
Stop breastfeeding and give formula until the levels fall
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.4.15: during phototherapy, use short breaks of up to 30 minutes for breastfeeding, nappy changing and cuddles; continue lactation and do not give additional fluids or feeds routinely to breastfed babies (expressed breast milk if extra is needed).

n.0: Short feeding breaks are encouraged during single phototherapy; tube feeding is not routine.
n.2: CG98 advises against giving additional water or dextrose routinely.
n.3: Breastfeeding should continue; stopping is not recommended.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Finn's phototherapy was stopped at 08:00 after his serum bilirubin fell well below the treatment threshold. When should his serum bilirubin be checked for rebound?
o: At 10:00, 2 hours after stopping
At 08:00 two days later, 48 hours after stopping
Between 12:00 and 14:00, 4 to 6 hours after stopping
Between 20:00 and 02:00, 12 to 18 hours after stopping
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.4.5, 1.4.6: stop phototherapy once serum bilirubin has fallen at least 50 micromol/L below the threshold, and check for rebound 12 to 18 hours after stopping (08:00 + 12 to 18 hours = 20:00 to 02:00).

n.0: 2 hours is too early to detect rebound.
n.1: 48 hours is later than the CG98 rebound check window.
n.2: 4 to 6 hours is the interval for repeat measurement after starting phototherapy (CG98 1.4.4).

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ivy, born at 40 weeks and breastfed, is 16 days old and still visibly jaundiced. Her mother says her stools have become pale and chalky and her urine is dark. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure her mother that breast milk jaundice is common at this age
Arrange conjugated bilirubin measurement and same-day medical review
Advise stopping breastfeeding for 48 hours to see if the jaundice fades
Recheck the jaundice at the 6 to 8 week infant examination
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE CG98 1.7.1-1.7.2: jaundice lasting over 14 days in a term baby is prolonged; look for pale chalky stools and dark urine and measure conjugated bilirubin. Pale stools and dark urine suggest cholestasis such as biliary atresia, needing urgent expert advice.

n.0: Pale stools and dark urine are not features of breast milk jaundice.
n.2: Interrupting breastfeeding is not recommended and delays investigation.
n.3: Waiting weeks could delay time-critical diagnosis of biliary atresia.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Theo, born at term, is 6 hours old on the postnatal ward. His axillary temperature is 36.2 C. He is pink, feeding and has normal breathing and heart rate. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Bathe the baby in warm water to bring the temperature up quickly
Warm him with skin-to-skin, a hat and dry blankets, then recheck
Admit the baby to the neonatal unit for incubator care at once
Record the reading as normal, as 36.2 C is within the newborn range
The Newborn Infant.w: Normal newborn temperature is 36.5 to 37.5 C (RCUK 2025 NLS; BAPM NEWTT2). For a low temperature, implement thermal measures: dry the baby, cover the head, wrap in warm dry blankets or use skin-to-skin, and recheck (NEWTT2 chart guidance).

n.0: Bathing causes evaporative heat loss and would worsen hypothermia.
n.2: A well baby with mild hypothermia can be warmed on the ward; admission is not the first step.
n.3: 36.2 C is below the normal range of 36.5 to 37.5 C.

The Newborn Infant.q: A community midwife visits baby Rosa, aged 5 days, at home. According to NICE NG194, which finding is a red flag for serious illness?
o: Sleeping for 3 hours between feeds
Axillary temperature of 35.8 C
Small possets of milk after feeds
Respiratory rate of 52 breaths/min
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.4.9: red flags for serious illness in young babies include a temperature of 38 C or over or under 36 C, respiratory rate over 60, grunting, chest indrawing, pallor or mottling, a weak or high-pitched cry, bulging fontanelle, seizures, bilious or projectile vomiting and non-blanching rash.

n.0: Sleeping 3 hours between feeds is normal for many newborns.
n.2: Small possets are common; bilious or forceful (projectile) vomiting is the red flag.
n.3: A respiratory rate of 52 is within the normal newborn range (the red flag is over 60).

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Jamal, 10 days old, has been refusing feeds since this morning and is much less responsive than usual, according to his mother. His temperature is 37.0 C. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Advise paracetamol and ask her to call back if he is no better tomorrow
Advise more frequent feeds and review him at the next routine visit
Arrange immediate medical assessment, as fever can be absent in infection
Reassure his mother, as a normal temperature makes infection unlikely
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.4.1, 1.4.4, 1.4.7 and 1.4.10: take parents' concerns seriously, be aware that fever may not be present in young babies with serious infection, and recognise the significance of feed refusal and reduced responsiveness. A baby thought seriously unwell needs immediate assessment by an emergency service.

n.0: Delaying until the next day risks deterioration from possible sepsis.
n.1: A change in behaviour with feed refusal needs assessment now, not a routine review.
n.3: A normal temperature does not exclude serious infection in young babies.

The Newborn Infant.q: Kiran has type 1 diabetes and has just given birth at 38 weeks. Her baby is well and is with her. According to NICE NG3, when should the baby first be fed and have a blood glucose test?
o: Feed within 30 minutes of birth; test blood glucose at 2 to 4 hours
Test cord blood glucose at birth before the first feed is given
Feed within 4 hours of birth; test blood glucose at 24 hours
Feed within 1 hour of birth; test blood glucose at 30 minutes
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG3 1.5.3 and 1.5.9: women with diabetes should feed their babies as soon as possible after birth (within 30 minutes) and then every 2 to 3 hours; carry out blood glucose testing routinely at 2 to 4 hours after birth.

n.1: Routine testing is at 2 to 4 hours; cord blood glucose is not the routine NG3 test.
n.2: 4 hours is too long to wait for a feed and 24 hours too late for the first test.
n.3: NG3 advises feeding within 30 minutes, and glucose at 30 minutes is too early for the routine test.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Leon's mother has gestational diabetes. At 3 hours his pre-feed capillary plasma glucose is 1.8 mmol/L. After maximal feeding support his next pre-feed reading is 1.9 mmol/L. He has no abnormal signs. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Continue routine feeds, as 1.9 mmol/L is above the 1.0 action level
Stop glucose testing, as the baby has no abnormal clinical signs
Escalate for additional measures such as tube feeding or IV dextrose
Give a formula top-up and plan discharge if the next value exceeds 1.5
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG3 1.5.9-1.5.10: feed frequently until pre-feed capillary plasma glucose is at least 2.0 mmol/L. Use additional measures (tube feeding or IV dextrose) if values are below 2.0 on 2 consecutive readings despite maximal feeding support, if there are abnormal signs, or if the baby will not feed effectively.

n.0: The NG3 target is at least 2.0 mmol/L; two consecutive lower values need more than routine feeding.
n.1: Monitoring must continue until feeding maintains glucose at 2.0 mmol/L or above.
n.3: 1.5 is not the NG3 target, and babies of women with diabetes stay at least 24 hours (NG3 1.5.6).

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ana, whose mother has type 2 diabetes, is 5 hours old. The midwife finds her jittery and floppy, with a weak cry, and she is not interested in feeding. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Give a feed and recheck the blood glucose in 3 hours
Offer skin-to-skin contact and observe her for 1 hour
Wait for a laboratory glucose result before taking action
Test blood glucose and arrange IV dextrose as soon as possible
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG3 1.5.11: for babies with clinical signs of hypoglycaemia, test blood glucose and provide intravenous dextrose as soon as possible. NG3 1.5.5: hypoglycaemia with abnormal clinical signs is a reason for neonatal unit admission.

n.0: A baby with abnormal signs needs urgent treatment; waiting 3 hours is unsafe.
n.1: Skin-to-skin does not treat symptomatic hypoglycaemia.
n.2: Treatment should not be delayed for a laboratory result when signs are present.

The Newborn Infant.q: On the postnatal ward, baby Elsie's observations give a NEWTT2 total score of 4. Using the BAPM NEWTT2 escalation tool, what is the expected response?
o: Refer to the Tier 1 neonatal doctor or ANNP for review within 1 hour
Request an immediate review and consider a neonatal emergency call
Refer to the Tier 1 neonatal doctor or ANNP for review within 15 minutes
Repeat the observations in less than 1 hour
The Newborn Infant.w: BAPM NEWTT2 (2023) escalation tool: score 1, repeat observations within 1 hour; score 2-3, Tier 1 review within 1 hour; score 4-5, Tier 1 review within 15 minutes (inform shift leader, consider SpO2 and glucose); score 6 or more, immediate review; any critical (purple) observation, immediate review and consider a 2222 call.

n.0: Review within 1 hour is the response to a score of 2 to 3.
n.1: Immediate review is for a score of 6 or more or any critical observation.
n.3: Repeating observations within 1 hour is the response to a score of 1.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Max, 20 hours old, has a NEWTT2 score of 0 on his latest observations. His parents say he 'just isn't himself', and the midwife also feels he looks unwell. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Request a neonatal review, as concern can trigger review at any score
Repeat his observations in 4 hours before deciding whether to escalate
Ask the parents to raise their concerns on the morning ward round
Continue routine care, as a score of 0 does not need escalation
The Newborn Infant.w: BAPM NEWTT2: healthcare professional concern can initiate a neonatal review at any time regardless of the score, and parental concern is part of the chart (reflecting Ockenden). NICE NG194 1.4.1: treat parents' concerns as an important indicator of possible serious illness.

n.1: Waiting 4 hours when both parents and the midwife are concerned risks missing deterioration.
n.2: Concerns should be acted on now, not deferred to a ward round.
n.3: NEWTT2 allows review regardless of score when there is clinical concern.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Ruby is 7 weeks old and is attending her 6 to 8 week review. Her mother asks what development is expected at this age. According to NICE NG194, which should be assessed?
o: Social smiling and visual fixing and following
Rolling over from her front to her back
Sitting steadily with support from cushions
Reaching for a toy and grasping it
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.3.5: at 6 to 8 weeks, assess the baby's social smiling and visual fixing and following. The NIPE infant examination also takes place at this age.

n.1: Rolling usually develops at around 4 to 6 months, so it is not expected at 6 to 8 weeks.
n.2: Sitting with support is a later milestone than 6 to 8 weeks.
n.3: Deliberate reaching and grasping develop later in the first months.

The Newborn Infant.q: Parents of a 3-day-old baby who is feeding well ask how often their baby will be weighed in the first weeks. Which answer reflects NICE NG194?
o: At birth and then at the 1-year review, unless the GP requests more
Every day for the first 2 weeks to check that feeding is going well
Every week until 6 months, then once a month until 1 year
In the first week and around 8 weeks, and if there are concerns
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.3.6: measure weight and head circumference of babies in the first week and around 8 weeks, and at other times only if there are concerns, plotting results on the growth chart.

n.0: NG194 recommends measurements in the first week and around 8 weeks as well as at birth.
n.1: Daily weighing is not recommended for well babies who are feeding effectively.
n.2: Routine weekly weighing is not the NG194 schedule.

The Newborn Infant.q: During play, 2-week-old Kai looks at his father's face, then turns his head away, yawns and arches his back. His father keeps trying to make eye contact. How should the midwife explain Kai's behaviour?
o: He is showing signs of colic that need review by the GP
He is showing hunger and should be offered a feed straight away
He wants more eye contact and play to keep him engaged
He is showing he needs a pause from interaction to calm down
The Newborn Infant.w: Turning away, yawning and arching are disengagement cues: the baby needs a break. NICE NG194 1.3.17: encourage parents to respond appropriately to the baby's cues to promote emotional attachment (SPM 3.16.2 understanding the newborn's needs).

n.0: These cues are normal communication, not signs of colic.
n.1: Feeding cues include rooting and hand to mouth, not turning away and yawning.
n.2: Continuing to seek eye contact when the baby is disengaging can overstimulate him.

The Newborn Infant.q: A first-time mother asks how she will know when her 4-day-old baby is ready to feed, as she wants to feed responsively. Which is an early feeding cue?
o: Rooting and bringing hands to mouth
Sleeping deeply with regular breathing
Crying loudly with an arched back
Yawning and turning the head away
The Newborn Infant.w: Early feeding cues include stirring, rooting, mouth opening and hand to mouth. Crying is a late cue. NICE NG194 defines responsive feeding as feeding in response to the baby's cues.

n.1: Deep sleep with regular breathing is a quiet sleep state, not a feeding cue.
n.2: Crying is a late hunger cue; feeding is easier before the baby is distressed.
n.3: Yawning and turning away are disengagement cues, not feeding cues.

The Newborn Infant.q: First-time parents of a 6-day-old baby are worried that they will not know if their baby becomes unwell. Which advice from the midwife best reflects NICE NG194?
o: Explain that serious infection in a baby will cause a high fever
Advise taking the baby's temperature every 4 hours, day and night
Advise waiting for the health visitor's first visit to raise worries
Give information on the Baby Check scoring system and when to call 999
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.3.12-1.3.13: consider giving parents information about the Baby Check scoring system, and advise them to seek advice if they think the baby is unwell and to call 999 if they think the baby is seriously ill. 1.4.4: fever may be absent in young babies with serious infection.

n.0: Fever may not be present in young babies with serious infection (NG194 1.4.4).
n.1: Routine 4-hourly temperatures are not recommended and can miss other signs of illness.
n.2: Parents should seek advice whenever they are worried, not wait for a scheduled visit.

The Newborn Infant.q: Leah asks how she can play with her 1-week-old daughter to support her development. Which advice about newborn vision is most accurate?
o: Hold her face about 20 to 30 cm away and talk, as newborns prefer faces
Hang a mobile about 1 metre above the cot, as newborns focus at a distance
Wait until 6 weeks before face-to-face play, as newborns cannot see faces
Show bright cartoons on a tablet held close to her face to train vision
The Newborn Infant.w: Newborns focus best at about 20 to 30 cm and show a preference for faces. NICE NG194 1.3.17: face-to-face interaction promotes emotional attachment and supports very early development (SPM 3.13.4).

n.1: Newborns focus best close up, not at a metre or more.
n.2: Newborns can see and prefer faces from birth; face-to-face play should start straight away.
n.3: Screens are not recommended for babies and do not replace face-to-face interaction.

The Newborn Infant.q: Baby Alfie is 10 days old and feeding well, and his mother is well. The midwife plans to transfer their care to the health visiting team today. According to NICE NG194, when should the first health visitor home visit be considered?
o: Within 36 hours after transfer from midwifery care
At the 6 to 8 week infant physical examination
Between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care
At around 3 months, with the first immunisations
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.1.15: consider arranging the first postnatal health visitor home visit between 7 and 14 days after transfer of care from midwifery care. 1.1.9: the transfer from midwife to health visitor must be clearly communicated to professionals and parents.

n.0: 36 hours is the standard for the first midwife visit after transfer from the place of birth.
n.1: The 6 to 8 week examination is usually done in primary care and is later than the health visitor visit.
n.3: Primary immunisations start at 8 weeks, and the health visitor visit is earlier than either.

The Newborn Infant.q: At a home visit, Ellie and her partner tell the midwife they plan to bring their 9-day-old baby, born at term weighing 3.4 kg, into their bed tonight. Ellie has had two glasses of wine (about 4 units) and her partner smokes. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Advise that bed sharing is safe because the baby was a healthy weight
Advise them to doze with the baby on the sofa instead of the bed
Strongly advise them not to share a bed with the baby tonight
Advise bed sharing with the baby on her side, facing Ellie
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG194 1.3.15: strongly advise parents not to share a bed with their baby if the baby was low birth weight or either parent has had 2 or more units of alcohol, smokes, has taken drowsiness-causing medicine or used recreational drugs. Both factors apply here.

n.0: Normal birth weight does not offset the risks from alcohol and smoking.
n.1: Sleeping on a sofa or chair with a baby is particularly dangerous (NG194 1.3.14).
n.3: Babies should sleep on their back, not on their side (NG194 1.3.14).

The Newborn Infant.q: A midwife is recording the Apgar score at 1 minute for baby Kofi, whose parents have dark skin. How should the colour element of the score be assessed?
o: Skin colour of the face, chest and trunk for central oxygenation
Score colour as 2 for any baby with darker skin
Palms of the hands and soles of the feet for central oxygenation
Inside the mouth for central, nail beds for peripheral oxygenation
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.2: assess central oxygenation by looking inside the mouth at the mucous membranes and tongue, and peripheral oxygenation by the colour of the nail beds. Skin colour is unreliable, particularly in babies with darker skin.

n.0: Facial and trunk skin colour is an unreliable guide to oxygenation, particularly with darker skin.
n.1: Assigning a default score is unsafe and could miss central cyanosis.
n.2: Palms and soles reflect peripheral circulation, not central oxygenation.

The Newborn Infant.q: At 1 minute of age, baby Erin has a heart rate of 110 bpm, slow irregular breathing, some flexion of the limbs, grimaces when stimulated, and a pink body with blue hands and feet. What is her Apgar score?
o: A score of 7
A score of 8
A score of 6
A score of 5
The Newborn Infant.w: Apgar scoring: heart rate over 100 = 2; slow or irregular breathing = 1; some flexion = 1; grimace = 1; pink body with blue extremities = 1. Total 6. NG235 1.11.1: record the Apgar at 1 and 5 minutes.

n.0: 7 would need a further point, for example vigorous crying or active movement.
n.1: 8 would need two further points, such as a strong cry and active motion.
n.3: 5 undercounts; the heart rate over 100 scores 2, not 1.

The Newborn Infant.q: Ten minutes after an uncomplicated birth, Dina is holding her baby skin-to-skin and the baby is rooting. A student midwife wants to take the baby to weigh and measure now. Dina has not asked for this. What should the midwife advise?
o: Weigh now, as birth weight must be recorded within 15 minutes
Bath the baby first to reduce the risk of infection, then weigh
Weigh quickly and return the baby to skin-to-skin afterwards
Delay weighing and measuring until after the first hour
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.10: avoid separating the woman and baby within the first hour for routine procedures such as weighing, measuring and bathing, unless she requests it or it is needed for the baby's immediate care. 1.11.14: record head circumference and birth weight soon after the first hour.

n.0: There is no 15-minute requirement; NG235 records weight soon after the first hour.
n.1: Bathing is a routine procedure that should not interrupt the first hour.
n.2: Even a brief separation for routine weighing goes against NG235 1.11.10.

The Newborn Infant.q: After a 20-hour labour, Sara is very sleepy and holding her baby skin-to-skin. The midwife notices the baby's face is pressed into Sara's breast with the head flexed forward. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Swaddle the baby tightly against Sara's chest to stop slipping
Leave the baby as they are, because the baby is warm and settled
Move the baby into a cot for the rest of the first hour
Reposition the baby with face visible and head supported, and explain
The Newborn Infant.w: NICE NG235 1.11.9: prioritise optimal baby airway positioning during skin-to-skin, ensuring the head is supported so the airway does not become obstructed, and explain to the woman and companion how to maintain the airway.

n.0: Tight swaddling does not protect the airway and limits skin contact.
n.1: A flexed head with the face covered risks airway obstruction.
n.2: Skin-to-skin can continue safely with correct positioning; separation is not needed.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Leah, 33, has asthma and is 35 weeks pregnant. She is admitted with a blood pressure of 158/104 mmHg and a diagnosis of pre-eclampsia. Oral labetalol has been prescribed by the junior doctor. As the midwife prepares the first dose, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Withhold it and ask the prescriber to review because of her asthma
Give the labetalol after she has used her salbutamol inhaler
Give oral methyldopa from stock instead and record the change
Give the labetalol and check her peak flow every hour afterwards
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Labetalol is a beta-blocker and is unsuitable in asthma because of the risk of bronchospasm. NICE NG133 recommends labetalol first line but nifedipine for women in whom labetalol is not suitable, so the midwife withholds the dose and asks the prescriber to review (SPM 3.18 contraindications; Code 18).

n.1: Pre-treatment with salbutamol does not make a contraindicated beta-blocker safe.
n.2: A midwife cannot substitute a different antihypertensive without a prescription.
n.3: Monitoring peak flow does not remove the risk of bronchospasm from a beta-blocker in asthma.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Precious, 30, took sertraline throughout her pregnancy for depression and has just given birth to a healthy-looking baby at 39 weeks. She wants to keep her baby with her on the postnatal ward. In line with NICE NG235, what is the most appropriate plan for the baby?
o: Advise Precious to stop sertraline so that she can breastfeed
Give a dose of naloxone to reverse any drug effects at birth
Admit the baby to the neonatal unit for 72 hours of observation
Carry out additional monitoring for signs of withdrawal or PPHN
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 1.11.17 recommends additional monitoring of the baby when the mother has taken an SSRI or SNRI in pregnancy, because of the risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal withdrawal. This can happen with the baby alongside the mother (SPM 3.18 adverse effects across the continuum of care).

n.0: Sertraline is generally compatible with breastfeeding, and stopping abruptly risks relapse of depression.
n.1: Naloxone reverses opioids, not SSRIs, and is not indicated for a well baby.
n.2: A well baby does not need routine separation and neonatal unit admission; monitoring can be done with the mother.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Isla, 28, has epilepsy controlled on lamotrigine and is 20 weeks pregnant. She tells the midwife she has had two brief seizures this month after being seizure-free for 2 years. She has been taking every dose. What is the best explanation and action?
o: Lamotrigine absorption is blocked by her folic acid, so stop folic acid
Pregnancy slows lamotrigine metabolism, so she should miss a dose
Seizures are expected in pregnancy, so review at the next routine visit
Lamotrigine clearance rises in pregnancy, so refer for urgent review
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Lamotrigine clearance increases markedly in pregnancy, so blood levels can fall and seizures return despite full adherence. Increased seizures need prompt referral to the obstetric and epilepsy team for dose review (SPM 3.18 pharmacology in pregnancy; SPM 4.3 complications). Folic acid should continue.

n.0: Folic acid does not block lamotrigine absorption and should be continued in women taking antiseizure medicines.
n.1: Clearance increases rather than slows, and missing doses would increase seizure risk further.
n.2: Increased seizures are not an expected finding to leave until a routine visit; they risk harm to woman and fetus.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Mei, 35, is 12 weeks pregnant and attends her booking appointment. She lists two prescribed medicines from her GP. The midwife is completing her medicines history. Which further step is most important to make the history complete and safe?
o: Ask her to bring her tablets to the 16-week appointment
Record the prescribed medicines and recheck them at 28 weeks
Ask about over the counter, herbal and supplement products
Ask the GP practice to fax the repeat prescription list
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: A full medicines history includes over the counter, herbal and supplement products as well as prescribed medicines, because these can interact or be unsafe in pregnancy. Code 18.3 requires care to be compatible with other treatment, including (where possible) over the counter medicines; SPM 3.18 covers polypharmacy and over the counter use.

n.0: Delaying to 16 weeks leaves the history incomplete at booking when it is needed.
n.1: Waiting until 28 weeks leaves non-prescribed products unchecked through organogenesis.
n.3: Confirming the repeat list adds nothing about non-prescribed products, which are the gap in this history.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Hannah, 32, is having a planned home birth. Her community midwife has no prescription chart or patient group directions for this birth. Which medicine can the registered midwife lawfully administer under the midwives exemptions in Schedule 17 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012?
o: Intramuscular oxytocin for the third stage
Intravenous tranexamic acid for heavy bleeding
Intravenous co-amoxiclav for suspected infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for a seizure
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: HMR 2012 Schedule 17 lists the parenteral prescription-only medicines a registered midwife may administer in professional practice, including oxytocins (natural and synthetic), ergometrine, carboprost, anti-D, phytomenadione and others (SPM 3.19 midwives exemptions).

n.1: Tranexamic acid is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.
n.2: Antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav are not on the Schedule 17 list.
n.3: Magnesium sulfate is not on the Schedule 17 list and needs a prescription or PGD.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Ellie, a third-year student midwife, is caring for Fatima, 27, in established labour. Fatima requests pethidine, which the registered midwife will give under the midwives exemptions. Ellie asks whether she can draw up and administer the injection herself under direct supervision. What is the correct response?
o: Yes, once she has been signed off as competent by a practice assessor
No, pethidine must be prescribed and given by a doctor in labour
No, students may not give pethidine under the midwives exemptions
Yes, if the registered midwife directly supervises the injection
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Schedule 17 allows student midwives to administer listed parenteral medicines under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, but this expressly excludes diamorphine, morphine and pethidine (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 1.2 act within the law; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Practice assessor sign-off does not change the legal exclusion of pethidine for student midwives.
n.1: Registered midwives can administer pethidine under the exemptions without a doctor's prescription.
n.3: Direct supervision covers other listed medicines but the Schedule excludes pethidine for students.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Sian, 29, is 3 days postnatal at home after a second-degree tear and reports perineal pain not relieved by paracetamol. She has no contraindications to NSAIDs. Which medicine can the registered midwife supply to her under the midwives exemptions?
o: Co-codamol 30/500 tablets
Diclofenac tablets
Amoxicillin capsules
Dihydrocodeine tablets
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Schedule 17 Part 1 allows registered midwives to sell or supply, in the course of their professional practice, prescription-only medicines containing diclofenac, hydrocortisone acetate, miconazole, nystatin and phytomenadione (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Co-codamol 30/500 contains codeine, which is not on the midwives supply list.
n.2: Antibiotics such as amoxicillin are not on the midwives supply list and need a prescription.
n.3: Dihydrocodeine is not on the midwives supply list.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Olivia, 25, is in labour and has a positive group B streptococcus result. Intravenous benzylpenicillin is not on the midwives exemptions list and no doctor is free to write a prescription. Which of the following authorises the midwife to administer it without an individual prescription?
o: The administration list in Schedule 17 of the regulations
An entry about antibiotics written in Olivia's birth plan
A verbal instruction from the labour ward coordinator
A trust PGD she is trained and authorised to use
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: A patient group direction (PGD) is a written instruction allowing named, trained and authorised professionals to supply or administer a specified medicine to a defined group of patients without an individual prescription. Medicines outside Schedule 17 need a prescription or a PGD (SPM 3.19).

n.0: Benzylpenicillin is not on the Schedule 17 administration list.
n.1: A birth plan records preferences and is not a legal authority to administer a medicine.
n.2: A coordinator is not a prescriber, and a verbal instruction does not authorise administration.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: A newly qualified midwife on the postnatal ward is asked by a woman with a perineal haematoma whether the midwife could inject local anaesthetic to drain it on the ward, using lidocaine under the midwives exemptions. Which statement about lidocaine under Schedule 17 is accurate?
o: It may be given by a midwife while attending a woman in childbirth
It needs a separate PGD for each perineal repair after birth
It may be given for any minor procedure in the postnatal period
It may be given by a student midwife without direct supervision
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Schedule 17 allows midwives to administer lidocaine hydrochloride only while attending a woman in childbirth (for example infiltration for episiotomy or perineal repair). Management of a postnatal haematoma needs medical review and a prescription (HMR 2012 Sch 17; SPM 1.2).

n.1: Lidocaine during childbirth is covered by the exemption and needs no PGD.
n.2: The exemption is limited to attending a woman in childbirth, not any postnatal procedure.
n.3: Student midwives must be under the direct supervision of a registered midwife.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Priya, a midwife newly arrived from overseas, is preparing for the third stage of labour on a midwife-led unit. Ana, 30, has chosen active management with Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms). Priya asks a colleague whether the midwives exemptions cover this combined product. What is the correct answer?
o: No, a combined product needs a patient group direction
Yes, because Syntometrine is classed as a pharmacy medicine
No, ergometrine needs an individual prescription from a doctor
Yes, both oxytocin and ergometrine are on the administration list
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Schedule 17 covers parenteral POMs containing the listed substances and no other prescription-only substance. Oxytocins and ergometrine maleate are both listed, so a registered midwife may administer Syntometrine (if not contraindicated, for example by pre-eclampsia) (HMR 2012 Sch 17; NG235 1.10.11).

n.0: A combined product is covered when every POM substance in it is on the list, as here.
n.1: Syntometrine is a prescription-only medicine, not a pharmacy medicine.
n.2: Ergometrine maleate is on the Schedule 17 administration list.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Beth, 34, is in established labour on the delivery suite and has been given pethidine 100 mg intramuscularly by her midwife under the midwives exemptions. Pethidine is a Schedule 2 controlled drug. Where must the midwife record this administration?
o: On Beth's medicines record, as the register is kept by pharmacy
In the handover sheet so the coordinator can update the register
In the ward controlled drug register and on Beth's medicines record
In the controlled drug register once the shift has finished
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Code 18.2 requires midwives to keep to guidance on recording the supply and administration of controlled drugs. Schedule 2 controlled drugs used on a ward are recorded contemporaneously in the ward controlled drug register and in the woman's medicines record (NICE NG46 1.2.1: a controlled drugs register is kept for each premises where Schedule 2 controlled drugs are stored, in line with regulation 20 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Wards hold their own controlled drug register; a medicines record entry alone is not enough.
n.1: A handover sheet is not a legal record and the coordinator did not witness the administration.
n.3: Controlled drug entries are made at the time of administration, not later in the shift.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Kerry has been a registered midwife for 4 years and wants to prescribe medicines such as antibiotics for women with postnatal infections in her community caseload. What must happen before she can prescribe independently?
o: She must hold a patient group direction for each antibiotic she uses
She must complete an NMC-approved prescribing programme and have it recorded
She must complete 2 years of community practice and a local competency
She must be authorised in writing by her head of midwifery
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Only nurses and midwives who have completed an NMC-approved prescribing qualification and had it recorded on the register can prescribe (Code 18, note to 18.5). SPM 3.19 expects the ability to progress to a prescribing qualification after registration.

n.0: A PGD allows supply or administration to a group; it is not prescribing.
n.2: Length of experience and a local competency do not confer prescribing rights.
n.3: A head of midwifery cannot authorise prescribing; it requires a recorded qualification.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Comfort, 30, has pre-eclampsia and is in the second stage of labour on the delivery suite. Her blood pressure is controlled on labetalol. She has chosen active management of the third stage. Which uterotonic is most appropriate after the birth of her baby?
o: Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intravenously
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 1.10.11-1.10.12 offers oxytocin 10 units IM for active management. Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia and severe cardiac, hepatic or renal disease (NG235 1.10.9), so oxytocin alone is used here.

n.1: Oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia because ergometrine raises blood pressure.
n.2: Carboprost is a treatment for PPH, not the routine prophylactic uterotonic.
n.3: Ergometrine is contraindicated in pre-eclampsia and is not a prophylactic option in NG235.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Jess, 27, is healthy and in labour with her first baby. She has chosen active management of the third stage and asks the midwife how oxytocin plus ergometrine (Syntometrine) compares with oxytocin alone. Which explanation is accurate?
o: It is equally effective but must be given intravenously after the birth
It is more effective at reducing blood loss but causes more nausea and vomiting
It is more effective at reducing blood loss and has similar side effects
It is less effective at reducing blood loss but causes fewer side effects
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 1.10.9 explains that oxytocin plus ergometrine may be more effective than oxytocin alone at reducing the risk of postpartum haemorrhage but is more likely to cause nausea and vomiting, so an antiemetic is offered (1.10.10). It is given IM after the birth of the baby, before cord clamping.

n.0: It is given intramuscularly, and it is somewhat more effective than oxytocin alone.
n.2: Side effects are greater: nausea and vomiting are more common.
n.3: It is more effective, not less, and has more side effects.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Lily, 29, is having her labour augmented with an oxytocin infusion at 9 cm dilatation. The midwife palpates 6 contractions in 10 minutes. The CTG is currently normal and Lily is coping with an epidural. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give terbutaline before deciding on the infusion rate
Continue the current rate and reassess in 30 minutes
Increase the rate to complete dilatation more quickly
Reduce or stop the infusion and inform the obstetrician
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 1.8.54 aims for 3 to 4 contractions in 10 minutes on oxytocin, and 1.8.55 advises reducing or stopping it if there are more than 4 in 10, until there are 4 or fewer. Excessive contractions (5 or more in 10 is an amber CTG feature, NG229) reduce fetal oxygenation.

n.0: Tocolysis is not the first step; the oxytocin causing the overactivity is reduced or stopped first.
n.1: Continuing unchanged leaves excessive contractions untreated for a further 30 minutes.
n.2: Increasing oxytocin with 6 contractions in 10 minutes worsens uterine hyperstimulation.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Nadia, 33, has a primary postpartum haemorrhage of 1,200 mL after a vaginal birth. Uterotonics have been given and the obstetrician asks the midwife to prepare tranexamic acid as NICE recommends. How should it be given?
o: 500 mg intravenously as a rapid bolus
1 g intramuscularly as a single injection
2 g orally with a glass of water
1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 1.10.35: alongside uterotonics, give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes for PPH, repeated after at least 30 minutes if bleeding continues. Tranexamic acid is not a midwives exemption medicine and needs a prescription or PGD.

n.0: The dose is 1 g, and it is given over 10 minutes rather than as a rapid bolus.
n.1: The intramuscular route is not the route recommended for PPH.
n.2: Oral tranexamic acid is not used for acute PPH.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Ruth, 31, received oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM for active management of the third stage. On the delivery suite, 20 minutes after the placenta is delivered complete, she bleeds heavily from an atonic uterus despite massage and an empty bladder. She has no history of asthma. According to NICE NG235, which uterotonic is appropriate next?
o: Misoprostol 200 micrograms orally
A second dose of oxytocin with ergometrine IM
Carboprost intramuscularly
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intravenously
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 table 12: after prophylaxis with oxytocin plus ergometrine, first-line treatment for atony is carboprost IM or an oxytocin infusion. Carboprost can be repeated at intervals of at least 15 minutes, up to 8 doses (NG235 1.10.34).

n.0: NG235 lists misoprostol 800 micrograms sublingually or rectally, not 200 micrograms orally.
n.1: NG235 keeps a repeat of oxytocin with ergometrine for settings where other drugs are unavailable, such as a home birth; on the delivery suite carboprost or an oxytocin infusion is first line.
n.3: Ergometrine has already been given and IV ergometrine is not the NG235 next step.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Asha, 36, is being treated for an atonic postpartum haemorrhage. She was given carboprost intramuscularly 5 minutes ago and is still bleeding. The junior doctor asks the midwife to draw up a second dose of carboprost to give straight away. What is the correct response?
o: Wait at least 60 minutes after the first dose
Wait at least 15 minutes after the first dose
Give it now because the bleeding is continuing
Give misoprostol as carboprost is a single dose
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 1.10.34: carboprost may be repeated at intervals of at least 15 minutes, up to a maximum of 8 doses. Meanwhile other measures continue (massage, oxytocin infusion, tranexamic acid, escalation to the senior team).

n.0: The minimum interval is 15 minutes, not 60 minutes.
n.2: A second dose at 5 minutes is earlier than the minimum 15-minute interval.
n.3: Carboprost can be repeated up to 8 doses; it is not a single dose.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Tamsin, 26, has severe pre-eclampsia and is receiving magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour after a 4 g loading dose. On her hourly check the midwife finds she is drowsy, her respiratory rate is 10 breaths/min and her patellar reflexes are absent. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Increase the infusion because absent reflexes signal seizure risk
Stop the infusion, call for help and prepare calcium gluconate
Give a further 2 g bolus of magnesium sulfate for drowsiness
Continue the infusion and recheck her reflexes in 4 hours
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Loss of patellar reflexes, respiratory depression and drowsiness are signs of magnesium toxicity. The infusion is stopped, urgent help called, airway and breathing supported and calcium gluconate (the antidote in the product SPC) prepared. NICE NG25 1.10.5 requires monitoring of pulse, BP, respiratory rate and patellar reflexes at least 4-hourly.

n.0: Absent reflexes indicate magnesium toxicity, not a need for more magnesium.
n.2: A further bolus is for recurrent fits, not drowsiness, and would worsen toxicity.
n.3: Continuing exposes her to worsening respiratory depression; this needs immediate action.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Joy, 38, has severe cardiac disease and received oxytocin 10 units IM for the third stage. Ten minutes after birth she has an atonic postpartum haemorrhage. The obstetric team is present. Which uterotonic option is most appropriate for her?
o: An oxytocin infusion
Ergometrine 250 micrograms intravenously
Ergometrine 500 micrograms intramuscularly
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG235 table 12: after oxytocin prophylaxis, first-line options are ergometrine IM (carboprost if contraindicated) or an oxytocin infusion. Ergometrine-containing drugs are contraindicated in severe cardiac disease (NG235 1.10.9), so an oxytocin infusion is chosen.

n.1: Intravenous ergometrine is contraindicated for the same reason.
n.2: Ergometrine is contraindicated in severe cardiac disease.
n.3: This combination contains ergometrine, which is contraindicated in severe cardiac disease.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Danielle, 37, has chronic hypertension treated with ramipril. She phones the community midwife to say she has just had a positive pregnancy test and estimates she is 6 weeks pregnant. Which plan is in line with NICE NG133?
o: Continue ramipril and add aspirin 75 mg daily from 12 weeks
Continue ramipril until her booking appointment at 10 weeks
Stop all her blood pressure medicine until she is seen in clinic
Arrange for ramipril to be stopped within 2 working days and replaced
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG133 1.3.3: stop ACE inhibitors or ARBs if a woman becomes pregnant, preferably within 2 working days of notification, and offer alternatives (labetalol first line). ACE inhibitors carry a risk of congenital abnormalities.

n.0: Aspirin may be advised from 12 weeks, but ramipril still needs to be stopped and replaced.
n.1: Waiting until 10 weeks prolongs exposure to an ACE inhibitor in early pregnancy.
n.2: Stopping all treatment leaves chronic hypertension uncontrolled; an alternative should be offered.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Kezia, 23, has epilepsy controlled with sodium valproate. She attends the early pregnancy unit with an unplanned pregnancy of 7 weeks, confirmed on scan. She is distressed and asks the midwife what she should do about her medication. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Stop valproate today and restart it after the first trimester
Halve the valproate dose until she sees her GP next month
Continue valproate as the main risk period has already passed
Keep taking it for now and arrange urgent specialist review today
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Valproate carries a high risk of malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders (MHRA safety advice; CG192 1.4.29). In epilepsy, stopping abruptly can cause seizures that harm woman and fetus, so she should not stop or change her dose without advice and needs urgent specialist review to plan the switch (SPM 3.18).

n.0: Abruptly stopping an antiseizure medicine risks status epilepticus; changes need specialist planning.
n.1: Self-adjusting the dose risks seizures and delays the specialist review she needs now.
n.2: Organogenesis is ongoing at 7 weeks and valproate also affects neurodevelopment, so urgent review is needed.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Ngozi, 32, had pre-eclampsia and is day 3 postnatal. She is breastfeeding and still needs antihypertensive treatment. She was on methyldopa antenatally, which the team plans to stop. Which medicine does NICE NG133 recommend offering?
o: Enalapril
Furosemide
Losartan
Methyldopa at a reduced dose
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG133 1.9.4 recommends enalapril for postnatal hypertension, including in women who are breastfeeding, with monitoring of maternal renal function and potassium. Methyldopa should be stopped within 2 days after birth (NG133 1.5.18), and diuretics and ARBs are avoided where possible when breastfeeding (NG133 1.9.8).

n.1: NG133 1.9.8 advises avoiding diuretics in women who are breastfeeding where possible.
n.2: Losartan is an ARB, which NG133 1.9.8 advises avoiding while breastfeeding where possible.
n.3: NG133 1.5.18 advises stopping methyldopa within 2 days after birth and changing to an alternative.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Freya, 30, is 10 days postnatal and exclusively breastfeeding. Her GP has prescribed a medicine for migraine and Freya asks the community midwife whether it is safe for her baby. Where should the midwife seek specialist evidence-based advice?
o: Her sister's experience of the same medicine
An online parenting forum with many replies
The patient information leaflet in the box
The UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: The UK Drugs in Lactation Advisory Service (Specialist Pharmacy Service) gives evidence-based advice on medicines in breastfeeding; the BNF and local medicines information services are also appropriate. Manufacturer leaflets often advise against use because medicines are not tested in breastfeeding, not because of proven harm (NG133 1.9.2; SPM 3.18).

n.0: Anecdotal experience is not evidence-based advice about this baby and this medicine.
n.1: An online forum is not a reliable, evidence-based source of medicines information.
n.2: Product leaflets often carry general disclaimers rather than evidence about breastfeeding.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Marta, 34, has bipolar disorder and is 24 weeks pregnant. After specialist discussion she has decided to continue lithium because she is at high risk of relapse. Which monitoring plan is in line with NICE CG192?
o: Check plasma lithium at booking, at 28 weeks and at 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium weekly from 20 weeks until the birth
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks
Check plasma lithium every 4 weeks, then stop it at 36 weeks
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE CG192 1.4.37: if lithium continues in pregnancy, check plasma levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from the 36th week; keep levels in range, maintain fluid balance, plan birth in hospital, stop lithium during labour and check levels 12 hours after the last dose.

n.0: Three checks in pregnancy is less frequent than the 4-weekly monitoring recommended.
n.1: Weekly checks are recommended from 36 weeks, not from 20 weeks.
n.3: Lithium is stopped during labour, not at 36 weeks, when weekly monitoring starts.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Ayesha, 29, has chronic kidney disease and attends for booking at 10 weeks. Her blood pressure is normal. The midwife identifies that she is at high risk of pre-eclampsia. What advice about aspirin is in line with NICE NG133?
o: Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 20 weeks until 36 weeks
Take aspirin 300 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth
Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from booking until 28 weeks
Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG133 1.1.2: women at high risk of pre-eclampsia (including chronic kidney disease) are advised to take aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth. For this indication aspirin must be prescribed rather than bought.

n.0: Aspirin starts at 12 weeks, not 20, and continues until the birth.
n.1: The recommended dose is 75 to 150 mg, not 300 mg.
n.2: Aspirin continues until the birth rather than stopping at 28 weeks.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Shanice, 27, is 5 days postnatal and breastfeeding her term baby. She takes enalapril for postnatal hypertension and says she is thinking of switching to formula because the medicine might harm her baby. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Give formula at night when the level in her milk is highest
Express and discard her milk for 2 hours after each dose
Keep breastfeeding and watch for drowsiness or poor feeding
Stop breastfeeding while she takes any antihypertensive medicine
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG133 1.9.1-1.9.3: the need for antihypertensives does not prevent breastfeeding; most lead to very low levels in milk. Advise monitoring the baby for drowsiness, lethargy, pallor, cold peripheries or poor feeding. Enalapril is recommended postnatally including when breastfeeding (NG133 1.9.4).

n.0: Night-time formula is not needed and could reduce her milk supply.
n.1: Discarding milk is not advised; levels in milk are very low.
n.3: Antihypertensive treatment can be adapted to accommodate breastfeeding; stopping is not needed.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Rosa, 31, is 34 weeks pregnant and has been prescribed nifedipine for gestational hypertension. She shows the midwife the product leaflet, which says the medicine should not be used in pregnancy, and says she will not take it. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree that she should not take it and record that she declined it
Explain leaflet warnings often reflect a lack of testing, and discuss it
Tell her the prescriber's decision overrides the leaflet's warning
Advise her to take half the prescribed dose to lower any risk
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: NICE NG133 notes (alongside 1.4.5) that some nifedipine brands are contraindicated in pregnancy by the manufacturer, and explains that most medicines are not tested in pregnant or breastfeeding women, so manufacturer disclaimers are not because of specific safety concerns or evidence of harm (NG133 1.9.2). The midwife explains this, answers her questions and involves the prescriber so Rosa can make an informed decision (SPM 3.18).

n.0: Simply recording a refusal misses the chance to give the information she needs to decide.
n.2: Her informed consent is required; a prescriber's decision does not override her choice.
n.3: Self-reducing the dose gives inadequate treatment and has not been prescribed.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Holly, 28, is day 2 after a caesarean birth on the postnatal ward. Her chart shows a new prescription for oral cefalexin written that morning, but there is no dose written, only the drug name, route and frequency. The doctor who wrote it has gone to theatre. What should the midwife do?
o: Give the usual adult dose and ask the doctor to add it later
Withhold the dose and contact a prescriber to complete it
Give the lowest dose in the BNF until the doctor is free
Ask a midwife colleague to confirm the usual dose, then give it
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: A prescription without a dose is incomplete and must not be administered. The midwife withholds the dose, contacts a prescriber (another doctor if needed) to correct it and documents the delay (Code 18; SPM 3.18 prescribing errors; SPM 3.19 safe administration).

n.0: Choosing a dose is prescribing, which the midwife is not authorised to do here.
n.2: Selecting any dose, even the lowest, is prescribing without authority.
n.3: A colleague's agreement does not make an incomplete prescription valid.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Bisi, 33, started a new antibiotic yesterday for mastitis. At a home visit she shows the community midwife a raised itchy rash on her arms that began this morning. The midwife arranges same-day medical review. How should the suspected adverse drug reaction be reported?
o: To the NMC as a fitness to practise concern
To the manufacturer by letter after discharge
Through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme
Once a doctor confirms the drug caused it
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Suspected adverse drug reactions are reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme. Certainty is not required: a suspicion is enough, and healthcare professionals and patients can report (SPM 3.18 adverse reactions).

n.0: The NMC regulates professionals; an adverse drug reaction is not a fitness to practise matter.
n.1: The national route is the Yellow Card scheme, and reporting should not wait until discharge.
n.3: Yellow Card reports are based on suspicion; proof of causation is not needed first.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Chloe, 30, is postnatal after a long labour. The midwife realises she has just given Chloe a dose of dihydrocodeine that was prescribed for the woman in the next bed. Chloe is sleepy but rousable and breathing normally. What is the midwife's first priority?
o: Assess Chloe and inform the doctor and coordinator now
Tell Chloe what happened at her discharge discussion
Refer herself to the NMC before the end of her shift
Complete an incident report before telling anyone else
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Code 14.1 requires the midwife to act immediately to put right the situation where harm has or could have occurred: assess and monitor Chloe (including respiratory rate and sedation) and get medical review. She then explains and apologises (Code 14.2) and documents and reports the incident (Code 14.3).

n.1: Chloe must be told promptly, not at discharge (Code 14.2).
n.2: Self-referral to the NMC is not the immediate priority and is not required for every error.
n.3: Reporting matters, but Chloe's safety and medical review come first.
