Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Two women with the surname Begum are on the same postnatal bay. Before giving prescribed oral iron to Jahanara Begum, 26, what is the most reliable way for the midwife to confirm she has the right woman?
o: Ask, 'Are you Mrs Begum?' and wait for her to agree
Check that the bed number matches the one on the chart
Check name, birth date and hospital number with the chart
Ask her partner to confirm her full name and the medicine
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Positive identification uses at least two identifiers (name, date of birth, hospital number) on the wristband checked against the prescription, and asking the woman to state her name and date of birth where she can. Closed questions and bed numbers are unreliable (SPM 3.19 safe administration).

n.0: A closed question invites agreement and both women share the surname.
n.1: Women can move beds, so a bed number does not identify a person.
n.3: A partner's confirmation is not a substitute for checking identifiers against the chart.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Emily, 35, had an intravenous antibiotic dose omitted overnight after a transcription error and has developed signs of infection needing extra treatment. The next morning she asks the midwife, 'Did something go wrong with my medicines?' What is the most appropriate response?
o: Say she can be told the details if she makes a complaint
Explain what happened, apologise and say what happens next
Say the risk team will contact her when the review has ended
Say an apology now would amount to admitting liability
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Code 14.2 requires the midwife to explain fully and promptly what has happened, including likely effects, and apologise. The statutory duty of candour (reg 20, Regulated Activities Regulations 2014) also applies to the organisation. An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence (Compensation Act 2006 s2).

n.0: Openness is owed when harm occurs, not in response to a complaint.
n.2: Delaying an honest answer until the review ends breaches the duty to explain promptly.
n.3: An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence under the Compensation Act 2006 s2.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Late in a busy shift on the delivery suite, a colleague asks the midwife to give an intravenous antibiotic to Maya, 29, from an unlabelled syringe the colleague drew up 20 minutes ago before being called to an emergency. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Label the syringe from the chart and then give the dose
Give it, as the colleague is an experienced registered midwife
Discard it and prepare and check a fresh dose herself
Give it after reading the drug name on the prescription chart
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: A midwife should administer only a medicine she has prepared or checked herself; an unlabelled syringe cannot be verified. Discarding it and preparing a fresh dose against the prescription keeps Maya safe (Code 18; Code 19.1 reduce the likelihood of mistakes; SPM 3.19).

n.0: Labelling a syringe she did not prepare does not confirm its contents.
n.1: Experience of the colleague does not allow the contents of an unlabelled syringe to be verified.
n.3: The chart shows what was prescribed, not what is in the syringe.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: While preparing medicines on the postnatal ward, a midwife picks up 2 tablets of labetalol for Aisha, 31, instead of the 1 tablet prescribed. She notices and corrects this before reaching the bedside. What should she do next?
o: Tell the coordinator verbally and take no further action
Report the near miss through the incident reporting system
Make no report as the error did not reach the woman
Refer herself to the NMC as a fitness to practise matter
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Near misses are reported through the local incident reporting system so that learning can reduce future harm. Code 19.1 requires measures to reduce the likelihood of mistakes, near misses and harm (SPM 3.18 medicines errors).

n.0: A verbal mention is not recorded and does not support organisational learning.
n.2: Near misses are reported for learning even when no harm occurred.
n.3: A corrected near miss is a learning event, not a fitness to practise referral.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Grace, 34, is 2 days post caesarean and has been prescribed daily low molecular weight heparin for 10 days. She tells the midwife she does not want the injection because she hates needles and feels fine. She has capacity. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the injection while explaining it is part of standard care
Withhold it and record that she declined, with no further action
Explore her reasons, explain the risks and inform the prescriber
Ask her partner to persuade her to accept the injection
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: A woman with capacity can decline a medicine. The midwife explores her concerns, explains the risk of venous thromboembolism after caesarean and alternatives, respects her decision, documents it and informs the prescriber (Code 4.2 informed consent; SPM 3.19 optimisation of medicines).

n.0: Giving a medicine against her stated wishes is treatment without consent.
n.1: Recording alone omits the information she needs and the prescriber's review.
n.3: Asking a partner to persuade her risks coercion; the discussion is with Grace.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Amira, 29, takes lithium for bipolar disorder and is 22 weeks pregnant. At an antenatal appointment she asks the midwife why her lithium blood levels are now being checked more often than before pregnancy. Which physiological change of pregnancy best explains the need for closer monitoring?
o: Higher glomerular filtration speeds renal clearance of lithium
Reduced plasma volume concentrates lithium in the circulation
Slower gastric emptying reduces the amount of lithium absorbed
Higher serum albumin binds more lithium within the plasma
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Glomerular filtration rises by around half in pregnancy, so renally cleared drugs such as lithium are excreted faster and levels can fall. NICE CG192 (1.4.35-1.4.37) advises lithium levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks. SPM 3.18 requires knowledge of pharmacology across the continuum of care.

n.1: Plasma volume increases in pregnancy; it does not fall.
n.2: Gastric emptying slows in pregnancy, but lithium absorption is not the main reason for closer level monitoring; renal clearance is.
n.3: Serum albumin falls rather than rises in pregnancy, and lithium is not significantly protein bound.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Grace, 31, is in established labour at term and is group B streptococcus positive. Her prescription chart shows intravenous benzylpenicillin. While checking her identity band before giving the dose, the midwife sees a red allergy band and Grace says penicillin gave her a widespread rash. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the dose slowly and observe her closely for a reaction
Withhold the dose and contact the prescriber to review it
Give clindamycin from ward stock and tell the doctor afterwards
Give a small test dose first and continue if no rash appears
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: The midwife must not administer a medicine to which the woman reports an allergy. Withholding the dose and asking the prescriber to review and prescribe an alternative keeps her safe (Code 19.1 reduce the likelihood of harm; SPM 3.18 allergies and drug sensitivities). The decision and allergy status are documented.

n.0: Giving a medicine she reports an allergy to risks anaphylaxis; slow administration does not make it safe.
n.2: Clindamycin is not a midwives exemption medicine; it needs a prescription or PGD before it can be given.
n.3: A midwife cannot decide to give a test dose of a drug to which an allergy is reported; this still exposes her to the allergen.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Zainab, 26, is 31 weeks pregnant and has lower back pain after a long day at work. She tells the community midwife she has been taking ibuprofen bought from the supermarket and asks if this is the best painkiller to use. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Stop ibuprofen and use paracetamol at the recommended dose
Change to codeine tablets from the pharmacy for stronger relief
Change to aspirin 300 mg tablets when the pain is severe
Continue ibuprofen for up to 3 days and take it with food
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen are avoided in pregnancy unless prescribed, particularly in the third trimester (risk of premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and reduced amniotic fluid). Paracetamol at the recommended dose is the first choice simple analgesic. SPM 3.18 includes the impact of over the counter medication.

n.1: Codeine is not a first-line choice in pregnancy and can cause neonatal withdrawal and respiratory depression with use near birth.
n.2: Analgesic-dose aspirin is also an NSAID and carries the same third trimester risks.
n.3: Ibuprofen should be stopped at 31 weeks rather than continued with food.

Medicines in Midwifery Practice.q: Ruth, 24, is 4 weeks postnatal and plans to start the progestogen-only pill. During the contraception discussion she mentions she has been taking St John's wort, bought from a health food shop, for low mood. What should the midwife explain about this combination?
o: St John's wort can make the pill less effective at preventing pregnancy
St John's wort is herbal, so it has no interaction with the pill
St John's wort can be taken safely if separated from the pill by 2 hours
St John's wort increases the pill's effect, so a lower dose suits
Medicines in Midwifery Practice.w: St John's wort induces liver enzymes and reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, so an alternative method (such as an intrauterine method) should be discussed, and her low mood assessed. Code 18.3 requires care to be compatible with other treatment, including over the counter products; SPM 3.18 covers interactions.

n.1: Herbal products can interact with medicines; St John's wort is a well-known enzyme inducer.
n.2: Enzyme induction is not avoided by spacing the doses; the effect persists.
n.3: Enzyme induction lowers, not raises, hormone levels; there is no lower-dose option.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Abena, 34, is a Black woman who is day 1 after a caesarean birth. She feels breathless and her respiratory rate is 26 breaths/min. The pulse oximeter reads 95% on air. Her heart rate is 112 beats/min. How should the midwife interpret these findings?
o: Pulse oximetry may overestimate her saturation, so escalate now
Saturation of 95% means the breathlessness is likely anxiety
Her heart rate is normal for pregnancy, so increase observations
Saturation of 95% is reassuring, so recheck in 4 hours
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.4.9 warns that pulse oximeters may overestimate oxygen saturation in people with dark skin. A respiratory rate of 26 is a high-risk criterion (NG255 table 1), so she needs urgent senior review whatever the saturation reading (SPM 4.6).

n.1: Attributing breathlessness to anxiety risks missing sepsis or pulmonary embolism.
n.2: A respiratory rate of 26 needs escalation, not just more observations; 112 is above her expected baseline.
n.3: A normal-looking saturation does not outweigh a high-risk respiratory rate, and may be overestimated.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Kayleigh, 25, is on the postnatal ward 3 days after a caesarean birth. She says she feels unwell. Her temperature is 35.8 C, heart rate 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min and blood pressure 118/74 mmHg. She has no other high-risk criteria. What is the most appropriate action under NICE NG255?
o: Recheck her observations at the next 4-hourly round
Start a 500 mL fluid bolus before any review by a clinician
Arrange bloods with lactate and review within 1 hour
Reassure her that sepsis is unlikely as she has no fever
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NG255 table 1 moderate-to-high criteria include temperature under 36 C, heart rate 100-130 and surgery in the last 6 weeks. With 2 or more such criteria, arrange bloods including lactate and a clinician review within 1 hour (NG255 1.7.10). Sepsis may be afebrile.

n.0: Waiting for the next round ignores 2 or more moderate-to-high criteria.
n.1: Fluid boluses are guided by lactate and blood pressure after review; this step comes first.
n.3: Sepsis can present with a low temperature; NG255 counts under 36 C as a risk criterion.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Harriet, 36, has severe pre-eclampsia. The midwife escalated her blood pressure of 168/112 mmHg and new headache to the registrar 30 minutes ago. The registrar said they would come but is still in theatre, and her blood pressure is now 172/114 mmHg. What should the midwife do?
o: Wait for the registrar, who has already been informed
Escalate to the obstetric consultant using the escalation policy
Record the new reading and recheck it in 30 minutes
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe an antihypertensive instead
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: When escalation does not produce a timely response and the woman is deteriorating, the midwife escalates further up the chain, usually to the consultant, using the unit's escalation policy, and documents this (SPM 4.6; Code 16 and 8.2). Severe hypertension needs prompt treatment (NG133).

n.0: Waiting while severe hypertension worsens delays treatment.
n.2: Rechecking without escalation leaves severe hypertension untreated.
n.3: Escalation should follow the obstetric chain and escalation policy rather than going around it.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Ellis was born at term after significant meconium-stained liquor and is being observed on the postnatal ward. At 2 hours the midwife finds a respiratory rate of 70 breaths/min with grunting. Heart rate is 140 beats/min. What should the midwife do?
o: Encourage a breastfeed and recheck after the feed
Wrap the baby and recheck in 30 minutes
Recheck the respiratory rate at the 4-hour observation
Call the neonatal team for urgent review
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG235 1.11.29: after meconium, escalate to a neonatal clinician if respiratory rate is over 60, there is grunting, heart rate under 100 or over 160, capillary refill over 3 seconds, temperature 38 C or above, saturation under 95% or central cyanosis (SPM 4.6 deterioration in the newborn).

n.0: Feeding a baby with respiratory distress risks aspiration and delays review.
n.1: Warming does not treat respiratory distress and delays review.
n.2: Two red flags (RR over 60 and grunting) need review now, not at the next observation.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Gemma, 28, gave birth vaginally 2 hours ago. Her measured blood loss is 650 mL. Her pulse is 88 beats/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg and her uterus is now well contracted. How should this blood loss be classified?
o: Major primary postpartum haemorrhage
Expected blood loss after a vaginal birth
Minor primary postpartum haemorrhage
Secondary postpartum haemorrhage
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Primary PPH is blood loss of 500 mL or more within 24 hours of birth; minor PPH is 500-1000 mL and major PPH over 1000 mL (RCOG GTG 52). 650 mL within 2 hours is a minor primary PPH and needs monitoring and documentation (SPM 4.7).

n.0: Major PPH is more than 1000 mL.
n.1: 500 mL or more within 24 hours meets the definition of PPH.
n.3: Secondary PPH occurs after the first 24 hours following birth.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Leanne, 31, has just given birth at home after an active third stage, and the placenta is complete. Ten minutes later the midwife sees a sudden heavy gush of blood and the uterus feels soft. A second midwife is in the next room. What should the first midwife do first?
o: Call for help and rub up a contraction
Weigh the soiled pads to measure the loss accurately
Start an intravenous infusion before calling anyone
Give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously from her bag
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG235 1.10.33: for PPH, call for help (here the second midwife and a 999 ambulance) and give immediate treatment: empty the bladder, uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids, while assessing blood loss and arranging transfer to obstetric-led care.

n.1: Quantifying loss is part of continuous assessment but does not come before calling for help and treatment.
n.2: IV access matters, but calling for help comes first so treatment can happen in parallel.
n.3: Tranexamic acid is not a midwives exemption drug and is not the immediate first step.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: A community midwife is discussing place of birth with four women. Which woman should be advised to plan birth in an obstetric unit because of her antenatal risk of postpartum haemorrhage?
o: Amina, 29, para 2, BMI 32 kg/m2
Becky, 24, who had a second-degree tear last time
Dana, 33, who had a PPH needing transfusion last time
Cara, 35, with a low-risk pregnancy and a fundal placenta
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG235 1.10.29 lists antenatal PPH risk factors that warrant advice to give birth in an obstetric unit, including previous PPH over 1000 mL or requiring transfusion, BMI over 35, grand multiparity (4 or more), pre-eclampsia, Hb under 85 g/L at onset of labour and placenta accreta spectrum.

n.0: BMI over 35 and parity 4 or more are the thresholds; 32 and para 2 do not meet them.
n.1: A previous second-degree tear is not an antenatal PPH risk factor in NG235.
n.3: A fundal placenta in a low-risk pregnancy is not a PPH risk factor.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Nicola, 26, is 40 minutes after birth with ongoing trickling blood loss. On palpation her uterus is soft and displaced to the right, above the umbilicus. She has not passed urine since before the birth. Uterine massage has been started. What is the next most appropriate action?
o: Empty her bladder, using a catheter if she cannot void
Repeat the observations in 15 minutes and review the loss
Give a second dose of oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly
Encourage her to put the baby to the breast for 30 minutes
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: A full bladder displaces the uterus and stops it contracting effectively. NICE NG235 1.10.33 includes emptying the bladder alongside uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids in the immediate treatment of PPH (SPM 4.8 first-line management).

n.1: Waiting allows ongoing bleeding; the cause should be treated now.
n.2: A repeat IM oxytocin dose is not the NG235 treatment step, and a full bladder will still stop the uterus contracting.
n.3: Breastfeeding helps but does not correct a uterus displaced by a full bladder.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Fern, 30, has had a home birth with a physiological third stage. Shortly after the placenta is delivered she bleeds heavily. Her blood pressure was normal throughout pregnancy and labour and she has no other medical conditions. Which uterotonic is the first-line choice under NICE NG235?
o: Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes
Oxytocin 10 units as a rapid intravenous bolus
Oxytocin 5 units with ergometrine 500 micrograms IM
Carboprost 250 micrograms intramuscularly
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG235 table 12: after a physiological third stage, first-line treatment for atonic PPH is oxytocin plus ergometrine IM (carboprost if contraindicated) or an oxytocin infusion once IV access is available. Fern has no contraindication to ergometrine.

n.0: Tranexamic acid is given alongside uterotonics, not as the first-line uterotonic.
n.1: Oxytocin is given as an infusion for PPH; a rapid IV bolus is not the NG235 treatment.
n.3: Carboprost is used first line when oxytocin plus ergometrine is contraindicated, which is not the case here.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Oona, 34, is having a major postpartum haemorrhage on the delivery suite. Help has arrived and uterotonics have been given. Her oxygen saturation is 93% on air. In line with NICE NG235, how should oxygen be given?
o: Oxygen is unnecessary until saturation falls below 90%
4 L/minute by simple face mask aiming for 92%
15 L/minute by non-rebreathe mask aiming for 94 to 98%
2 L/minute by nasal cannula aiming for 88 to 92%
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG235 1.10.33: consider supplementary oxygen starting at 15 L/minute using a non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag, to obtain a target saturation of 94% to 98% (SPM 4.7).

n.0: Her saturation is already below the 94 to 98% target, so oxygen is indicated now.
n.1: Low-flow oxygen by simple mask is not what NG235 advises in PPH.
n.3: 88 to 92% is the target for people at risk of hypercapnia, not for PPH.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During a major postpartum haemorrhage in the birth room, the team is busy treating Rachel, 29. Her partner is standing in the corner, crying and asking repeatedly what is happening. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Allocate a team member to stay with them and explain
Ask him to wait outside until the emergency is over
Tell him everything is fine so that he stays calm
Ask the most junior doctor to explain once Rachel is stable
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG235 1.10.36: allocate a member of the healthcare team to stay with the woman and her birth companions, explain what is happening, answer questions and offer support throughout the emergency (SPM 4.7).

n.1: Sending him out without support or information is not in line with NG235.
n.2: False reassurance is dishonest and undermines trust (Code 20.2).
n.3: Support should be given during the emergency, not deferred until afterwards.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Bella, 27, is in a midwife-led unit. Her placenta has not delivered 35 minutes after the birth despite active management. Her blood loss is 200 mL, her uterus is contracted and her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Attempt manual removal in the room with Entonox for pain
Site intravenous access and arrange transfer to obstetric care
Start an intravenous oxytocin infusion to expel the placenta
Inject oxytocin into the umbilical vein to aid separation
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: A third stage over 30 minutes with active management is prolonged (NICE NG235 1.10.20). Secure IV access and explain why (1.10.21); do not use umbilical vein agents (1.10.22) or routine IV oxytocics unless bleeding excessively (1.10.23-1.10.24); arrange transfer to an obstetric unit (1.10.27); no manual removal without anaesthetic (1.10.28).

n.0: Manual removal needs an anaesthetic in an obstetric unit (NG235 1.10.28).
n.2: IV oxytocics are given for a retained placenta when bleeding is excessive, which it is not here.
n.3: NG235 1.10.22 advises against umbilical vein agents for a retained placenta.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Precious, 33, is giving birth on a midwife-led unit. The baby's head has been born but has retracted tightly against the perineum, and the shoulders have not delivered with the next contraction and routine axial traction. What is the midwife's first action?
o: Perform an episiotomy to make more room for the shoulders
Ask Precious to push harder with the next contraction
Call for help, stating that this is shoulder dystocia
Apply firm downward traction to the baby's head
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Retraction of the head (turtle sign) and failure of routine axial traction to deliver the shoulders indicate shoulder dystocia. The first step is to call for help, clearly stating the emergency, so manoeuvres can begin with the right team present (RCOG GTG 42; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Shoulder dystocia is a bony problem; episiotomy is not the first action and is not needed in every case.
n.1: Maternal pushing alone will not release an impacted shoulder and can worsen the impaction.
n.3: Downward or excessive traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury and is avoided.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Help has arrived for Ama, 30, whose baby has shoulder dystocia. The senior midwife asks the team to put Ama into the McRoberts position. What does this involve?
o: Laying her flat and hyperflexing her hips onto her abdomen
Raising the foot of the bed with her legs in stirrups
Asking her to kneel on all fours with her head lowered
Turning her onto her left side with the upper leg raised
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: McRoberts manoeuvre: lie the woman flat and hyperflex and abduct her hips so her thighs are brought up towards her abdomen. This straightens the lumbosacral angle and rotates the symphysis, and is a first-line manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure (RCOG GTG 42).

n.1: Stirrups with the foot of the bed raised is a lithotomy, head-down position, not the flat, hyperflexed position of McRoberts.
n.2: All fours is a separate manoeuvre, not McRoberts.
n.3: The left lateral position is not McRoberts.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During shoulder dystocia, Rhiannon, 28, is in the McRoberts position. The baby's back is on her left side. A midwife is asked to apply suprapubic pressure. How should this be done?
o: From Rhiannon's right side, pressing on her lower abdomen towards the fetal back
From the foot of the bed, pressing upwards on the baby's head to disimpact it
From Rhiannon's left side, pressing behind the anterior shoulder towards the fetal chest
From Rhiannon's right side, pressing down on the uterine fundus towards the pelvis
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Suprapubic pressure is applied from the side of the fetal back, just above the symphysis and behind the anterior shoulder, pushing towards the fetal chest to adduct and rotate the shoulder into the wider oblique diameter (RCOG GTG 42).

n.0: Pressure towards the fetal back abducts the shoulder and widens the bisacromial diameter.
n.1: Pushing the head back is not suprapubic pressure and does not free the shoulder.
n.3: Pressure on the fundus is fundal pressure, which is avoided in shoulder dystocia.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During a shoulder dystocia, a junior doctor who has just arrived tells Lauren's partner to push down hard on the top of her abdomen. What should the midwife do?
o: Stop it at once, as fundal pressure is avoided
Allow it, as it adds force to the McRoberts manoeuvre
Ask the doctor to apply it instead of the partner
Allow it once suprapubic pressure has been tried
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Fundal pressure is avoided in shoulder dystocia because it increases impaction of the shoulder and is associated with brachial plexus injury and uterine rupture (RCOG GTG 42). The midwife intervenes to protect the woman and baby (SPM 4.7).

n.1: Fundal pressure does not assist McRoberts and worsens impaction.
n.2: Fundal pressure is avoided whoever applies it.
n.3: Fundal pressure is not a later step after suprapubic pressure.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Imani, 31, is in the McRoberts position and the team is managing shoulder dystocia. The midwife delivering the baby is about to apply traction to the head again to check whether the shoulders have been released. What type of traction is appropriate?
o: Lateral traction while rotating the head sideways
Routine axial traction in line with the fetal spine
Strong downward traction towards the floor
Steady upward traction towards the symphysis
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Only routine axial traction, in line with the fetal spine, is used to assess whether manoeuvres have worked. Downward, lateral or excessive traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury (RCOG GTG 42).

n.0: Lateral flexion of the neck stretches the brachial plexus.
n.2: Downward traction increases the risk of brachial plexus injury.
n.3: Upward traction is not used to deliver the anterior shoulder.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: After shoulder dystocia was resolved by McRoberts and suprapubic pressure, the midwife is completing the documentation for Olivia, 36. Which detail is especially important to include alongside the times and manoeuvres?
o: The colour of the liquor when the membranes ruptured
Which of the baby's shoulders was anterior
The time of her last vaginal examination before birth
Her pain score during the second stage of labour
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Documentation after shoulder dystocia should include time of birth of the head and body, the anterior shoulder, the manoeuvres used with their timing and sequence, staff present and their arrival times, the condition of the baby and cord blood gases (RCOG GTG 42). The anterior shoulder is linked to the side of any brachial plexus injury.

n.0: Liquor colour is recorded in labour but is not a key shoulder dystocia record.
n.2: The last vaginal examination time is routine labour documentation, not specific to this emergency.
n.3: Pain scores may be recorded but are not a key element of shoulder dystocia documentation.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Noah was born after a shoulder dystocia that took 3 minutes to resolve. At the first examination, his right arm lies limp, extended and internally rotated, and he does not move it, while the left arm moves normally. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Reassure the parents that this is normal bruising after a fast birth
Recheck the arm movements at the 6 to 8 week examination
Ask the parents to exercise the arm at each nappy change
Refer to the neonatal team for assessment of a brachial plexus injury
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: A limp, internally rotated arm after shoulder dystocia suggests brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy), a recognised complication (RCOG GTG 42 reports 2.3-16%). The baby needs neonatal assessment and referral (SPM 4.7 and 4.8 first-line management and referral).

n.0: This is not explained by bruising and needs assessment, not reassurance.
n.1: Delaying assessment to 6 to 8 weeks could delay specialist care.
n.2: Exercises should only follow specialist assessment and advice.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Shoulder dystocia for Bea, 34, was resolved after 2 minutes and her baby is crying. The placenta is about to be delivered. Which maternal complication should the midwife be especially alert for?
o: Urinary tract infection
Pre-eclampsia
Post-dural puncture headache
Postpartum haemorrhage
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Shoulder dystocia is associated with maternal morbidity including postpartum haemorrhage (around 11%) and obstetric anal sphincter injury (around 3.8%) (RCOG GTG 42). NICE NG235 1.10.30 lists shoulder dystocia as an intrapartum risk factor for PPH.

n.0: Urinary tract infection is not the key immediate complication of shoulder dystocia.
n.1: Pre-eclampsia is not a complication of shoulder dystocia.
n.2: Post-dural puncture headache follows epidural complications, not shoulder dystocia.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Esme, 29, is 6 cm dilated on the labour ward when her membranes rupture spontaneously. Within a minute the fetal heart rate drops to 70 beats/min. On vaginal examination the midwife feels a pulsating loop of cord in front of the fetal head. What should the midwife do first?
o: Document the findings before taking further action
Ask Esme to push to speed up the birth
Leave to fetch the CTG machine from the next room
Call for help and elevate the presenting part
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: In cord prolapse, call for help immediately (emergency bell, obstetric and neonatal teams) and relieve cord compression by keeping fingers in the vagina to elevate the presenting part, then position her knee-chest or left lateral head down while preparing for birth (RCOG GTG 50; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Documentation follows emergency treatment, not before it.
n.1: At 6 cm pushing will not achieve birth and worsens cord compression.
n.2: Leaving the woman removes the elevation of the presenting part when cord compression is causing bradycardia.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Bronwen, 34, has a cord prolapse at home with a loop of cord lying outside the vagina. The community midwife has called 999. What should she do with the cord?
o: Hold it firmly to feel pulsation throughout
Wrap it tightly in a dry towel to keep it warm
Handle it as little as possible
Push it back into the vagina above the head
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: minimal handling of loops of cord outside the vagina to prevent vasospasm. Manual replacement of the cord above the presenting part is not recommended. Relieving compression is achieved by elevating the presenting part.

n.0: Repeated handling causes vasospasm and should be kept to a minimum.
n.1: Tight wrapping compresses the cord; handling is kept to a minimum.
n.3: Manual replacement of the cord above the presenting part is not recommended in GTG 50.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Theo's mother, Ruby, 27, has a cord prolapse on the labour ward at 8 cm dilatation. A midwife is elevating the presenting part while theatre is prepared. Which position should Ruby be helped into?
o: Semi-recumbent, sitting up on the bed
Knee-chest, on her knees with her chest down
Squatting, with support from her partner
Upright, standing beside the bed
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: knee-chest position, or left lateral with head down and a pillow under the left hip, uses gravity to reduce pressure of the presenting part on the cord while birth is arranged.

n.0: Sitting up increases pressure on the cord.
n.2: Squatting brings the presenting part down onto the cord.
n.3: Standing increases pressure of the presenting part on the cord.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Lara, 31, has a cord prolapse at a planned home birth. Paramedics arrive to transfer her to the nearest consultant unit. Which position is recommended for her during the ambulance journey?
o: Exaggerated Sims position
Sitting upright on the stretcher
Knee-chest position
Supine with a pillow under her knees
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: knee-chest is potentially unsafe in a moving vehicle, so the exaggerated Sims position (left lateral, head down, pillow under the left hip) is used during ambulance transfer, with elevation of the presenting part.

n.1: Sitting upright increases pressure of the presenting part on the cord.
n.2: Knee-chest is advised while waiting at home but is potentially unsafe in a moving ambulance.
n.3: Supine positioning does not reduce pressure on the cord and risks aortocaval compression.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Saffron, 26, has a cord prolapse at a freestanding midwifery unit 40 minutes from the obstetric unit. The midwife has been elevating the presenting part manually. How can elevation be maintained during the long transfer?
o: Ask Saffron to push with each contraction to speed the birth
Give Entonox so that the contractions become weaker
Fill her bladder through a urinary catheter
Replace the cord inside the vagina above the presenting part
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: compression can be prevented by elevating the presenting part manually or by filling the urinary bladder via a catheter (community midwives should carry a Foley catheter), which is useful when transfer will take time.

n.0: Pushing before full dilatation increases cord compression.
n.1: Entonox is analgesia and does not reduce contractions or relieve cord compression.
n.3: Manual replacement of the cord is not recommended.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Zara, 30, is 5 cm dilated on the labour ward and has a cord prolapse. The CTG shows a prolonged deceleration. The obstetrician is present and theatre is ready. What is the recommended category of caesarean birth?
o: Category 3, aiming for birth within the day
Category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes
Category 1, aiming for birth within 60 minutes
Category 2, aiming for birth within 75 minutes
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: caesarean is recommended when vaginal birth is not imminent; category 1, aiming for birth within 30 minutes or less, if the fetal heart rate pattern is suspicious or pathological. Category 2 can be considered if the FHR is normal.

n.0: Category 3 is for births needing early but not urgent delivery.
n.2: Category 1 aims for 30 minutes or less, not 60.
n.3: Category 2 is considered when the fetal heart rate is normal, not with a prolonged deceleration.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Keira, 32, is fully dilated and pushing when the cord prolapses. The fetal head is at the level of the ischial spines plus 2 cm, in a direct occipito-anterior position, and the fetal heart rate is 80 beats/min. An experienced obstetrician is present. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Move to theatre for a category 2 caesarean birth
Assisted vaginal birth in the room
Knee-chest position until spontaneous birth occurs
Give tocolysis and transfer to theatre for caesarean
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: vaginal birth, usually assisted, can be attempted at full dilatation if it is anticipated that birth would be quick and safe. With a low head and a skilled operator present, this is quicker than transferring to theatre.

n.0: Category 2 is too slow with bradycardia, and birth can be achieved vaginally here.
n.2: Waiting for spontaneous birth in knee-chest delays birth of a compromised baby.
n.3: Tocolysis is for delays before caesarean; birth can be achieved now vaginally.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Wendy, 35, para 3, is in early labour at 4 cm. Her contractions are irregular and the fetal head is 4/5 palpable and mobile above the brim. A colleague suggests artificial rupture of membranes to speed things up. What should the midwife do?
o: Perform the amniotomy once she is lying flat on the bed
Avoid amniotomy and discuss the high head with obstetrics
Start oxytocin to bring the head down into the pelvis
Perform the amniotomy now, as she has had 3 births
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 50: artificial rupture of membranes should be avoided where possible when the presenting part is high or mobile, because of the risk of cord prolapse. Any decision needs obstetric discussion (SPM 4.7).

n.0: Maternal position does not remove the cord prolapse risk of amniotomy with a high head.
n.2: Oxytocin is not indicated in early labour without diagnosed delay (NG235) and is not used to engage the head.
n.3: Parity does not reduce the cord prolapse risk of amniotomy with a high, mobile head.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Yasmin, 24, is 35 weeks pregnant with pre-eclampsia and is on the antenatal ward. The midwife finds her having a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in bed. What should the midwife do first?
o: Insert a cannula and take bloods for platelets and liver function
Start a CTG to assess the fetal heart rate during the fit
Put a tongue depressor between her teeth to protect her airway
Call for help and keep her safe from injury, then turn her to the left
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: In an eclamptic fit, summon help (emergency bell, obstetric and anaesthetic teams), protect her from injury, place her in the left lateral position when possible to protect the airway and avoid aortocaval compression, and give oxygen. Magnesium sulfate is then given (NICE NG133 1.8.1, 1.8.4; SPM 4.7).

n.0: Bloods are needed but come after calling for help and securing her safety.
n.1: The woman is stabilised first; fetal assessment follows once she is safe.
n.2: Nothing should be forced into the mouth during a seizure; it can cause injury and airway obstruction.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Chantelle, 29, has severe pre-eclampsia and the consultant has decided to start magnesium sulfate. Which regimen is recommended by NICE NG133?
o: 4 g IV over 30 minutes, then 1 g/hour until birth
2 g IV over 5 minutes, then 2 g/hour for 12 hours
4 g IM into each buttock, then 2 g/hour for 24 hours
4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, then 1 g/hour for 24 hours
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 1.8.4 (Collaborative Eclampsia Trial regimen): a 4 g IV loading dose over 5 to 15 minutes, followed by an infusion of 1 g/hour maintained for 24 hours; after a fit, continue for 24 hours after the last fit.

n.0: The loading dose is given over 5 to 15 minutes and continues for 24 hours, not until birth.
n.1: The loading dose is 4 g and maintenance 1 g/hour for 24 hours.
n.2: NG133 uses intravenous loading and 1 g/hour maintenance, not this IM regimen.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Mercy, 31, had an eclamptic fit 6 hours ago and has been receiving magnesium sulfate 1 g/hour since then. She has a second fit. What treatment is recommended by NICE NG133?
o: Diazepam 10 mg IV, continuing the infusion as originally planned
A further 2 to 4 g IV, continuing the infusion for 24 hours after this fit
A phenytoin loading dose, stopping the magnesium sulfate infusion
A further 4 g IV, stopping the infusion at the original 24-hour point
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 1.8.4: recurrent fits are treated with a further 2 g to 4 g IV over 5 to 15 minutes, and the infusion continues for 24 hours after the last fit. NG133 1.8.5: do not use diazepam, phenytoin or other anticonvulsants as alternatives.

n.0: NG133 1.8.5 advises against diazepam as an alternative to magnesium sulfate.
n.2: NG133 1.8.5 advises against phenytoin; magnesium sulfate continues.
n.3: After a fit, the infusion continues for 24 hours after the last fit, not the original end point.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Harper, 27, is 34 weeks pregnant and has gestational hypertension. She phones the maternity triage line. Which symptom she describes needs immediate assessment for pre-eclampsia?
o: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Leg cramps that wake her at night
Flashing lights in her vision since today
Backache after standing at work
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 1.1.1 advises women to report immediately severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing before the eyes, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (SPM 4.8).

n.0: Gradual ankle swelling is common in pregnancy; sudden swelling of face, hands or feet is the warning sign.
n.1: Night cramps are common in pregnancy and are not a pre-eclampsia symptom.
n.3: Backache after standing is common and not a symptom of pre-eclampsia.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Nia, 30, has severe pre-eclampsia and is on the delivery suite awaiting induction. She has no ongoing blood loss and is not receiving hydralazine. The midwife is setting up her intravenous maintenance fluids. What rate does NICE NG133 recommend as the limit?
o: 125 mL/hour
80 mL/hour
150 mL/hour
40 mL/hour
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 1.8.12: in severe pre-eclampsia limit maintenance fluids to 80 mL/hour unless there are other ongoing fluid losses such as haemorrhage, because of the risk of pulmonary oedema. Volume expansion is not used unless hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive (1.8.11).

n.0: 125 mL/hour exceeds the recommended limit and risks pulmonary oedema.
n.2: 150 mL/hour exceeds the limit and risks pulmonary oedema.
n.3: 40 mL/hour is not the NG133 limit; maintenance fluids are limited to 80 mL/hour.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Olu, 33, is in established labour with severe hypertension; her last blood pressure was 164/112 mmHg and treatment has been given. How often does NICE NG133 recommend measuring her blood pressure?
o: Every 15 to 30 minutes until under 160/110
Every 4 hours, as for all women in labour
Every 2 hours until the birth of the baby
Every hour until it is below 140/90 mmHg
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 1.7.3: during labour, measure blood pressure hourly in women with hypertension, and every 15 to 30 minutes until it is less than 160/110 mmHg in women with severe hypertension.

n.1: 4-hourly blood pressure is for women without hypertension (NG235).
n.2: 2-hourly measurement is too infrequent for severe hypertension.
n.3: Hourly measurement is for hypertension that is not severe.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Sadia, 28, is 37+2 weeks pregnant and has pre-eclampsia with blood pressure controlled on labetalol. Her blood results are stable and the CTG is normal. According to NICE NG133, when should birth be planned?
o: Continue surveillance until spontaneous labour
Continue surveillance and plan birth at 40 weeks
Initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours
Arrange a category 1 caesarean birth today
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 (table 3, timing of birth in pre-eclampsia): from 37 weeks onwards, initiate birth within 24 to 48 hours. Before 34 weeks surveillance continues unless there are indications, and from 34+0 to 36+6 birth is considered case by case.

n.0: Waiting for spontaneous labour does not follow the 24 to 48 hour recommendation.
n.1: Waiting until 40 weeks is not advised once pre-eclampsia is present at 37 weeks.
n.3: A category 1 caesarean is for an immediate threat to life; her condition is stable.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Gabby, 26, is on day 3 after a vaginal birth. She had pre-eclampsia but did not need antihypertensive treatment. Today her blood pressure is 152/102 mmHg and she has no headache or epigastric pain. What should the midwife do?
o: Recheck the blood pressure on day 5 as planned
Advise rest and recheck the blood pressure in a week
Reassure her that blood pressure peaks and settles by itself
Seek medical review to start antihypertensive treatment
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG133 1.5.14: in women with pre-eclampsia who did not take antihypertensives, start treatment if blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher. Ask about severe headache and epigastric pain at each measurement (1.5.15). Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia can occur after birth (SPM 4.8).

n.0: A reading of 152/102 meets the treatment threshold now; waiting is not appropriate.
n.1: Rest without treatment ignores the 150/100 threshold.
n.2: This reading meets the threshold for treatment and needs review.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Tia, 26, is 6 days after a caesarean birth and at home. At a postnatal visit she feels very unwell, with offensive lochia. Her heart rate is 134 beats/min, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min and blood pressure 108/66 mmHg. What should the community midwife do?
o: Call 999 and pre-alert the hospital
Ask her GP to see her at the surgery later today
Take a high vaginal swab and revisit her tomorrow
Advise paracetamol and phone triage if she worsens
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: A heart rate over 130 is a high-risk criterion (NICE NG255 table 1). Outside hospital, a person meeting any high-risk criterion is referred for emergency care, usually by 999 ambulance, and secondary care is pre-alerted (NG255 1.6.1, 1.6.2).

n.1: A GP appointment later delays emergency care for a high-risk woman.
n.2: A swab and revisit delays treatment of possible sepsis with a high-risk criterion.
n.3: Paracetamol can mask fever and delays urgent assessment.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Kemi, 33, is 2 days postnatal on the ward and meets a high-risk criterion for sepsis. The senior doctor has assessed her and taken blood cultures. Within what time should she receive a broad-spectrum antimicrobial?
o: Within 6 hours
Within 3 hours
After the culture results are known
Within 1 hour
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.7.2: for suspected sepsis with 1 or more high-risk criteria, give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial at the maximum recommended dose without delay, within 1 hour of meeting the high-risk criterion, after taking blood cultures if this does not delay treatment.

n.0: 6 hours is too long for a woman meeting a high-risk criterion.
n.1: 3 hours is the senior review window for 2 or more moderate-to-high criteria with normal lactate.
n.2: Waiting for culture results would delay treatment by a day or more.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: A midwife is teaching students about NICE NG255. Which of these women is in the group at higher risk of sepsis because of a recent pregnancy, birth, termination or miscarriage?
o: Dee, who had a stillbirth 8 weeks ago
Chloe, who had a miscarriage 5 weeks ago
Ruth, who gave birth 10 weeks ago
Anya, who had a termination 9 weeks ago
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.2.1 identifies people who are pregnant, or who gave birth or had a termination or miscarriage in the past 6 weeks, as at higher risk of sepsis. Chloe, 5 weeks after a miscarriage, is within this period.

n.0: 8 weeks after a stillbirth is outside the 6-week window.
n.2: 10 weeks after birth is outside the 6-week window.
n.3: 9 weeks after a termination is outside the 6-week window.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Jade, 29, is in the obstetric unit with suspected sepsis 3 days after birth. She meets high-risk criteria, her lactate is 4.6 mmol/L and her systolic blood pressure is 88 mmHg. The doctor asks the midwife to give an intravenous fluid bolus. What does NICE NG255 recommend?
o: 1000 mL of 5% glucose given over 1 hour
500 mL of crystalloid given over 4 hours
500 mL crystalloid over under 15 minutes
250 mL of colloid given over 30 minutes
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.9.2: use crystalloids containing sodium 130-154 mmol/L as a 500 mL bolus over less than 15 minutes. With lactate over 4 or systolic 90 or less, give the bolus within 1 hour and refer to critical care (1.7.4); reassess, and give a second bolus if no improvement (1.9.4).

n.0: 5% glucose does not contain sodium in the recommended range and the volume and rate are wrong.
n.1: Giving the bolus over 4 hours is far slower than recommended.
n.3: NG255 recommends crystalloid in 500 mL boluses, not colloid.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Leila, 31, is day 4 after a forceps birth on the postnatal ward. She has a respiratory rate of 23 breaths/min and a heart rate of 118 beats/min, which are moderate-to-high risk criteria. Her blood results show a lactate of 2.8 mmol/L and normal kidney function. What does NICE NG255 recommend next?
o: Repeat the lactate in 4 hours before deciding on antibiotics
Repeat her observations hourly and ask for a senior review within 3 hours
Treat as high risk, with antibiotics and an IV fluid bolus within 1 hour
Give oral antibiotics and review her at the next ward round
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.7.11: with 2 or more moderate-to-high criteria and lactate over 2 mmol/L (or AKI), treat as if high-risk criteria are met: antimicrobial within 1 hour (1.7.2) and, with lactate 2-4, an IV fluid bolus within 1 hour (1.7.5).

n.0: Waiting 4 hours delays antibiotics for a woman who should be treated as high risk.
n.1: Hourly reassessment and a 3-hour review apply when lactate is 2 mmol/L or lower.
n.3: Oral antibiotics and a later review do not meet the high-risk pathway.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Hope, 30, is 5 days postnatal and has been admitted to the gynaecology ward with suspected puerperal sepsis. Her baby is at home with her partner and is breastfeeding by expressed milk. What should the midwife arrange for the baby?
o: An assessment of the baby for signs of infection
Antibiotics for the baby to start at once as a precaution
Formula feeds until Hope's blood cultures are negative
A routine check at the baby's 6 to 8 week examination
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG194 1.2.8: if sepsis is suspected in the woman, assess the baby for infection. Group A streptococcus and other organisms can spread between mother and baby (SPM 4.8 first-line management, including the newborn).

n.1: Antibiotics are a decision after assessment of the baby, not an automatic step.
n.2: Expressed breast milk need not be stopped; the baby needs assessment.
n.3: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks misses early infection in the baby.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Emma, 27, meets high-risk criteria for sepsis on the delivery suite 1 day after birth. Antibiotics and a fluid bolus have been given. How often does NICE NG255 recommend monitoring her?
o: Every 2 hours until her lactate is normal
Hourly for the first 4 hours, then 4-hourly
Every 4 hours with a full set of observations
Continuously, or at least every 30 minutes
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.7.7: monitor people with suspected sepsis who meet any high-risk criteria continuously, or a minimum of once every 30 minutes depending on setting, using a physiological track and trigger system, and monitor mental state (1.7.8).

n.0: 2-hourly observations are less frequent than recommended.
n.1: Hourly observations are less frequent than the 30-minute minimum.
n.2: 4-hourly observations are far too infrequent for high-risk sepsis.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Aaliyah, 34, has suspected sepsis 2 days after a caesarean birth and meets high-risk criteria. One hour after antibiotics and two fluid boluses, her systolic blood pressure remains 86 mmHg and she is more confused. The registrar has reviewed her. What should happen now?
o: Give a third fluid bolus and recheck after 1 more hour
Change the antibiotics and await the microbiology result
Continue current treatment and repeat the lactate in 2 hours
Alert the consultant to attend her in person
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG255 1.7.9 and 1.9.4: if a high-risk person does not respond within 1 hour of any intervention, or there is no improvement after a second fluid bolus, alert a consultant to attend in person. Critical care referral is also needed with systolic 90 or less (1.7.4).

n.0: NG255 calls for a consultant to attend after no improvement following a second bolus, not a third bolus.
n.1: Waiting for microbiology does not address her failure to respond now.
n.2: Waiting 2 more hours delays senior input for a deteriorating woman.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Rosie, 34, is 32 weeks pregnant and attends maternity triage with painless, bright red vaginal bleeding that has soaked one pad. Her 20-week scan reported a low-lying placenta. Her observations are normal and the fetal heart rate is 140 beats/min. Which action should the midwife avoid?
o: A digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
Blood tests including a full blood count and group and save
An ultrasound scan to locate the placenta
A speculum examination by the obstetrician
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63: if placenta praevia is possible (previous low placenta, high presenting part or painless bleeding), digital vaginal examination should not be performed until ultrasound has excluded placenta praevia, as it can provoke major haemorrhage.

n.1: Bloods are recommended for all women with APH (FBC and group and save as a minimum).
n.2: Ultrasound is needed to locate the placenta before any digital examination.
n.3: A speculum examination can safely identify cervical dilatation or a lower genital tract cause.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Imogen, 29, is 35 weeks pregnant and has pre-eclampsia. She presents with constant severe abdominal pain and a small amount of dark vaginal bleeding. Her uterus feels hard and is tender all over, and she looks pale and clammy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
o: Placenta praevia
Onset of normal labour
Placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63: abruption should be considered when pain is continuous; a tense, 'woody' uterus indicates a significant abruption. Visible loss may underestimate concealed bleeding, so maternal signs of shock can be out of proportion. Pre-eclampsia is a risk factor (SPM 4.3).

n.0: Placenta praevia typically causes painless bleeding with a soft, non-tender uterus.
n.1: Labour pain is intermittent with relaxation between contractions, not a constantly hard uterus.
n.3: A cervical ectropion causes painless spotting with a soft uterus and no shock.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Mia, 27, is RhD negative with no anti-D antibodies. She received routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis at 28 weeks. At 31 weeks she presents with a small antepartum haemorrhage that has now settled. What does RCOG GTG 63 recommend about anti-D?
o: No anti-D is needed because routine prophylaxis was given at 28 weeks
Give anti-D immunoglobulin and do a Kleihauer test
Give anti-D after the birth if her baby is RhD positive
Wait for the Kleihauer result before deciding on anti-D
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63: anti-D immunoglobulin should be given to all non-sensitised RhD-negative women after any presentation with APH, independent of whether routine antenatal prophylaxis has been given. After 20 weeks, give at least 500 iu and do a test for fetomaternal haemorrhage (Kleihauer) to see whether more is needed.

n.0: Routine prophylaxis does not remove the need for anti-D after a sensitising event.
n.2: Waiting until after the birth leaves her unprotected after a potentially sensitising event now.
n.3: Anti-D is given after any APH without waiting; the Kleihauer test decides whether additional anti-D is needed.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Ffion, 30, is 33 weeks pregnant. She attends triage after losing an estimated 300 mL of fresh blood at home. She has no signs of shock and the bleeding has now settled. Using the RCOG GTG 63 definitions, how is this antepartum haemorrhage classified?
o: Major haemorrhage
Massive haemorrhage
Spotting
Minor haemorrhage
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63 definitions: spotting is staining on underwear or pads; minor haemorrhage is under 50 mL that has settled; major haemorrhage is 50-1000 mL with no signs of shock; massive haemorrhage is over 1000 mL and/or signs of shock.

n.1: Massive haemorrhage is over 1000 mL or with signs of shock.
n.2: Spotting is staining or streaking only, not 300 mL.
n.3: Minor haemorrhage is under 50 mL.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Kim, 36, is brought to the labour ward at 34 weeks with heavy continuing vaginal bleeding. She is confused, her heart rate is 135 beats/min and her blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg. The team is gathering. What is the immediate priority?
o: Resuscitate Kim using an ABC approach
Take a full history of the bleeding and any pain
Start a CTG to establish the fetal condition
Arrange an ultrasound scan to locate the placenta
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63: with major or massive haemorrhage or maternal compromise, assess maternal wellbeing and start resuscitation immediately. The mother is the priority and should be stabilised before the fetal condition is established, using an ABC approach (SPM 4.7).

n.1: A full history is taken once there is no maternal compromise.
n.2: Fetal assessment comes after the mother is stabilised.
n.3: Imaging is not the priority while she is shocked and bleeding.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Precious, 25, is 30 weeks pregnant and attends with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain. She has a bruise on her upper arm. Her partner answers questions for her and will not leave the room. The fetal heart rate is 150 beats/min. Which action is most appropriate?
o: Discharge her once the bleeding settles, with a leaflet
Assess for abruption and ask about abuse when she is alone
Ask her about domestic abuse with her partner present
Accept her partner's explanation and focus on the bleeding
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63 lists abdominal trauma, including from domestic violence, as a risk factor for placental abruption, so clinical assessment for abruption is needed. Routine enquiry about domestic abuse must happen when she is alone (SPM 4.3; safeguarding).

n.0: Discharge without assessing for abruption or abuse risks harm to her and the baby.
n.2: Asking with the partner present is unsafe and unlikely to lead to disclosure.
n.3: Accepting the partner's account risks missing both abruption and abuse.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Zoe, 32, is 38 weeks pregnant and in early labour. Her membranes rupture spontaneously and there is a sudden fresh vaginal bleed of about 100 mL. Within minutes the fetal heart rate falls to 80 beats/min. Zoe is well, with a normal pulse and blood pressure. What should the midwife suspect?
o: Minor placental abruption
Cervical ectropion
A show from cervical change
Ruptured vasa praevia
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63: if APH is associated with rupture of the membranes, bleeding from a ruptured vasa praevia should be considered. The bleeding is fetal blood, so the fetus is rapidly compromised while the mother stays well; this needs immediate obstetric help and urgent birth.

n.0: An abruption would usually cause pain and maternal signs; rapid fetal compromise with a well mother at membrane rupture suggests vasa praevia.
n.1: An ectropion does not cause sudden fetal bradycardia at membrane rupture.
n.2: A show is blood-stained mucus, not a 100 mL bleed with fetal bradycardia.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Ines, 28, is 29 weeks pregnant and was admitted after an antepartum haemorrhage of about 150 mL. The bleeding has now stopped, placenta praevia has been excluded on scan and the CTG is normal. She asks if she can go home tonight. What does RCOG GTG 63 recommend?
o: She can go home after one normal CTG, with a phone call tomorrow
She should remain in hospital at least until the bleeding has stopped
She can go home now, as placenta praevia has been excluded
She should remain in hospital until she gives birth
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 63: women with APH heavier than spotting, or with ongoing bleeding, should remain in hospital at least until the bleeding has stopped; discharge after a reassuring assessment applies to spotting that has settled with praevia excluded. Each woman is assessed individually.

n.0: A single normal CTG does not meet the GTG 63 advice for bleeding heavier than spotting.
n.2: Going home immediately applies to spotting that has settled, and this was a heavier bleed.
n.3: GTG 63 does not require admission until birth; it advises admission at least until bleeding stops.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: A midwife enters a side room on the antenatal ward and finds Olga, 30, who is 33 weeks pregnant, slumped in a chair. She does not respond to voice or a firm shake and is not breathing normally. What should the midwife do?
o: Check a capillary blood glucose before calling anyone
Put out an obstetric arrest call and start CPR
Lay her flat and listen for the fetal heart
Put her in the recovery position and observe her
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: An unresponsive woman who is not breathing normally is in cardiac arrest: call for help (cardiac arrest call stating maternal or obstetric arrest so obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams attend) and start CPR, relieving aortocaval compression as she is over 20 weeks (RCUK 2025 special circumstances: pregnancy).

n.0: Glucose is checked as part of finding reversible causes, after help is called and CPR started.
n.2: The fetal heart is not assessed during maternal arrest; maternal resuscitation is the priority.
n.3: The recovery position is for an unresponsive person who is breathing normally.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Sara, 28, is 32 weeks pregnant and in cardiac arrest on the labour ward. CPR is under way on a firm surface. The midwife is asked to relieve aortocaval compression. According to RCUK 2025, which method is preferred?
o: Manual displacement of the uterus to her left
Tilting the whole bed 30 degrees to the left
Turning her fully onto her left side
Placing a wedge under her right hip
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025: above 20 weeks, relieve aortocaval compression as early as possible and maintain it throughout resuscitation. Manual left uterine displacement is preferred over lateral tilt because it allows effective chest compressions.

n.1: RCUK 2025 prefers manual displacement over lateral tilt, which reduces compression quality.
n.2: Full lateral positioning prevents effective chest compressions.
n.3: A wedge creates a lateral tilt, which RCUK 2025 ranks below manual displacement.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: A student midwife asks when relief of aortocaval compression becomes part of resuscitation for a pregnant woman in cardiac arrest. According to RCUK 2025, from what point is this recommended?
o: From 16 weeks, when the uterus becomes palpable
From 28 weeks, when the fetus is viable
From the start of the second trimester at 13 weeks
From above 20 weeks of gestation
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025: above 20 weeks of gestation, relieve aortocaval compression as early as possible and maintain it throughout resuscitation, as the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and aorta and reduces cardiac output.

n.0: 16 weeks is not the RCUK threshold.
n.1: 28 weeks is later than the RCUK threshold of above 20 weeks.
n.2: 13 weeks is not the RCUK threshold; the uterus is not yet large enough to cause significant compression.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During a maternal cardiac arrest, the resuscitation team leader asks the team to consider the pregnancy-specific causes (the 4Ps) as well as the standard 4Hs and 4Ts. Which of the following is one of the 4Ps in RCUK 2025?
o: Peripartum cardiomyopathy
Hyperkalaemia
Hypothermia
Coronary artery thrombosis
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 pregnancy-specific causes (4Ps): pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, puerperal sepsis, placental and uterine complications, and peripartum cardiomyopathy. These are considered alongside the 4Hs and 4Ts.

n.1: Hyperkalaemia is one of the 4Hs (hypo or hyperkalaemia and metabolic causes).
n.2: Hypothermia is one of the 4Hs.
n.3: Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary) is one of the 4Ts.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Bisi, 31, is 34 weeks pregnant and has had a cardiac arrest on the antenatal ward. CPR with manual uterine displacement is under way. The obstetric registrar says a resuscitative hysterotomy is needed. Where should it be performed?
o: Where she arrested, as soon as possible
In the obstetric theatre, after transfer on the bed
In the intensive care unit, once stabilised
In the emergency department, after a CT scan
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025: resuscitative hysterotomy is time-sensitive; preparation should begin early and it should be performed as soon as possible at the site of the cardiac arrest by a skilled team. Moving her delays it and interrupts CPR.

n.1: Transfer to theatre delays the procedure and interrupts effective CPR.
n.2: Waiting for stabilisation defeats the purpose; the hysterotomy is part of resuscitation.
n.3: Imaging is not part of the decision and would cause harmful delay.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Freya, 29, collapses 20 minutes after a vaginal birth. She is pale and drowsy, with heart rate 142 beats/min and blood pressure 70/40 mmHg. There is blood on the bed and her uterus feels soft and high. What is the most likely cause and the immediate response?
o: Eclampsia: give magnesium sulfate 4 g IV
Vasovagal faint: lie her flat and raise her legs
Pulmonary embolism: give oxygen and wait for a CT scan
Haemorrhage: get help, massage, uterotonic, fluids
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Collapse soon after birth with tachycardia, hypotension, visible bleeding and a soft uterus points to hypovolaemia from atonic PPH. Call for help, uterine massage, uterotonics and IV fluids (NICE NG235 1.10.33), within an ABC approach to maternal collapse.

n.0: There is no seizure or hypertension; she is hypotensive.
n.1: A faint does not cause a soft uterus with heavy bleeding and persistent shock.
n.2: A pulmonary embolism would not explain the bleeding and boggy uterus.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Leah, 33, is in labour and has just been given intravenous benzylpenicillin. Within minutes she develops wheeze, stridor, widespread hives and a blood pressure of 78/42 mmHg. The infusion has been stopped and help called. What drug should be given first?
o: Adrenaline 500 micrograms intramuscularly
Chlorphenamine 10 mg by slow IV injection
Salbutamol 5 mg by oxygen-driven nebuliser
Hydrocortisone 200 mg by slow IV injection
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Anaphylaxis (airway or breathing problems with hypotension after a trigger) is treated first with intramuscular adrenaline 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) for adults, repeated after 5 minutes if needed (RCUK 2025 special circumstances guideline, anaphylaxis section). Adrenaline is on the midwives exemptions list (HMR 2012 Sch 17).

n.1: Antihistamines are not first-line emergency treatment for anaphylaxis.
n.2: Nebulised salbutamol does not treat the hypotension and is not first line.
n.3: Corticosteroids are not first-line emergency treatment for anaphylaxis.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Esther, 26, is 37 weeks pregnant and has a cardiac arrest in the antenatal clinic within the hospital. The midwife makes the emergency call. Which teams should be summoned?
o: Obstetric and anaesthetic teams, with no need for neonatal staff
The cardiac arrest team, with obstetrics informed afterwards
Cardiac arrest, obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams
The midwife coordinator, who will decide which teams to call
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Maternal arrest needs the cardiac arrest team plus obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, because a resuscitative hysterotomy may be needed as soon as possible and the baby will need resuscitation (RCUK 2025 special circumstances: pregnancy).

n.0: A baby born by resuscitative hysterotomy needs the neonatal team.
n.1: Obstetric staff are needed at once to prepare for resuscitative hysterotomy.
n.3: Delegating the call to the coordinator delays the multidisciplinary response.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Ama, 32, is having a planned home birth and is pushing involuntarily. As the midwife watches the perineum, she sees fetal buttocks and genitalia rather than a head. No one has suspected breech before. What should the midwife do first?
o: Call for help, including a 999 ambulance and a second midwife
Carry Ama to the car for an immediate hospital transfer
Ask Ama to stop pushing until an ambulance arrives
Apply gentle traction to the buttocks to speed the birth
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: In an unexpected breech at advanced labour, call for help (999 ambulance, second midwife) and prepare for a vaginal breech birth. RCOG GTG 20b: women near or in the active second stage should not routinely be offered caesarean, and all midwives should be familiar with breech birth techniques.

n.1: Moving her during the active second stage risks the birth happening in transit without help.
n.2: Asking her to stop pushing will not halt the birth and wastes time needed to call help.
n.3: Traction risks extension of the arms and head; GTG 20b advises a hands-off approach.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Ingrid, 29, is giving birth to a baby in breech presentation. The buttocks are distending the perineum with each contraction. The midwife is waiting with hands ready. Which principle should guide her care at this stage?
o: Bring down a loop of cord as soon as it is visible
Keep hands off and let maternal effort deliver the baby
Pull gently on the baby's legs with each contraction
Perform an episiotomy for all breech births
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 20b: encourage maternal effort once the breech is visible and use a 'hands-off' approach, avoiding traction; touching the baby can cause reflex extension of the arms or head. Intervene if there is delay or poor fetal condition. Episiotomy is selective rather than routine.

n.0: Handling the cord is not recommended; it can cause vasospasm.
n.2: Traction can cause the arms and head to extend and become trapped.
n.3: GTG 20b recommends selective, not routine, episiotomy.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During a breech birth, Nadia's baby has been born to the umbilicus with the back anterior. The buttocks were born 2 minutes ago. The baby has good tone and colour and is descending with each contraction. What should the midwife do?
o: Ask Nadia to stop pushing to protect the perineum
Keep her hands off and continue to observe progress
Grasp the legs and apply traction to deliver the arms
Deliver the head at once using Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 20b: a hands-off approach with timely intervention if progress is not made once the umbilicus has delivered, or if there is poor tone, extended arms or neck. Intervention is generally required if more than 5 minutes from buttocks to head or more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head. Good tone and progress mean no intervention yet.

n.0: Stopping maternal effort delays the birth when cord compression is likely.
n.2: Traction is avoided because it can cause arm and head extension.
n.3: The arms and body have not yet been born, and the head is not the next step.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Bethan, 26, is having an unexpected breech birth on a midwife-led unit. The baby was born to the umbilicus 4 minutes ago with no further progress over the last 2 contractions. The baby looks pale and has poor tone. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Assist the birth with manoeuvres, without traction
Ask Bethan to stand up and walk to aid descent
Apply firm traction to the baby's pelvis to deliver the shoulders
Wait for 2 more contractions as the mother is still pushing
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 20b: intervention to expedite breech birth is required if there is poor fetal condition or delay of more than 3 minutes from umbilicus to head (or 5 minutes from buttocks to head). Assistance is given without traction, using manoeuvres to release arms and deliver the head.

n.1: Changing position by walking is not the response to delay with a compromised baby.
n.2: Traction risks extension of the arms and head; manoeuvres are used without traction.
n.3: With poor tone and over 3 minutes since the umbilicus, waiting increases the risk of hypoxia.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During an assisted breech birth, Lena's baby needs help after the umbilicus is born. When the midwife needs to hold the baby to guide the birth, how should she hold it?
o: By the neck and shoulders, extending the head backwards
By the ankles, lifting the baby high over the abdomen
By the abdomen, with thumbs on the baby's soft tissues
Around the bony pelvic girdle, avoiding soft tissues
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 20b: care must be taken to avoid fetal trauma; the fetus should be grasped around the pelvic girdle, not the soft tissues, and the neck should not be hyperextended.

n.0: Hyperextending the neck can cause spinal and other injury.
n.1: Lifting the baby by the ankles risks hyperextension of the neck.
n.2: Pressure on the abdomen can injure internal organs.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: In a breech birth, Tara's baby is born to the level of the scapulae but the arms are not visible and have not delivered with the next contraction. The baby's back is anterior. Which manoeuvre does RCOG GTG 20b describe for this situation?
o: Burns-Marshall manoeuvre to lift the baby by its feet
Suprapubic pressure to bring the arms down
McRoberts manoeuvre to widen the pelvic outlet
Hooking the arms down by flexing at the elbow
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 20b: once the scapula is visible, the arms can be hooked down by inserting a finger in the elbow and flexing the arm across the chest; if an arm is nuchal, Lovset's manoeuvre is advised.

n.0: Burns-Marshall is for the after-coming head and GTG 20b does not advise it because of neck overextension.
n.1: Suprapubic pressure helps flex the head, not deliver extended arms.
n.2: McRoberts is a shoulder dystocia manoeuvre in cephalic births.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: The arms and shoulders of Kemi's breech baby have been born, but the after-coming head has not delivered. The baby's back is anterior. Which approach is recommended in RCOG GTG 20b?
o: Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit, with suprapubic pressure to flex the head
Burns-Marshall, lifting the baby by its feet over the abdomen
Firm downward traction on the baby's shoulders
Fundal pressure from an assistant to push the head out
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCOG GTG 20b: the head is delivered by the Mauriceau-Smellie-Veit manoeuvre or forceps; suprapubic pressure aids flexion if there is delay due to an extended neck. Burns-Marshall is not advised because of concern about overextension of the neck.

n.1: GTG 20b does not advise Burns-Marshall because of neck overextension.
n.2: Traction on the shoulders risks hyperextension and injury.
n.3: Fundal pressure is not the recommended way to deliver the after-coming head.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Mona, 30, attends the labour ward at 39 weeks in early labour at 3 cm dilatation. A scan confirms an unexpected breech presentation with flexed legs and an average-sized baby. She is unsure what to do. In line with NICE NG121, what should the midwife and obstetrician do?
o: Discuss the risks and offer a choice of labour or caesarean
Advise caesarean, as vaginal breech birth is not offered in labour
Advise she continues labour, as caesarean is unsafe in labour
Attempt external cephalic version before any other discussion
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG121 1.15.1-1.15.3: discuss the benefits and risks of vaginal birth and caesarean (more serious problems for the woman with caesarean, for the baby with vaginal birth), explain any benefit of caesarean for the baby may be greater in early labour, and offer a choice between continuing labour and caesarean.

n.1: NG121 offers a choice; vaginal breech birth is an option after discussion.
n.2: Caesarean is a valid option in labour; NG121 offers a choice.
n.3: ECV in established labour is not the NG121 approach; informed choice of mode of birth is.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Kai is born at 40 weeks on a midwife-led unit. After drying and stimulation he is floppy, pale and not breathing, with a heart rate of about 70 beats/min. The midwife has called for help and placed him on the resuscitaire with his head in a neutral position. What is the next step?
o: Give 5 inflation breaths at 30 cm H2O in air
Suction the mouth and nose before any breaths
Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3:1
Give oxygen at 100% by face mask held over his face
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if not breathing adequately, open the airway and give 5 inflation breaths of 2-3 seconds each, starting at 30 cm H2O for babies 32 weeks or more, in 21% oxygen (air). NICE NG235 1.11.22 also advises starting basic resuscitation in air.

n.1: Routine suction is not recommended and delays lung inflation.
n.2: Compressions start only if the heart rate is under 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
n.3: Term babies start in air; free-flow oxygen does not inflate fluid-filled lungs.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: During newborn resuscitation, the midwife gives inflation breaths to Baby Lily, born at 39 weeks, using a bag-valve-mask with a pressure-limiting device. How long should each inflation breath last?
o: 2 to 3 seconds
Under 1 second
10 seconds
5 to 6 seconds
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: give 5 inflation breaths, each sustained for 2 to 3 seconds, to help clear lung fluid and aerate the lungs; then reassess the heart rate and chest movement.

n.1: Short breaths do not adequately aerate fluid-filled lungs at birth.
n.2: 10 seconds is longer than the recommended 2 to 3 seconds.
n.3: 5 to 6 seconds is longer than the recommended 2 to 3 seconds.
