Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Rhys is born at 29 weeks and is not breathing adequately despite stimulation. The neonatal team is on the way. Which inflation pressure and starting oxygen concentration does RCUK 2025 recommend?
o: 20 cm H2O in 21% oxygen
30 cm H2O in 100% oxygen
25 cm H2O in 30% oxygen
30 cm H2O in 21% oxygen
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: start inflation at 25 cm H2O for babies under 32 weeks (30 cm H2O at 32 weeks or more), and start in 30% oxygen or more under 32 weeks (21% at 32 weeks or more). PEEP of 6 cm H2O if possible.

n.0: 20 cm H2O and air are not the RCUK starting settings for any gestation.
n.1: 100% oxygen is not the starting concentration; it is used during chest compressions.
n.3: 30 cm H2O and 21% oxygen are for babies of 32 weeks or more.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Isla is born at 28 weeks in the delivery suite. The room is warm and the resuscitaire heater is on. How should the midwife manage her temperature immediately after birth?
o: Place her skin-to-skin and cover both with a warm towel
Put her body into a plastic bag without drying, and add a hat
Give her a warm bath to bring her temperature up quickly
Dry her thoroughly and wrap her in a dry warm towel
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: for babies under 32 weeks, dry the head, put on a hat and place the body in a plastic (polyethylene) bag without drying, under a radiant heater; aim to keep temperature 36.5 to 37.5 C. Babies of 32 weeks or more are dried and wet towels removed.

n.0: A 28-week baby needs a plastic bag under a radiant heater and is likely to need stabilisation.
n.2: Bathing causes heat loss and is not part of newborn resuscitation.
n.3: Drying and wrapping is for babies of 32 weeks or more.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Max was born at 38 weeks. After inflation breaths with good chest rise, he has received 30 seconds of effective ventilation breaths. His heart rate is now 50 beats/min. What should the team do next?
o: Give adrenaline before any chest compressions
Start compressions at 15:2 and keep the oxygen at 21%
Start compressions at 3:1 and increase oxygen to 100%
Continue ventilation in air and reassess in 2 minutes
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if the heart rate is under 60 after at least 30 seconds of effective ventilation, start chest compressions at 3 compressions to 1 breath (two-thumb encircling technique) and increase oxygen to 100%. Reassess every 30 seconds.

n.0: Adrenaline is considered if heart rate stays under 60 despite effective ventilation and compressions.
n.1: 15:2 is the paediatric ratio; newborns receive 3:1 with 100% oxygen.
n.3: Waiting 2 minutes delays compressions when heart rate is under 60 despite effective ventilation.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: The midwife gives 5 inflation breaths to Baby Tom, born at 41 weeks, but sees no chest rise and the heart rate is not increasing. What should she do next?
o: Start chest compressions at a ratio of 3 compressions to 1 breath
Give ventilation breaths at 30 per minute as planned
Reposition the head and use a two-person jaw thrust, then repeat
Increase the inflation pressure to 50 cm H2O and continue
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if there is no chest rise, check and correct head position, consider two-person jaw thrust or a supraglottic airway, then repeat the 5 inflation breaths. Compressions are not effective until the lungs are aerated.

n.0: Compressions are not started until the lungs have been effectively aerated.
n.1: Ventilation breaths will not work until airway obstruction is corrected and chest rise is seen.
n.3: Pressure may be increased cautiously after airway manoeuvres, not jumped to 50 cm H2O first.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Rose is born at 31 weeks. She cries at birth and has good tone. The midwife is supporting her mother, Asha, and the neonatal team is present. In line with NICE NG25 and RCUK 2025, what should happen to the cord?
o: Clamp after 10 seconds while Rose is held above her mother
Wait at least 60 seconds with Rose at or below the placenta
Milk the cord towards Rose three times and then clamp it
Clamp at once and pass Rose straight to the neonatal team
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: NICE NG25 1.14.1-1.14.2: for preterm babies, wait at least 60 seconds before clamping, with the baby at or below the level of the placenta. RCUK 2025 also advises delayed cord clamping of at least 60 seconds while assessing the baby.

n.0: 10 seconds is too short, and the baby should be at or below the placenta level.
n.2: Cord milking is not recommended in this situation (RCUK 2025 advises against it under 28 weeks).
n.3: Immediate clamping is not recommended for a preterm baby who does not need resuscitation.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Baby Leo, born at 37 weeks, has a heart rate that remains under 60 beats/min despite effective ventilation in 100% oxygen and 30 seconds of good quality chest compressions. The neonatal registrar has placed an umbilical venous catheter. Which drug does RCUK 2025 recommend?
o: Naloxone 100 micrograms/kg intramuscularly
Adrenaline 20 micrograms/kg intravenously
Sodium bicarbonate 4.2% at 2 mL/kg
Atropine 20 micrograms/kg intravenously
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: RCUK 2025 NLS: if the heart rate stays under 60 despite effective ventilation and compressions, give adrenaline 20 micrograms/kg IV or IO (0.2 mL/kg of 1:10,000), preferably via a UVC, repeated every 4 minutes. Sodium bicarbonate was removed in the 2025 guidance.

n.0: Naloxone is not part of newborn resuscitation for a baby with persistent bradycardia.
n.2: Sodium bicarbonate was removed from the RCUK 2025 newborn algorithm.
n.3: Atropine is not part of the newborn life support algorithm.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Joanne, 32, is 8 hours after a vaginal birth on the postnatal ward. Her maternity early warning chart shows a total score in the red zone. The chart's escalation instructions state that this score needs immediate medical review. What should the midwife do?
o: Give paracetamol and recheck the observations in an hour
Record the score and pass it on at the next handover
Repeat the observations in 4 hours to confirm the trend
Call for immediate medical review and increase observations
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Early warning scores work only if the escalation response is followed. A trigger requiring immediate review means calling the doctor now, increasing observation frequency and staying with the woman (SPM 4.6 respond promptly to deterioration; NG255 1.1.8 consider an early warning score in pregnant and recently pregnant women).

n.0: Treating a number without escalation may mask deterioration and delays review.
n.1: Deferring to handover delays review of a woman who is deteriorating now.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours ignores a trigger that requires immediate review.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Mariam, 27, is day 2 after a caesarean birth. The midwife phones the obstetric registrar using SBAR. Having given her observations, she says: 'I think the problem is sepsis, possibly from her wound.' Which part of SBAR does this statement belong to?
o: Background
Recommendation
Assessment
Situation
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: SBAR: Situation (who and the immediate problem), Background (relevant history), Assessment (observations and the clinician's interpretation, for example 'I think the problem is...'), Recommendation (what is needed, such as review within a set time). Structured communication supports escalation (SPM 4.6).

n.0: Background gives relevant history, such as the caesarean and medicines.
n.1: Recommendation states what the midwife needs, such as review within 30 minutes.
n.3: Situation states who is calling, about whom and the immediate concern, before the clinical interpretation is given.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Siobhan, 30, is 12 hours after an emergency caesarean birth. Her observations are: respiratory rate 26 breaths/min, heart rate 98 beats/min, temperature 37.4 C and blood pressure 112/70 mmHg. Which finding is of most concern?
o: Respiratory rate 26/min
Heart rate 98/min
Temperature 37.4 C
Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: A respiratory rate of 25 or more is a high-risk criterion in NICE NG255 (table 1) and an early sign of deterioration that is often missed. The other values are within expected ranges for a recently pregnant woman (SPM 4.6).

n.1: A heart rate of 98 is below the NG255 moderate-to-high band of 100-130 and baseline HR is higher in pregnancy.
n.2: 37.4 C is within the normal range.
n.3: 112/70 mmHg is a normal blood pressure.

Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.q: Lucy, 29, had a postpartum haemorrhage and the midwife escalated her rising heart rate to the obstetric registrar, who attended and agreed a plan. Which documentation best meets professional standards?
o: A completed incident form in place of entries in her notes
Times, observations, who was called, when they came and the plan
A note at the end of the shift summarising the day's events
The observations, with a note that the doctor was informed
Obstetric & Neonatal Emergencies.w: Records should be completed at the time or as soon as possible after an event, and show what was found, who was contacted and when, and the agreed plan (Code 10.1-10.3). Clear escalation records support continuity and safety (SPM 4.6).

n.0: Incident reports do not replace the clinical record.
n.2: Records should be made as soon as possible after events, not summarised at the end of a shift.
n.3: This omits times, who attended and the agreed plan.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Rosa, 31, is 30 weeks pregnant with gestational hypertension and has started oral labetalol. She asks what blood pressure the team is aiming for now that she is on treatment. Which target is correct?
o: 150/100 mmHg or less
135/85 mmHg or less
140/90 mmHg or less
120/80 mmHg or less
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG133 table 1 (rec 1.4.3) sets a target blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg or less once a woman with gestational hypertension is on antihypertensive treatment.

n.0: 150/100 mmHg is the postnatal threshold for starting treatment in women with pre-eclampsia, not the antenatal target.
n.2: 140/90 mmHg is the threshold for diagnosis and for starting treatment, not the target once treated.
n.3: Aiming for 120/80 mmHg is lower than the NG133 target and risks reducing placental perfusion unnecessarily.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Bisi, 29, is 30 weeks pregnant. At a routine appointment her blood pressure is 144/94 mmHg on two readings, having been normal before. Dipstick urinalysis is negative and she feels well. The obstetric team suspects pre-eclampsia may be developing. Which test does NICE recommend to help rule it out?
o: Uterine artery Doppler assessment
A 24-hour urine collection for total protein
First morning urine sample for protein:creatinine ratio
Placental growth factor (PlGF)-based testing
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG133 1.4.4 recommends PlGF-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia in women presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia (for example, with gestational hypertension) between 20+0 and 36+6 weeks. Bisi is at 30 weeks.

n.0: Uterine artery Doppler is used at 18+0 to 23+6 weeks to assess risk of early fetal growth restriction (SBL v3 2.7), not to rule out pre-eclampsia at 30 weeks.
n.1: NG133 1.2.5 advises against routine 24-hour urine collection to quantify proteinuria.
n.2: NG133 1.2.4 says not to use the first morning void to quantify proteinuria; and the dipstick is negative, so quantification is not indicated.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Chloe, 24, is 34 weeks pregnant with pre-eclampsia. On the antenatal ward she reports a severe frontal headache and seeing spots. Her blood pressure is 168/112 mmHg and she has three beats of ankle clonus. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the midwife?
o: Give oral paracetamol for the headache and recheck her blood pressure in one hour
Call the obstetric team urgently and prepare magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive treatment
Prepare diazepam for seizure prophylaxis and start intravenous fluids at 125 mL/hour
Increase her blood pressure checks to every four hours and repeat her bloods tomorrow
Complications & Additional Care.w: Severe hypertension with severe headache, visual disturbance and clonus are features of severe pre-eclampsia. NG133 1.8.3 advises considering IV magnesium sulfate when there are severe features, and severe hypertension needs urgent antihypertensive treatment (1.8.6) with BP every 15 to 30 minutes until below 160/110. The midwife's role is to escalate immediately and prepare.

n.0: Treating the headache symptomatically and waiting an hour delays treatment of a woman at imminent risk of eclampsia or stroke.
n.2: NG133 1.8.5 advises against diazepam as an alternative to magnesium sulfate, and maintenance fluids should be limited to 80 mL/hour (1.8.12).
n.3: Four-hourly checks are far too infrequent with severe hypertension; NG133 advises every 15 to 30 minutes until BP is under 160/110 mmHg.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Imani, 28, is 37+2 weeks pregnant in her first pregnancy. She was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia two days ago; her blood pressure is 146/92 mmHg on labetalol, her bloods are stable and the CTG is normal. She asks when her baby will be born. Which response reflects NICE guidance?
o: Birth is usually planned at 40 weeks if her condition stays stable
Birth is considered once her blood pressure exceeds 160/110 mmHg
Birth is usually planned at 39 weeks to allow further fetal maturity
Birth is recommended now, with labour started within 24 to 48 hours
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG133 (table 3) recommends initiating birth within 24 to 48 hours for women with pre-eclampsia from 37+0 weeks. Imani is 37+2 weeks.

n.0: Continuing to 40 weeks is not recommended once pre-eclampsia is diagnosed at term.
n.1: Birth from 37 weeks does not wait for severe hypertension; severe features before 37 weeks are an indication in their own right.
n.2: There is no NICE recommendation to wait until 39 weeks in pre-eclampsia; birth is initiated from 37+0 weeks.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Farah, 32, books at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2 and her first baby weighed 3.6 kg. She has no previous gestational diabetes and no family history of diabetes. Which plan for gestational diabetes testing is most appropriate?
o: Offer a 75 g 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks
Test her urine for glucose at each visit and arrange testing if positive
Offer an HbA1c test at booking to assess her risk
Offer an oral glucose tolerance test as soon as possible after booking
Complications & Additional Care.w: A BMI of 30 kg/m2 or over is a risk factor for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.2.2). Women with risk factors other than previous GDM are offered a 75 g 2-hour OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks (NG3 1.2.5, 1.2.7).

n.1: NG3 1.2.3 says not to use urinalysis for glucose to assess risk; Farah already has a risk factor that warrants an OGTT.
n.2: NG3 1.2.3 says not to use HbA1c to assess the risk of developing gestational diabetes.
n.3: Early testing after booking is for women who had gestational diabetes in a previous pregnancy (NG3 1.2.6); Farah has not.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Mei, 30, has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks. Her fasting plasma glucose is 5.8 mmol/L and her 2-hour value is 7.1 mmol/L. How should these results be interpreted?
o: The test is normal because the 2-hour value is below 7.8 mmol/L
The result is borderline and the OGTT should be repeated at 32 weeks of pregnancy
She has type 2 diabetes because the fasting value is above 5.5 mmol/L at 26 weeks
She has gestational diabetes because the fasting value is 5.6 mmol/L or above
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.2.8 diagnoses gestational diabetes if the fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or above OR the 2-hour value is 7.8 mmol/L or above. Either threshold is enough.

n.0: Both values do not have to be raised; a fasting level of 5.8 mmol/L alone meets the diagnostic criterion.
n.1: NG3 has no borderline category requiring repeat testing; the threshold is met now.
n.2: These are the diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes, not type 2 diabetes.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Nadia, 29, was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 28 weeks and is learning to check her capillary blood glucose. She asks what fasting level she should aim for. Which target is correct?
o: 7.0 mmol/L
6.0 mmol/L
4.0 mmol/L
5.3 mmol/L
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.3.5 advises pregnant women with any form of diabetes to aim for a fasting plasma glucose of 5.3 mmol/L, and NG3 1.3.6 advises staying above 4 mmol/L if taking insulin.

n.0: 7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis is the level at which immediate insulin is offered (NG3 1.2.22), not the target.
n.1: 6.0 mmol/L is above the NG3 fasting target.
n.2: 4 mmol/L is the level to stay above if taking insulin, not the target to aim for.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Precious, 34, had gestational diabetes treated with metformin. She gave birth to a healthy baby two hours ago and asks what happens to her metformin now. Which advice is correct?
o: Continue metformin for six weeks and then have an HbA1c test with her GP
Continue metformin until her capillary glucose is normal for three days
Reduce metformin to half dose and stop it at the six to eight week check
Stop metformin now; a fasting glucose test is offered 6 to 13 weeks after birth
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.6.3 advises women with gestational diabetes to stop blood glucose-lowering therapy immediately after birth. A fasting plasma glucose test is offered 6 to 13 weeks after birth (NG3 1.6.11), with annual HbA1c if negative.

n.0: Glucose-lowering therapy is stopped immediately after birth, not continued for six weeks.
n.1: Waiting for three days of normal readings is not the NG3 approach; therapy stops at birth.
n.2: Tapering to half dose is not recommended; treatment stops immediately after birth.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Kemi, 31, is 29 weeks pregnant and has just been diagnosed with gestational diabetes. Her fasting plasma glucose at diagnosis was 6.3 mmol/L, and the scan shows no macrosomia or polyhydramnios. Which first-line management is most appropriate?
o: Start insulin straight away because her fasting glucose is above 6.0 mmol/L at diagnosis
Start metformin and insulin together because she was diagnosed after 28 weeks
Diet and exercise changes, adding metformin if targets are not met in 1 to 2 weeks
Start glibenclamide straight away and review her capillary glucose results in 4 weeks
Complications & Additional Care.w: With a fasting plasma glucose below 7.0 mmol/L at diagnosis, NG3 1.2.18 and 1.2.19 recommend a trial of diet and exercise first, offering metformin if targets are not met within 1 to 2 weeks. Immediate insulin is considered for 6.0 to 6.9 mmol/L when there is macrosomia or polyhydramnios, which Kemi does not have.

n.0: Immediate insulin is offered when the fasting level is 7.0 mmol/L or above, or considered at 6.0 to 6.9 mmol/L with macrosomia or polyhydramnios; neither applies.
n.1: Gestation at diagnosis does not dictate combined therapy in NG3.
n.3: Glibenclamide is not first line, and a 4-week review is too slow if targets are not being met.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Ruth, 33, has type 1 diabetes and is in established labour at 38 weeks. Her capillary blood glucose has been 8.4 mmol/L and then 8.9 mmol/L an hour apart. She is otherwise progressing normally. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Escalate to the obstetric and diabetes team to start intravenous dextrose and insulin
Recheck her capillary glucose in 4 hours because both readings are below 10 mmol/L
Give her a small carbohydrate snack and recheck her capillary glucose in an hour
Ask her to give her usual subcutaneous dose of rapid-acting insulin
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.4.12 advises keeping capillary plasma glucose between 4 and 7 mmol/L in labour and starting intravenous dextrose and insulin if it is not maintained in that range. Two readings above 7 mmol/L need escalation per the unit protocol.

n.1: The intrapartum target is 4 to 7 mmol/L; waiting 4 hours with readings above range risks neonatal hypoglycaemia.
n.2: Extra carbohydrate would raise a glucose level that is already above target.
n.3: Managing intrapartum glucose with ad hoc subcutaneous doses is not the NG3 approach; IV dextrose and insulin are used.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Ines gave birth to a baby boy at 39 weeks an hour ago. She has gestational diabetes treated with insulin. The baby is well, pink and alert, and has breastfed once 20 minutes after birth. When should the baby's first blood glucose be measured?
o: At 6 hours after birth if he is feeding well
At 24 hours, before transfer home
Within the first 30 minutes, before the first feed
At 2 to 4 hours after birth, before a feed
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.5.3 recommends routine blood glucose testing at 2 to 4 hours after birth in babies of women with diabetes. Babies feed within 30 minutes and then every 2 to 3 hours until pre-feed levels are at least 2.0 mmol/L (NG3 1.5.9).

n.0: Waiting 6 hours would miss the period when neonatal hypoglycaemia most commonly occurs.
n.1: Testing at 24 hours is far too late; NG3 sets 2 to 4 hours.
n.2: Testing before the first feed in a well baby is not recommended; the first feed should come within 30 minutes and the test at 2 to 4 hours.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Josie, 35, has gestational diabetes controlled with diet alone. She is now 40+2 weeks with normal growth scans and no other complications. She asks how long she can wait for labour to start naturally. Which response reflects NICE guidance?
o: Birth is advised no later than 40+6 weeks, with induction or caesarean if needed
Birth should already have been planned between 37+0 and 38+6 weeks of pregnancy
Induction is offered from 41+0 weeks, as for other women with uncomplicated pregnancies
She can wait until 42 weeks because her diabetes is controlled by diet and exercise
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.4.4 advises women with uncomplicated gestational diabetes to give birth no later than 40+6 weeks, offering induction or caesarean if they have not given birth by then.

n.1: 37+0 to 38+6 weeks is the range for women with type 1 or type 2 diabetes without complications (NG3 1.4.2).
n.2: Gestational diabetes has its own NG3 timing rule; the general prolonged-pregnancy pathway does not apply.
n.3: NG3 sets 40+6 weeks for gestational diabetes; waiting to 42 weeks is not advised.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Tola, 26, is 31 weeks pregnant and phones triage because she has had a gush of clear fluid and is now leaking steadily. She has no contractions. On speculum examination in the unit, the midwife sees a pool of amniotic fluid in the posterior fornix. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Treat as P-PROM and start oral erythromycin as prescribed
Discharge her home with advice to monitor her temperature
Send a swab for an IGFBP-1 test to confirm membrane rupture
Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess the cervix
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.3.1: if pooling of amniotic fluid is seen on speculum, do not perform any diagnostic test but offer care for P-PROM, including oral erythromycin 250 mg four times a day for up to 10 days or until established labour (NG25 1.4.1).

n.1: Confirmed P-PROM at 31 weeks needs antibiotics, steroids and a care plan; discharge without treatment is unsafe.
n.2: Diagnostic tests such as IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 are used when pooling is NOT seen; with pooling, NG25 says not to test.
n.3: Digital examination is avoided in P-PROM without labour because it increases infection risk and adds no information here.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Cara, 29, is 28 weeks pregnant with intact membranes. She has regular painful contractions and the obstetrician confirms suspected preterm labour. Which tocolytic does NICE recommend first line?
o: Atosiban
Indometacin
Nifedipine
Terbutaline
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.8.3 recommends offering nifedipine for tocolysis to women between 26+0 and 33+6 weeks with intact membranes in suspected or diagnosed preterm labour. An oxytocin receptor antagonist is considered if nifedipine is contraindicated.

n.0: Atosiban, an oxytocin receptor antagonist, is the second choice when nifedipine is contraindicated (NG25 1.8.4).
n.1: Indometacin is not one of the NG25 recommended tocolytics.
n.3: NG25 1.8.5 advises not to offer betamimetics such as terbutaline for tocolysis.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Hana, 32, is 30 weeks pregnant with P-PROM confirmed yesterday. She is taking oral erythromycin and asks why she needs an injection of corticosteroid. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It helps the baby's lungs mature and reduces breathing problems if born early
It relaxes the uterus and lowers the chance of labour starting this week
It protects the baby's brain and lowers the risk of cerebral palsy
It reduces her risk of developing an infection of the womb before birth
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.9.2 recommends maternal corticosteroids between 24+0 and 33+6 weeks in suspected, diagnosed or established preterm labour, planned preterm birth or P-PROM. They accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce neonatal respiratory complications.

n.1: Corticosteroids are not tocolytics; nifedipine is used to delay labour.
n.2: Neuroprotection against cerebral palsy is the purpose of magnesium sulfate, not corticosteroids.
n.3: Erythromycin, not a corticosteroid, is the prophylaxis against intrauterine infection.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Abi, 34, is 27 weeks pregnant and in established preterm labour, 6 cm dilated. Her midwife is preparing for birth. Which intervention for the baby should the midwife make sure has been offered now?
o: A second course of antenatal corticosteroids
Oral erythromycin for prophylaxis against infection
Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
Intramuscular progesterone to slow cervical change
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.10.2: offer IV magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection to women between 24+0 and 29+6 weeks who are in established preterm labour or having a planned preterm birth within 24 hours. SBL v3 5.20 sets the same standard for births under 30 weeks.

n.0: Repeat courses are avoided where possible (SBL v3 5.19) and nothing suggests she had a first course long ago.
n.1: Erythromycin is prophylaxis against infection in P-PROM; it does not protect the baby's brain before an imminent preterm birth.
n.3: Progesterone is a preventive measure started at 16 to 24 weeks, not treatment for established labour.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Lucy, 30, is 18 weeks pregnant. Her first baby was born spontaneously at 31 weeks. A transvaginal scan at 18 weeks shows a cervical length of 22 mm. Which preventive option should be discussed with her?
o: Bed rest at home until 34 weeks of pregnancy
A choice of vaginal progesterone or cervical cerclage
Prophylactic nifedipine taken daily until 34 weeks
Repeat cervical scan at 24 weeks before any treatment
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.2.1: women with a history of spontaneous preterm birth (up to 34+0 weeks) or mid-trimester loss (from 16+0) and a cervix of 25 mm or less on a scan between 16+0 and 24+0 weeks are offered a choice of prophylactic vaginal progesterone or cerclage.

n.0: Bed rest is not an NG25 intervention for preventing preterm birth.
n.2: Nifedipine is used for acute tocolysis in suspected preterm labour, not as daily prophylaxis.
n.3: With a short cervix already found, waiting until 24 weeks delays an effective intervention.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Zara, 28, is 32 weeks pregnant and presents with irregular tightenings and intact membranes. The obstetric team is unsure whether she is in preterm labour. Which diagnostic test does NICE suggest considering first at this gestation?
o: Transvaginal ultrasound measurement of cervical length
A high vaginal swab for group B streptococcus
Serum C-reactive protein and white cell count
A digital vaginal examination repeated after 4 hours
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.7.4: at 30+0 weeks or more with suspected preterm labour, consider transvaginal cervical length measurement. A length over 15 mm makes preterm labour unlikely. NG25 1.7.5 lists fetal fibronectin as an alternative, but Saving Babies' Lives v3.2 (5.9) reports that fetal fibronectin cassettes have been discontinued.

n.1: A GBS swab does not diagnose preterm labour.
n.2: CRP and white cell count are used with other findings to diagnose intrauterine infection in P-PROM, not preterm labour.
n.3: Serial digital examinations are not the recommended diagnostic test and add infection risk.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Megan, 25, is 25 weeks pregnant and in suspected preterm labour at a local unit with a special care baby unit but no neonatal intensive care. She has been given her first steroid dose. Which plan best reflects Saving Babies' Lives v3?
o: Plan birth locally and ask the NICU team to attend for the birth
Plan birth locally and transfer the baby to a NICU after stabilisation
Transfer her once the second steroid dose has been given in 24 hours
Arrange in utero transfer to a maternity service on the same site as a NICU
Complications & Additional Care.w: SBL v3 5.18: babies born under 27 weeks (or under 800 g, or multiples under 28 weeks) should be born in a maternity service on the same site as a designated NICU, moving them in utero whenever possible. Acute tocolysis may be used to allow in utero transfer (5.17).

n.0: Bringing a team in does not replace birth on a NICU site, which is the SBL v3 standard.
n.1: Postnatal transfer of an extremely preterm baby carries higher risk than in utero transfer, which SBL v3 prefers.
n.2: Delaying transfer for 24 hours risks birth in a unit without NICU; the second dose can follow at the receiving unit.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Nina, 33, gives birth to a baby girl at 32 weeks. The baby cries at birth and has good tone. The neonatal team is present. What is the most appropriate cord management?
o: Clamp the cord straight away so the neonatal team can begin their assessment
Delay clamping for at least 60 seconds, holding the baby at or below the placenta
Milk the cord towards the baby three times and then clamp and cut it
Wait until the cord stops pulsating, usually about 5 minutes, before clamping
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG25 1.14.1 and 1.14.2: wait at least 60 seconds before clamping the cord of preterm babies unless earlier clamping is needed, and position the baby at or below the level of the placenta. SBL v3 5.22 sets the same standard for births under 37 weeks.

n.0: A vigorous preterm baby does not need immediate clamping; delayed clamping improves outcomes.
n.2: Cord milking is not the NG25 recommendation, and RCUK 2025 advises against it under 28 weeks.
n.3: Waiting for pulsation to stop risks hypothermia in a preterm baby; the NG25 standard is at least 60 seconds.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Olivia, 26, is on the low-risk pathway for fetal growth restriction in her first pregnancy. She asks when the midwife will start measuring her bump. According to Saving Babies' Lives v3, when should symphysis fundal height measurement begin?
o: From 20+0 weeks, measured weekly until birth
At 32+0 weeks, once the fetus is large enough to measure
At appointments after 24+0 weeks, with the first by 28+6 weeks
At every appointment from booking, plotted on a growth chart
Complications & Additional Care.w: SBL v3 2.10: women at low risk of FGR have serial SFH measurement at each antenatal appointment after 24+0 weeks (no more often than every 2 weeks), with the first measurement by 28+6 weeks, plotted on charts by trained clinicians.

n.0: SBL v3 starts SFH after 24+0 weeks and says no more often than every 2 weeks, not weekly from 20 weeks.
n.1: Starting at 32 weeks would miss earlier growth restriction; the first measurement is due by 28+6 weeks.
n.3: SFH is not useful in the first half of pregnancy and is not started at booking.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Aisha, 30, is 33 weeks pregnant on the low-risk pathway. Her symphysis fundal height today plots below the 10th centile on her growth chart; two weeks ago it was on the 40th centile. She reports normal fetal movements. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Remeasure the fundal height at her next routine appointment
Refer her for an ultrasound assessment of fetal growth
Reassure her because the fetal movements are normal
Ask a colleague to remeasure and record the higher of the two values
Complications & Additional Care.w: A fundal height plotting below the 10th centile, or a drop across centiles, is an indication for an ultrasound growth assessment. SBL v3 2.11 requires staff measuring SFH to interpret and refer when indicated, and 2.14 sets the assessment of wellbeing once FGR is suspected.

n.0: Waiting for the next routine visit delays detection of possible FGR, a major risk factor for stillbirth.
n.2: Normal movements do not exclude growth restriction; the measurement still needs investigating.
n.3: Choosing the higher of two readings is unsafe and does not address the fall across centiles.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Grace, 34, smokes and had a previous baby below the 3rd centile. She has been placed on serial ultrasound surveillance for fetal growth starting at 28 weeks. At her 30-week community appointment, what should the midwife do about fundal height measurement?
o: Measure fundal height and refer for a scan if it falls below the 50th centile
Stop measuring fundal height, as serial scans have replaced it
Measure and plot fundal height at each visit alongside the scans
Measure fundal height weekly between her scan appointments
Complications & Additional Care.w: SBL v3 2.12: women on planned serial scan surveillance should stop having SFH measured once serial surveillance begins; growth is assessed by ultrasound.

n.0: SFH has been stopped for this pathway, and the 50th centile is not a referral trigger.
n.2: SBL v3 2.12 says SFH should cease once serial scan surveillance starts.
n.3: Weekly SFH is not part of any SBL v3 pathway and adds no information to serial scans.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Divya, 38, books at 10 weeks. She has chronic hypertension and her previous baby was growth restricted with pre-eclampsia. The FGR risk assessment places her in the high-risk category. In addition to aspirin, which surveillance does Saving Babies' Lives v3 recommend?
o: Uterine artery Doppler at 18+0 to 23+6 weeks, then serial growth scans
Fundal height measurement every 2 weeks from 24+0 weeks of pregnancy
Weekly computerised CTG from 28 weeks of pregnancy until birth
A single growth scan at 36 weeks to estimate the fetal weight
Complications & Additional Care.w: SBL v3 2.7 recommends uterine artery Doppler at 18+0 to 23+6 weeks for women at high risk of FGR, and 2.13 serial ultrasound surveillance of fetal growth (3 to 4 weekly) for women at increased risk.

n.1: SFH is the surveillance for low-risk women; high-risk women need ultrasound.
n.2: Routine weekly CTG is not the SBL v3 surveillance method; computerised CTG is used once FGR is suspected (2.14).
n.3: A single late scan would miss early-onset FGR in a high-risk pregnancy.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Lena, 29, is 36+2 weeks pregnant. Her growth scan shows an estimated fetal weight below the 3rd centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler. She has no other risk factors. When does Saving Babies' Lives v3 recommend birth?
o: Await spontaneous labour with weekly growth scans and Doppler
Initiate labour or birth at 37+0 weeks and no later than 37+6
Plan birth at 40+0 weeks if the Doppler stays normal
Consider birth at 39+0 weeks, achieving birth by 39+6
Complications & Additional Care.w: SBL v3 2.18: when the EFW is below the 3rd centile with no other risk factors, initiation of labour or delivery should occur at 37+0 weeks and no later than 37+6 weeks, after discussion with the mother.

n.0: An EFW below the 3rd centile carries a high stillbirth risk; expectant management to spontaneous labour is not advised.
n.2: Waiting until 40 weeks exceeds the 37+6 limit set in SBL v3.
n.3: 39+0 to 39+6 weeks applies to an EFW between the 3rd and 10th centile (SBL v3 2.19).

Complications & Additional Care.q: Freya, 31, is 35 weeks pregnant. Her scan shows an estimated fetal weight on the 6th centile with normal Doppler and steady growth velocity. She has no other risk factors. She asks when her baby should be born. Which response reflects Saving Babies' Lives v3?
o: Birth should be considered at 39+0 weeks and achieved by 39+6
Birth should be planned at 41 weeks if growth continues
Birth should be initiated at 37+0 weeks and by 37+6
Birth should be planned at 34 weeks after a course of steroids
Complications & Additional Care.w: SBL v3 2.19: for an EFW between the 3rd and under the 10th centile, delivery should be considered at 39+0 weeks and achieved by 39+6 weeks; other risk factors are needed to recommend birth before 39 weeks.

n.1: Continuing past 39+6 weeks with an SGA fetus is not advised by SBL v3.
n.2: 37+0 to 37+6 weeks applies to EFW below the 3rd centile (SBL v3 2.18).
n.3: She is already 35 weeks with normal Doppler; there is no indication for preterm birth.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Mia, 27, has an ultrasound at 13 weeks showing a twin pregnancy. The sonographer cannot confidently determine chorionicity, and a second opinion from a senior sonographer is also inconclusive. How should the pregnancy be managed?
o: Repeat the scan with 3D ultrasound to confirm chorionicity
As a dichorionic pregnancy until the 20-week scan
As a monochorionic pregnancy until proven otherwise
As a dichorionic pregnancy if the twins are discordant in sex later
Complications & Additional Care.w: NICE NG137 1.1.7: if it is difficult to determine chorionicity even after referral, manage the pregnancy as monochorionic until proven otherwise, because monochorionic twins carry higher risks (such as feto-fetal transfusion syndrome).

n.0: NG137 1.1.12 advises not to use 3D ultrasound to determine chorionicity.
n.1: Assuming dichorionicity would leave a possibly monochorionic pregnancy without the closer surveillance it needs.
n.3: Discordant sex later confirms dichorionicity, but until then the safer assumption is monochorionic.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Bea, 30, has an uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy and is now 34 weeks. She asks when the babies are likely to be born. Which response is consistent with NICE NG137?
o: Await spontaneous labour up to 38 weeks of pregnancy
Planned birth at 37 weeks, as for dichorionic diamniotic twins
Planned birth between 32+0 and 33+6 weeks by caesarean
Planned birth at 36 weeks, after considering antenatal steroids
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG137 1.9.10: offer planned birth at 36 weeks for uncomplicated monochorionic diamniotic twins, after a course of antenatal corticosteroids has been considered; continuing beyond 36+6 weeks increases the risk of fetal death (1.9.5).

n.0: Continuing past 36+6 weeks in MCDA twins increases the risk of fetal death.
n.1: 37 weeks is the timing for uncomplicated dichorionic diamniotic twins (NG137 1.9.9).
n.2: 32+0 to 33+6 weeks is for monochorionic monoamniotic twins.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Joy, 28, attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks. She has no known mental health history. As part of a general discussion about her wellbeing, which approach does NICE CG192 recommend the midwife considers?
o: Ask her to complete the full Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale at booking
Ask about mood if she shows visible signs of distress during the appointment
Ask the two depression identification questions and consider the GAD-2 for anxiety
Refer her to her GP for a mental health review before her dating scan
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.5.4: at booking and in the early postnatal period, consider asking the two depression identification questions (feeling down, depressed or hopeless; little interest or pleasure in the past month) and consider the GAD-2 for anxiety, as part of a general discussion.

n.0: The EPDS or PHQ-9 is used as part of a full assessment after a positive response or clinical concern (CG192 1.5.5), not as the first step for everyone.
n.1: Waiting for visible distress misses women who are unwilling to disclose, which CG192 1.5.1 warns is common.
n.3: Routine GP referral without any identified concern is not recommended; the midwife asks the questions herself.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Selin, 31, is 14 days postnatal. At a home visit she answers yes to both depression identification questions. She is caring for her baby, has no thoughts of self-harm and no history of severe mental illness. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Advise her to stop breastfeeding so that she can start antidepressants
Consider a full assessment with the EPDS or PHQ-9, or refer to her GP
Refer her urgently to the crisis team for assessment within 4 hours
Reassure her that these are baby blues and review her in four weeks
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.5.5: if a woman responds positively to either depression identification question, consider a full assessment using the EPDS or PHQ-9 or refer her to her GP (or to a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.0: Breastfeeding does not need to stop to treat depression, and medication decisions follow assessment.
n.2: A 4-hour emergency assessment is for suspected postpartum psychosis; Selin has no features of psychosis or high risk.
n.3: Low mood persisting at two weeks needs assessment; dismissing it as baby blues and waiting four weeks risks missing postnatal depression.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Lauren, 30, is 20 weeks pregnant. Using the GAD-2, she scores 4 out of 6 for feeling nervous and being unable to stop worrying. What does NICE CG192 advise the midwife to consider?
o: Referring her directly to a specialist mother and baby unit
Using the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring her to her GP
Repeating the GAD-2 at her 28-week appointment before acting
Asking the avoidance question, as her score is below the threshold
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.5.6: if a woman scores 3 or more on the GAD-2, consider using the GAD-7 for further assessment or referring her to her GP (or to a mental health professional if a severe problem is suspected).

n.0: Mother and baby units provide inpatient care within 12 months of birth for women who need admission (CG192 1.10.1), not first-line assessment of anxiety.
n.2: A score of 3 or more is the threshold for action now, not after a delay of eight weeks.
n.3: The avoidance question is for women scoring less than 3 who still cause concern (CG192 1.5.7); Lauren scored 4.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Hannah, 27, books at 10 weeks. She has bipolar disorder, currently well and managed by her GP, with no admission for five years. Which referral is most appropriate?
o: Ask her GP to review her medication and mood before 20 weeks
No referral, because her condition has been stable for five years
Refer to secondary care, ideally a specialist perinatal mental health team
Refer to the health visitor for extra postnatal mood monitoring at home
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.5.10: refer all women who have, or have any history of, severe mental illness (including bipolar disorder) to a secondary mental health service, preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service, for assessment and treatment, and make sure the GP knows.

n.0: GP review alone does not meet CG192, which requires secondary or specialist perinatal input for severe mental illness.
n.1: A history of severe mental illness at any time triggers referral; stability does not remove the high risk of perinatal relapse.
n.3: A health visitor referral alone leaves the pregnancy and immediate postnatal period, the highest-risk time, without specialist planning.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Precious, 24, gave birth four days ago. Her partner calls the community midwife because she has not slept for two nights, is talking rapidly, believes the baby has been swapped and is frightened. She had no previous mental health problems. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Complete an EPDS questionnaire at the next routine postnatal visit
Advise her partner to let her sleep and call back if she is no better tomorrow
Book a GP appointment for later this week to review her mood
Arrange immediate referral for specialist mental health assessment within 4 hours
Complications & Additional Care.w: Sudden onset of insomnia, agitation and delusional beliefs in the first days after birth suggests postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. CG192 1.5.12: refer to a secondary (preferably specialist perinatal) mental health service for immediate assessment within 4 hours of referral.

n.0: The EPDS screens for depression and is not the response to an acute psychotic presentation.
n.1: Waiting until tomorrow leaves a woman with possible psychosis and her baby at serious risk.
n.2: A GP appointment later in the week delays assessment of a condition that can deteriorate within hours.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Rania, 29, has just had her first baby. She has never had a mental illness, but her mother had postpartum psychosis after Rania's birth. During which period does CG192 advise professionals to be particularly alert for symptoms of postpartum psychosis?
o: Between 3 and 6 months after birth
The third trimester of pregnancy
The first 2 weeks after birth
The first 6 weeks after birth
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.5.11: if a woman has past or present severe mental illness or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal mental illness, be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after childbirth.

n.0: Onset is typically within days of birth; CG192 sets the first 2 weeks as the alert period.
n.1: Postpartum psychosis arises after birth, not in the third trimester.
n.3: Six weeks is broader than the specific CG192 alert period of the first 2 weeks.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Sophie, 33, has bipolar disorder and has decided with her psychiatrist to continue lithium through pregnancy. She is now 36 weeks. Which plan is most consistent with NICE CG192?
o: Check a lithium level once labour starts and continue her usual dose
Stop lithium at 36 weeks and restart it on the second postnatal day
Weekly plasma lithium levels from now, and plan birth in hospital
Lithium levels every 4 weeks until birth, with birth at home if she chooses
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.4.37: if lithium continues in pregnancy, check plasma levels every 4 weeks, then weekly from 36 weeks; maintain fluid balance; ensure she gives birth in hospital; monitor in labour; stop lithium during labour and check levels 12 hours after the last dose.

n.0: Lithium is stopped during labour because of dehydration and toxicity risk, with a level 12 hours after the last dose.
n.1: CG192 does not advise stopping lithium at 36 weeks; it is stopped during labour.
n.3: Levels become weekly from the 36th week, and CG192 advises birth in hospital.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Kate, 32, has had antenatal depression treated with an SSRI throughout pregnancy. Her baby girl was born 12 hours ago at term and is breastfeeding. Which action by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Arrange for the baby to be admitted to the neonatal unit for observation
Carry out a full neonatal assessment, alert to possible medication effects
Advise her to stop the SSRI now that the baby has been born
Advise formula feeding to avoid exposing the baby through breast milk
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG192 1.9.2: if a woman has taken psychotropic medication during pregnancy, carry out a full neonatal assessment, bearing in mind the variation in onset of adverse effects and the need for further monitoring, and keep relevant professionals and the family informed.

n.0: A well baby does not need neonatal unit admission; assessment and monitoring can continue with the mother.
n.2: Stopping an effective antidepressant abruptly after birth risks relapse at a high-risk time; decisions belong with the prescriber.
n.3: SSRIs are not a reason to stop breastfeeding; decisions are individual and made with the woman.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Amir was born at 39 weeks by spontaneous vaginal birth. His mother had GBS found on a urine culture at 30 weeks; membranes ruptured 6 hours before birth. At 2 hours old he is pink, feeding well, with normal observations and tone. Which plan best follows NICE NG195?
o: Start intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour without waiting for results
Transfer him to the neonatal unit for blood cultures and observation
Use clinical judgement and, if monitoring, observe him for at least 12 hours
Continue routine postnatal care as he has no risk factors for infection
Complications & Additional Care.w: Maternal GBS bacteriuria is a non-red-flag risk factor (NG195 box 1). With no red flags and only 1 risk factor, NG195 1.10.3 says use clinical judgement about withholding antibiotics and, if monitoring is needed, continue for at least 12 hours using a newborn early warning system.

n.0: Antibiotics without delay are for any red flag or 2 or more non-red-flag risk factors or indicators; Amir has 1 risk factor.
n.1: A well baby with one risk factor can be monitored with his mother; neonatal unit admission is not indicated.
n.3: Maternal GBS colonisation or bacteriuria IS a risk factor in NG195, so routine care without assessment is not appropriate.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Twins Ella and Isla were born at 37 weeks. At 10 hours old, Ella develops signs of shock and is started on antibiotics for suspected sepsis. Isla is feeding well and her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate plan for Isla?
o: Take investigations and start antibiotics without waiting for results
Continue routine postnatal care because she has no clinical signs
Monitor her observations every 4 hours for 12 hours before deciding
Wait for Ella's blood culture result before deciding about Isla
Complications & Additional Care.w: Suspected or confirmed infection in another baby of a multiple pregnancy is a red flag risk factor (NG195 box 1). Any red flag means investigations then antibiotics without waiting for results (NG195 1.10.3), given within 1 hour of the decision to treat (1.15.2).

n.1: A red flag risk factor applies even when the baby looks well.
n.2: Observation alone is for babies without red flags and with only 1 risk factor or indicator.
n.3: Waiting for the sibling's culture delays treatment of a baby with a red flag.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Leo was born at 35 weeks after spontaneous preterm labour, with membranes intact until birth. At 3 hours old he has a temperature of 35.8 C despite a warm environment and is grunting with mild recession. Which action is most appropriate under NG195?
o: Monitor him for at least 12 hours using a newborn early warning chart
Use the Kaiser calculator on the postnatal ward outside any audit
Repeat his temperature in 1 hour after skin-to-skin contact
Take investigations and start antibiotics without waiting for results
Complications & Additional Care.w: Leo has a risk factor (preterm birth after spontaneous labour) and two clinical indicators (temperature under 36 C unexplained by environment; respiratory distress). Two or more non-red-flag risk factors or indicators mean investigations and antibiotics without waiting for results (NG195 1.10.3).

n.0: Monitoring alone is for babies with 1 risk factor or indicator and no red flags.
n.1: NG195 1.10.4 allows the Kaiser calculator for babies over 34+0 weeks only as part of a prospective audit.
n.2: Rewarming and rechecking delays treatment when he already meets the threshold for antibiotics.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Noor, 2 days old and born at term, needs intravenous antibiotics for suspected early-onset infection. The paediatrician asks the midwife to prepare the first-line regimen. Which regimen does NICE NG195 recommend?
o: Benzylpenicillin with gentamicin
Amoxicillin with cefotaxime
Co-amoxiclav alone
Flucloxacillin with gentamicin
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG195 1.20.1: use intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin as first-choice empirical treatment for suspected early-onset infection, unless local resistance data indicate otherwise.

n.1: Cefotaxime is added if there is evidence of Gram-negative sepsis (NG195 1.20.8), not used first line with amoxicillin.
n.2: Co-amoxiclav is not the NG195 empirical regimen for early-onset neonatal infection.
n.3: Flucloxacillin is not the NG195 first-line choice for early-onset infection.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Tom, born at 40 weeks, is noticed by the midwife to look yellow at 18 hours old. He is feeding and otherwise well. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Check with a transcutaneous bilirubinometer and repeat it in 24 hours
Place him near a sunny window and review him at the next visit
Measure serum bilirubin within 2 hours and get an urgent medical review
Encourage more frequent breastfeeds and reassess at 48 hours
Complications & Additional Care.w: Jaundice within the first 24 hours is a risk factor for significant hyperbilirubinaemia. CG98 1.2.10 to 1.2.12: measure serum bilirubin urgently (within 2 hours) and arrange urgent medical review within 6 hours.

n.0: CG98 1.2.15 to 1.2.16 restricts transcutaneous measurement to babies over 24 hours old; under 24 hours, serum bilirubin is needed.
n.1: Sunlight is not a treatment for neonatal jaundice and delays measurement.
n.3: Jaundice under 24 hours may be haemolytic; waiting until 48 hours is unsafe.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Zoe, 4 days old and breastfed, is starting phototherapy on the postnatal ward. Her mother asks whether she should give formula top-ups to help clear the jaundice. Which advice is correct?
o: Give cooled boiled water between feeds to keep her well hydrated and clear it
Give formula top-ups after each feed to help flush out the bilirubin
Stop breastfeeding until the bilirubin is below the treatment threshold
Keep breastfeeding in short breaks from phototherapy; top-ups are not needed
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG98 1.4.4 to 1.4.15: during phototherapy allow short breaks (up to 30 minutes) for breastfeeding and do not give additional fluids or feeds routinely to breastfed babies; expressed breast milk is preferred if extra is needed.

n.0: Water is not given; it does not reduce bilirubin and can harm feeding and fluid balance.
n.1: Routine formula top-ups are not recommended for breastfed babies having phototherapy.
n.2: Stopping breastfeeding is not needed and undermines feeding.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Kofi, born at 38 weeks, is 16 days old and still visibly jaundiced. He is breastfeeding well and gaining weight. His mother says his stools have become pale and chalky. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat a transcutaneous reading at the 6 to 8 week check
Arrange measurement of conjugated bilirubin and refer for expert advice
Advise a 48-hour break from breastfeeding to see if it settles
Reassure her that breast milk jaundice can last for several weeks
Complications & Additional Care.w: Prolonged jaundice is jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby. Pale chalky stools suggest cholestasis such as biliary atresia. CG98 1.7.1 to 1.7.2: look for pale stools and dark urine and measure conjugated bilirubin; over 25 micromol/L needs expert advice.

n.0: Waiting until 6 to 8 weeks could delay diagnosis of biliary atresia, where timing of surgery matters.
n.2: Stopping breastfeeding is not recommended and delays investigation.
n.3: Pale chalky stools are a warning sign of liver disease, not breast milk jaundice; reassurance is unsafe.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Baby Sam was born at 38 weeks to a mother with type 1 diabetes. He is well, pink and feeding, and his 3-hour blood glucose is 2.4 mmol/L before a feed. The postnatal ward is busy and a staff member suggests taking him to the neonatal unit for convenience of monitoring. Which response is best?
o: Admit him to the neonatal unit for monitoring for 24 hours
Keep him with his mother, continuing feeds and glucose monitoring
Separate him from his mother overnight so that she can rest
Start intravenous dextrose to prevent a later fall in glucose
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG3 1.5.2: babies of women with diabetes should stay with their mothers unless complications or abnormal clinical signs require admission. A well baby with a pre-feed glucose of at least 2.0 mmol/L continues 2 to 3 hourly feeding and monitoring (NG3 1.5.9). Keeping mother and baby together supports feeding (SPM 4.10).

n.0: Admission is for clinical indications such as hypoglycaemia with abnormal signs (NG3 1.5.5), not ward workload.
n.2: Separation disrupts feeding and is not indicated for a well baby.
n.3: IV dextrose is not needed for a well baby with a pre-feed glucose above 2.0 mmol/L who is feeding.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Kayleigh, 25, is 8 weeks pregnant and attends her booking appointment. She tells the midwife for the first time that she uses cocaine most weekends and drinks heavily. She is anxious and asks whether this will be reported. Which response is most appropriate first?
o: Make a referral to the police because she has disclosed illegal drug use
Offer referral to a substance misuse service and explain how care is coordinated
Tell her the booking cannot continue until she has stopped using any drugs
Record the disclosure and plan to discuss it again at the 28-week visit
Complications & Additional Care.w: NICE CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses that she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme. Care is coordinated across agencies (1.2.2, 1.2.3) with a named midwife or doctor (1.2.4), and staff attitudes should not deter her from using services (1.2.1).

n.0: Drug use disclosed in a health consultation is not a police matter; the concern is her and her baby's health and wellbeing.
n.2: Making care conditional on abstinence creates a barrier that CG110 1.2.1 asks staff to overcome.
n.3: Delaying discussion until 28 weeks wastes months of potential support and treatment.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Bella, 30, is 22 weeks pregnant and on opiate substitution therapy. She misses appointments and tells the midwife she is frightened that her baby will be taken away at birth. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Explain honestly what to expect after birth, including care for the baby and any social care role
Reassure her that social care will not be involved if she attends every appointment from now
Advise her to stop her opiate substitution therapy so the baby will not need extra care
Avoid discussing social care so that she does not stop attending her appointments
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG110 1.2.1 and 1.2.10: address women's fears about children's services with information tailored to their needs, and explain what to expect when the baby is born, including medical care the baby may need, where the baby will be cared for and any potential involvement of social services.

n.1: Promising no involvement is not honest and may not be true; it undermines trust later.
n.2: Stopping opiate substitution therapy abruptly is unsafe and should only be considered with specialist input.
n.3: Avoiding the subject leaves her fears unaddressed, which is a recognised barrier to engagement.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Fatima, 29, is 16 weeks pregnant and speaks little English. She attends with her husband, who offers to interpret because he speaks English well. The midwife needs to discuss screening results and ask routine questions about domestic abuse. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange a professional interpreter, not a family member, for the appointment
Use a translation app on the midwife's phone to save waiting time
Give her written leaflets in English to take home for her husband to explain
Accept her husband's offer, as he knows her history and preferences well
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG110 1.3.10: provide an interpreter who can communicate in the woman's preferred language and who should not be a family member, legal guardian or partner. CG110 1.1.14 also requires at least one one-to-one consultation without the partner present to allow sensitive issues to be raised.

n.1: An unverified app is not a safe substitute for a professional interpreter when discussing screening results and abuse.
n.2: Leaflets in English do not meet her communication needs and still rely on her husband.
n.3: Using her husband prevents safe enquiry about domestic abuse and may filter what she says or hears.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Jess, 16, books at 12 weeks. She is living with her mother, is still at school and finds hospital clinics intimidating. Which care arrangement best follows NICE CG110?
o: Care deferred until her mother can attend every appointment with her
Standard consultant-led clinic care, as she is under 18
A named midwife providing most of her care, with a direct phone number
Antenatal care through her school nurse until 28 weeks
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG110 1.4.4: offer young women under 20 a named midwife who provides most of their antenatal care, with a direct-line telephone number. Services should be age-appropriate, community-based where possible and alert to safeguarding (1.4.1, 1.4.5).

n.0: Jess can attend herself; deferring care until her mother is available is a barrier to antenatal care.
n.1: Age alone is not an indication for consultant-led care; young women need accessible, age-appropriate services.
n.3: School nurses do not provide antenatal care; the midwife does.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Rana, 27, is 26 weeks pregnant. Her partner attends every appointment, answers questions for her and does not leave the room. She has missed two appointments. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Document that she is accompanied and continue care as usual at each appointment
Arrange a one-to-one consultation without her partner present to ask about her safety
Refer her straight to the police based on her partner's controlling behaviour
Ask her about domestic abuse in front of her partner so the question is clear
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG110 1.1.14: provide each woman with a one-to-one consultation, without her partner or family present, on at least one occasion to allow sensitive issues such as domestic abuse to be discussed. Controlling behaviour and missed appointments are warning signs of domestic abuse, and NICE NG201 1.2.5 advises asking about domestic abuse when the woman is alone.

n.0: Continuing as usual ignores clear warning signs and misses the chance to ask safely.
n.2: A police referral without her disclosure or consent, before any assessment, is premature and may increase her risk.
n.3: Asking in front of a possibly abusive partner may endanger her and is unlikely to lead to disclosure.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Ayan, 24, is an asylum seeker who is 30 weeks pregnant. She tells the community midwife she is being moved by the Home Office to accommodation in another city next week. Which action by the midwife is most important?
o: Delay her 32-week appointment until her new address is confirmed
Advise her to rebook with a GP in the new city after she has settled in
Make sure her hand-held notes are complete and she knows to keep them with her
Ask her to come back to this unit for each appointment after she moves
Complications & Additional Care.w: CG110 1.1.5, 1.1.10 and 1.3.8: women should take a copy of their hand-held maternity notes when moving, the notes should contain a full record of care and all test results, and women should keep them with them at all times. The midwife should also share information with the receiving service.

n.0: Delaying care creates a gap at a time when antenatal checks are important.
n.1: Waiting until she has settled risks a gap in care at 30 weeks; continuity of records and referral are needed now.
n.3: Travelling back from another city is impractical and risks missed appointments.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Ruby, 26, has a mild learning disability and is 20 weeks pregnant. She lives with her partner and has come alone to discuss her anomaly scan results. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Postpone the discussion until her partner can attend to make the decisions
Use accessible information, allow extra time and check her understanding
Give the standard written leaflet and ask her to phone with any questions
Assume she lacks capacity and ask the consultant to decide on her behalf
Complications & Additional Care.w: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1, capacity is presumed and all practicable steps must be taken to help a person decide. The Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments, such as easy read information and longer appointments. CG110 1.3.11 advises checking understanding of spoken information.

n.0: Ruby is entitled to make her own decisions; her partner cannot decide for her.
n.2: Standard leaflets without adjustment may not meet her needs and are not a reasonable adjustment.
n.3: A learning disability does not mean she lacks capacity (MCA 2005 s2(3)); capacity is presumed.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Chantelle, 22, is 24 weeks pregnant. Her two older children were removed into care last year because of neglect linked to her partner's alcohol use. She still lives with the same partner. What is the most appropriate action by the midwife?
o: Wait until the baby is born and then decide whether a referral to social care is needed
Refer to children's social care but avoid telling Chantelle to protect the relationship
Make no referral, as the previous removal has already been dealt with by the court
Explain her concerns and refer to children's social care for a pre-birth assessment
Complications & Additional Care.w: Previous removal of children with the same risk factor present is a clear safeguarding concern for the unborn baby. Multi-agency assessment and a coordinated plan are needed before birth (CG110 1.1.7), and the woman should be told why and when information may be shared (CG110 1.1.9) unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Pre-birth assessment allows support and safety planning; waiting until after birth wastes this time.
n.1: Openness is the default; CG110 1.1.9 says tell her why and when information is shared, and nothing here suggests telling her would increase the risk.
n.2: The previous proceedings concerned the older children; the unborn baby faces the same unresolved risk.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Laila, 31, is 36 weeks pregnant. A scan confirms an intrauterine fetal death. She is physically well, her membranes are intact and there are no signs of infection or bleeding. She says she cannot face labour today. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Send her home and ask her to return to the unit when labour starts naturally
Advise immediate induction of labour today to reduce the risk of infection
Discuss expectant management, induction and caesarean, and respect her choice
Arrange a caesarean birth today as the quickest way to end the pregnancy
Complications & Additional Care.w: NICE NG207 1.2.28: after intrauterine fetal death, if the woman is physically well with intact membranes and no infection or bleeding, discuss the options for birth (expectant management, induction or caesarean) and respect her decision. Support for her and her family is offered (1.2.27).

n.0: Expectant management is a valid option but is a decision to be discussed and agreed, with support and follow-up, not a default discharge.
n.1: Immediate induction is offered when there are ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding (NG207 1.2.29), which Laila does not have.
n.3: Caesarean carries surgical morbidity; it is one option to discuss, not the default recommendation.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Carys, 28, is 33 weeks pregnant and has an intrauterine fetal death confirmed. She has a temperature of 38.4 C, offensive vaginal loss and her membranes ruptured two days ago. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Offer a choice including expectant management over the next week
Start oral antibiotics and plan induction in 48 hours
Offer mifepristone and plan induction in 48 hours
Offer immediate induction of labour or caesarean birth
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG207 1.2.29: after intrauterine fetal death, if there is evidence of ruptured membranes, infection or bleeding, offer immediate induction of labour or caesarean birth. Carys also needs sepsis assessment.

n.0: Expectant management is not offered when there is infection or ruptured membranes.
n.1: Infection with ruptured membranes after fetal death needs immediate birth and sepsis management, not a 48-hour delay.
n.2: The usual mifepristone interval is for a well woman with intact membranes; with infection, birth is immediate.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Megan, 30, has chosen induction of labour after an intrauterine fetal death at 38 weeks. She has had no previous caesarean birth. Which regimen does NICE NG207 recommend?
o: Artificial rupture of membranes followed by a 24-hour wait
Vaginal dinoprostone gel alone, repeated every 6 hours
Oral mifepristone 200 mg, then dinoprostone or misoprostol
Intravenous oxytocin alone from the start of the induction
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG207 1.2.31: for women choosing induced labour after intrauterine fetal death, offer oral mifepristone 200 mg followed by vaginal dinoprostone or oral or vaginal misoprostol (or a mechanical method), based on clinical circumstances and national protocols.

n.0: Artificial rupture of membranes is not the recommended first step and increases infection risk.
n.1: NG207 combines mifepristone with a prostaglandin for fetal death; dinoprostone alone is not the recommended regimen.
n.3: NG207 lists intravenous oxytocin alone among methods the evidence does not support for induction.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Priya and her partner have just had a stillborn daughter at 37 weeks. They seem unsure about seeing or holding her. Which approach by the midwife is most appropriate?
o: Take the baby to the mortuary while they rest and ask them again tomorrow
Advise them not to see her because it may make their grief harder
Offer them the choice, with time and gentle explanation, and respect what they decide
Encourage them to hold her now because they will regret it later if they do not
Complications & Additional Care.w: Compassionate bereavement care (SPM 4.11; National Bereavement Care Pathway stillbirth pathway) offers parents personalised choices about seeing, holding and making memories with their baby, without pressure either way, and respects their decision. They can change their mind later.

n.0: Removing the baby without agreement takes away the choice; parents may want time with her now.
n.1: Advising against seeing the baby removes a choice many parents value; the decision is theirs.
n.3: Pressuring parents to hold the baby is not person-centred; they should be offered the choice without coercion.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Following the stillbirth of Baby Aria at 39 weeks, the community midwife visits the parents at home. They ask whether anyone will look into what happened. Which statement about the Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) is most accurate?
o: The coroner investigates stillbirths, so the hospital does not hold a review
The hospital reviews the care once the parents request a review in writing
The review is confidential to staff and the findings are not shared with parents
The hospital reviews the care, and they are told about the review and can contribute
Complications & Additional Care.w: The PMRT supports systematic multidisciplinary review of care for stillbirths and neonatal deaths from 22 weeks. Parents are told a review will take place and how they can contribute, and a plain-language explanation of the findings is discussed with them (NPEU PMRT).

n.0: Coroners in England and Wales do not currently have jurisdiction over stillbirths; the hospital reviews the care using the PMRT.
n.1: The PMRT review happens for every eligible death; parents do not have to request it.
n.2: Parent involvement and sharing the findings with parents are core aims of the PMRT.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Sophie, 26, had a miscarriage at 19 weeks. On discharge she asks whether she must register her baby's birth and death. Which response is accurate for England and Wales?
o: The baby must be registered as a neonatal death within 5 days
The loss must be registered as a stillbirth within 42 days
Registration is required because the loss was after 16 weeks
There is no legal requirement to register a loss before 24 weeks
Complications & Additional Care.w: A stillbirth in law is a baby born after the 24th week of pregnancy who did not breathe or show any other signs of life (Births and Deaths Registration Act 1953 s41); stillbirths must be registered. A pregnancy loss before 24 weeks is not legally registrable, although parents in England may apply for a voluntary baby loss certificate.

n.0: Neonatal death applies to a baby born alive who dies; this was a loss before 24 weeks without signs of life.
n.1: Stillbirth registration applies to babies born after 24 weeks with no signs of life.
n.2: 16 weeks is not a legal threshold for registration in England and Wales.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Jade, 34, is being cared for after a stillbirth at 35 weeks. She is distressed that her breasts are becoming full and leaking on day 3. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Acknowledge how distressing this is and discuss options to manage lactation
Advise her to express fully every 3 hours to prevent mastitis
Explain that this does not happen after a stillbirth and arrange a GP review
Tell her to bind her breasts tightly and restrict her fluid intake
Complications & Additional Care.w: Lactation commonly begins after a stillbirth and can be very distressing. Bereavement care includes preparing parents for this and discussing options, such as suppression measures or donating breast milk, in a sensitive, personalised way (National Bereavement Care Pathway; SPM 4.11).

n.1: Frequent full expression stimulates supply and is not the advice for a woman who wishes to suppress lactation.
n.2: Milk does come in after a stillbirth because lactation is triggered by birth of the placenta.
n.3: Tight binding and fluid restriction are not recommended and can cause discomfort and harm.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Ellen, 29, and her partner are leaving hospital after the neonatal death of their son at 2 days old. Which follow-up arrangement best reflects good bereavement care?
o: Arrange a routine postnatal visit on day 10 and close her midwifery care
Book their son's 6 to 8 week check as planned so they stay in contact with services
Inform the GP and health visitor, cancel baby appointments and offer a follow-up meeting
Leave them to contact the unit themselves if they want a follow-up appointment in future
Complications & Additional Care.w: The National Bereavement Care Pathway emphasises communication with the GP and health visitor, cancelling routine baby-related appointments and screening invitations, and offering a follow-up appointment with a senior clinician to discuss what happened and any review findings.

n.0: Closing care after one visit does not provide the ongoing support and follow-up the pathway expects.
n.1: Sending routine baby appointments after a death causes avoidable distress; they should be cancelled.
n.3: Leaving all contact to bereaved parents risks them receiving no support or follow-up.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Amara, 33, attends her booking appointment at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. She has had chronic hypertension for three years, controlled on medication, and her blood pressure today is 132/84 mmHg. Which advice about aspirin is most appropriate?
o: Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 20 weeks until 36 weeks
Take aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the baby is born
Start aspirin if her blood pressure rises above 140/90 mmHg
Start aspirin if a second risk factor for pre-eclampsia is identified
Complications & Additional Care.w: Chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia. NICE NG133 1.1.2 advises women with any high-risk factor to take 75 mg to 150 mg of aspirin daily from 12 weeks until the birth of the baby.

n.0: The start point is 12 weeks and aspirin continues until birth; starting at 20 weeks and stopping at 36 weeks departs from NG133 1.1.2.
n.2: Aspirin is prophylaxis based on risk at booking, not treatment triggered by a rise in blood pressure.
n.3: A single high-risk factor is enough; the 'more than one' rule applies to moderate risk factors (NG133 1.1.3).

Complications & Additional Care.q: Ellie, 41, is 10 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her BMI is 27 kg/m2, her blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg and she has no medical history. Her mother had pre-eclampsia. Which statement about aspirin is most accurate?
o: Her age is a high-risk factor, so aspirin from 20 weeks is advised
Her family history is a high-risk factor, so aspirin from 16 weeks is advised
She has more than one moderate risk factor, so aspirin from 12 weeks is advised
She has one moderate risk factor, so aspirin is not indicated at this stage
Complications & Additional Care.w: Nulliparity, age 40 or older and a family history of pre-eclampsia are all moderate risk factors. With more than one moderate risk factor, NG133 1.1.3 advises aspirin 75 to 150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth. Ellie has three.

n.0: Age 40 or over is a moderate risk factor, and aspirin starts at 12 weeks, not 20.
n.1: Family history is a moderate, not high, risk factor and the advised start is 12 weeks.
n.3: Ellie has three moderate risk factors (first pregnancy, age 41, family history), not one.

Complications & Additional Care.q: Leah, 27, is 32 weeks pregnant. Her booking blood pressure at 10 weeks was 114/70 mmHg. Today it is 146/94 mmHg and remains at that level on a repeat reading. Urinalysis shows no protein and she has no symptoms. Which term best describes her condition?
o: Severe gestational hypertension
Gestational hypertension
Pre-eclampsia
Chronic essential hypertension
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG133 defines gestational hypertension as new hypertension (140/90 mmHg or more) presenting after 20 weeks without significant proteinuria. Leah's booking BP was normal and there is no proteinuria or organ dysfunction.

n.0: Severe hypertension in NG133 is over 160 mmHg systolic or over 110 mmHg diastolic; 146/94 mmHg is not in that range.
n.2: Pre-eclampsia needs new hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or another maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction; none is present.
n.3: Chronic hypertension is present at booking or before 20 weeks; Leah's booking BP was normal.
