Complications & Additional Care.q: Sana, 30, is 35 weeks pregnant and has gestational hypertension managed in the community. She asks which symptoms should make her contact the maternity unit straight away. Which symptom should the midwife highlight?
o: Severe headache with blurred vision or flashing lights
Heartburn after large meals that eases with antacids
Needing to pass urine more often during the night
Ankle swelling at the end of the day that settles overnight
Complications & Additional Care.w: NG133 1.1.1 advises women to report immediately any severe headache, problems with vision such as blurring or flashing before the eyes, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet.

n.1: Meal-related heartburn relieved by antacids is common; severe pain just below the ribs is the warning sign.
n.2: Nocturia is a normal effect of pressure on the bladder in late pregnancy, not a pre-eclampsia warning symptom.
n.3: Gradual dependent ankle oedema that resolves overnight is common in late pregnancy; it is sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet that needs urgent review.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: After a shoulder dystocia that ended with a healthy baby, the team leader runs a short debrief. She asks the team to describe what went well and what made that possible, as well as what could be improved. Which approach is she using?
o: A clinical audit against the shoulder dystocia guideline
A formal disciplinary review of the team's practice
A strength-based approach that learns from what went well
A root cause analysis to find who made the error
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Strength-based approaches (SPM 5.4, 5.13.5) look at what went well and why, so successful behaviours can be reinforced and spread, alongside identifying improvements.

n.0: Audit measures practice against standards across many cases, not a single team debrief.
n.1: A disciplinary review addresses individual conduct, not team learning after a good outcome.
n.3: Root cause analysis looks for causes of failure, and the aim is not to find who made an error.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Grace, a midwife, is 11 hours into a 12.5-hour night shift with no break. She notices she has read the same CTG twice without taking it in. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask a student midwife to interpret the CTG on her behalf for now
Finish her current tasks and then take her break after handover
Drink a strong coffee and carry on with her care until the end of her shift
Tell the coordinator, take a break and ask a colleague to review the CTG
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Fatigue is a recognised human factor that impairs attention and decision-making. Recognising it, telling the coordinator, taking a break and getting a second review keeps care safe (SPM 5.4, 5.14; Code 16.3 tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity about problems that may prevent you working within the Code; Code 19.2 human factors).

n.0: A student cannot take responsibility for CTG interpretation; review must be by a competent registrant.
n.1: Waiting until handover leaves a fatigued midwife making decisions for another 90 minutes.
n.2: Caffeine does not reliably restore performance, and continuing leaves her impaired while interpreting a CTG.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Maya is the midwife at a freestanding birth centre when a woman has a sudden, heavy postpartum haemorrhage. One other midwife and a maternity support worker are on duty. What should Maya do first?
o: Phone the obstetric unit for advice before starting any treatment
Ask the support worker to estimate the blood loss before any other action
Call for help, request a 999 ambulance and give each colleague a clear role
Start the haemorrhage protocol herself and call for help once bleeding slows
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: In an unpredictable emergency, calling for help early, arranging transfer and allocating clear roles makes best use of a small team (SPM 5.13.6; NICE NG235 1.10.33: call for help, transfer to obstetric-led care).

n.0: Advice is useful but treatment and transfer must not wait for it.
n.1: Measuring blood loss matters, but it is not the first priority over summoning help.
n.3: Delaying the call for help until bleeding slows wastes time a small team cannot afford.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: During a category 1 caesarean, the anaesthetist, obstetrician and midwife all focus on the baby's delivery. Nobody notices that the woman's oxygen saturations have fallen. Which human factors concept best describes this?
o: Loss of situational awareness
Confirmation bias
Authority gradient
Diffusion of responsibility
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Situational awareness is perceiving what is happening, understanding its meaning and anticipating what comes next. When all attention narrows onto one task, other important information is missed (SPM 5.4).

n.1: Confirmation bias is favouring information that supports an existing belief.
n.2: An authority gradient is a steep hierarchy that discourages juniors from speaking up.
n.3: Diffusion of responsibility is assuming someone else will act on a known task; here the change was not noticed.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Yasmin, a midwife on the antenatal ward, is about to phone the obstetric registrar about Mrs Okoro, 34 weeks pregnant, whose blood pressure is 162/108 mmHg with a severe headache. Using SBAR, how should Yasmin open the call?
o: Ask the registrar to come and review Mrs Okoro within 15 minutes
Describe Mrs Okoro's obstetric history, booking bloods and her previous pregnancies
Give her own interpretation that this is probably severe pre-eclampsia
Give her name, ward, the woman's name and the severe hypertension with headache
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SBAR begins with the Situation: who is calling, from where, about whom, and the immediate concern. Background, Assessment and Recommendation follow. A clear opening helps the receiver prioritise (SPM 5.13.2).

n.0: The request for review is the Recommendation, which closes the call rather than opening it.
n.1: History is the Background, which comes after the Situation.
n.2: Her clinical interpretation is the Assessment, the third step.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A midwife has given an SBAR handover to the registrar about a woman with a suspected sepsis score. Which statement best fits the 'Recommendation' part of SBAR?
o: "I think she is septic and I am worried that she is deteriorating quickly."
"Please review her within 15 minutes; I will take blood cultures now."
"Her temperature is 38.6 C, her heart rate 124 and her respiratory rate 24."
"She had a caesarean birth five days ago and was discharged on day 2."
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: The Recommendation states clearly what the caller wants and in what time frame, and what she will do meanwhile, so that expectations are explicit and can be read back (SPM 5.13.2).

n.0: Her clinical judgement is the Assessment; it does not say what action is needed or when.
n.2: Observations form part of the Situation or Assessment, not the Recommendation.
n.3: The surgical history is Background.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Abi is caring for a woman in labour on continuous CTG monitoring. According to Saving Babies' Lives v3, how often should a separate 'fresh eyes' review of the CTG and overall wellbeing take place?
o: At least every 2 hours
When the CTG is classified as pathological
At least hourly
At least every 4 hours
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SBL v3 4.3 and 4.4: a regular (at least hourly) systematic review of maternal and fetal wellbeing, with a separate fresh eyes review at least hourly when CTG is used, or at least 4-hourly with intermittent auscultation, unless triggered earlier.

n.0: Two-hourly is less often than the SBL v3 minimum for CTG.
n.1: Fresh eyes is a scheduled safeguard; waiting for a pathological trace defeats its purpose of earlier detection.
n.3: Four-hourly fresh eyes applies to intermittent auscultation, not CTG monitoring.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: At 07:30 the night midwife hands over care of a woman in labour on an oxytocin infusion to the day midwife. Which handover approach is safest?
o: A verbal handover at the desk so the woman is not disturbed during labour
A written handover left in the notes because the night midwife is late to leave
A brief handover of the CTG findings, as the infusion is recorded on the chart
Bedside handover with the woman, using a structured tool and checking CTG and pump
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Structured, face-to-face bedside handover that involves the woman allows both midwives to review the CTG, infusion rate and plan together and reduces information loss (SPM 5.13.2; NMC Code 8.6 share information to identify and reduce risk).

n.0: A desk handover misses checking the CTG, pump and the woman herself together.
n.1: A written note alone gives no chance to clarify or ask questions at a high-risk point.
n.2: Limiting handover to the CTG leaves out the oxytocin rate, maternal condition and plan.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Mo, a band 6 midwife, has escalated a pathological CTG to the obstetric registrar, who says to continue and review in an hour. Mo remains very concerned as the fetal heart rate has had a prolonged deceleration. What should Mo do next?
o: State her concern clearly and escalate to the consultant obstetrician
Document her disagreement and review the CTG again in an hour
Ask another midwife whether she agrees before taking any action
Accept the registrar's plan because the decision is a medical one
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: When concerns remain after escalation, the midwife should use the escalation or conflict of clinical opinion policy to go to the consultant. Ockenden IEA 3 requires trusts to support staff in escalating clinical concerns when professionals disagree (SPM 5.6; Code 16.1).

n.1: Documenting without acting leaves the fetus at continuing risk for another hour.
n.2: Seeking a second midwifery view is reasonable but should not delay escalation when she is already concerned.
n.3: The midwife remains accountable for acting on her concerns; deferring to hierarchy despite clear risk is unsafe.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: During a night shift, Tara notices that her colleague smells strongly of alcohol, is slurring her words and is about to check a controlled drug. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop her taking part in drug checks and tell the coordinator straight away
Report her directly to the NMC before speaking to anyone at the unit
Wait until the end of the shift and then discuss it privately with her
Complete the drug check together so that a second person is present
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: A colleague who appears impaired poses an immediate risk to women and babies. The Code 16.1 and 17 require raising concerns without delay to protect people; the immediate step is to remove the risk and inform the person in charge, who will follow local policy.

n.1: Referral to the NMC may follow, but the immediate risk on the shift must be managed locally first.
n.2: Waiting until the end of the shift leaves women exposed to an impaired practitioner for hours.
n.3: Continuing the check with an impaired colleague does not remove the risk.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Holly, a newly qualified midwife, is uneasy because the registrar is about to attempt a rotational instrumental birth without the consultant present, which local policy says requires consultant agreement. Which statement by Holly is most appropriate?
o: "I'm concerned our policy needs consultant agreement. Can we call them first?"
"I'll fill in an incident form afterwards if anything goes wrong for her."
"I'm not happy, but I don't want to hold things up, so carry on."
"You're the doctor, so I'll go along with whatever you decide is best here."
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Speaking up clearly, naming the concern and the policy, and proposing a safe action is the core of graded assertiveness and challenging a steep hierarchy (SPM 5.6, 5.13.2; Code 16.1).

n.1: Reporting after the event does not prevent the risk; concerns should be raised at the time.
n.2: Voicing unease but then letting things proceed does not protect the woman.
n.3: Deferring to hierarchy despite a safety concern breaches the duty to raise concerns.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Over three months, Chloe has repeatedly reported to her ward manager that night staffing falls below safe levels, with no response or action. What should she do next?
o: Post about the staffing on social media to raise public awareness
Escalate to a more senior manager or the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
Stop reporting, as her concerns have already been recorded
Resign from her post so that she is not accountable for the risk
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: If concerns are not addressed, the midwife should escalate further, for example to senior managers, the Freedom to Speak Up Guardian and, if needed, external bodies such as the CQC (NMC raising concerns guidance; Code 16.1 raise and, if necessary, escalate concerns; SPM 5.6).

n.0: Social media is not an appropriate route and may breach confidentiality and Code 20.10.
n.2: Recording a concern does not discharge the duty if the risk continues unaddressed.
n.3: Resigning does not address the risk to women and babies.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Nell, a midwife, prepares an oxytocin infusion using a quarter of the prescribed dose. Her colleague spots the discrepancy during the independent second check, before the infusion is connected. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Correct the dose and report Nell to the NMC for making a medicines error
Correct the dose and report the event as a near miss on the incident system
Correct the dose; no report is needed because the woman was not harmed
Correct the dose and tell the woman that a serious incident has occurred
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: A near miss is an event that could have caused harm but was intercepted. Reporting near misses allows the system to learn before harm occurs (SPM 5.2; PSIRF focus on learning).

n.0: A single intercepted error is a learning event for the organisation, not a fitness to practise matter.
n.2: Near misses are reportable precisely because they reveal risks before anyone is harmed.
n.3: No harm occurred and the error was intercepted, so calling it a serious incident is inaccurate; the priority is correcting the dose and reporting so the system learns.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Following a delay in escalating a pathological CTG, Baby Jacob needed therapeutic cooling for moderate encephalopathy. Under the statutory duty of candour in England, what must the trust do?
o: Inform the parents in writing after the trust's legal team has approved the letter
Tell the parents if they ask directly whether anything went wrong with their baby's care
Tell the parents in person as soon as reasonably practicable, with an account and apology
Wait until the investigation is complete before telling the parents what happened
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014: for a notifiable safety incident, notify the relevant person as soon as reasonably practicable, in person, giving a true account, an apology, details of further enquiries and reasonable support, followed by written notification.

n.0: The initial notification must be in person; written notification follows it.
n.1: The duty is proactive; it does not depend on the family asking.
n.3: Notification must not wait for the investigation; further findings are shared later in writing.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: After an incident, a midwife tells a woman, "I am so sorry this happened to you and your baby." A colleague warns her that saying sorry admits legal liability. Which response is correct?
o: An apology admits liability unless the woman has signed a waiver
An apology is acceptable when it is made in writing, not in person
An apology admits liability, so it should come from the legal team
An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence or breach of duty
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Section 2 of the Compensation Act 2006 states that an apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty. Regulation 20 defines an apology as an expression of sorrow or regret, and Code 14.2 requires an apology when harm occurs.

n.0: There is no waiver mechanism; an apology is not of itself an admission.
n.1: The duty of candour requires the apology in person first, then in writing.
n.2: Compensation Act 2006 s2 means an apology is not of itself an admission of liability.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A trust in England has moved from the Serious Incident Framework to the Patient Safety Incident Response Framework (PSIRF). A midwife asks what has changed. Which description is most accurate?
o: Investigations now identify the individual staff member who is responsible for the harm
System learning and proportionate responses, with compassionate engagement of families
Every incident now has a full root cause analysis completed within 60 working days
Families are no longer involved, so that staff can speak freely
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: PSIRF replaced the Serious Incident Framework (2015). Its four aims are compassionate engagement and involvement of those affected, system-based approaches to learning, considered and proportionate responses, and supportive oversight (NHS England PSIRF).

n.0: PSIRF focuses on systems and contributory factors, not on blaming individuals.
n.2: PSIRF moves away from a fixed timescale and investigation for everything towards proportionate responses.
n.3: Compassionate engagement of patients and families is a core PSIRF aim.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A baby born at term needs therapeutic cooling after a difficult labour in an NHS trust in England. The parents ask whether an independent body will look into the care. Which body carries out independent maternity safety investigations in England?
o: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
Maternity and Newborn Safety Investigations (MNSI)
The Perinatal Mortality Review Tool (PMRT) team
The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC)
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: MNSI carries out independent investigations of certain maternity and newborn safety events reported by NHS trusts in England, working with families and staff and making safety recommendations without blaming individuals (MNSI).

n.0: The Ombudsman considers complaints after local processes are exhausted, not safety investigations.
n.2: The PMRT supports local hospital reviews of perinatal deaths; it is not an independent investigation body.
n.3: The NMC regulates individual registrants' fitness to practise; it does not investigate maternity safety events.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Lucy, a midwife, realises she gave a woman's prescribed antibiotic 4 hours late because she forgot it during a busy shift. The woman is well. What should Lucy do first?
o: Report the incident but not tell the woman, because no harm has occurred
Tell the woman, apologise, give the dose as advised and report the incident
Give the dose now and record it at the scheduled time to avoid confusion
Ask a colleague to give the dose so that the error is not linked to her
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Code 14.1 to 14.3: act immediately to put right the situation, explain to the person what has happened and apologise, and document events. The incident should be reported so the system can learn (SPM 5.2).

n.0: Openness with the woman is required by Code 14 when an error occurs.
n.2: Recording a false time is dishonest and breaches Code 10 and 20.2.
n.3: Concealing her involvement breaches the duty of candour and honesty.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A trust has completed a learning response after a woman had a major postpartum haemorrhage with a delayed transfer. Following Ockenden, what should the team make sure happens with the findings?
o: Share them with the family in plain language and feed them into training
File the report and repeat the review if a similar incident happens
Send the report to the family in technical terms for accuracy
Keep the report internal to protect staff who took part in interviews
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Ockenden IEA 5: investigations must be meaningful for families and staff, reports written in language families understand, and lessons fed into multidisciplinary training and changes in practice audited. SPM 5.3 requires sharing feedback and learning with families and colleagues.

n.1: Filing without action fails to implement learning; Ockenden expects timely change.
n.2: Ockenden requires language families can understand, with medical terms explained.
n.3: Families should be involved and informed; withholding findings breaches openness.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Jo, a midwife, was involved in a shoulder dystocia that is now the subject of a trust learning response. She is asked to attend an interview and give a written account. What is her professional responsibility?
o: Give an account after checking it with colleagues so the stories match
Decline the interview until the trust guarantees she will not be named
Cooperate fully and give an honest, factual account of her involvement
Ask her union to give an account so she does not have to take part
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Code 23 requires registrants to cooperate with investigations and audits, and Code 10 and 20.2 require honest, accurate accounts. Critical reflection on the incident supports learning (SPM 5.2).

n.0: Aligning accounts with colleagues undermines the integrity of the investigation.
n.1: Making cooperation conditional on anonymity conflicts with the duty to cooperate.
n.3: A union may support her, but the account must be her own.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A student midwife asks Rachel, her practice supervisor, what the leading cause of maternal death in the UK is during pregnancy and up to six weeks after, according to the latest MBRRACE-UK data (2022-24). Which answer is correct?
o: Cardiac disease in pregnancy
Maternal suicide
Thrombosis and thromboembolism
Sepsis from genital tract infection
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: MBRRACE-UK data brief (2022-24): thrombosis and thromboembolism remained the leading cause of maternal death during or up to six weeks after pregnancy, followed by cardiac disease and then psychiatric causes.

n.0: Cardiac disease was the second most common cause in 2022-24.
n.1: Maternal suicide is the leading cause between six weeks and one year after pregnancy, not up to six weeks.
n.3: Sepsis was a less common direct cause, behind thromboembolism and suicide.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A community midwife is planning postnatal visits to women up to a year after birth. According to MBRRACE-UK 2022-24, what is the leading cause of maternal death between six weeks and one year after the end of pregnancy?
o: Thrombosis and thromboembolism
Epilepsy and stroke
Maternal suicide
Cardiac disease
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: maternal suicides remained the leading cause of maternal death occurring between six weeks and one year after the end of pregnancy; psychiatric causes accounted for 33% of late maternal deaths.

n.0: Thromboembolism is the leading cause during pregnancy and up to six weeks after.
n.1: Neurological causes are important indirect causes but not the leading late cause.
n.3: Cardiac disease is the second leading cause up to six weeks, not the leading late cause.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A midwife is reviewing data on inequalities to plan an outreach project. According to MBRRACE-UK 2022-24, how did the maternal mortality rate for Black women compare with that for White women?
o: Nearly three times higher
About five times higher
About the same
About twice as high
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: MBRRACE-UK 2022-24: there was a nearly three-fold difference in maternal mortality rates for Black women compared with White women; women in the most deprived areas had twice the rate of those in the least deprived.

n.1: The 2022-24 data show a nearly three-fold, not five-fold, difference.
n.2: A large and persistent inequality was reported; the rates were not similar.
n.3: A twofold difference is the gap between the most and least deprived areas, not between Black and White women.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A newly appointed midwife in England is told that the trust is still working through the Ockenden final report (2022). How many themes of immediate and essential actions (IEAs) did the report set for all trusts?
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: The Ockenden final report (30 March 2022) set out 15 immediate and essential action themes for all maternity services in England, including safe staffing, escalation and accountability, multidisciplinary training, and bereavement care.

n.0: The final report set 15 IEA themes, not 10.
n.2: Four is the number of areas for action in the East Kent report.
n.3: Seven was the number of IEAs in the first (emerging findings) Ockenden report in 2020; the final report set 15.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A maternity governance meeting is discussing the East Kent report, "Reading the signals" (Kirkup, 2022). Which list matches the report's four areas for action?
o: Safe staffing, multidisciplinary training, complex antenatal care, bereavement care
Smoking, fetal growth, fetal movements, fetal monitoring, preterm birth, diabetes
Identifying poor performance, compassion and kindness, teamworking, responding with honesty
Listening to women, workforce, safety culture, standards and structures
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: East Kent (19 October 2022): identifying poorly performing units; giving care with compassion and kindness; teamworking with a common purpose; responding to challenge with honesty.

n.0: These are among the Ockenden immediate and essential action themes.
n.1: These are the six elements of Saving Babies' Lives v3.
n.3: These are the four themes of the NHS England three-year delivery plan (2023).

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A midwife is explaining Saving Babies' Lives Care Bundle v3 to a new colleague. Which list correctly describes its six elements?
o: Smoking; fetal growth; fetal movements; fetal monitoring; stillbirth; postnatal care
Smoking; obesity; fetal growth; induction of labour; caesarean birth; neonatal care
Smoking; fetal growth; fetal movements; fetal monitoring; preterm birth; diabetes
Smoking; folic acid; vitamin D; aspirin; fetal growth; preterm birth
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SBL v3 elements: 1 reducing smoking; 2 fetal growth risk assessment, surveillance and management; 3 raising awareness of reduced fetal movement; 4 effective fetal monitoring in labour; 5 reducing preterm births and optimising perinatal care; 6 management of pre-existing diabetes.

n.0: Element 5 is preterm birth and element 6 is pre-existing diabetes; there is no stillbirth or postnatal element.
n.1: Obesity, induction, caesarean and neonatal care are not SBL v3 elements.
n.3: Folic acid, vitamin D and aspirin are interventions within elements, not elements themselves.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Following a cluster of maternal deaths from venous thromboembolism reported in national data, a midwife wants to use the findings in her practice. Which action best applies national report findings to individual care?
o: Reassess VTE risk at booking and on admission, and support informed choices
Wait for the trust to update its guideline before changing her practice
Share the national report with women at booking and let them decide what to do
Advise all pregnant women to take low molecular weight heparin from their booking visit
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SPM 1.5 requires midwives to use and apply lessons from data and reports to inform practice and support women's evidence-informed decisions. Applying VTE learning means individualised risk assessment at booking, repeated on any admission or new problem and around birth (NICE NG201 1.2.18; RCOG GTG 37a), and shared decision-making about prophylaxis.

n.1: Applying current national guidance on VTE risk assessment does not depend on waiting for a local update.
n.2: Handing over a report without discussion does not support informed decision-making.
n.3: Universal prophylaxis is not recommended; prophylaxis follows individual risk assessment.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A midwife is preparing a teaching session on the NHS England three-year delivery plan for maternity and neonatal services (2023). Which theme is part of the plan?
o: Reaching a national target for continuity of carer by March 2024
Moving all births into obstetric units for safety
Reducing caesarean birth rates to a fixed national target
Developing and sustaining a culture of safety, learning and support
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: The three-year delivery plan (30 March 2023) has four themes: listening to and working with women and families with compassion; growing, retaining and supporting the workforce; developing and sustaining a culture of safety, learning and support; and standards and structures that underpin safer, more personalised and more equitable care.

n.0: NHS England removed the national target date for continuity of carer in September 2022.
n.1: The plan supports personalised choice of place of birth, including midwifery-led settings.
n.2: The plan does not set a fixed national caesarean rate target.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Priya, a midwife, wants to reduce delays in giving women pain relief on the induction suite. She plans to trial a new medicine round time for one week on one bay, collect data, then adjust. Which quality improvement method is she using?
o: A root cause analysis
A randomised controlled trial
A Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle
A clinical audit and re-audit cycle
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: PDSA cycles test small changes on a small scale: plan the change, do it, study the results, and act by adopting, adapting or abandoning it before the next cycle (SPM 5.1).

n.0: Root cause analysis investigates why an incident happened, not how to test an improvement.
n.1: A randomised controlled trial is research with random allocation, ethics approval and a comparison group, not a small local test of change.
n.3: Audit measures current practice against an agreed standard; it does not test a change in rapid cycles.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: After a one-week trial of a new triage call script, Ola collects data on call times and compares it with the previous month. Which stage of the PDSA cycle is she completing?
o: The Do stage
The Plan stage
The Study stage
The Act stage
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: In the Study stage the team analyses the data, compares results with predictions and reflects on what was learned. Act then decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change (SPM 5.1).

n.0: Do was the one-week trial itself.
n.1: Planning set out the change and predictions before the trial.
n.3: Act follows Study and decides what to do next with the change.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A midwifery team wants to check whether all women with a BMI of 40 kg/m2 or over were referred for an anaesthetic review as set out in the unit guideline. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: A clinical audit measuring practice against the guideline standard
A service evaluation of women's satisfaction with the clinic
A PDSA cycle testing a new referral form on one clinic
A research study comparing two referral pathways
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Clinical audit measures current practice against a defined standard (here, the referral requirement in the guideline), identifies gaps and drives improvement, with re-audit to close the loop.

n.1: Satisfaction is a different question from compliance with a referral standard.
n.2: A PDSA cycle tests a change; the question is whether an existing standard is being met.
n.3: Research generates new knowledge by comparing interventions; the standard already exists.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Funmi is leading the introduction of a new postnatal discharge checklist on her ward. Previous changes have failed because staff felt they were imposed. What should she do first?
o: Ask the ward manager to make use of the checklist mandatory from Monday
Introduce the checklist on night shifts first when the ward is quieter
Involve ward staff and women in identifying the problem and shaping the change
Issue the checklist by email with a start date and a compliance target
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Effective change management engages the people affected early, builds shared understanding of the need for change and involves service users. This increases ownership and sustainability (SPM 5.11, 5.13.4).

n.0: Mandating use without engagement is likely to meet the same resistance.
n.1: Choosing a quieter shift does not address why previous changes were resisted.
n.3: Imposing change by email repeats the approach that has failed before.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A labour ward midwife notices that the nitrous oxide and oxygen (Entonox) supply in empty rooms is often left connected and that a regulator has a faint hiss. In the context of sustainable healthcare, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Record the hiss in the ward diary for the next equipment check
Report the leak, and turn off supplies in rooms not in use
Leave the supply connected so it is ready for the next woman
Advise women to use pethidine instead of Entonox to reduce emissions
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas and much is lost through leaks in piped systems. Reporting leaks and avoiding waste reduces environmental harm without restricting women's choice of analgesia (SPM 5.10, 5.13.3).

n.0: Waiting for a routine check leaves a known leak releasing gas.
n.2: Leaving supplies connected in empty rooms increases waste and does not deal with the leak.
n.3: Women's choice of pain relief should not be restricted; the aim is to cut waste, not to deny Entonox.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A health visitor phones to ask a community midwife for the discharge summary of a woman who has moved home. The midwife is on a home visit. What is the most appropriate way to share the information?
o: By reading the summary aloud over the phone in the woman's home
By asking the woman to take her notes to the health visitor
Through the approved secure electronic record or secure email system
By sending a photo of the notes from her personal phone
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Information should be shared using approved, secure digital systems that protect confidentiality and create an audit trail (SPM 5.12; Code 5.1 and 10).

n.0: Reading confidential information aloud in another person's home risks disclosure to others.
n.1: Relying on the woman delays information the health visitor needs and does not use the professional route.
n.3: Personal devices and messaging are not approved routes and risk a data breach.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Several women of Black African origin tell a community midwife that they felt their concerns were dismissed during labour. What is the most effective way for the midwife to advocate for change?
o: Advise each of the women to make an individual complaint to the trust
Share the stories on social media to raise public awareness of racism
Apologise to each woman and explain that the staff on duty were very busy
Gather the feedback, raise it through governance and work with the local MNVP
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Advocating for change (SPM 5.13.4) means collecting evidence and raising it through the right channels, co-producing improvements with service users such as the Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnership (MNVP). MBRRACE-UK shows Black women have nearly three times the maternal mortality of White women, so these concerns are a safety issue.

n.0: Complaints are their right, but leaving it to women alone puts the burden on them and misses system learning.
n.1: Social media is not an appropriate route and may breach confidentiality.
n.2: Explaining it away as busyness fails to recognise a pattern that needs action.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: After a successful PDSA cycle reduced triage delays, the team leader wants the improvement to last when the project ends. Which step is most likely to sustain the change?
o: Thank the team and close the project now that the target has been reached
Build the new process into the guideline, training and data monitoring
Rely on the project champion to remind staff about the new process
Repeat the original baseline audit in two years to check progress
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Sustaining improvement means embedding the change in standard processes (guidelines, induction, training) and continuing to monitor data so any slippage is noticed (SPM 5.11, 5.13.3).

n.0: Closing the project without embedding the change risks a return to old habits.
n.2: Dependence on one person is fragile; the process must not rely on an individual.
n.3: Waiting two years leaves any slippage unnoticed for too long.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Immediately after a cord prolapse that ended in a category 1 caesarean and a healthy baby, the coordinator gathers the team for a ten-minute 'hot debrief'. What is the main purpose of this debrief?
o: To agree a single account of events to give to the investigators
To check on staff wellbeing and capture learning while it is fresh
To decide which team member should complete the incident report form
To identify which team member was responsible for the delay
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: A hot debrief is a short, supportive team reflection soon after an event. It checks on staff wellbeing, captures what went well and what could improve, and flags issues for follow-up (SPM 5.9, 5.13.1).

n.0: Agreeing a single account undermines honest individual reporting.
n.2: Allocating paperwork is not the purpose of a debrief.
n.3: Debriefs are supportive and system-focused, not about blaming individuals.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Zainab, 30, is 36 weeks pregnant and asks her midwife whether a herbal tea her family recommends will help start labour. The midwife finds no good-quality evidence about its safety or effect in pregnancy. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Avoid the topic and advise her to ask her GP at her next visit
Tell her it is safe to try because it is a natural plant-based product
Explain there is no reliable evidence, discuss possible risks and record it
Tell her it will not work, as no published research supports its use
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Acting safely without good-quality evidence means being honest about uncertainty, sharing what is known about possible risks, supporting her informed decision and documenting it (SPM 5.7; Code 6.1 and 6.2).

n.0: Deflecting to the GP leaves her without the information she asked for.
n.1: 'Natural' does not mean safe; claiming safety is not supported by evidence.
n.3: Absence of evidence is not proof of no effect; the honest answer is that it is unknown.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A midwife is caring for a woman with a rare genetic condition. There is no national guideline and the local policy does not mention it. The woman is now in early labour. What is the safest approach?
o: Transfer her care to the consultant and stop providing midwifery care
Follow the standard low-risk pathway until a relevant guideline can be found
Delay any decisions until a specialist can see her the next working day
Seek senior and multidisciplinary advice, agree a plan with her and record why
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: When evidence or guidance is absent, safe practice means drawing on senior and multidisciplinary expertise, involving the woman in planning, and recording the reasoning (SPM 5.7, 5.13.1; Code 13.2 make a timely referral to another practitioner and 13.3 ask for help with anything beyond your competence).

n.0: Consultant involvement is appropriate, but the midwife continues to provide midwifery care alongside.
n.1: Treating a rare condition as low risk without advice may miss specific risks.
n.2: She is in labour now; waiting until the next working day is unsafe.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Holly is writing a reflective account using Gibbs' reflective cycle about a difficult conversation with a bereaved family. She has described the event, explored her feelings and evaluated what was good and bad. Which stage comes next?
o: Action plan
Analysis
Description
Conclusion
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Gibbs' cycle runs: description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan. After evaluation comes analysis, making sense of the situation and drawing on theory or evidence (SPM 5.13.1).

n.0: The action plan is the final stage, after the conclusion.
n.2: Description is the first stage, which Holly has already completed.
n.3: The conclusion follows analysis.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Lydia, a midwife, is writing a reflective account for revalidation about care she gave to a woman with a postpartum haemorrhage. What must she make sure of when writing it?
o: It names the colleagues involved so that the reflection is complete
It includes the woman's hospital number so the case can be checked
It is signed by the woman to confirm the account is accurate
It contains no information that could identify the woman or colleagues
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: NMC revalidation guidance requires reflective accounts to be anonymised, with no information that could identify any person, in line with Code 5 (respect privacy and confidentiality).

n.0: Naming colleagues identifies them and is not required.
n.1: A hospital number is identifiable and breaches confidentiality.
n.2: Reflective accounts are the midwife's own reflection; the woman does not sign them.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A coordinator faces a sudden surge: three women arrive in labour, one with bleeding, while a fourth needs transfer to theatre. Which approach best reflects structured problem solving in a stressful situation?
o: Assess each woman quickly, prioritise by risk, allocate staff and review often
Deal with the women in the order they arrived to be fair to everyone
Ask each midwife to manage whichever woman they meet first
Focus on the theatre transfer first and assess the new arrivals afterwards
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Structured problem solving in pressured situations means assessing, prioritising by risk (the woman who is bleeding needs immediate assessment), allocating roles, communicating the plan and reviewing as things change (SPM 5.13.1, 5.13.6).

n.1: Order of arrival ignores clinical urgency and risks delaying care for the woman who is bleeding.
n.2: Uncoordinated allocation loses oversight and may leave the highest-risk woman without the right skills.
n.3: Fixing on one task risks missing deterioration in the new arrivals.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A senior colleague tells Sara that low-risk women in established labour must have nil by mouth "because that's what we've always done here". Sara is unsure. What should she do?
o: Check current guidance and discuss it with the colleague and the coordinator
Follow the colleague's practice, as she has more experience on the unit
Wait for the next guideline update before raising it with anyone
Disregard the instruction and offer women food without discussing it
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Practice should be based on current evidence. NICE NG235 1.8.18 advises that women may eat a light diet in established labour unless they have had opioids or develop risk factors. Checking guidance and discussing it openly is safe, team-based problem solving (SPM 5.7, 5.9).

n.1: Experience alone does not justify practice that conflicts with current guidance.
n.2: Delaying leaves women receiving care that is out of step with current guidance.
n.3: Acting unilaterally without discussion undermines teamwork and does not change the unit's practice.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A team holds a multidisciplinary meeting each month where staff reflect on recent cases, including those that went well, and agree changes to practice. Which statement best describes the value of this activity?
o: Shared reflection helps the whole team learn and improve the service
It replaces the need to report incidents through the formal system
It is mainly a way to identify staff who need performance management
It satisfies mandatory training requirements for every attendee
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Team reflection activities promote shared learning and improvements in practice and services (SPM 5.9). They complement, not replace, formal incident reporting.

n.1: Incidents must still be reported through the formal system.
n.2: The purpose is learning and improvement, not performance management.
n.3: Reflective meetings are not a substitute for mandatory training.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Two weeks after caring for a woman whose baby was stillborn, Kemi, a midwife, has become withdrawn, tearful at handover and is calling in sick more often. Her colleague Amy notices. What is the most appropriate action for Amy?
o: Suggest Kemi swaps to night shifts so she is under less scrutiny
Speak to Kemi privately, listen, and encourage her to access staff support
Report Kemi's sickness pattern to the ward manager for formal review
Avoid mentioning it so that Kemi does not feel singled out
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SPM 5.14 requires midwives to recognise signs of vulnerability in colleagues and act to minimise risks to their health and wellbeing. A private, compassionate conversation and signposting to support (such as the Professional Midwifery Advocate, occupational health or employee assistance) is the right first step.

n.0: Changing shifts does not address her distress and may increase isolation.
n.2: A formal sickness review is not the first response to a colleague showing distress after a traumatic event.
n.3: Ignoring signs of distress leaves Kemi without support and may risk her health and practice.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: After a difficult shift, Freya would like confidential, restorative support to reflect on her experiences. Under the A-EQUIP model in England, who provides restorative clinical supervision for midwives?
o: The NMC fitness to practise team
Her named practice assessor
A Supervisor of Midwives (SoM)
A Professional Midwifery Advocate
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: A-EQUIP (advocating and educating for quality improvement), published by NHS England in 2017, replaced statutory supervision of midwives. Professional Midwifery Advocates deliver restorative clinical supervision to support midwives' wellbeing and practice.

n.0: The NMC regulates registrants; it does not provide restorative supervision.
n.1: Practice assessors assess students under the SSSA; they do not supervise qualified midwives.
n.2: Statutory supervision and the Supervisor of Midwives role were removed in 2017.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Nadia, a midwife, has been diagnosed with depression. She is struggling to concentrate and worries this may affect her clinical decisions. What does the NMC Code require of her?
o: Self-refer to the NMC for a fitness to practise investigation
Tell someone in authority promptly and act to address the concern
Continue working and see whether her concentration improves
Keep her diagnosis private, because health information is confidential
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Code 16.3: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity if you experience problems that may prevent you working within the Code, taking prompt action to tackle the causes. SPM 5.14 covers recognising vulnerability in oneself.

n.0: A health condition managed with support does not require self-referral to the NMC.
n.2: Waiting to see risks unsafe decisions while she is struggling.
n.3: Her diagnosis is confidential, but the effect on her practice must be raised so that safe adjustments can be made.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Tom, a community midwife, regularly works through his lunch break and stays late to finish notes. He feels exhausted and short-tempered at home. Which action best reflects compassionate self-care?
o: Carry on as he is, as the workload should settle in a few weeks
Take work notes home to finish them in the evenings
Discuss workload with his manager and protect regular breaks
Reduce the time spent at each postnatal visit to catch up
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SPM 5.15 requires midwives to manage the personal and emotional challenges of work and workload and incorporate compassionate self-care. Raising workload concerns and taking breaks reduces burnout risk and protects safety.

n.0: Ignoring signs of exhaustion increases the risk of burnout and errors.
n.1: Taking notes home risks confidentiality breaches and extends working hours further.
n.3: Cutting visit time reduces quality of care and does not solve the workload problem.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A newly qualified midwife says she feels she is "not good enough" after a busy shift. Her preceptor wants to use a strength-based approach. Which response best fits?
o: "You'll toughen up once you've worked here for a year."
"Everyone feels like that, so try not to worry about it."
"Let's list all the mistakes you made today so you can avoid them."
"Let's look at what you handled well today and how you can build on it."
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Strength-based approaches (SPM 5.13.5) recognise and build on what the person does well, supporting confidence and resilience while still planning development.

n.0: Telling her to toughen up is unsupportive and ignores her wellbeing.
n.1: Dismissing her feelings does not support her or build on her strengths.
n.2: Focusing on mistakes alone is deficit-based and may lower confidence further.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A maternity unit announces that community and hospital teams will be restructured in three months. Several midwives feel anxious and uncertain. Which response by a midwife best manages the personal challenges of this change?
o: Seek accurate information, join the consultation and use support
Share worries about the change on a public social media group
Avoid the consultation meetings so that the change causes her less stress
Hand in her notice before the details of the restructure are known
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: SPM 5.15 asks midwives to manage the challenges of uncertainty and change. Engaging with accurate information and consultation, and using support, helps manage anxiety and lets her influence the change.

n.1: Public posting may breach Code 20.10 and does not help resolve concerns.
n.2: Avoidance increases uncertainty and removes her voice from the process.
n.3: Resigning before knowing the details is a premature response to uncertainty.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: After a maternal collapse on the labour ward, the woman survived but several staff are visibly shaken. Two days later the ward manager arranges a facilitated team session. What is the main aim of this session?
o: To support staff wellbeing and help the team process the event
To ask staff to write statements for the coroner
To replace the formal learning response with an informal one
To decide which staff members should be moved off the labour ward
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Facilitated team sessions after traumatic events support staff wellbeing, help people make sense of what happened and reduce the risk of lasting psychological harm, while learning continues through formal processes (SPM 5.14, 5.15).

n.1: The woman survived; coroner statements are not relevant here.
n.2: Team support sessions do not replace formal learning responses.
n.3: Moving staff is not the aim and may feel punitive.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Grace, a senior midwife, notices she has become cynical about women's concerns, feels emotionally drained most days and dreads coming to work. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Keep her feelings to herself so colleagues are not burdened
Wait until her annual appraisal to mention how she feels
Take on extra shifts to keep busy and distract herself
Recognise these as signs of burnout and seek support early
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Emotional exhaustion, cynicism and dread are recognised signs of burnout. SPM 5.14 asks midwives to recognise vulnerability in themselves and act to minimise risks; seeking support early (manager, PMA, occupational health) protects her wellbeing and women's care.

n.0: Withholding her feelings delays support and risks her health and practice.
n.1: Waiting for appraisal delays help that is needed now.
n.2: Extra shifts increase workload and worsen exhaustion.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: On a busy maternity triage unit, Bea notices that a woman reporting reduced fetal movements has waited 45 minutes before being seen by a midwife. Under NICE NG4, what does this delay represent and what should Bea do?
o: An expected delay at busy times; record it in the notes
A complaint; give the woman details of the complaints process
A midwifery red flag event; notify the midwife in charge
A serious incident; report it directly to the chief nurse
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: NICE NG4 box 3: a delay of 30 minutes or more between presentation and triage is a midwifery red flag event. When a red flag occurs, the midwife in charge should be notified to decide whether staffing is the cause and what action is needed.

n.0: NG4 treats this delay as a warning sign about staffing, not an acceptable norm.
n.1: The woman may complain, but the immediate step is to notify the midwife in charge.
n.3: A triage delay without harm is not a serious incident; NG4 classes it as a red flag event for the midwife in charge.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Jess is caring for a woman in established labour when the coordinator asks her to also take over care of a second woman in established labour in the next room, as no other midwife is free. Which statement is most accurate?
o: This is a matter for the coordinator, so Jess has no duty to raise a concern
This is acceptable when both women are low risk and their labours are progressing normally
This is acceptable if a maternity support worker stays with one of the women
This is a red flag event; she should raise it with the coordinator for escalation
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: NICE NG235 recommends one-to-one care in established labour, and NG4 box 3 lists any occasion when one midwife cannot provide continuous one-to-one care in established labour as a red flag. Code 16.1 and 16.2 require raising concerns about safety and being asked to practise beyond safe limits.

n.0: Every registrant has a duty under Code 16 to raise concerns; it is not left to the coordinator alone.
n.1: Low risk does not remove the standard of one-to-one midwifery care in established labour.
n.2: A support worker cannot replace the midwife in providing one-to-one care in established labour.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Marta gave birth 90 minutes ago and is still waiting for her second-degree tear to be sutured because both midwives on the birth centre are busy. According to NICE NG4, what is the significance of this?
o: This becomes a red flag event once the delay goes beyond 2 hours
A delay of 60 minutes or more in suturing is a red flag event
This is a red flag if the woman makes a complaint about it
Suturing can safely wait up to 4 hours, so no action is needed
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: NG4 box 3 gives 'missed or delayed care (for example, delay of 60 minutes or more in washing and suturing)' as a midwifery red flag event, to be reported to the midwife in charge.

n.0: Two hours relates to the delay between admission for induction and beginning the process.
n.2: Red flags are about the delay itself, not whether a complaint is made.
n.3: NG4 uses 60 minutes as the example threshold for delayed washing and suturing.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Leanne is the midwife in charge of a maternity unit. Three midwifery red flag events have been reported in the past hour. What is her responsibility under NICE NG4?
o: Decide whether staffing is the cause and what action is needed
Record the events and review them at the monthly governance meeting
Close the unit to all admissions until the next shift starts
Ask the staff who reported them to resolve the issues themselves
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: NG4 box 3: when a red flag event occurs, the midwife in charge should be notified and should determine whether midwifery staffing is the cause and the action needed, such as redeploying staff or escalating per the staffing policy.

n.1: Monthly review is part of monitoring, but immediate assessment and action are needed now.
n.2: Closure may be one option under escalation policy, but it is not automatic and other actions are considered first.
n.3: The midwife in charge holds responsibility for assessing staffing and acting on red flags.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: At the start of a night shift, the labour ward coordinator is also allocated a woman in labour because two midwives have called in sick. Following the Ockenden findings, why is this a concern?
o: The coordinator role is held by an obstetrician during the night
A coordinator with a caseload cannot readily support staff and oversee care
Coordinators are not trained to care for women who are in established labour
It breaches the rule that coordinators must work day shifts
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Ockenden found the labour ward coordinator often lacked supernumerary status and had their own caseload, preventing them from being accessible to junior staff for advice, care planning and support. Trusts must recognise the coordinator as a specialist role (IEA 2).

n.0: The labour ward coordinator is a senior midwife role on all shifts.
n.2: Coordinators are experienced midwives able to provide care; the issue is loss of oversight.
n.3: No such rule exists; the issue is supernumerary status, not shift pattern.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: On a day shift the maternity unit falls below its agreed minimum midwifery staffing level, and redeployment from the community has not filled the gap. Following Ockenden, what should happen next?
o: Ask midwives to skip their breaks until the shift is over
Escalate under the staffing policy to senior managers and on-call leaders
Ask student midwives to cover the shortfall under indirect supervision
Continue as normal, as staffing usually improves in the afternoon
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Ockenden IEA 2 (safe staffing): trusts must maintain a clear escalation and mitigation policy when staffing falls below minimum levels, escalating to senior management, obstetric leads, the chief nurse, medical director and others. SPM 5.5 links safe staffing with safety and quality of care.

n.0: Removing breaks increases fatigue and error; it is not a mitigation strategy.
n.2: Students are supernumerary learners and cannot be counted in staffing numbers.
n.3: Hoping staffing improves leaves women at risk and ignores the escalation policy.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Ana is a newly qualified midwife in her second week of preceptorship. The coordinator allocates her a woman with severe pre-eclampsia on a magnesium sulfate infusion and no experienced midwife is assigned to support her. What is the most appropriate response from Ana?
o: Explain her experience to the coordinator and ask for support or reallocation
Accept the allocation and ask the obstetric registrar to check on her hourly
Accept the allocation and look up the magnesium protocol as she goes
Refuse to work the shift until a different allocation is offered
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Skill mix should match the acuity of the women. Code 13 (recognise and work within the limits of competence) and 16.2 (raise concerns if asked to practise beyond your role, experience and training) apply. Ockenden supports protected preceptorship for newly qualified midwives.

n.1: Medical checks do not replace experienced midwifery oversight of a high-acuity woman.
n.2: Learning a high-risk protocol while providing care without support puts the woman at risk.
n.3: Refusing to work at all abandons her duty of care; the right step is to raise the concern and seek support.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A trust has paused its midwifery continuity of carer teams because it cannot staff them safely. A woman asks why her named midwife will not be at her birth. Which explanation is accurate?
o: Continuity of carer now covers antenatal and postnatal care but not labour
The national target date for full continuity of carer requires a short pause
Continuity of carer has been stopped nationally following the final Ockenden report
Trusts that cannot staff it safely were told to suspend it and transfer women safely
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: NHS England's letter of 21 September 2022 removed the national target date for MCoC and said trusts unable to meet safe staffing must immediately suspend existing MCoC provision and transfer women safely; it is rolled out where safe staffing allows (SPM 5.5).

n.0: Midwifery continuity of carer spans pregnancy, labour and the postnatal period; labour has not been removed from the model.
n.1: The national target date was removed in September 2022.
n.2: MCoC has not been banned; it continues where safe staffing allows.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: During a postpartum haemorrhage in a birth room, the coordinating midwife shouts "Can someone get the registrar?" Three staff are in the room; two minutes later no one has called. Which human factors problem does this illustrate, and what would have prevented it?
o: Diffusion of responsibility; naming one person to act and confirm back
Fatigue; rotating staff out of the birth room every 30 minutes
Fixation error; asking everyone to stop and recheck the blood loss
Normalisation of deviance; reporting the delay on an incident form
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: A request addressed to no one can leave everyone assuming someone else has acted. Directed, closed-loop communication (naming the person, giving a clear task, and having it read back) is a core human factors strategy in emergencies (SPM 5.4, 5.13.2).

n.1: Nothing suggests fatigue; the problem was how the request was made.
n.2: Fixation error is focusing on one problem while missing others; the failure here was an unassigned task.
n.3: Normalisation of deviance is gradual acceptance of unsafe practice; an incident report afterwards would not have prevented the delay.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: Lena, the labour ward coordinator, holds a five-minute safety huddle with the midwives, obstetricians and anaesthetist at the start of each shift. A new midwife asks what the main purpose of the huddle is. Which answer is most accurate?
o: To record staff attendance for mandatory training compliance
To allocate blame for any problems from the previous shift
To replace individual handovers between midwives for each woman
To build a shared picture of current risks, workload and priorities
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Safety huddles support shared situational awareness: the whole multidisciplinary team agrees which women are highest risk, where pressures lie and who to escalate to. This reflects human factors and interdisciplinary working (SPM 5.4, 5.8).

n.0: Training compliance is recorded through training systems, not huddles.
n.1: Huddles look forward to risks and plans; they are not for blaming individuals.
n.2: Huddles supplement, not replace, structured handover of each woman's care.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: A maternity unit's multidisciplinary emergency skills training is attended by midwives on one day and by obstetricians and anaesthetists on another. Following the Ockenden report, what change should the unit make?
o: Keep separate sessions so each profession can focus on its own role
Hold joint sessions so that staff who work together train together
Replace face-to-face drills with an online module for all staff
Train the labour ward coordinators and ask them to cascade it
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Ockenden immediate and essential action 7 (multidisciplinary training): staff who work together must train together, with regular joint multidisciplinary training. SPM 5.8 recognises why interdisciplinary learning matters.

n.0: Separate sessions miss the teamworking and communication skills that joint training develops.
n.2: Online modules cannot rehearse team responses to emergencies in the way practical drills do.
n.3: Cascading through coordinators does not give every team member joint practice.

Working With Others: Safety & Quality.q: On a busy postnatal ward, ampoules of two different intravenous medicines with similar packaging are stored next to each other. A midwife picks up the wrong one but notices before giving it. From a human factors perspective, what is the most effective response?
o: Remind the midwife to concentrate harder when checking her medicines
Report the near miss so the storage can be redesigned to separate them
Add a note to the ward diary asking staff to take more care
Ask the midwife to complete a medicines competency reassessment
Working With Others: Safety & Quality.w: Human factors focuses on designing systems that make errors less likely, such as separating look-alike products, rather than relying on vigilance alone. Reporting near misses allows learning before harm occurs (SPM 5.2, 5.4).

n.0: Exhorting individuals to try harder does not change the system that made the error likely.
n.2: A diary note relies on memory and vigilance and does not remove the hazard.
n.3: Retraining one person leaves the hazard in place for every other member of staff.

Scholar & Leader.q: A trial of a new antenatal education programme reports the risk of caesarean birth in the intervention group compared with usual care as a relative risk of 0.80 (95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.98). Sophie, a student midwife, asks her practice supervisor how to interpret this. Which explanation is correct?
o: An 80% relative reduction that is statistically significant at the 5% level
A 20% relative reduction that is statistically significant at the 5% level
A 20% relative reduction that is not statistically significant
A 20% relative increase that is statistically significant at the 5% level
Scholar & Leader.w: A relative risk of 0.80 means the risk is 80% of the comparison risk, a 20% relative reduction (1 minus 0.80). The 95% confidence interval (0.65 to 0.98) lies entirely below 1.0, the line of no effect, so the result is statistically significant at the 5% level.

n.0: An RR of 0.80 is a 20% reduction, not 80%; an 80% reduction would be an RR of 0.20.
n.2: The interval does not include 1.0 (its upper limit is 0.98), so the result is statistically significant.
n.3: A relative risk below 1.0 shows a reduction in risk, not an increase.

Scholar & Leader.q: Fatima appraises a trial of 600 women comparing two methods of fetal heart monitoring across three hospitals. The primary outcome was validated and prespecified, and follow-up was 98%. Women were allocated by date of admission: even dates to method A, odd dates to method B. What is the main weakness in this trial?
o: The sample is too small to detect any difference in outcome
The primary outcome was chosen after the data were analysed
Follow-up was too incomplete to trust the results
Staff could predict allocation, introducing selection bias
Scholar & Leader.w: Allocating by date is quasi-randomisation: recruiting staff can know which group the next woman will enter and may consciously or unconsciously decide whom to enrol, causing selection bias. Concealed random allocation is a key question in appraisal checklists such as CASP for RCTs.

n.0: Nothing in the stem suggests the trial was underpowered; 600 women across three sites is a substantial sample, and the flaw described is in allocation.
n.1: The stem states the primary outcome was prespecified, so selective outcome reporting is not the problem.
n.2: Follow-up was 98%, which is high and not a meaningful source of attrition bias.

Scholar & Leader.q: Hannah, a labour ward midwife, reads a small single-centre study suggesting a new upright birthing position reduces assisted births. She is keen to start using it with every woman she cares for from her next shift. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Appraise the study and weigh it against systematic reviews and guidance
Start offering the position to all women she cares for and record the outcomes
Email the study to all colleagues and recommend they adopt the position
Ask the next woman in labour whether she would like to try the new position
Scholar & Leader.w: SPM 5.16 requires midwives to use research to inform decisions and develop practice, and Code 6.1 requires advice to be evidence-based. One small single-centre study should first be appraised for bias and weighed against the wider body of evidence (systematic reviews, NICE guidance) before any change is proposed through local governance.

n.1: Changing practice for all women on the basis of one unappraised small study bypasses appraisal and governance, and collecting outcomes informally is not a substitute.
n.2: Recommending adoption to colleagues spreads an unappraised finding before its quality and fit with wider evidence are known.
n.3: Offering the position before appraisal means the information given to the woman is not yet evidence-based, contrary to Code 6.1.

Scholar & Leader.q: In a trial, 10% of women given usual care developed an obstetric anal sphincter injury, compared with 6% of women given a perineal protection bundle. Zainab, a practice development midwife, wants to explain the result to colleagues in terms of how many women need the bundle to prevent one injury. What is the number needed to treat?
Scholar & Leader.w: Absolute risk reduction = 10% minus 6% = 4% (0.04). Number needed to treat = 1 / ARR = 1 / 0.04 = 25 women given the bundle to prevent one injury. Interpreting trial data in this way is part of SPM 1.4.

n.0: 4 is the absolute risk reduction expressed as a percentage, not the number needed to treat.
n.2: 17 is 1 divided by 0.06, which uses the intervention group risk instead of the difference between groups.
n.3: 40 is the relative risk reduction as a percentage (4 divided by 10), not the NNT.

Scholar & Leader.q: Leila, a public health midwife, wants to find out what proportion of women booked in the last 6 months were offered a carbon monoxide test at booking, and to compare this with the NICE NG209 recommendation that every woman is offered one. What type of project is this?
o: Clinical audit
Health surveillance
Research
Service evaluation
Scholar & Leader.w: The HRA defining research table describes clinical audit as answering 'Does this service reach a predetermined, recognised or pre-established standard?' and measuring against a standard. Leila is measuring current practice against the NG209 standard (CO test offered at booking).

n.1: Health surveillance detects and manages threats to population health such as outbreaks, not compliance with a care standard.
n.2: Research aims to generate or test a hypothesis and produce generalisable new knowledge; Leila is checking local practice against an existing standard.
n.3: Service evaluation measures current service without reference to a standard ('What standard does this service achieve?'), whereas Leila has a defined standard.

Scholar & Leader.q: A new midwife-led postnatal drop-in clinic opened 3 months ago. Joanne, the team leader, plans to give a short questionnaire to women attending, asking how satisfied they are and what could be better. No external standard exists for the clinic. What type of project is this?
o: Research
Service evaluation
Health surveillance
Clinical audit
Scholar & Leader.w: Service evaluation is designed to judge current care, asking 'What standard does this service achieve?', usually by asking those receiving the service, without reference to a set standard (HRA defining research table). It does not require NHS REC review.

n.0: Joanne is not testing a hypothesis or aiming for generalisable knowledge; she is judging a local service.
n.2: Health surveillance monitors threats to population health, not satisfaction with a local clinic.
n.3: Audit measures practice against a predetermined standard, and the stem states no such standard exists for the clinic.

Scholar & Leader.q: Megan, a labour ward midwife, has repeated an audit of documentation of the third stage of labour against the trust standard. Compliance was 62% last year. Since then, a new documentation sticker and teaching sessions were introduced. In which stage of the audit cycle is Megan now working?
o: Selecting the standard against which practice is measured
Collecting baseline data on current practice
Re-audit to measure whether the changes have improved practice
Comparing baseline data with the standard for the first time
Scholar & Leader.w: The audit cycle runs: select a standard, measure current practice, compare with the standard, implement change, then re-audit to see whether practice has improved, closing the loop. Megan has already introduced changes after a baseline audit, so this is the re-audit (SPM 5.17).

n.0: The standard was already chosen before last year's audit.
n.1: Baseline data (62%) were collected last year; this is the repeat measurement.
n.3: The first comparison with the standard produced the 62% figure that led to the changes.

Scholar & Leader.q: A practice development team trials a new handover tool on one postnatal ward for a single week. At the end of the week they compare missed-observation rates with what they predicted, before deciding whether to adapt or spread the tool. In the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle, which stage is the comparison?
o: Do
Plan
Study
Act
Scholar & Leader.w: In PDSA, Plan sets out the change and predictions, Do carries out the small test, Study analyses the data and compares them with the predictions, and Act decides whether to adopt, adapt or abandon the change before the next cycle (NHS England quality improvement guidance).

n.0: Do is running the test on the ward for the week and collecting the data.
n.1: Plan is when the change is designed and predictions are made, before the test.
n.3: Act follows the comparison and is the decision to adopt, adapt or abandon.

Scholar & Leader.q: Chloe, a specialist diabetes midwife, wants to interview women with gestational diabetes about cultural beliefs around diet, aiming to develop a theory that could be transferred to other maternity services. She plans to start next month. Which governance step is most appropriate before she begins?
o: Register it as a service evaluation with the maternity governance lead
Register it with the clinical audit department and start next month
Start interviews once women give verbal consent, as there is no intervention
Treat it as research and apply for HRA and NHS ethics committee approval
Scholar & Leader.w: Chloe aims to generate new, transferable knowledge, which meets the UK Policy Framework definition of research (para 3.1), including non-interventional qualitative research. Research normally requires NHS REC review, arranged through HRA approval; audit and service evaluation do not (HRA defining research table).

n.0: Service evaluation judges a local service without seeking transferable findings; Chloe's aim takes it into research.
n.1: It is not an audit: there is no standard being measured, and the purpose is new transferable knowledge.
n.2: Non-interventional research is still research under the policy framework; the absence of an intervention does not remove the need for ethical review and written informed consent processes.

Scholar & Leader.q: Rosa, 31, is 20 weeks pregnant and has been invited to join a randomised trial of an iron supplement. She tells her midwife she is worried that saying no will mean she is treated differently at the clinic. Which response by the midwife is best?
o: 'If you decline, you will be booked into the consultant clinic instead.'
'Your partner will also need to agree because the baby is involved.'
'You can decline, or withdraw later, and your care will not change.'
'You need to give your answer today so that the trial can include you.'
Scholar & Leader.w: Valid consent to research must be voluntary and informed; participants can decline or withdraw at any time without their standard care being affected (UK Policy Framework for Health and Social Care Research; Code 4.2 make sure you get properly informed consent). A pregnant woman with capacity gives her own consent.

n.0: Linking refusal to a change in her care pathway is coercive and has no clinical basis.
n.1: A pregnant woman with capacity consents for herself; the partner's agreement is not a legal requirement for her participation.
n.3: Pressure to decide on the spot undermines voluntary consent; she should have time to consider the information.

Scholar & Leader.q: The maternity unit plans to redesign its antenatal clinic appointment system after complaints about long waits. Ellie, the band 7 midwife leading the project, wants women's views to shape the new design from the start. What is the most appropriate way to achieve this?
o: Introduce the new system and then invite women to complain if needed
Ask the clinical director to approve a design based on staff rotas
Survey the clinic midwives and receptionists about the best design
Co-produce it with the local Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnership
Scholar & Leader.w: SPM 5.17 highlights midwives' contribution to practice and policy through engagement and consultation. Maternity and Neonatal Voices Partnerships bring service users, staff and commissioners together to co-produce maternity services, so women's views shape the design from the outset.

n.0: Seeking views after implementation is reactive and does not let women shape the design from the start.
n.1: A design based on rotas and approved by the clinical director leaves out women's experience altogether.
n.2: A staff survey gathers useful views but does not involve the women who use the service.

Scholar & Leader.q: Tess, a band 6 midwife, completes an audit showing that 70% of women with a postpartum haemorrhage had a documented quantitative blood loss measurement against a trust standard of 95%. She presents the findings at the governance meeting. What is the most appropriate next step?
