o: Publish the result in a journal as evidence of poor national practice
Agree an action plan to improve practice and set a date for re-audit
Lower the trust standard to 70% to reflect what is achievable
Repeat the same audit next month to confirm the figure
Scholar & Leader.w: After comparing practice with the standard, the audit cycle moves to implementing change through an agreed action plan and then re-auditing to close the loop. Audit findings are local and are not generalisable research (HRA defining research table).

n.0: A local audit measures practice in one service against a local standard; it does not produce generalisable evidence about national practice.
n.2: Lowering the standard to match performance defeats the purpose of audit, which is to raise practice to the standard.
n.3: Repeating the audit without any change will show the same gap; change must be made before re-auditing.

Scholar & Leader.q: Naomi, a midwife on a busy postnatal ward, is working with Carol, a maternity support worker who has been trained and assessed as competent in maternal observations. Which task is most appropriate for Naomi to delegate to Carol?
o: Giving the first dose of intravenous antibiotics to a woman with a fever
Assessing a perineal wound and deciding whether the woman can go home
Carrying out the newborn and infant physical examination before discharge
Recording 4-hourly observations for a well woman after a straightforward birth
Scholar & Leader.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence, making sure they understand the instructions. Routine observations for a well woman are within Carol's assessed competence; assessment, clinical decision-making and IV medicines stay with registered practitioners.

n.0: Administering IV antibiotics is a registered practitioner's task and outside an MSW's scope.
n.1: Assessing a wound and making a discharge decision require a registered midwife's clinical judgement.
n.2: The newborn and infant physical examination is carried out by a trained registered practitioner, not an MSW.

Scholar & Leader.q: Carol, a maternity support worker, has recorded observations for Mrs Ahmed, who is 6 hours after a caesarean birth, as delegated by the midwife, Naomi. Carol tells Naomi the observations are done. What should Naomi do next?
o: Ask another support worker to check Carol's figures before the next round
Review the recorded observations and confirm they meet the required standard
Note in the handover that the observations were completed by Carol
Countersign the chart so that the record is complete for the shift
Scholar & Leader.w: Code 11.3: confirm that the outcome of any task you have delegated meets the required standard. Naomi remains accountable for the decision to delegate and must review the observations herself so she can act on any abnormal findings.

n.0: Passing the check to another support worker does not meet Naomi's own duty under Code 11.3.
n.2: Recording who did the task in handover does not check the result or act on it.
n.3: Countersigning without reviewing the values does not confirm the outcome of the task and could miss deterioration.

Scholar & Leader.q: Dana is the labour ward coordinator. Four requests arrive at the same moment. Which should she attend to first?
o: A woman at 38 weeks with a mild headache whose blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg
A postnatal woman 2 hours after birth asking for her prescribed paracetamol
A woman in established labour whose fetal heart rate has been 85 bpm for 4 minutes
A woman booked for elective caesarean tomorrow who needs her bloods taken
Scholar & Leader.w: SPM 5.19 requires safe prioritising. A prolonged fetal bradycardia lasting several minutes is an obstetric emergency needing immediate assessment and escalation; Code 25.1 asks leaders to identify priorities and deal with risk.

n.0: A mild headache with normal blood pressure needs review, but a prolonged fetal bradycardia is the more urgent threat.
n.1: Analgesia is important but can follow within minutes without risk to life.
n.3: Pre-operative bloods for tomorrow are routine and can be planned later in the shift.

Scholar & Leader.q: Yasmin, a band 7 midwife, overhears a colleague telling a woman in early labour, in front of others, that she is 'making a fuss' about her contractions. As a leader on the unit, what is the most appropriate response?
o: Support the woman, then speak privately with the colleague
Report the colleague directly to the NMC for unprofessional conduct
Take over the woman's care and avoid working with the colleague in future
Raise the issue with the whole team at next month's meeting
Scholar & Leader.w: SPM 5.20 requires positive leadership and role modelling; Code 1.1 requires kindness and respect, and Code 9.1 requires honest, constructive feedback to colleagues. Yasmin first ensures the woman is supported, then addresses the behaviour privately and promptly.

n.1: A single lapse is first addressed locally through feedback and support; an immediate NMC referral is disproportionate on these facts.
n.2: Avoiding the colleague does not address the behaviour or help the colleague improve.
n.3: Waiting a month for a team meeting leaves the woman unsupported now and denies the colleague timely, private feedback.

Scholar & Leader.q: Lucy is coordinating the birth centre on a night shift. Two midwives have called in sick, leaving three women in established labour with two midwives. No bank staff are available. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask the women's birth partners to call a midwife when contractions change
Escalate to the manager on call under the staffing escalation policy
Continue to manage the shift and complete an incident report in the morning
Ask the two student midwives on shift to care for the third woman
Scholar & Leader.w: Code 25.1 requires leaders to identify priorities, manage staff and resources effectively and deal with risk; Code 16.1 requires raising and escalating concerns about safety, and standard 16 to act without delay. Escalating through the staffing policy allows the manager on call to redeploy staff or divert admissions.

n.0: Relying on birth partners to monitor labour transfers a professional responsibility to people without training.
n.2: Waiting until morning delays action while women in labour are receiving unsafe staffing levels.
n.3: Students are supernumerary and must be supervised; they cannot replace a registered midwife to make up numbers.

Scholar & Leader.q: Ruth, a midwife, asks Jen, a maternity support worker, to carry out a heel-prick blood glucose test on a baby at risk of hypoglycaemia. Jen says she has not yet been trained or assessed in this test. What is Ruth's most appropriate action?
o: Ask the baby's mother to help Jen carry out the test
Carry out the test herself and arrange for Jen to receive training
Talk Jen through the steps so she can carry out the test now
Ask Jen to watch a training video before doing the test
Scholar & Leader.w: Code 11.1: delegate only tasks within the other person's scope of competence. Jen has not been trained or assessed, so Ruth carries out the time-sensitive test herself and supports Jen's development through proper training (Code 9.4).

n.0: Involving the mother does not address Jen's lack of competence and delays a time-sensitive test.
n.2: Verbal instructions at the bedside do not make Jen competent; she has not been trained or assessed.
n.3: A video is not training and assessment of competence for a clinical procedure.

Scholar & Leader.q: Two midwives on the postnatal ward disagree about how best to support a woman who is finding breastfeeding painful. One favours advising nipple shields; the other wants to observe a full feed first. The woman is well and the baby is feeding. What is the most appropriate way to resolve this?
o: Ask the woman to choose between the two midwives' suggestions
Discuss the evidence together and agree a plan
Refer the disagreement to the ward manager to decide
Defer to the midwife with the longer length of service
Scholar & Leader.w: Code 9.3: deal with differences of professional opinion with colleagues by discussion and informed debate. Here there is no immediate safety risk, so the midwives discuss the evidence (observing a feed to assess attachment) and agree a plan.

n.0: Presenting an unresolved professional disagreement to the woman shifts the professional judgement onto her.
n.2: Escalating to the manager is premature when the midwives can resolve a non-urgent issue through informed debate.
n.3: Length of service does not determine which approach is best supported by evidence.

Scholar & Leader.q: Kiran is coordinating a delivery suite. She must allocate staff: Midwife A (newly qualified, 3 months), Midwife B (8 years' experience), and a maternity support worker. Women needing care include one with severe pre-eclampsia on intravenous magnesium sulfate and one in early labour with no risk factors. Which allocation is most appropriate?
o: Midwife B to the woman on magnesium; Midwife A to the woman in early labour
The support worker to the woman on magnesium with Midwife A overseeing
Midwife B to the woman in early labour; the support worker to the woman on magnesium
Midwife A to the woman on magnesium; Midwife B to the woman in early labour
Scholar & Leader.w: SPM 5.19 requires appropriate assignment of care responsibilities. Kiran first assesses acuity: a woman on IV magnesium for severe pre-eclampsia needs one-to-one care from an experienced midwife. The low-risk woman in early labour is suitable for the newly qualified midwife, who can seek support (Code 13).

n.1: Monitoring a woman on IV magnesium is outside an MSW's scope, even with oversight.
n.2: An MSW cannot provide the registered care needed for magnesium therapy, and this leaves no registrant with that woman.
n.3: Placing the least experienced midwife with the highest-risk woman mismatches skill mix to acuity.

Scholar & Leader.q: Ava, a second-year student midwife, has a two-week spoke placement in a pelvic health clinic run by Tom, a registered physiotherapist. Ava's link lecturer asks whether Tom can act as her practice supervisor for the placement. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment, what is the correct position?
o: Tom can supervise her if a midwife countersigns each shift record
Tom can be her practice supervisor as a registered health professional
Tom can host her, but supervision must come from a midwife on another site
Tom can supervise her once he completes the practice assessor preparation
Scholar & Leader.w: SSSA (NMC 2018, republished 2023) standard 2.7: students are supervised in practice by NMC registered nurses, midwives, nursing associates and other registered health and social care professionals. A registered physiotherapist can be Ava's practice supervisor.

n.0: There is no SSSA requirement for a midwife to countersign each shift; Tom's own registration makes him eligible to supervise.
n.2: Supervision by another registered health professional is expressly allowed, so remote midwife supervision is not required.
n.3: Practice assessor preparation is for the assessor role; practice supervisors do not need it, and a midwifery student's practice assessor must be a registered midwife (6.4).

Scholar & Leader.q: Sam, a third-year student midwife, starts a gynaecology placement. The ward manager suggests that Bethany, an experienced registered adult nurse with practice assessor preparation, should be Sam's practice assessor for this placement. What is the correct response?
o: Decline: a midwifery student's practice assessor must be an NMC registered midwife
Accept, because Sam's academic assessor is a registered midwife
Accept, because Bethany has completed practice assessor preparation
Accept for this placement, then assign a midwife assessor for the final part
Scholar & Leader.w: SSSA 6.4: midwifery students are assigned to practice and academic assessors who are NMC registered midwives. Bethany can act as a practice supervisor (2.7) but cannot be Sam's practice assessor.

n.1: 6.4 applies to both the practice and the academic assessor; a midwife academic assessor does not make a nurse eligible as practice assessor.
n.2: Preparation does not override 6.4; the practice assessor for a midwifery student must be a registered midwife.
n.3: 6.4 applies to every practice assessor assignment, not just the final part of the programme.

Scholar & Leader.q: Olivia, a community midwife, has been Lily's practice supervisor for the first four weeks of a placement. Lily's nominated practice assessor goes on long-term sick leave and the manager asks Olivia to become Lily's practice assessor for the same placement while still supervising her. What is the correct position?
o: Olivia can take both roles for the remaining weeks of this placement
Olivia should not hold both roles for Lily at the same time
Olivia can take both roles because she knows Lily's practice best
Olivia can take both roles if the academic assessor agrees in writing
Scholar & Leader.w: SSSA 7.10: practice assessors are not simultaneously the practice supervisor and academic assessor for the same student. Holding both roles at the same time removes the separation between supporting learning and assessing it.

n.0: The separation applies throughout the period the roles are held, including the rest of this placement.
n.2: Knowing the student well is why supervisor feedback informs assessment (7.2), but the roles must still be held by different people.
n.3: The standards contain no written-agreement exception to the separation in 7.10.

Scholar & Leader.q: Zara, a third-year student midwife, is completing her final practice placement. Several registered midwives have supervised her. Under the NMC Standards for student supervision and assessment, who conducts the assessment that confirms Zara has achieved her practice proficiencies?
o: The practice supervisor who has worked the most shifts with her
Her nominated practice assessor, using feedback from supervisors
Her academic assessor, based on her university assignments
The ward manager, as the person accountable for the placement area
Scholar & Leader.w: SSSA 7.1: practice assessors conduct assessments to confirm student achievement of proficiencies and programme outcomes for practice learning; 7.2: decisions are informed by feedback from practice supervisors. The academic assessor confirms achievement in the academic environment (9.1) and works with the practice assessor on progression (7.5).

n.0: Practice supervisors contribute observations to assessment (4.1, 4.2) but do not confirm proficiency.
n.2: The academic assessor collates and confirms achievement in the academic environment, not the practice assessment itself.
n.3: The ward manager's role is not the practice assessor's unless formally nominated as such.

Scholar & Leader.q: Mia, a second-year student midwife, is caring for a woman in labour with her practice supervisor, Claire. The woman requests intramuscular pethidine, which has been prescribed. Mia asks if she can give it under Claire's direct supervision. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Mia gives it if the woman agrees to a student administering her medicine
Mia gives it if she has passed her university medicines calculation test
Claire administers the pethidine herself and Mia observes and assists
Mia gives it under Claire's direct supervision as a listed midwife exemption
Scholar & Leader.w: Human Medicines Regulations 2012 Schedule 17 Part 3: student midwives may administer listed parenteral medicines under the direct supervision of a registered midwife, but not diamorphine, morphine or pethidine. Claire gives the pethidine; Mia learns by observing.

n.0: The woman's agreement cannot override the legal exclusion for student midwives.
n.1: Passing a calculation test does not change the legal exclusion of pethidine for students.
n.3: Pethidine is excluded from the medicines a student midwife may administer, even under direct supervision.

Scholar & Leader.q: During a shift, Kezia, a first-year student midwife, gives an unclear handover about a postnatal woman, leaving out her blood loss. Her practice supervisor, Rachel, wants to give feedback that helps Kezia improve. Which approach is best?
o: Wait until the end of placement and include the issue in the final report
Correct Kezia in front of the team so that everyone learns from the error
Re-do the handover herself and model a complete one for Kezia
Give private, specific feedback that day and agree a plan
Scholar & Leader.w: SPM 5.21: support students, promoting reflection and providing constructive feedback. Code 9.1: give honest, accurate and constructive feedback. Feedback is most useful when timely, private, specific about the behaviour, linked to its impact on safety, and ends with an agreed plan.

n.0: Delaying until the final report denies Kezia the chance to improve during the placement.
n.1: Public correction can humiliate the student and is not constructive feedback.
n.2: Modelling a good handover helps, but without direct feedback Kezia may not recognise the omission or why blood loss matters.

Scholar & Leader.q: Nadia, a practice supervisor, has noticed that a student midwife has arrived late on four shifts and has twice given women advice that conflicts with unit guidelines, despite feedback. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Wait to see whether things improve before the final assessment
Discuss the student's performance with the other students on placement
Document the concerns and raise them with the practice and academic assessors
Tell the student she can no longer attend the placement area
Scholar & Leader.w: SSSA 4.4: practice supervisors are expected to raise and respond to student conduct and competence concerns, and 4.3 lets them share observations with practice and academic assessors. Concerns persisting after feedback, including unsafe advice, should be documented and raised promptly.

n.0: Waiting allows unsafe advice to continue and delays support for the student.
n.1: Discussing a student's performance with peers breaches confidentiality and is unprofessional.
n.3: Removing a student from placement is not a practice supervisor's decision; it goes through the assessors and university process.

Scholar & Leader.q: Ellen, a registered midwife, has supervised a student midwife on four shifts this week but is not her practice assessor. Before the student moves to another area, what is Ellen's responsibility regarding documentation?
o: Leave documentation to the academic assessor at the next tripartite meeting
Record her observations of the student in the assessment document
Give verbal feedback, as written records are for the practice assessor
Sign off the proficiencies she has seen the student achieve this week
Scholar & Leader.w: SSSA 4.1: practice supervisors contribute to the student's record of achievement by periodically recording relevant observations on conduct, proficiency and achievement. SPM 5.21 includes evaluating and documenting student performance. Confirming proficiency is the practice assessor's role (7.1).

n.0: The academic assessor relies on practice records; Ellen's observations need recording now.
n.2: Verbal feedback is valuable, but supervisors are also expected to record observations (4.1).
n.3: Signing off proficiencies is the practice assessor's assessment role (7.1), not the supervisor's.

Scholar & Leader.q: Jodie, a registered midwife, is preparing for revalidation. Over the past 3 years she has logged 35 hours of continuing professional development, of which 12 hours were participatory learning such as workshops and simulation. What does she need to do to meet the CPD requirement?
o: Record her 35 hours as complete, since the total is met
Complete at least 8 more hours of any type of CPD
Complete at least 20 more hours of participatory CPD
Complete at least 8 more hours of participatory CPD
Scholar & Leader.w: NMC revalidation: 35 hours of CPD in the 3 years since last renewal, of which at least 20 must be participatory. Jodie has 12 participatory hours, so she needs 20 minus 12 = 8 more participatory hours.

n.0: The 35-hour total is met, but fewer than 20 hours are participatory, so the requirement is not yet satisfied.
n.1: Extra individual (non-participatory) learning would not close the participatory shortfall.
n.2: 20 is the total participatory requirement; she already has 12, so the shortfall is 8.

Scholar & Leader.q: Angela is registered with the NMC as both a nurse and a midwife and wants to revalidate both registrations. How many practice hours must she have completed in the 3 years since her registration was last renewed?
o: 1,350 hours, including 450 hours in each role
450 hours across nursing and midwifery combined
900 hours in whichever role she practises most
900 hours, with 450 in each role
Scholar & Leader.w: NMC revalidation: a midwife needs 450 practice hours over 3 years; a dual nurse and midwife registrant needs 900 hours, 450 in each role. 1,350 applies to triple registration.

n.0: 1,350 hours is the requirement for triple registration.
n.1: 450 hours applies to a single registration, not dual registration.
n.2: The 900 hours must include 450 in each registered role, not all in one.

Scholar & Leader.q: Bisi, a community midwife, is completing her revalidation portfolio. Which statement about her written reflective accounts meets the NMC requirement?
o: Five accounts on the NMC form, written in academic essay style
Five accounts in any format, each linked to her job description
Five accounts on the NMC form, each linked to the Code
Three accounts on the NMC form, each linked to the Code
Scholar & Leader.w: NMC revalidation: five written reflective accounts in the 3-year period, recorded on the NMC reflective accounts form, each explaining what was learned from CPD, feedback or an experience and how it relates to the Code. They do not need to be lengthy or academic.

n.0: The NMC states accounts do not need to be lengthy or academic-style pieces of writing.
n.1: The NMC form is required, and accounts must relate to the Code rather than a job description.
n.3: Five accounts are required, not three.

Scholar & Leader.q: During a long second stage, Precious, a midwife, notices that the woman is becoming exhausted with directed pushing. She changes her approach there and then, encouraging the woman to rest and push with her urges. According to Schön, what kind of reflection is this?
o: Reflection-in-action
Reflection-before-action
Critical incident analysis
Reflection-on-action
Scholar & Leader.w: Schön distinguished reflection-in-action (thinking on your feet and adjusting practice during the event) from reflection-on-action (looking back afterwards). Precious adjusted her care during the event. SPM 1.27 requires continuous self-reflection.

n.1: Reflection-before-action is anticipatory planning, not adjusting care during the event.
n.2: Critical incident analysis is a structured retrospective review of a significant event.
n.3: Reflection-on-action happens after the event, for example when writing a reflective account.

Scholar & Leader.q: Helen, a labour ward midwife, uses Gibbs' reflective cycle to write about a shoulder dystocia she attended. She has described what happened and how she felt. She now writes about what went well and what did not go well. Which stage of the cycle is this?
o: Action plan
Analysis
Conclusion
Evaluation
Scholar & Leader.w: Gibbs' cycle runs: description, feelings, evaluation (what was good and bad), analysis (making sense of the situation), conclusion (what else could have been done) and action plan. Judging what went well and badly is evaluation.

n.0: The action plan sets out what she will do if the situation arises again.
n.1: Analysis follows evaluation and asks why things happened, drawing on evidence and theory.
n.2: Conclusion considers what else could have been done and what was learned.

Scholar & Leader.q: Ngozi, a midwife, is revalidating. Her line manager, who will act as her confirmer, is a registered physiotherapist. Ngozi asks how to meet the reflective discussion requirement. Which advice is correct?
o: Replace the reflective discussion with a sixth written reflective account
Hold the reflective discussion with an NMC registrant before confirmation
Hold the reflective discussion with any colleague who knows her practice
Hold the reflective discussion with her line manager as her confirmer
Scholar & Leader.w: NMC revalidation: the reflective discussion must be with another NMC registered nurse, midwife or nursing associate and cover the five reflective accounts. Where the confirmer is not on the NMC register, the reflective discussion is held separately before the confirmation meeting.

n.0: There is no option to replace the reflective discussion with an extra written account.
n.2: The discussion partner must be an NMC registrant, not any colleague.
n.3: The line manager is not on the NMC register, so cannot be the reflective discussion partner; they can still act as confirmer.

Scholar & Leader.q: At her annual appraisal, Hollie, a midwife with 2 years' experience, receives feedback from colleagues that she rarely asks for help when unsure and sometimes delays escalating concerns. She feels upset by this. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Reflect on the feedback, discuss it with her manager and agree a development plan
Accept the feedback politely and continue practising in the same way
Request a transfer to another ward where colleagues know her less well
Ask which colleagues gave the feedback so that she can challenge their view
Scholar & Leader.w: Code 9.2: gather and reflect on feedback from a variety of sources, using it to improve your practice. SPM 1.27 requires midwives to seek and respond to support and feedback. A development plan addresses the safety issue (Code standard 13 recognise and work within the limits of your competence).

n.1: Accepting feedback without changing practice ignores a safety-relevant pattern.
n.2: Moving wards avoids the feedback and leaves the development need unaddressed.
n.3: Focusing on who gave the feedback is defensive and does not use it to improve practice.

Scholar & Leader.q: Isla, a midwife, has worked 300 practice hours in the 3 years since her registration was last renewed, after a long career break. Her revalidation date is in 2 months. She has met all the other requirements. What is the correct position?
o: She needs a return to practice programme or the test of competence
She can revalidate if her confirmer verifies her competence
She can revalidate by completing 150 extra CPD hours instead
She can revalidate because she has met all the other requirements
Scholar & Leader.w: NMC revalidation requires 450 practice hours for a midwife in the 3 years since last renewal. Isla has 300, which is 150 short; a registrant who cannot meet the practice hours requirement must complete an approved return to practice programme or the test of competence.

n.1: A confirmer confirms the requirements have been met; they cannot waive the practice hours requirement.
n.2: CPD hours cannot be substituted for practice hours.
n.3: Practice hours are a mandatory requirement; meeting the others does not offset the 150-hour shortfall.

Scholar & Leader.q: Priya, a community midwife, is preparing a teaching session on whether warm compresses applied to the perineum in the second stage of labour reduce severe perineal trauma. She wants to base her session on the strongest type of evidence about the effectiveness of this intervention. Which source should she look for first?
o: A systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
A single large randomised controlled trial from one maternity unit
A prospective cohort study following women through the second stage
A consensus statement from a panel of experienced consultant midwives
Scholar & Leader.w: For questions about the effectiveness of an intervention, a systematic review that pools randomised controlled trials (meta-analysis) sits at the top of the evidence hierarchy, because it combines all eligible trials and reduces the effect of chance and bias in any one study. SPM 5.16 expects midwives to use research to inform decision-making; Code 6.1 requires advice to be evidence-based.

n.1: A well-conducted RCT is strong evidence, but one trial from a single unit ranks below a systematic review that pools all relevant trials.
n.2: A cohort study is observational and cannot control for confounding as randomisation does, so it ranks below RCTs and reviews of RCTs for effectiveness.
n.3: Expert opinion is the lowest level of evidence in the hierarchy; it is useful where trials are lacking but is not the strongest source.

Scholar & Leader.q: Grace, a midwife researcher, wants to understand how women who had a traumatic first birth experience their next pregnancy, including their fears and what helped them feel safe. She plans to recruit 15 women from a birth reflections clinic. Which research approach best fits her question?
o: A randomised controlled trial of two birth reflections models
A case-control study comparing women with and without trauma
A qualitative study using in-depth semi-structured interviews
A cross-sectional survey recording mode of birth and birthweight
Scholar & Leader.w: Questions about lived experience, meaning and feelings are best answered with qualitative methods such as in-depth semi-structured interviews, which produce rich, transferable findings from a small purposive sample (HRA defining research table: qualitative findings are described so they can be transferred to other settings).

n.0: An RCT tests whether one intervention works better than another; Grace is exploring experiences, not comparing interventions.
n.1: A case-control design looks back for risk factors linked to an outcome; it does not capture how women experience their pregnancy.
n.3: Recording mode of birth and birthweight gives numerical data and cannot describe women's fears or what helped them feel safe.

Scholar & Leader.q: Amara, a band 6 midwife, leads a team meeting on the MBRRACE-UK data brief covering maternal deaths in 2022 to 2024. She wants to plan targeted antenatal outreach in her diverse inner-city area. Which finding from the report should she present accurately to the team?
o: Maternal suicide was the leading cause of death during pregnancy
Black women died at nearly three times the rate of White women
Black women died at nearly twice the rate of White women
The overall maternal death rate fell by 20% compared with 2009 to 2011
Scholar & Leader.w: The MBRRACE-UK 2022-24 data brief (Sept 2026) reported a rate of 12.80 per 100,000 maternities, with Black women dying at nearly three times the rate of White women; the rate was 20% higher than in 2009-11. SPM 1.4 requires midwives to critically interpret local, national and international data and reports.

n.0: Thrombosis and thromboembolism were the leading cause during pregnancy and up to 6 weeks after; maternal suicide was the leading cause from 6 weeks to 1 year.
n.2: Twice is the gap between the most and least deprived areas, not the ethnic disparity for Black women, which was nearly three times.
n.3: The rate was 20% higher than in 2009 to 2011, not lower.

Scholar & Leader.q: Researchers want to find out whether going to sleep on the back in late pregnancy is linked to late stillbirth. Stillbirth is a rare outcome, and asking women to sleep in a particular position as an intervention would be unethical. Which study design is most efficient for this question?
o: A cross-over trial in which each woman tries both sleep positions
A randomised controlled trial allocating women to a sleeping position
A qualitative study of women's beliefs about sleep in pregnancy
A case-control study of women with and without a stillbirth
Scholar & Leader.w: Case-control studies start with the outcome (cases with stillbirth, controls without) and look back at exposures, which makes them the efficient design for rare outcomes where an experiment would be unethical. Interpreting why a design was chosen is part of critical appraisal (SPM 1.4, SPM 5.16).

n.0: A cross-over trial still allocates women to a possibly harmful exposure and cannot measure a single, irreversible outcome such as stillbirth.
n.1: Randomly allocating women to a position suspected of increasing stillbirth risk would be unethical, as the stem states.
n.2: Qualitative research describes beliefs and experiences; it cannot measure the association between sleep position and stillbirth.
